item.title: [Lex Clips] Greatest boxer of all time | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、意外的观察：伟大的拳击手需要一个"伟大的敌人"来完成

Khabib 这段对话里藏着一个反直觉的判断——Mike Tyson 不是最伟大的拳击手，因为他缺少一个"配得上他"的敌人。这颠覆了我们对"伟大"的常规定义：我们习惯把伟大视为个人属性（力量、技巧、胜率），但 Khabib 揭示的其实是一个关系性的伟大——一个拳手的历史地位，不取决于他多强，而取决于是否有人强到能与他构成叙事张力。

Holyfield 对 Tyson 来说不够"重"，所以 Tyson 的传奇是残缺的。这就像哈姆雷特没有克劳狄斯，福尔摩斯没有莫里亚蒂——主角的完整性，寄生在对手的浓度里。

二、跨领域连接：体育史其实是"叙事密度"的竞争，不是"运动表现"的竞争

Khabib 在无意中提出了一个非常接近文学理论的观点：伟大的比赛之所以被记住，是因为它们外溢出体育本身——Ali vs Frasier 有越战、有宗教、有种族；Louis vs Schmeling 有罗斯福 vs 希特勒、有民主 vs 法西斯。

这里有一个惊人的隐藏结构：一场比赛的"历史保鲜期"，与它当时"承载了多少非体育信息"成正比。这条法则同样解释了： - 为什么 1969 阿波罗登月比后续所有登月都更被记住（冷战叙事密度） - 为什么 AlphaGo vs 李世石比 AlphaZero 全胜任何人更有文化重量（人机之战的存在焦虑） - 为什么苹果 1984 广告比它卖出的任何一台电脑都更长寿（反乌托邦叙事嫁接）

Pacquiao vs Mayweather 数据上无懈可击，但 Khabib 说"没有那种能量"——因为它只是一场拳赛，不是一场时代的替身战争。

三、更深的洞见：Khabib 在为自己（和 MMA）做一个隐蔽的诊断

注意这段对话的起点——他在讨论"MMA 与拳击的对比"，然后立刻把话题拉进"拳击最伟大的比赛"。这是一个精妙的心理转移：他其实在焦虑 MMA 缺乏 Ali–Frasier 级别的历史重量。

MMA 只有 30 年历史，胜负更快、故事更碎、冠军流转更频繁。当 Khabib 反复强调"政治、宗教、国家全都汇聚在一起了"时，他实际上在暗示一个悲伤的现实：在算法推荐、注意力碎片化、地缘政治不再具备"两极清晰对立"的今天，可能再也不会有 Ali vs Frasier 那样的比赛了——不是因为拳手不够强，而是因为世界不再能提供那样浓度的对立叙事作为背景板。

这就是最出人意料的一层：Khabib 谈的表面是"谁最伟大"，深层是在哀悼一个能让体育承载文明重量的时代已经结束。他自己作为一个从达吉斯坦走出来、退役时全胜、带着穆斯林身份和普京背景的选手，可能是最后一批还能"外溢"的运动员，而他知道这一点。

📝 转录文本

一、拳击的历史底色：150 年，谁才是那张脸？

Take for example the sport most similar to MMA, which is — well, let's say boxing. How old is boxing? 150 years. Like, when you think boxing, what pops into your head?

Thrilla in Manila.

Yeah. Yeah. Well, I love Mike Tyson a lot too. So — well, Tyson had big fights, but Mike Tyson never had that signature rival like Muhammad Ali had in Joe Frazier.

Mhm. Yeah. He just didn't have one. I mean, who do we have? Evander Holyfield. Look, Holyfield–Tyson is no Muhammad Ali.

二、20 世纪 vs 21 世纪：无可比拟的"马尼拉惊悚战"

Take Ali and Frazier — Thrilla in Manila, right? People called it the greatest rivalry. And it still is. In the 20th century, there was nothing that could compare.

In the 21st century, the only thing you could compare to it, purely based on the numbers, is Pacquiao and Mayweather. Yes, there was public interest, but there wasn't the energy that there was with Muhammad Ali and Joe Frazier.

Yeah. If I can just pause for a second, I'll check on Perplexity. Mhm. — "List the biggest boxing fights of all time." It's Ali and Frazier, like you said. Yeah. Yeah. The first, the third —

Well, when he lost, and then the third fight, the Thrilla in Manila. And Foreman — I must say Ali versus Foreman.

三、全球关注度的顶点：Ali vs Foreman，10 亿人观看

Well, Foreman — that was the year, I think '74, right? The fight was watched by up to a billion people worldwide.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. It was one of those things. Politics got mixed into it, too. Yeah, it — well, it was actually a very big fight.

四、80 年代的黄金一代：Leonard、Durán、Hearns、Hagler

Sugar Ray Leonard, Durán — Sugar Ray Leonard versus Thomas Hearns. Hagler versus Hearns. Well, Hagler — Hagler and Durán in Montreal. Yeah, Sugar Ray Leonard and Durán in Montreal, when they fought — when he admitted after the fight that he lost the mental game and broke down before the fight. But then Sugar Ray beat him later.

Yeah. He came back and won. Yeah.

五、被遗忘的巅峰对决：Joe Louis vs Max Schmeling —— 罗斯福对希特勒

Uh, well, if you look at it, out of everything that stands out, I think you can mention Frazier and Muhammad Ali. And there was also Joe Louis against the German, Max Schmeling. Hitler stood behind Schmeling, and Roosevelt stood behind Louis.

For those who don't know this story — I just watched it recently. It was something incomparable. They were so big. They were two of the most famous athletes of their time. Roosevelt was promoting Joe Louis. You know, at that moment for America, it was like something incredible that a white president was promoting a Black world champion. And on the other hand, Hitler stood behind Schmeling.

It was what — 1936, 1938. They had — they fought twice. Twice. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. They fought two times.

六、超越体育：当比赛承载起国家、政治与信仰

This wasn't just a good boxing match, just a good fight. This was politics. Those were nations. This was politics. This was nations. Everything. It all came together.

And it's the same thing with Ali, too. Muhammad Ali with the Vietnam War — all that stuff. Yes. Yes. And his — and even religion is tied into it. Everything here came together.

They simply went beyond sports.

item.title: [Business of Sport] From $6bn to $300m: How Can LIV Keep Going?
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：$6B 失败之后，$300M 却被期待能"成功"——这不是投资，这是"资本的葬礼经济学"

沙特用 60 亿美元、五年时间证明了 LIV 的商业模式无法闭合。然而下一轮 2.5–3 亿美元的资金进来，居然被叙述为"新愿景"。这里藏着一个几乎没有人指出的系统性真相：这不是一次投资，这是一次"体面清算"（graceful liquidation）。

BC Partners 投的这笔钱，从体量上看根本不足以维持一个球员的合同，更别说整个赛季。它真正的功能，不是"重建 LIV"，而是为 PIF 提供一个可以退场的叙事出口——让沙特不至于以"我们烧了 60 亿然后关灯走人"的姿态收场。它买的不是资产，是声誉的缓冲垫。这是主权资本退出体育时最典型的"葬礼式融资"结构：新钱进来的目的是让旧钱走得体面。

二、隐藏的循环结构：BC Partners → GSE Worldwide → Bryson DeChambeau——一场"影子谈判"

主持人无意间揭出了一个惊人的关联：BC Partners 也是 GSE Worldwide（Bryson 的经纪公司）的投资方。这不是巧合，这是一个教科书级的"结构性绑架"：

  • BC Partners 表面上"投资 LIV"，实质上是在为自己已经持股的经纪公司客户续保。
  • Bryson 说"新投资者有清新的愿景，但不会改变太多"——这不是记者会话术，这是被资本关系锁定的球员在替资本发声。
  • 沙特欠球员的钱如果转为 LIV 股权，那么 GSE 的客户价值就与 LIV 的存续绑定，而 BC Partners 又同时持有两端——双边套保。

这种结构让我想到 2000 年互联网泡沫末期的"投行研报–承销–做市"三位一体：同一家机构在利益链的多个节点上，同时扮演"分析师、承销商、做市商"。当年 SEC 花了十年拆解这套嵌套。今天在体育资产的边缘，同样的结构正以更精致的形式复活。

三、跨领域连接：LIV 的"股权替现金"骗局 = WeWork 的员工期权 + 政治学的"死猫策略"

Charlie 提到最担心的一点——把欠球员的现金转为股权——这在硅谷有一个精确的对应词叫 "underwater equity trap"（水下期权陷阱）：

WeWork 崩盘前，员工被反复告知"你的期权将来会更值钱"；Uber 上市前，司机被劝说"接受股权激励代替时薪"。最终结果几乎无一例外：现金放弃者血本无归，坚持要现金的成为唯一赢家。

数学是残酷的：Bryson 的 5 亿美元合同若换成 2% 股权，LIV 需要以 250 亿美元估值退出 才能让球员打平。而 LIV 目前是负值资产。这在概率上等价于要求 Bryson 用一份保底合同去交换一张彩票。

而 Scott O'Neil 在此刻抛出"我们已找到新投资者"的声明——这正是英国政治学中经典的 "dead cat strategy"（死猫策略）：当你即将有极糟的新闻要发布时，把一只死猫扔在桌上，让所有人先讨论那只死猫。结果如主播所说：媒体铺天盖地报"新投资"，几乎无人报"最终站赛季直接取消"。这不是公关失误，这是精心设计的注意力再分配。

四、更深层的系统真相：LIV 的失败不是"高尔夫的失败"，而是"主权资本 vs. 私募资本操作系统"的第一次公开对撞

主播说了一句被轻轻带过、但极其重要的话：

"LIV 现在必须从一个 sovereign wealth entity（主权资本实体）转变为 private capital entity（私募资本实体）。"

这是整个故事的隐藏骨架。主权资本的逻辑是 "钱是工具，目的是软实力/地缘/合法性"；私募资本的逻辑是 "钱是目的，一切都是回报率的函数"。这两套操作系统对同一个资产给出的估值可以相差 10 倍以上。

LIV 的球员合同、赛制设计、40 亿美元的市场投入，全都是在主权 OS下写就的代码。现在要在私募 OS上继续运行，几乎所有函数都会返回 error。这就像把一个用户体验极佳但从不考虑单位经济学的 To-C 产品，交给一家只看 LTV/CAC 的对冲基金——不是产品不好，是操作系统不兼容。

这为未来 5 年所有"主权资本进入体育后再退出"的资产（沙特/卡塔尔/阿联酋支持的俱乐部、联赛、赛事），提供了一份提前泄露的验尸报告：当主权退潮时，暴露出来的不是"低估值资产"，而是"根本无法在私募逻辑下定价的资产"。

📝 转录文本

1. 序幕：LIV 的坏消息终于开始集中释放

We've just seen over the last 10 days or so, we've seen the first significant bits of news flow since the problems which we predicted really hit back in March, April. We predicted this would happen back in January, and in March, April it would — the Saudis announced that they would not be continuing to fund the LIV tour after this season. And there were even rumors at the time, Charlie, that LIV would struggle to make it to the end of this season.

And so it has proven, right? So it has proven.

2. LIV 赛制的"少打多赚"结构

So just to bring listeners up to date, the LIV tour is quite a limited thing in any case. Only 15 events, right? And the last of those events — and this is one of the big attractions for some of the players, actually — was the last of the events was to be held at the sort of start of September, which then basically meant that from mid-September until the end of the year, LIV golfers were basically on holiday. Um, they could cram their playing into a time period that was January until August, right? And then have 4 months off. What's not to like about that when you've got guaranteed money on the table.

So the the last —

big fan of that, yeah. What? What's that? Dustin Johnson was a big fan of that. Dustin Johnson was a big fan of that. Pay me more money to play less golf, perfect. Yeah, absolutely.

3. 4000 万美元的团队总决赛被砍掉

Um so the the last event of this season was meant to be the end of season team championship, which was in Michigan. Um and the prize pool for this event was intended to be 40 million bucks, right? So this was the big conclusion to the team element of the LIV thing.

And don't forget this is one of the few innovations that they brought in which could truly be said to be an innovation. I don't regard not having a cut as being an innovation. That's just a sort of easy for players. Um but team golf was an innovation on a week-to-week basis.

So by canning the team championships and bringing the team element into the end of season singles championship, which is happening um I think this week, in fact, in Indianapolis. Um that basically means that this — yeah, this week's event in Minneapolis is the last event of LIV 2026.

And it basically says that the Saudi pulled, the Saudis pulled their funding to the degree that they couldn't even fund that last tournament, right? So, it makes the whole thing very real.

4. Scott O'Neil 的"死猫策略"公告

So, that's one bit of news flow. The other bit of news flow is that at the same time as this was becoming apparent, Scott O'Neil, who's the commissioner of LIV, um, chief executive —

CEO, yeah. CEO of LIV, whatever it might be, announced, in a rather curious fashion, Charlie, I don't know what you think, that that he had secured new investment for LIV 2027. Couldn't say who it was. Couldn't say the deal had actually been signed and agreed. Simply said, "By the way, we have been able to attract new investment for next season."

It felt to me like what we call in PR a dead cat, right? Which is you throw something on the table because you know there's some really bad news coming. And you hope that the thing you throw on the table distracts from the bad news.

And to a degree, it kind of worked, which is that I saw in the mainstream sort of English language international media, there was quite a lot of coverage over this new investment. There's actually been very little coverage over the fact that the final event of the season has been ditched.

5. Rahm 与 DeChambeau 的悬而未决

Now, at the same time, there are obviously major question marks over whether Jon Rahm and Bryson DeChambeau, who are the two global stars who are currently playing on LIV, will still be playing in it next year. There are rumors that that that not all the bills have been paid, that not all the players have been paid, and so on and so forth.

And there was a players meeting recently, um, that I think was led by Bryson, um, at at a recent, um, LIV event to consider what next steps would be.

6. "Dean Burmester 是地球上最大的球星"——爱丽丝梦游仙境式发言

But, it's quite clear from Scott O'Neil's, um, comments, which I'll come on to in a moment, which bordered on the delusional, that he is seriously contemplating a LIV in 2027 that exists without Rahm and DeChambeau. And I'm not sure where this statement sits. It's not a Belgian Football Federation statement. It's not an HP statement. It's not a UEFA statement. It's it's more of a sort of Alice in Wonderland statement, right?

So, he's asked effectively what LIV would be like without its two stars. And he said, "I define it," by which he means stardom, "a little bit differently. For instance, I don't think that there was a bigger star on the planet than Dean Burmester in South Africa recently."

Um now, uh Dean Burmester, for those who don't who don't know, is a journeyman South African player who was on the US PGA Tour and without anyone outside South Africa even noticing it, moved across to LIV as part of the flock of golfers who went across there to earn easier money for less golfers, as Charlie says. And LIV has had a relative success, or should I say a lesser degree of failure, with their South African event than they have with other events, right?

So, they're clearly hanging their hat on, well, you know, we got quite a few people to come to our South African event and our leading South African golfer is Dean Burmester. Am I pronouncing that Burmester right, by the way Charlie?

Yeah, I think so. Yeah. I mean, so well known, obviously so well known that you're — And and as a golf fan yourself, you know, you it's it's un- I'm surprised you don't know that. Well, I'm sure that's on me, as they say, given that he — given that he is the biggest star on the planet, according to Scott O'Neil. Right?

7. "10 场赛事、没有巨星、有神秘大投资人"——你信吗？

So, we are being asked to believe that there is going to be a 10-event LIV Tour next year, right? That's the background briefing, that will exist without Rahm and DeChambeau, where the biggest stars on the planet, Dean Burmester and Cameron Smith, are going to be the big draws, and that there is a massive investor who's coming in to back this concept. Are you buying it, Charlie?

Um No. I'm not. Charlie, I've been questioned — I've been questioned — I think we can both agree that if it does happen, it'll be a ripping failure. But do you think it's going to happen? Do you think there is an investor? look, Charlie, we've we've played this game in life and what — and we we both have ventures before — what you — I've been — you you've been told that money is coming. You think an investment's going to land. Like until that money is in the bank, you you cannot say otherwise. Indeed. So with them saying that documents have been signed and it's going to September in a vote and announcing it now, there's probably something in there where they have to do that. Again, for the players and the relationships with the players as their contracts are now moving into the next season where they probably have to make some of those announcements. But let's be very real. Until that cash is there, it is very much up in the air.

8. 60 亿美元失败之后，2.5–3 亿美元凭什么成功？

And look, do what you — you said I joke. No, I don't buy it. I've genuinely been questioning my own sanity and everything that you understand about good investments and where to make money and and and what looks like value and and what doesn't.

Um because let's let's just be very clear, right? LIV Golf has failed with a $6 billion injection injection of capital. $6 billion. The reported investment here — and that's sorry, $6 billion over five five years. The reported investment here is $250 to $300 million for the next — I think — well, basically to take it on for the next year, but I think internally they think that could secure it for at least the next couple of years.

What makes you think you could achieve something with $250 million that you couldn't with six? Let's just be really basic on that, okay? And and the the truth is you can't.

So then it asks the bigger question. Let's be realistic, right? LIV Golf is dead. LIV 1.0 is is gone. So everything that we know when we're talking about LIV, that that is over. With $250 million coming in, that cannot sustain one player contract that they were signing, let alone a whole field plus the events, plus everything that comes with running this.

So, whatever we're going to see moving forward, whether it happens or not, is going to be dramatically different. Bryson came out in a press conference a few days ago and said the investor from the conversations I've had has a new and fresh vision on this product, followed up by it won't be changing too much. Well, if that is the case, then we might as well just quit and go home now because it cannot sustain the spend that it's had previously.

9. Chapter 11 与"股权换现金"——最令人担忧的部分

Charlie, look, there's a number of things. Firstly, I don't know and we haven't been privy to it that the nature of this other than Scott O'Neil's statement saying that there's an agreement in place with the lead investor. We're going to have to assume this is an equity investment rather than a distressed debt or more complex financial structuring, which by the way could well happen and could be far above our abilities to scrutinize on on this show.

But, if we're just assuming it is that type of investment, they've got huge issues running forward. As the debt within the company, they've got player contracts that are huge liabilities for them. Now, there's been talk about a Chapter 11 bankruptcy, which, you know, essentially means that they would have the right to restructure some of that and move some of those contracts and the money owed into things like equity schemes for the players.

Don't even get me started on this. This is probably the bit that I'm most concerned about because in the statement that was put out, they tried to make this a huge win for everyone. This is the first time the players will be the majority equity holders in a major sporting tour. Equity means value. What what value? What what value are these players going to have moving forward? This business has no value right now.

So, if you're transferring cash owed to players to equity, that's assuming that one day those players are going to be better off than they would be if they'd got that cash for them to actually look at this as a really good deal. I don't know about you, there is nothing to me that says you can get rid of all of the liabilities that LIV has now. You can turn it around with 250 to 300 million dollars. You can create value on top of that to make a percentage of that equity worth something to all of these players so that eventually one day you can miraculously find a buyer who's going to pay you something significant enough to give those players back a proper portion of cash.

10. Bryson 的数学：需要 250 亿美元退出才能"划算"

Let's play this out if it's Bryson's contract, right? Let's say — Let's just use the big numbers, right? If you got a 500 million deal which was being talked about previously as him renewing on LIV. Let's say he got a 2% ownership of the whole of LIV. LIV would need to sell for 25 billion for him to back a like equity model over his cash model to make that worthwhile. So, it's a complete — like the Gazi fallacy, whatever we want to call it, to suggest that this equity model for the players is a good thing.

11. BC Partners 与 GSE Worldwide——那个惊人的关联

We have to say this with a big reported — in the golf world, it's widely reported that BC Partners, which is a PE — private equity credit firm, are the investor. Now, they supposedly have said that the continuation and participation of some of those key players is important to their investment. So, you're going to have to find a way to keep those players other than just pay them huge sums of cash. I'm very keen to see how they managed to do that.

I'm going to massively speculate, but if PIF owe a huge amount of money to some of those players on contracts, I could see maybe a settlement agreement with some of those players which would still give them a significant amount of money and a significant enough portion to keep them involved in a LIV structure for X amount of time that would allow BC Partners to take that majority stake and not have to worry about serious injections of cash just from play — for player contracts. That's huge speculation on my side, but that's the only way that I could see that happening.

More importantly, Charlie, I had a little look at BC Partners. Do you know another big investment that they made in sports? Do you know what that that was?

No, who was that? They invested in a company called GSE Worldwide. Now, GSE Worldwide is a big sports marketing representation talent agency. Do you know who GSE's major client is on the golfing front? Bryson. So, the same company that has invested significant cash in the represent — in one of the representation agencies for Bryson DeChambeau is going to be the company reportedly that puts money into LIV Golf. [snorts]

12. "Wheels within wheels"——世俱杯、DAZN、Trump 家族式的循环交易

Yeah, and this is going to be my speculation was that when I when I heard that there was a supposed investor into LIV Golf, I sort of thought it's likely to be some an entity or somebody or something who could be lent on or who or who would have some sort of ulterior motive. You know, I was going to speculate that it might be someone close to the Trump family. Many of the LIV events are played at Trump venues for instance, or somebody who might want to be on PIF's right side who comes in with a face saver um which enables the whole thing to continue.

Um you know, so it that that kind of wheels within wheels type um thing. Like you remember when it came to um the whole TV deals around the Club World Cup. And —

Yeah. the circularity between Saudi winning the contract to to host the World Cup at the same time as Sa- as Saudi and DAZN paying what didn't seem to be an obviously good value amount for the TV rights to the Club World Cup which enabled Infantino to say the Club World Cup was a success. There was a sort of circularity going on.

So, I I don't know. My my instinct is since there is no business case that can be made for it whatsoever, um my instinct is is it'll be one of those wheels within wheels type transactions where there's enough face saving benefits/ benefits/ being good friends with PIF benefits — because one thing that is true, Charlie, is a vast amount of money has been raised in the last 3 years by the major private equity firms to invest in sport.

13. 私募资本的"部署压力"如何扭曲体育资产估值

And that money has to find a home, right? Uh and that's what's driving some asset valuations to slightly strange levels in the round the sort of fringes of sport, which is that once they've raised the money, the only way which they then attract management fees on deploying that money is when they actually make investments. So, even if the investment might be a bit a bit high on the risk-reward scheme, um higher than might normally be attractive, it can still be better than not deploying the money at all. Um and —

So, Charlie, I agree with that, but interestingly BC is not an Apollo, a KKR, an Ares, right? One of one of the big US funds, let's say at 5-plus billion where you know, okay, I I still personally I still think it's mad, other people may disagree, but as you've said there, deploying that capital is is actually tough in this market at that level when you have that amount of it and you've got a number of organizations operating.

So, you know, could you have done something with one of them potentially? The number is what it would actually take to invest properly in this if you were going to have a crack at it. I mean, 250 to 300 million, you know, all I'm looking at is what's going to be the future injections. Just like you would Charlie, if you're buying a football club, right? It's not about necessarily what you pay for it, you know that. It's about what you're going to have to put into it to continue to not just run it properly, but build value into it so that one day you can hopefully make some money out of it.

14. 主权资本 → 私募资本：操作系统的切换

And this is the big change, right? LIV is now going to have to operate as a sovereign wealth entity as into a private capital entity.

Yeah. And the minute like you go from that to that, money is important.

I keep — I kept checking myself going, "Hang on, Charlie, you always criticize people just for looking at the monetary value of things. What about the secondary nature?" You just touched on maybe some of the secondary natures here, but I don't really see the secondary nature for a BC of doing this if they if they didn't genuinely believe they could make some value out of it.

But I — you know, I was asking myself, "Why did players come and play for LIV in the first place?" The only reason was for cash, right? So, you even just from a motivations perspective —

Well, actually, I say that, that's a lie. Dustin, as I've just said, Dustin Johnson said that he was playing a bit less and he loved that as well and got more time. So, you know, find the package was was good, but the majority of it, let's not kid ourselves, was the huge fees that the the a lot of the players got. It was the you get paid for turning up, not just for making a cut.

15. 奖金池腰斩、签约金消失、股权变水下期权

They're saying that, you know, now prize pools will go down to $10 million an event. They were at $25 to $30 million an event. You're not going to get the major sign-on fees. Your equity, as we've discussed previously, is is only — is only worth anything in a few — in what, 5 to 10 years' time — a few eventually manage to put something together and even then it's probably not going to reach the cash that you thought you were going to get when you came in.

There's a lot of it that to me I — I I just don't understand it. I I genuinely don't. And I think Scott O'Neil, look, to be fair to him, look, he's the CEO and his job is to try and keep this thing alive and he's going to put across a narrative and talk about it in ways that anyone who is slightly critical of this whole thing will pull apart like like we've just done. I don't blame him for that. It's the reality of his position.

16. 收尾：为那些正在被"股权画饼"的球员担忧

So, yeah, if I can leave it on one thing, there's a craziness to it from a financial perspective. The thing I really worry about is who's getting in the players' ears going, "Hey, guys, you know, this is an amazing equity scheme for you. Be a part of this. Honestly, it's all going to be good. You owed that money, but we're going to give you more equity."

I hope there's really good people around them, the ones that are getting promised a lot of this value, to to put some of that into context and and build a realistic picture of it because otherwise you can see a an unfortunate position for a few of them coming — um coming to fruition.

观看原视频 →

## 一、最反直觉的观察：$6B 失败之后，$300M 却被期待能"成功"——这不是投资，这是"资本的葬礼经济学"
沙特用 60 亿美元、五年时间证明了 LIV 的商业模式无法闭合。然而下一轮 2.5–3 亿美元的资金进来，居然被叙述为"新愿景"。这里藏着一个几乎没有人指出的系统性真相：**这不是一次投资，这是一次"体面清算"（graceful liquidation）**。
BC Partners 投的这笔钱，从体量上看根本不足以维持一个球员的合同，更别说整个赛季。它真正的功能，不是"重建 LIV"，而是**为 PIF 提供一个可以退场的叙事出口**——让沙特不至于以"我们烧了 60 亿然后关灯走人"的姿态收场。它买的不是资产，是**声誉的缓冲垫**。这是主权资本退出体育时最典型的"葬礼式融资"结构：**新钱进来的目的是让旧钱走得体面**。
## 二、隐藏的循环结构：BC Partners → GSE Worldwide → Bryson DeChambeau——一场"影子谈判"
主持人无意间揭出了一个惊人的关联：BC Partners 也是 GSE Worldwide（Br

item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib on meeting Fedor Emelianenko | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"保温杯里的冠军哲学"——被忽略的最强隐喻

大多数人听这段访谈会记住"Fedor击败巨人"的画面，但真正的信号藏在那个保温杯里。2004年，一个正在统治世界的Pride重量级冠军，跑到达吉斯坦地方赛去打比赛，打完一场，走回后台，倒茶、就着蜂蜜、慢慢喝——然后再上场。

这不是"放松"，这是一种拒绝仪式化紧张的姿态。绝大多数顶级运动员会在场边用音乐、跺脚、拍脸、嘶吼来"进入状态"，把自己的神经系统调到高频；Fedor 反其道而行——他用日常动作稀释比赛的重量，让"打Pride冠军战"和"在家喝茶"处于同一个能量层级。Khabib 15岁的记忆里最强烈的画面不是拳头，而是茶壶，这本身就说明：真正的威慑力来自把非凡场景当作平常事的能力。

二、跨领域连接：Fedor的"幼儿园老师脸"与日本能剧的"面"

Khabib提到俄罗斯圈子里开玩笑说 Fedor "长得像幼儿园老师"，然后他一拳KO巨人。这个对比让我想起日本能剧的"中间面"（中間面）——那种表面上无表情、微微下垂、看起来温和的木刻面具。能剧大师会告诉你：越是"无表情"的面，越能承载复杂情绪。观众必须自己把恐惧、悲伤、愤怒投射上去。

Fedor 的脸就是格斗界的"中间面"。他不给对手任何情绪坐标——你看不到愤怒（可以对抗），看不到恐惧（可以利用），看不到快乐（可以打断）。这种"空"是一种心理战武器：对手在这张空白的脸上读到的一切，都是他自己内心投射出来的怪物。这就是为什么Khabib说"他用冷静征服了很多人的头脑"——不是Fedor做了什么，而是对手在这面空白镜子前吓到了自己。

三、意料之外的观察：Khabib其实在承认自己"不如"Fedor

整段话里最微妙、也最少被注意的一点是——Khabib 主动划了一条线："我认为Fedor在气质上比我更平静。That's my impression."

一个从未败绩、无可挑剔的传奇冠军，在自己的播客里、面对全球观众，主动承认另一个人在某个维度上超越自己。这在顶级运动员中极其罕见。这里藏着一个反常识的真相：真正的强者不需要争"谁最强"，因为他们知道"最强"是个多维空间。

更深一层——Khabib 说"内心沸腾，表面冷静"，然后又说 Fedor "内心可能真的就没有沸腾"。这两种"冷"是完全不同的技术路径： - Khabib 的冷 = 控制（emotional regulation，需要能量） - Fedor 的冷 = 本质（emotional flatness，天生结构）

这就像古典音乐里两种极端：一种是Argerich那样把狂暴压进指尖的爆发力；另一种是Michelangeli那种从骨子里就克制的冰冷。听众常以为它们是同一种"高级"，其实是两种完全相反的神经系统解决同一个问题。Khabib 敏锐地识别出了这个差别，并诚实地承认——自己走的是"控制路径"，而Fedor走的是"结构路径"。

四、最后的钩子

Fedor那句名言"能打败我的只有我自己"被引用了无数次，但Khabib给出了这句话真正的技术解读："主要的比赛是先跟自己比。你先打败自己，然后才真正开始跟对手比。"

这句话可以直接搬进创业、写作、投资——任何一个"表面上你在跟外部竞争，实际上你在跟自己的恐惧、贪婪、走神做搏斗"的领域。Fedor 和 Khabib 不是在描述格斗，他们是在描述所有高压表现的底层物理定律。

📝 转录文本

关于Fedor：不得不问的那个人

Well, I have to ask about Fedor. What can you say about him? He had some legendary fights. He beat Cro Cop, Big Nog, Mark Coleman.

Yeah, and Kevin Randleman. And then, he had those legendary fights with the Japanese fighters who were big stars over there. Man, I loved it. Honestly, he inspired me just by the fact that he was from Russia, and he was a fighter. He was closer to our school of training combat.

2004年，达吉斯坦：Pride冠军来打地方赛

And there was this moment, back in 2004, the Dagestan combat championship. Can you imagine? 2004, the Dagestan combat championship, and Fedor showed up. He showed up. He came to compete in the Dagestan open combat championship while being the reigning Pride champion.

I was 15 years old at the time. I was right there in the venue. My father actually invited him. He was sending out invitations to different schools back then. It was Stary Oskol, where he used to train. Fedor's coaches were sent an invitation. He came with his brother Alexander. They both made it to the finals back then.

I just remember — $5,000, $3,000, $1,000. First, second, third place. At heavyweight, they gave a car. When the two brothers arrived, they beat everyone to get to the finals. They didn't fight each other. One of them took first place, that was Fedor. Alexander took second place.

那个保温杯：15岁少年的近距离观察

I remember back then, when he was warming up, I was standing next to him while he warmed up. It was this building, you know, a venue that fits maybe 1,500 people, and over there was this partition, like a wall, and everyone was warming up behind that wall.

At that time, well, practically very few people even knew who Fedor was, but I knew Fedor. I knew who he was, that he was the Pride champion. At that time, he beat Nogueira, beat Mark Coleman, beat Randleman. This was before his championship fight against Cro Cop.

I would come over and just sit there, watching how he warmed up, what he did. I just remember very well — I don't know, maybe Fedor will see this podcast — he had a thermos.

[laughter]

He had a thermos and he was just drinking tea. And I remember he fought Ibrahim Magomedov. He was also a legendary fighter of ours, a heavyweight who fought in Pride, too. He fought against him. It was either his first or second fight.

热身细节：连鼻子和耳朵都要热身

And he was warming up incredibly well. I remember how he was warming up his nose and his ears. I watched him and it was unusual for me at that time. I never warmed up my nose and ears. I just — I just remember how Fedor was really working on his nose, his ears, his whole face.

And he went, fought, came back. This was in Makhachkala, 2004. It's the same as a UFC champion now coming and fighting at the Dagestan Combat Championship. Can you imagine that? Back then, it was the best heavyweight organization in the world. He comes there and fights.

So, he finished a fight, goes back, and he had this big thermos with him. His team was sitting separately over there.

[sighs]

Uh — he was drinking tea. He just fought, walked back, poured some tea, and drank it. He had something to snack on with it, maybe honey or something. I just don't remember. And I was, "Wow, Fedor is right here." For me, that was just such a, you know, great source of motivation back then. It's really hard to put those emotions into words.

想问Fedor：茶里到底放了什么？

By the way, maybe you could ask him about that on the podcast.

Uh — about the thermos?

No, no. About the tea, what was in it? Thyme, mint? What did he put in there?

Uh, well, I would love to talk to him on this podcast, but I think he rarely does interviews.

I think you can reach him. I can help you.

Well, if you could put in a good word for me.

Yeah, of course. I think it would be interesting for people to hear him.

Absolutely.

冷静的气场：像幼儿园老师，却KO巨人

Yeah. But psychologically, he's kind of like you in a way.

You mean calm?

Yeah.

Yes, that calmness. You see the Pride era, those huge fights, those really tough matchups, and still he always stayed calm.

It's his aura. Yeah. I don't know about others, but for me that was his aura. The fact that he'd come out with such a calm, cool-headed look, and knock out giants, strong fighters at that time, right?

Yeah.

You know, we used to joke about his face that he — uh — kind of looks like a kindergarten teacher, you know? And then he goes out there and knocks out absolute giants.

And he was like that. Both before and after the fight, he never showed much emotion. But I think we're a little different in that regard. I think Fedor by temperament is calmer than I am. That's my impression. But with that cold-blooded calmness of his, I think he got to a lot of people mentally.

内心沸腾与表面冷静：两种不同的"冷"

It's like something's happening inside both of you. Like something's boiling inside. So, when we look at your face —

of course it's boiling. What do you think?

You know what? It's one thing when it's boiling inside and you show it, but there are some who can't hide their feelings.

[gasps]

But, it's a different thing when it's boiling inside and on the surface you stay cold, cold-blooded, calm, and you can handle all these different emotions that hit you at the same time. There are a lot of them, and they all hit differently.

顶级运动员的独特之处：同时处理多种情绪

When you compete, what makes a fighter and athlete at the highest level so unique is that so many different emotions hit you at the same time. Fear, nerves, the fact that people are watching you, the thought that you might perform badly, that you might not show what you've trained for, that you might mess it up, that you might, I don't know, fall.

So much enters your head, and you can put each emotion where it belongs. So, you know, if all of that gets inside your head and turns into chaos, you won't be able to handle it emotionally. But, you stay cold-blooded. And you know that if you don't handle these emotions that are coming at you, if you don't handle this pressure, then it will be difficult for you to compete, because the main competition is against yourself first.

You fight yourself, you beat yourself, and only then do you actually start competing with your opponent. So, I think it happens to everyone, not just him or me. The big difference here is how much you can control it.

Fedor 的名言：能打败我的只有我自己

Fedor himself famously said, "The only person who can defeat me is me. The only person who can beat me is me."

He was talking about that fight with yourself, I'm sure. Because if you lose to yourself, then you'll lose to your opponent very easily.

Mhm.

观看原视频 →

item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib and Islam speak different languages - Dagestan has 30+ languages | Khabib Nurmagomedov
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、语言的"不可通约性"：一种被低估的文明基础设施

最令人意外的观察是：Khabib 和 Islam 作为师徒、兄弟、同乡，日常竟然"根本听不懂彼此的母语"。这不是方言差异，而是两套完全独立的语言系统（Avar 与 Kumyk/Lak 语族分属完全不同的语系）。他们能并肩训练二十多年、共同征服 UFC，靠的其实是第三方语言（俄语）作为"中立协议层"。

这颠覆了我们对"团队亲密度"的常识——通常我们认为"共享母语"是信任的前提，但达吉斯坦的案例揭示：当没有人能强迫他人使用自己的母语时，反而催生出一种更平等的沟通契约。这与硅谷早期工程师文化异曲同工——正因为大家母语各异，英语作为"降级过的通用协议"反而促成了更快的协作。

二、跨领域连接：达吉斯坦是"生物多样性"的语言学镜像

30+ 种语言挤在一个略大于苏格兰的地区——这个密度在全球仅有巴布亚新几内亚、亚马逊河上游可比。有趣的是，这三个地方有一个共同的物理特征：地形极度破碎（高加索山脉、热带雨林、山地部落）。

这里藏着一个跨学科的"啊哈时刻"：语言多样性遵循的是生态学中的"岛屿生物地理学"定律。每一个山谷就是一个"进化孤岛"，语言像加拉帕戈斯的雀鸟一样各自演化。Khabib 一句轻描淡写的"我们有 30 多种语言"，实际上在陈述一个地理学、进化生物学、认知科学交汇的深层规律。

更反直觉的是：格斗冠军的密集产出与语言的高度碎片化，可能共享同一个根源。当每个村庄都必须自我防御、每一次跨谷通婚都需要谈判与力量证明时，"身体语言"（摔跤、khash 摔法）就成了唯一超越语言隔阂的通用协议。MMA 冠军之乡的秘密，或许写在语言地图上，而不是训练馆里。

三、隐藏的系统真相：文化"消化力"决定文明韧性

Khabib 提到达吉斯坦"吸收了很多文化和信仰"——伊斯兰是主流，但饮食里同时能看到欧洲、亚洲、高加索的层叠痕迹。这是一个值得放大的系统性观察：

一个地区能在 1500 年里保留 30 多种语言而不被同化，同时又"消化"了无数外来元素——这需要一种极特殊的文化代谢机制：吸收营养但保留骨架。

与之形成鲜明对比的是许多"熔炉型"文明（比如美国的 Melting Pot 隐喻）——它们通过同质化换取效率。而达吉斯坦走的是另一条路：分布式冗余的文明架构。用软件工程的话说，这是"微服务架构"对"单体架构"——每个山谷是一个独立服务，故障不会蔓延，但系统整体依然能对外接口。

这或许解释了一个更深的悖论：为什么在全球化最凶猛的今天，这些"看似落后"的碎片化文化区反而展现出惊人的输出能力（顶级格斗手、独特音乐、独立的道德叙事）。碎片化不是弱点，而是一种反脆弱的战略储备。

📝 转录文本

语言的多样性

We have so many languages — more than 30 different languages — and people just don't understand each other.

Take Islam and me: we have different languages, come from different backgrounds. Islam is Lak and I'm an Avar. When we talk, it's not like it's a dialect — we don't understand each other at all. But since Islam has been with us for nearly 25 years, he actually picked up some Avar over time.

历史的印记

But anyway, the deep history of the region — it all left its mark. It created many different languages and traditions.

Basically, of course, Islam is our primary religion, but Dagestan has actually absorbed a lot of cultures and faiths. Even our food culture, it is incredibly rich: we have European, and Asian, and Caucasian — our own unique cuisine.

独一无二的达吉斯坦

So on the people themselves, the last 1,500 years of history have left a huge mark.

If you're into history and you start reading about Dagestan, I think you'll get completely immersed and be amazed by what a unique place it is.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一、语言的"不可通约性"：一种被低估的文明基础设施
最令人意外的观察是：**Khabib 和 Islam 作为师徒、兄弟、同乡，日常竟然"根本听不懂彼此的母语"**。这不是方言差异，而是两套完全独立的语言系统（Avar 与 Kumyk/Lak 语族分属完全不同的语系）。他们能并肩训练二十多年、共同征服 UFC，靠的其实是**第三方语言（俄语）作为"中立协议层"**。
这颠覆了我们对"团队亲密度"的常识——通常我们认为"共享母语"是信任的前提，但达吉斯坦的案例揭示：**当没有人能强迫他人使用自己的母语时，反而催生出一种更平等的沟通契约**。这与硅谷早期工程师文化异曲同工——正因为大家母语各异，英语作为"降级过的通用协议"反而促成了更快的协作。
## 二、跨领域连接：达吉斯坦是"生物多样性"的语言学镜像
30+ 种语言挤在一个略大于苏格兰的地区——这个密度在全球仅有巴布亚新几内亚、亚马逊河上游可比。有趣的是，**这三个地方有一个共同的物理特征：地形极度破碎**（高加索山脉、热带雨林、山地部落）。
这里藏着一个跨学科的"啊哈时刻"：**语言多样性遵循的是生态学中的"岛屿生物地

item.title: [No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups] How Nuclear Will Unlock Energy Abundance with Valar Atomics Founder Isaiah Taylor
item.dc:creator: No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

洞察一：核能行业的"模拟陷阱"——一个跨行业的隐蔽病理

Isaiah 说了一句非常锋利的话："大多数核能公司其实是建模仿真公司。" 这不只是对核工业的批评，而是揭示了一种普遍的组织病理——当一个行业因监管或恐惧而无法迭代真实硬件时，它会退化成一个"论文工业"。

有趣的跨领域连接：这与生物医药行业的"临床前动物模型工业"惊人相似。药企养了成千上万只小鼠，产出无数漂亮的机制论文，但真正让新药通过 FDA 的成功率却低于 10%。同样的病理也出现在自动驾驶——多年来 Waymo 之外的公司大都在"模拟里数亿英里"，但真实道路的边角案例才是决定性的。当反馈周期被切断，任何行业都会用"复杂性"替代"真实性"，因为复杂性可以被作者控制，而真实世界不能。

Valor 真正的哲学突破不是核物理，而是重新恢复"tick rate"作为组织的第一性度量——这个词借自游戏引擎，暗示了一件让人意外的事：Isaiah 把核反应堆公司当成了一个实时游戏系统在设计。

洞察二："事故概率" vs "事故后果"——一个被误用了半个世纪的心智模型

传统核能安全的整个哲学是降低事故发生概率（odds）；Valor 的哲学是降低事故后果（consequence）。这两者在数学上是等价的风险控制手段，但在组织行为学上完全不同。

出人意料的观察：追求"低概率"会让组织变慢，追求"低后果"会让组织变快。因为降低概率需要无穷的冗余、审查、模拟、防御性工程，每一层都会滋生官僚化和责任回避；而降低后果只需要在架构层做一次正确的物理选择（TRISO 燃料 + 石墨慢化 + 氦冷却 + 被动散热几何），之后组织可以自由地快速迭代。

这是一个非常深的元规律：你在设计上把"最坏情况"处理好了，你在流程上就可以放开了。 这个原则不仅适用于核能，它解释了： - SpaceX 为什么敢炸火箭（可回收 + 无人驾驶 = 最坏后果被架构消除） - Netflix 为什么敢在生产环境放 Chaos Monkey（微服务架构本身容忍失败） - 加密协议为什么可以开源审计（密码学保证最坏情况的安全边界）

"架构上的悲观主义"是"执行上的乐观主义"的前提。 这几乎是所有能高速迭代的高风险系统的共同秘密。

洞察三：能源是"一切成本的极限"——AI + 机器人正在把这个哲学论点变成会计事实

Isaiah 最后那个"麦克风思想实验"看似漫谈，但藏着一个可能重塑二十一世纪经济学的观察：当 AI 和机器人把"人力"这一输入项转换为"能源"时，能源就变成了所有物品成本的渐近极限。

传统经济学的三大生产要素——土地、劳动、资本——正在被悄悄地归约为一个单一变量：焦耳。土地是能量场的空间承载；劳动是热力学做功；资本是过去凝结的能量。当机器人可以替代几乎所有物理劳动时，边际成本函数会退化成一条纯能源曲线。

跨领域的意外连接：这与信息论中的朗道尔极限（Landauer's limit）在哲学上是同构的——擦除一比特信息的最小能量代价是 kT ln 2。物理学告诉我们，信息、计算、制造，最终都是能量的不同形态。Valor 押注的不是"更便宜的电"，而是"把整个文明的成本函数压缩到一个变量上"——一旦这件事发生，那么"能源便宜 10 倍"意味着 "GDP 便宜 10 倍"，这是一个远超普通商业机会的赌注。

最让人意外的暗示：如果 Isaiah 的世界观成立，那么"AI 竞赛"和"能源竞赛"其实是同一场竞赛，只是从对偶的两端逼近同一个瓶颈。谁先把"能源单位成本"打下一个数量级，谁就先获得了下一个文明台阶的入场券——而这个洞察，恰恰是大多数 AI 公司和大多数能源公司都还没真正内化的。

📝 转录文本

开场：一次历史性的启动

Welcome to War 250. First advanced reactor to ever make power by a startup.

We did something pretty awesome today. The first ever AI chip powered by a nuclear reactor.

First trico reactor to turn on in over 50 years in the United States.

How much of the premise of Valor is possible now comes from increasing demands for power in the United States largely driven by AI compute. Energy being a commodity, the demand is set by the price. If you can figure out how to make energy cheaper, you will have demand.

When SpaceX started going, people were like, there's no way they're going to hit the numbers that they're hitting today. Most of the nuclear industry is a modeling and simulation industry. They're not focused on hardware iteration, hardware execution, building the simplest and safest reactor that allows them to scale. And Valor just demonstrated that we are.

主持人开场

Hi listeners, welcome back to No Priors. Today I'm here with Isaiah Taylor, the founder and CEO of Valor Atomics. We're here in their Utah nuclear facility where we're going to do a tour, talk about why speed and scale are the only path to making nuclear reactors in the United States again. Um why energy is the only input to our hyper techchnoindustrial future and why there's an open regulatory environment for progress in energy R&D for the first time in years.

Welcome Isaiah. Thanks so much for doing this.

Of course. Welcome to Valor Atomics at San Rafll. Thanks for coming.

Valor 在做什么？

So what is what are you doing here at Valor?

We are making nuclear reactors built for planetary scale. So nuclear fision is kind of an old technology. It's around the 1940s that we really started working on it. Um and we've built a lot of nuclear reactors, but we've never built them from mass scale. Nuclear's never had its Ford moment or its Tesla moment, if you want to put it that way. And that's what Valor Atomics is working on doing. We have nuclear reactors that are more manufactured than constructed and uh they're extremely safe and we think the combination of these two things is going to allow us to scale nuclear fision and make energy 10 times cheaper for humanity. So that's what we're working on.

为什么是 Isaiah？——个人起点

We're going to dig into why you think this is possible and why you're making it happen after decades of like no real activity in this space. But first for you personally um you don't have the you know credentialed decades of nuclear research background that is often required to work in the space like you know why you and what triggered it?

I have been uh reluctant to start this company for a long time um and eventually did out of sheer frustration that uh nobody else was was working on it with the pace required and understanding the scale that would be required um and uh you know I I think any problem that uh you want to work on that's that's as hard as this. You have to really really believe in it. And after a certain amount of time, I just realized that I was never going to stop thinking about this. And so I I might as well build it.

It started for me. My great-grandfather was a nuclear physicist on the Manhattan project. Um my great-grandfather and great-grandmother were both in the secret city um during uh World War II. And I just grew up thinking about nuclear as this incredible technology. I've I've always wanted to build thousands of machines. Um I didn't know which ones I was going to build. It was just very clear to me since I was like six that I was supposed to build thousands of machines.

Um and at some point um I I went from thinking about nuclear as like a totally solved problem, right, which was my first um you know outside view of the industry. It was like, okay, people know how to build reactors. They're doing fine at it. to suddenly realizing that this was an entirely unsolved problem. Um that we we sort of thought we solved in the '60s and there was like a good run into the 70s and then we suddenly stopped.

So I came to that realization. It was u very disorienting for me actually. I I suddenly realized it actually remember the afternoon. I was like wait a minute did we actually stop building reactors in the 70s? Like who why did nobody tell me that? Um and really since that moment I had been like obsessively trying to understand why. Um, and I I came to some conclusions about why uh when I was in high school, and I I still hold those conclusions today. And then it was a, you know, 10-year journey of like waiting for someone to solve the problem, watching every nuclear startup that popped up, trying to figure out if they were going to solve the problem. And eventually realizing that that no one was going to solve it at the pace and scale that was necessary. Uh, and so I started Valor.

为什么美国停止建造反应堆？

So for people who come from outside the nuclear industry, like why did we stop building reactors in this country?

Yeah, we stopped for a pretty simple reason, which is 3M Island. So, we were building a lot of reactors. We were doing really well. Um, we had a a nuclear incident in the 3M 3M island reactor. And in that incident, we essentially lost the ability to uh cool the reactor. And in traditional uh lightwater reactors, you have to always be able to cool them, right? So, if you shut a reactor down in traditional nuclear, you have to keep cooling it even after shutdown. And in this case, the cooling system failed and so you had core meltdown.

Now, nobody died, right? Uh in fact, not only did nobody die, nobody was injured and there was no radiation dose to the public. But, uh it was sort of a optics and PR situation um that was mismanaged in many many different ways and the public uh became fearful and and lost interest in nuclear.

Now I think that actually turned around even like 15 20 years ago where suddenly uh people looked back on that and they said okay actually we do know how to build reactors really safe even learnings from that uh we've taken and incorporated into new designs but then there was a second problem which was once you stop an industry it's very hard to start it again and in the intervening time between 3M island and when people gained interest in nuclear again we also really changed how we build things in the United States.

We went from a country that was very good at large scale civil infrastructure, right? Bridges, roads, um huge power plants, dams, highway systems, right? We were really good at large scale civil infrastructure. Um and we kind of atrophied at that skill set and we got much better at advanced manufacturing.

And so my realization, one of the first realizations I had about this was if you're going to reboot nuclear and you're actually believe in in the atomic energy century, which I absolutely do, it's probably not going to look like what it did in the '60s. It's not going to look like civil infrastructure because we're not that good at that anymore. And what we're way better at is producing, you know, more complicated and uh more functional pieces of manufactured equipment. And so you're going to shift from the civil infrastructure way of building to a manufacturing way of building.

And I think even though some people did realize that, and this is generally what you'd call SMRs, right, small modular reactors, what was missing is that people did not realize that you're going to have to pursue that model through hardware iteration. And that's where really where Valor is unique is that yes, we believe in SMRs, we believe in reactors that are manufactured, but we also know that in order to get there, you have to do it through hardware iteration. You have to turn some plants on. You have to turn on 100 kilowatt reactor like the one behind us. You have to go cold critical like we did in project nova. And then you have to take the next steps after that. And it's going to be driven by hardware iteration. And I think that's what nobody else realized before us.

打破监管"鸡与蛋"：DOE 路径

So that's a whole company philosophy for you, but it has to interact with a regulatory environment where I think the assumed status quo is you can't iterate because you can't turn anything on because it's going to take you 15 years to go through a permitting process and several billion dollars to get a no or try again. And so like why why isn't that true?

No, there's this chicken and egg that existed for nuclear in the last 20 years where you need data in order to go to the regulator, but in order to go to the regulator with data, you have to have run a plant, right? And so there's this like, okay, how do you get the empirical data?

And the way that people tried to solve that was with modeling and simulation, right? So if you look at the nuclear industry outside of Valor, it's mostly a modeling and simulation uh industry. Like when you think of a nuclear company, right, there's like nuclear companies out there that everyone knows the name of. And you kind of look under the cover. It's actually a modeling and simulation company, right? They produce um very very precise what we call paper reactors which have really good predictions of how a theoretical thing might behave. And that was sort of the hack to try to get around this regulatory chicken and egg.

But the alternative is that you actually just do what Congress originally intended. Um if you look back at the early days of nuclear legislation um there were actually two pathways for nuclear in the United States. There was the um testing pathway and the commercial pathway. So the commercial pathway everyone knows is called the NRC the nuclear regulatory commission. The NRC is solving for largecale commercial deployment of mature systems. So yeah if you try to do the iteration under the regulator that's concerned with large scale commercial deployment of mature systems that's going to be tough, right? you're you're going to be asked commercial deployment questions when you're just trying to figure out how to bend some steel and get some atom splitting.

Um, but there's another pathway and that pathway is the Department of Energy. So, most people don't know this, but the Department of Energy was originally called the ERDA, the Energy Research and Development Agency. And people don't know that because it was only called the ERDA for about 2 years. There was a little 2-year period where uh it was it was renamed shortly after, but its origin is actually a spin out of the Atomic Energy Commission.

So where the DOE comes from originally is Congress taking the Atomic Energy Commission, which was one agency responsible for both commercial deployment and for testing. And they said, "Actually, let's split these out. Let's make the NRC in charge of commercial deployment. Let's make the ERDA in charge of testing, and we'll have these just two two separate agencies." And then two years later, uh, Congress said, "Actually, we're just going to call the ERDA the Department of Energy, right? The DOE." But the origin of this agency is testing nuclear reactors. That's that's what it's for.

Um, and everyone sort of forgot this. Um, it's just been sitting there in legislation for like 40 years and no one's really taken advantage of it except for one government program here or there where they want to, you know, do a NASA space reactor or something like that. But it has from a legal perspective been waiting for an administration to say, "Hey, this might be a way to accelerate nuclear R&D."

Uh, and that's exactly what the Trump administration has done. So, the reactor that's uh behind us here um was turned on under an executive order. It was EO14301, which called for three advanced reactors to go critical on American soil by July 4th. Um and and we built it under Department of Energy uh authority under that executive order.

So, I mean, this is an incredibly exciting time in nuclear. This is really breaking that chicken and egg, right? It's the first time where we've been able to to shortcut that, you know, problem of how do you get data and uh and we have data now. We're currently, as we're sitting here, making 100 kow uh splitting something like 10 to the 17 atoms per second uh in this reactor behind us.

参观控制室

So, this is the control room. There's two sections. This is the uh control half. This door's closed. We have to have senior reactor operators permission to enter here, which we just got. Thank you, Brent. And uh out here is sort of our uh observation room.

It looks like the control room in Hawthorne.

It's it is the exact control room in Hawthorne. We literally picked this up, put it on an airplane, and flew it here. So the entirety of the plant, including a control room, flew with us on the C17s. Uh first time that's ever been done, which is pretty cool.

How many people um operate?

We got one one operator at the controls who's the reactor operator who's controlling all this. And then you got an senior reactor operator who provides oversight and kind of ensures that we're staying within our safety limits and stuff, but we always have to have one person that controls maintaining safety, maintaining the reactor.

Scram 演示与被动安全

So, in a couple of days here, we're going to do a scram. So, we're going to press that big red button right there. Uh big red button scrams the reactor. So, basically drops the rods, right? Dropping the control rods will introduce a lot of boron carbide into the core. When we scram that, rods will drop. Boron carbide enters the core. Boron is a strong neutron absorber and so there will not be enough neutrons to maintain criticality because the neutron population gets absorbed into the into the rods. So that'll cause the reaction to stop.

Now in a nuclear reactor, this is getting to the core of like what is Valor doing differently? Why do we really believe that the technology that we have here is going to scale? Traditionally, um when you scram the reactor in a lightwater reactor, your work is nowhere near done yet, right? the next really day of operations is incredibly important because when you turn the reactor off in a traditional nuclear reactor um you still have a lot of heat produced and you have a lot of heat produced because in a nuclear core you still have about 5% uh heat production from recently split atoms.

So when a reactor is running you have a bunch of atoms being split. They're producing a ton of energy and even after the reaction shuts down, you you have recently split atoms that are continuing down their decay chains. So, this is called decay heat. Um, and decay heat is about 5 to 6% of what your continuous power was before you shut down.

And in a traditional reactor, the the reactor would melt down if you wouldn't if you didn't continue to run the cooling pumps after turning the reactor off. So, there's no more fision occurring. you don't have a a chain reaction anymore, but you do have this decay heat. And if you were just sort of let it sit there, that heat would build up and you would have meltdown. That's exactly what happened in Fukushima and 3M Island.

Um, and so the way that they deal with this in traditional plants is they have very very carefully built cooling systems that they continue to run for about 24 hours after shutdown. Um, and they try to build in all these redundancies and and make sure that in any circumstance the cooling systems never ever ever fail. Um, and that works pretty well. And nuclear is is the safest form of energy ever made. Um, even with sort of that caveat, um, 3M Island, you know, even though it melted down, nobody died, right? Fukushima, uh, arguably maybe one person died. It's sort of a debate among scientists whether that person died from radiation or not.

Um, so even as traditional nuclear is, it's very safe, but we want to do even better. And we want to do better because we are interested in scale. We want to make thousands of reactors, tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands. And when you're doing that, you really just want it to never ever melt down for any reason, right? And so the best way to do that is actually just to make active cooling systems unnecessary altogether.

And that's actually what we're going to demonstrate on Friday. We're going to scram this reactor. Immediately after we scram, we're actually going to turn off the entire electrical supply to the plant. We're going to turn off the circulator. We're going to turn off the RCCS pump. Every safety system in this plant, we're going to shut off and we're going to watch what happens.

Now, we have a cheat code. We know what's going to happen uh because we did this in Hawthorne before we had uh neutrons in it. Uh we ran the the plant at full power uh with electrical simulators. So, we basically have these electrical resistors in the plant in Hawthorne. We put about 15 city blocks worth of LA power into this and got it up to full nuclear temperatures, pressures.

Right. I remember seeing the sim.

Yeah. Uh and so we we held it there and then we did exactly what we're about to do, which is we turned off all safety systems at once and we watched the plan for 2 days. Um and exactly what we had hoped uh happened which is that the uh RCCS panels which are these water jackets around the core um went into passive circulation mode meaning the water boils the steam leaves it condenses that removes heat and you have natural circulation with no moving parts. Um, so zero input from the operators, no moving parts, no electrical control. It's just the geometry of that system that slowly just removes that decay heat over a period of two days.

So we're about to demonstrate that uh right here starting on Friday after 72 hours of at full power. So that'll be really exciting demonstration and it's really the basis of of scale, right? If we're going to do this uh many times, we want to make sure that just from the basic physics this reactor doesn't melt down. Not because of operator control, not because of really good engineering, but the physics of the plant make it safe for meltdown.

关于核安全的两大误解

One of the huge reasons for um the slowdown in investment in real R&D in this space has been concerns about the safety profile. You and your team are you know very respectful of but not particularly concerned that this is an insurmountable problem. What do people outside nuclear misunderstand about safety of these SMRs and your design in particular?

There's two big misunderstandings. One is that people, you know, generally perceive nuclear as like stable, cheap base load but kind of dangerous with downsides. I think that's just a complete misperception. Nuclear energy is the safest form of energy empirically. If you look at the amount of power generated versus the amount amount of deaths, um it's even safer than solar, which is very strange because how does someone die from solar? that actually most solar is installed on roofs and people sometimes die falling off of a roof installing solar and if you add those deaths up it is actually a higher death per energy than the totality of nuclear energy in the world. Um so that's actually kind of crazy. Nuclear as it is today is already the safest form of energy.

Now the only problem with existing nuclear is that I I think the ex the existing philosophy again it's the safest in the world but we can do better and where we'd like to improve is the existing philosophy says okay there's if you look at risk it's actually composed of two different things right it's composed of the odds of the thing happening and the consequence if it does happen and traditional nuclear has focused on risk reduction by reducing the odds right so they say okay Yeah, a meltdown could have some bad consequence. So, let's make sure that it never ever ever happens. And all of the effort into risk reduction goes into low odds of anything ever happening.

The alternative way that you can reduce risk is actually just reducing consequence, right? And we would argue that that's a much better way to reduce risk. Odds uh are stochastic, right? Even if you do an enormous amount of risk reduction on odds and you do all this engineering, something's still going to happen, right? like just something's going to come out of left field and you can't predict everything.

Um and so advanced reactors tend to focus on consequence more than odds. Now we still don't you know we we still try to protect against things like um you know we have sight security here for example right so someone can't come and compromise the control room but from an engineering perspective we also say well what if someone did you compromise the control room how do we still make sure that it's perfectly safe? Um and so advanced reactors really focus on that that second thing.

Um our safety basis when we go to the regulator is everything in the plant has failed. Absolutely everything right. Everything we know what happens.

Yeah. In fact it is it is safe. Right. So we have regulatory limits where we say okay in an accident scenario you can't dose the public with radiation. Right. That's really ultimately what a nuclear regulator is trying to prevent. You can't dose public and workers with radiation. And so our safety basis says, "All right, let's look at the reactor design and pretend that everything in it has failed. Are we dosing the, you know, workers in the public with radiation?" And the answer is no.

Um, and that's super super important because even though we do still try to reduce the odds, we have site security, we make sure that our operators are well trained, we start with the worst case possible scenario where everything has failed and we say, "How do we make that fa that safe?" And that's really a physics problem. It's really about the geometry of the core. It's about the materials that you use. Trico is a huge part of that. Um, and and that's how we pursue safety.

So, I think that that people miss that a nuclear is already very safe. But b, the new breed of root of nuclear is much more focused on just making sure that these plants are intrinsically and inherently safe regardless of odds, right? Regardless of what crazy thing comes out of left field. Um, and that's a much better way to scale.

可靠性挑战：氦、石墨与湿度

What are the major causes of um like reliability issues for a reactor of this design?

Let's see. Helium circulator is one area that people have had trouble with in the past. Um the heat exchanger between the main helium loop and the secondary power conversion loop is something that Fort St. Brands has had issues with. Uh I don't know Jess, what do you think?

Moisture as well. For brain had problems with moisture. So graphite is hydrophilic meaning that it loves to take moisture even in the hot desert air hot dry desert air it still sucks up moisture. Um so we have mitigated that risk by having the helium purification system and part of that is taking the moisture and the and trying to condense that moist air out of the system and then put it into some supply tanks or excuse me some storage tanks outside of that.

Um and so yeah, I think like in the long term we'll maybe start to do some of these deals where a dedicated customer wants their own gigasite for their hypercluster or something like that. Um but it'll be driven by speed even in that case, right? We'll go to the customers who say um you know and we want it delivered in a year, right? Not the customers who say oh we're thinking about this in 3 to four years.

So really speed and scale. If you honestly if you ask me any question and you keep digging back you will find speed and scale like that really is what nuclear is missing. It's missing its its Ford moment it's Toyota moment it's SpaceX moment where you have a company that realizes that the actual thing that nuclear is missing is scale deployment and and that's really what we care about. And so the gigasite, you we've got a site here. We're going to build more reactors here. We have a a planned gigasite nearby. We get to go with conviction, build power. Um and yes, I'm absolutely confident that load will follow.

作为 CEO 如何推动速度与规模

How do you um if you just think of your primary objectives as speed and scale? Yes. Given safety, right? Um how do you like drive that personally as CEO? What do you wake up every day and like think about problems to solve or what to focus on?

Yeah, this is one of those things that I think is the probably the most irreplaceable attribute of a company is its internal pace. We call it tick rate.

That's a sort of a metric that we've designed around going critical in in new systems, but you could probably translate that to any uh industry. You know, in software, it's probably something like, you know, new uh continuous integration builds per hour or something like that. But um I think it's the hardest thing to replicate. You have to start it from the first day of the company. Um, it has to come from the CEO and the first five team members have to have it deep in their bones. The first 20 team members have to have it deep in their bones. They have to be trained that when they hire people, they're looking for that in their, you know, those people's bones.

Um, and that's also not enough. Also, once you're in that setup, I have to constantly, and I, this is really what I do, go around the organization and speed things up, right? you know, continuously ask u my chief of staff's laughing over here because she's seen this happen many times. Um, you know, I go I go war mode on things, right? So, like look around and like, okay, that's going slow. And we will we will set up a a literal war room and I guess not literal war room, but we'll set up a physical war room um and we will say, how do we turn a six-month timeline into a four-week timeline, right? And maybe we'll hit 8 weeks, right? But it's not six months.

Um, and I think I've realized like there is no autopilot for that. There's no automatic mode that makes a company faster inherently. There are lots of things you can do to set it up for success. Um, but

but you have to push.

You will always I will always have to push and I will always push and it's because um I know that the physics are here, right? I know that energy will be a thousand times cheaper than it is today. I know that nuclear fision will make energy a thousand times cheaper than it is today. somebody will do that and it's really up to us as a team whether or not that's going to be in the future decades or the future centuries because that time is up to us right it's up to us how quickly we go down that path how quickly we make energy more abundant um and that feeds into everything else so it's it's highly motivating for us um and we are are tackling it as fast as we can.

能源丰盛的未来图景

People in their daily lives thinking about what happens for them if this works and you get very cheap abundant nuclear energy like imagine that future for us.

Energy is the fundamental input to uh the quality of human life. U if you look backward into time and say how did humanity go from one standard of living to the next, it's always unlocked by cheaper energy, right? Right.

So when we went from essentially a solar powered world, which is what we were in agrarian age, um like literally human muscles were solar powered because you were either eating plants or eating animals and both of those things were essentially um chemical energy that is built up by the energy of the sun through photosynthesis. Um life was hard, right? Life was really, really hard.

Um when we got into underground hydrocarbons, you had this massive uh explosion of quality of life, right? where we have, you know, heat in the winter and we have AC in the summer. Um, where we're able to drive cars to get to the hospital. Um, even really simple things, you know, we're in an aluminum strut building right now. Um, every one of these these struts that you could see behind us are made of aluminum. There was a time when aluminum was considered a precious metal. Um, where kings would literally make jewelry out of aluminum because it was that rare. And the thing that changed it to a literally structural metal that we make buildings out of uh is energy becoming cheaper, right? We figured out, you know, Charles Hall here in the United States figured out aluminum electrolysis. Um and cheap enough energy means that you can actually just separate that oxide from the aluminum. Uh and you can have pure aluminum metal. Um and that is that is entirely downstream of of energy.

So I would say that the standard of living that we enjoy today is entirely downstream of the fact that we figured out you can make pretty cheap energy with hydrocarbons. Now our goal is not pretty cheap energy. It's insanely cheap energy and that's going to be unlocked by by nuclear.

Um what it will look like I think is fundamentally unpredictable but I I have a few ideas. Um first of all I'm very very excited about transportation. Um, like if you think about the fundamental limits of why is it that I can't go see grandma every week, you know, on a plane, like why is it just so hard to do? Why is it so expensive? Why is it so complicated? It really just comes down to the fact that we've kind of squeezed as much juice out of jet fuel as we can, right? It it's just hard to imagine jet fuel getting 10 times cheaper than it is today. Uh, and it's polluting the environment and all of these different things. Um, if you could make energy 10 times cheaper, um, then you probably could go visit grandma every other day. You know, just on a on a Saturday it takes 30 minutes and, you know, she lives across the country, but you you go and visit her on the weekend.

Hyper-technoindustrialism：思想实验

I'm very excited about what I would call uh hyper techchnoindustrialism. This is a term I invented for

Okay. Haven't heard it.

Yeah. Um, for basically everything becoming free. Uh it is this sounds like I'm I'm talking sci-fi here, but like an approximation of this will happen.

Um let me put out a thought experiment for you. So uh let's take a a a physical good that's manufactured today, right? Let's let's take this microphone. So this microphone came from a factory and the factory had um sort of three inputs, right? It had people in the factory that are working on it, assembling things. It had input materials, right? And I would include in those input materials, you know, the plastic on here and this foam thing. Also the machines, right, that you know, maybe injection molded that plastic. And then the last thing it consumed was energy, right? So energy is one of the three things that made this.

What's interesting is um with the introduction of AI, we're actually converting the human input element to energy, right? So instead of uh a person having to pick something up and put it onto the next tray, right? you're going to have a robot pick some up, put on onto the next tray and consume energy, right? Um, and instead that human will be able to coordinate hundreds of robots, right? So, their personal output will go from picking up an object and putting onto a tray to essentially picking up 100 objects and putting it onto 100 trays. And the trade-off we're making there is that we're increasing the consumption of energy.

Now, you could still say, okay, but you are consuming physical inputs. What's interesting about that, though, is let's dig into that. All right. So, there were some physical inputs and some machines that went into that factory. Well, where did those come from? Right? Those don't grow on trees. Those also came from factories. And you can ask the same question. What went into that factory? It was energy. It was machines and it was people, right? Apply the same rubric and you realize, okay, actually, it's really just machines and energy. Well, where did those machines come from?

If you keep asking this question, what you realize is energy is the fundamental input. When we figure out AI and robotics that allows us to do semi-aututonomous manufacturing, energy will become the cost of all things, right? The cost of buying a thing will become the cost of energy used to make it. And to the extent that we can make energy 10 times cheaper and then 10 times cheaper, uh that is the extent to which we will be able to make basically everything free.

Um and that's very exciting to me. Uh because if we're going to go explore the stars and we're going to set up, you know, a place for us to live on Mars and explore the universe, we're going to need a lot of stuff and it's going to be it's going to need to be a lot cheaper than it is right now. So that's very exciting to me.

Exciting to me, too. That's a great place to end. Thanks, Isaiah.

Thanks so much for having me.

结语

item.description:
## 洞察一：核能行业的"模拟陷阱"——一个跨行业的隐蔽病理
Isaiah 说了一句非常锋利的话："大多数核能公司其实是建模仿真公司。" 这不只是对核工业的批评，而是揭示了一种普遍的组织病理——**当一个行业因监管或恐惧而无法迭代真实硬件时，它会退化成一个"论文工业"**。
有趣的跨领域连接：这与生物医药行业的"临床前动物模型工业"惊人相似。药企养了成千上万只小鼠，产出无数漂亮的机制论文，但真正让新药通过 FDA 的成功率却低于 10%。同样的病理也出现在自动驾驶——多年来 Waymo 之外的公司大都在"模拟里数亿英里"，但真实道路的边角案例才是决定性的。**当反馈周期被切断，任何行业都会用"复杂性"替代"真实性"**，因为复杂性可以被作者控制，而真实世界不能。
Valor 真正的哲学突破不是核物理，而是**重新恢复"tick rate"作为组织的第一性度量**——这个词借自游戏引擎，暗示了一件让人意外的事：Isaiah 把核反应堆公司当成了一个实时游戏系统在设计。
## 洞察二："事故概率" vs "事故后果"——一个被误用了半个世纪的心智模型
传统核能安全的整个哲学是**

item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib on Dana White: He is a cold-blooded businessman | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"冷血"不是缺陷，而是一种基础设施

多数人把 Dana White 的"cold-blooded"理解为性格特质，但 Khabib 在无意间揭示了一个更深的结构性真相：冷血本质上是一种"决策带宽"。当一个组织的领导者能够把"人际关系"从"业务判断"中彻底剥离，他实际上是把自己变成了一台不会因情感噪音而降频的处理器。这不是道德问题，而是信息论问题——情感耦合越多，决策熵越高，长期系统就越难维持一致性。

有意思的是，Khabib 引用了"黑帮电影里家族至上"的比喻，但这里出现了一个反直觉的置换：Dana 的"家族"不是人，而是品牌本身。UFC 这个抽象实体被拟人化为"家人"，而具体的血肉之躯（包括冠军、员工、朋友）反而被降级为"业务变量"。这是一种极其罕见的忠诚对象的抽象化转移——很多创业者做不大，恰恰是因为他们效忠的仍是具体的人。

二、被忽略的悖论：UFC 的"品牌免疫力"来自它敢于让单场比赛失败

Khabib 说了一句几乎所有人都会滑过去、但极其关键的话："即便某场比赛不成功，UFC 还是 UFC。"

这是一个隐藏的反脆弱结构。传统体育联盟（尤其是欧洲足球俱乐部、传统拳击推广公司）的品牌价值高度依赖"每一场都要精彩"，一旦砸了就动摇根基。而 UFC 反其道而行：它把"品牌"从"单一产品质量"中解耦出来，让品牌成为一种"入场券资格"而非"质量承诺"。

这里可以做一个跨领域的连接：这正是苹果 App Store 的逻辑，也是米其林指南的逻辑——策展平台的品牌力，来自"我在场"而不是"这一场很好"。UFC 30 年做到别的体育 100 年才达到的高度，秘诀可能不是"办了多少好比赛"，而是成功地让自己变成了 MMA 世界里的"操作系统"，而所有具体比赛只是运行其上的 App。你可以卸载某个 App，但你不会因此卸载 iOS。

三、真正让人意外的观察：Khabib 在赞美 Dana 的同时，也在为自己的"退出"辩护

这段访谈表面上是"退役传奇谈论老板"，但如果你把它放在 Khabib 自己的人生弧线里——他在职业巅峰急流勇退、拒绝金钱诱惑、回归家庭和信仰——你会发现一个镜像结构：

  • Dana：把"人"抽象为"品牌"，让 UFC 成为家人。
  • Khabib：把"品牌"抽象回"人"，让家人重新超越 UFC。

Khabib 说"我也运营过自己的联盟，我懂那种关系"——这句话看似谦逊补充，其实是在为自己当初 walk away 的选择提供了一个隐晦的合理化：正因为他理解 Dana 那种"必须冷血"的位置，他才更清楚自己不愿意成为那样的人。他对 Dana 的尊敬是真诚的，但也是一种保持距离的尊敬——像一个僧侣在赞美一位战功赫赫的将军。

跨领域连接：这与乔布斯之于 Wozniak、马斯克之于早期 PayPal 团队是同一模式——最出色的"人性化奉献者"往往主动让位给"冷血系统化者"，因为他们意识到：规模化的爱，需要有人愿意暂时放下爱。这是所有伟大组织背后一个几乎无人明说的、令人心碎的分工。

📝 转录文本

Dana White 是谁？——一个罕见的商业天才

Lex： From where you are now, you can see the entire fight business and you know Dana White very well. I'd say he's one of those rare geniuses in sports business. In business, period. I don't think the UFC would exist without Dana White. There are important people there, of course, but he's really at the center of it all. What can you say about him? What qualities, what traits have made him such a successful businessman?

双重视角：既是格斗者，也是联盟运营者

Khabib： First of all, I think if you look at it, I also—kind of, well, not kind of—I understand his position a little. I also ran my own league for a couple of years. I know what the relationship between a promoter—well, a league owner—and the fighters is like, not just as a fighter. Dealing with a league owner. I've been on both sides of it.

冷血的商业哲学：业务与情感的绝对分离

He's very good at separating business from personal relationships. For him, the two never, never overlap. He draws a clear line between them.

In business, he's extremely cold-blooded. He's made decisions, some major decisions, regardless of whether people like them or not. And those decisions, they were best for the league and for the UFC.

He always had that mentality, you know, like in those mafia movies where family comes first, right?

Lex： Mhm.

Khabib： Well, for him, the UFC always came first. That's the only way he was able to push their brand forward.

团队功不可没，但"樱桃"始终是 Dana

Of course, a lot of people contributed to that success. There were a lot of them. You have to give credit to Bruce Buffer, to Joe Rogan, to the commentators who were there. There were a lot of things that made the UFC unique, but the cherry on top was always Dana.

Dana did an incredible job promoting the UFC, and he still does. No matter what, the UFC is always there. You know, no matter how—no matter how unsuccessful a particular event might be, the UFC is still the UFC.

When they go into a new market outside the United States, even if a show doesn't go so well, people will still come back for the next event simply because it's the UFC. Over the last 30-plus years, they've established themselves as the premier MMA league in the world, and they put on the best fights.

So, in that respect, I think a huge part of the credit goes to Dana. The fact that the UFC has come this far is a major achievement.

建立这样的联盟有多难？

Lex： Building a league like that is incredibly difficult.

Khabib： Yeah, a lot of people have money, and a lot of people have tried. Many have come in, but building what the UFC has built is extremely hard.

And what they've achieved now with Paramount—that's something unique. It's a unique achievement. In just 30 years, they've grown to a level that some entire sports needed 100 or 150 years to reach.

归功于一人：Dana White

And you have to give credit where it's due, and that credit goes to one person: Dana White.

So, I think that his genius as a promoter—the way he promotes and pushes fights, and pushes his league as a whole—that is just remarkable. In my opinion, that's something a lot of people could learn from him.

item.title: [All-In Podcast] Anthropic's $2T IPO, Zuck's AI Manifesto, Nvidia's $500B AI Bet, Grok's Comeback
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三个反直觉的观察

1. Anthropic 的"两万亿定价"其实是一封投降书——败选投行故意泄露的"耻辱标签"

表面上大家在惊叹 2 万亿估值创纪录，但 Gavin 揭穿了一个华尔街的隐藏机制：这个数字几乎肯定是从"未拿到 Lead Left"的投行嘴里流出去的。当承销团里输掉主承销权的银行知道自己出局后，它们的第一动作不是庆祝，而是故意向 FT 泄露一个"看似高"的数字，逼中标的 Lead Left 陷入两难——定价低了显得无能，定价高了引发破发。

这里有个反直觉的推论：如果 Anthropic 真的以 2 万亿定价，恰恰说明路演反响炸裂，而不是"贵"。IPO 定价的博弈论几乎是反着读新闻的。这和你熟悉的产品发布的"预期管理"游戏是同一套代码——只不过这里的玩家是穿着定制西装的人。

2. Dario 的"Anthropic 可能是世界上唯一的私营公司"是一句结构性的自杀宣言

Gavin 点出了这句话时说"我建议 Dario 永远别再对任何人说这话"——这不只是公关失误。它触发了一个跨领域的镜像模式：SBF 说过类似的话（"有效利他 + 全世界的钱由我最优分配"）、Elizabeth Holmes、WeWork 的 Neumann——历史上所有说过"只有我们能拯救人类"的创始人，最后都倒在了同一堵墙前。

更深的洞察是：这句话不是傲慢，它是一种商业模式的自我暴露。Anthropic 的商业逻辑必须依赖"我们是唯一被允许存在的高智能"——这就是为什么他们同时游说政府监管、鼓吹开源危险、支持 Cartel 化。"世界上唯一的私营公司"不是幻想，是他们的收入模型的言下之意。Zuckerberg 那篇 6500 字檄文精准地打中了这一点："如果 AI 如此危险，你为什么急着造它？"——这不是伦理质问，这是商业模式的解构。

3. Nvidia 正在变成"AI 的美联储"——而 Anthropic 的 S-1 会是整个宏观周期的领先指标

这里有一个几乎没人在讲的跨领域连接：Jensen 的融资平台设计本质上和央行的公开市场操作一模一样。他提供 residual value guarantee（相当于折现窗口）、通过 Blackstone/KKR/Apollo 做通道（相当于一级交易商）、通过 telemetry 掌握全市场真实供需（相当于宏观数据）——Nvidia 已经不是芯片公司，它是 AI 经济的货币当局。

而真正让我震撼的推论是 Sax 那句话的言外之意：Anthropic 上市后的季度财报，将取代 CPI、非农就业成为 AI 时代最重要的宏观指标。因为整个 AI capex 链条是刚性传导的——Anthropic 一踩刹车，SpaceX 拿不到 500 亿，Nvidia 拿不到 300 亿，TSMC/Micron/SK Hynix 全线连环追尾。这是史上第一次，一家单一公司的季报会决定一个万亿美元产业的生死节奏。

隐藏的系统性真相：AI 时代的经济周期正在从"美联储主导"迁移到"anthropic S-1 + nvidia telemetry 主导"——而这场权力交接，几乎没有主流经济学家意识到正在发生。

一个额外的跨领域彩蛋：Zuckerberg 的这篇宣言不是写给公众的，它是开源版的《共产党宣言》的资本主义翻版——马克思用"生产资料私有化 vs 社会化"作为轴，Zuck 用"智能中心化 vs 分布化"作为新轴。AI 时代的意识形态战争，正在用完全对称的语法结构重演 19 世纪的辩论——只是这次，"资本家"变成了 EA，"无产阶级"变成了开源社区。

📝 转录文本

开场：本周阵容

All right, everybody. Welcome back to the All-In podcast, the number one podcast in the world. David Sacks and Gavin Baker are with us this week. We got a short crew, but a long docket and we are going to rock it.

How are you doing, Gavin? Nice to see you.

Fantastic.

You're still in that SpaceX afterglow. This is the biggest win of your career, correct?

You know, SpaceX was a magical moment. There's only one SpaceX but — to quote Bill Belichick, you know, it's on to Cincinnati.

Got it.

And there's a lot I think ahead for SpaceX. So the SpaceX story isn't over.

Yeah. And you're only as good as your last investment in our business. I guess everybody's like, "What now?" Sacks, you're back. How are you doing, brother? How's the summer wrapping up for you?

Good. I'm looking forward to talking to Gavin.

Oh, fantastic. Well, I'll try to stay with you and not step on you. You missed a really great discussion we had on the all-in interview show with your guy Rahm Emanuel. How did that go? I heard actually it got kind of spicy.

You know,

it got super spicy. Rahm came in like full guns blazing, but it's a really great interview and we'll take anybody who wants to do the interview show who's running in 2028. Did you catch it, Gavin, by chance?

I haven't watched it yet.
