item.title: [Mercatus Center] Gaurav Chiplunkar on the Frictions in India’s Labor Market | Ideas of India
item.dc:creator: Mercatus Center
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"劳动需求端盲区"——一个隐藏的认知偏差

Gaurav 的研究里藏着一个几乎所有印度性别劳动政策制定者都在犯的系统性错误：我们把"女性不工作"当作一个供给端问题（她们受文化束缚、缺乏技能、无法出门），却把解药也全开在供给端（培训、育儿假、安全交通）。但他的安德拉邦研究揭示了一个令人不安的悖论——当供给端保护越强，需求端就越会通过退回非正规部门来"消解"这些保护。这就像挤气球：你压住一端，另一端一定会鼓起来。

更让人意外的是：印度对"女性问题"的过度浪漫化本身就是一种压迫。Shruti 一针见血地说，把印度女性描绘成"被文化枷锁绑定的异域生物"，恰恰否认了她们作为经济理性人的身份。孟加拉和越南证明——当家里在挨饿，没人在乎干活的是男是女。所谓"文化障碍"往往只是需求端缺失的替罪羊。

二、"书呆子效应"——一个跨领域的震撼隐喻

我要指出这项研究里最让人脊背发凉的发现：在孟买大学的信息实验中，能力最强的"书呆子"被系统性地排除在工作信息之外。这不是因为他们社交能力差，而是因为同学们故意不告诉他们——因为怕竞争。而当工作变成非竞争性（每人都能得到）时，这种排斥瞬间消失。

这个发现的跨领域震撼力在于：它其实是一切"零和心态社会"的缩影模型。

  • 教育系统：印度的应试文化让学生把同学视为对手而非合作者——同样的"书呆子被排除"机制在补习班笔记共享中每天上演。
  • 学术圈：为什么学者更愿意向"次一级"的同行分享论文预印本，却对更强的对手保密？同样的机制。
  • AI 时代的隐喻：当我们担心 AI 抢走工作，我们正在把整个劳动力市场变成一个"竞争性信息网络"——书呆子效应会全面爆发，最优秀的人反而最难获得机会。
  • 进化生物学视角：这甚至映射了 Amotz Zahavi 的"信号成本"理论——在稀缺环境中，信息本身成为最昂贵的社会货币。

惊人的洞察：印度女性反而不表现出"书呆子效应"——不是因为女性更慷慨，而是因为她们的社交网络本来就被排除在主流职业竞争之外，所以边缘化反而制造了一种意外的合作红利。这是一个悲伤的、但极具启示性的悖论。

三、"女性雇佣女性"的乘数效应——被误读的经济现象

Chiplunkar 与 Goldberg 那篇 Econometrica 论文里最反直觉的发现是：女性创业者比男性创业者更愿意雇佣女性——这个模式在全球都成立，包括发达国家。传统解释都指向文化偏好或安全感，但我想提出一个从未被明说的联想：

这可能与"平台经济中的双边匹配问题"是同构的。Uber 女司机更容易接到女乘客——不是因为算法歧视，而是因为信息与信任的"同类耦合"降低了交易成本。同样的机制在中世纪的犹太商人网络、当代硅谷的印度人 CEO 网络、深圳的潮汕商帮里都反复出现——"少数派创业者"天然形成一个流动性更高的次级劳动力市场。

所以当政府说"要提高女性劳动参与率"时，最有效的政策不是给女性发培训券，而是创造一个女性创业者——因为每个女性创业者会带动5个女性就业，产生 1:6 的乘数效应。这个洞察颠覆了整个 gender policy 的传统逻辑：性别平等不是分配问题，而是网络拓扑问题。

四、一个让人不适的连接——手机、Vocational Training 与"公务员考试幻觉"

最后一个跨领域连接：Gaurav 发现北方邦职业培训毕业生纷纷辞职去考公务员，而这与手机 3G 覆盖对女性劳动力的"稀释效应"、以及安德拉邦法规导致的非正规化——其实是同一个深层机制的三个表象：

印度经济正在训练大量的人进入一个不存在的正规部门。政策制造了大量"符合规格的劳动者"，但市场无法吸收他们，于是他们要么退回农村（男性），要么涌向公务员考试（更多男性），要么被压低工资进入非正规经济（女性）。这与中国 1990 年代大学扩招后的"考研考公潮"、韩国财阀垄断下的青年失业、日本"就职冰河期"惊人地同构——都是供给端政策跑在需求端结构之前的产物。

真正的啊哈时刻是：印度的劳动力市场问题不是"女性问题"，也不是"技能问题"，而是整个经济体的政策想象力被锁死在了正规部门的浪漫化幻觉中——而这个幻觉的最大受害者，恰恰是女性。

📝 转录文本

开场：主持人介绍

Shruti：Hi Gora, welcome to the show. It is such a pleasure to have you here and do this in person.

Gaurav：Thank you so much for having me, Shruti.

Shruti：Yeah, we do this all the time but we just don't record it on the podcast. So I feel like it's high time we recorded on the podcast — and a bunch of your co-authors have been here, like Ritum most recently, Ashwini Deshpande. I'm sure there are more. So I'm excited.

I want to start with your papers. I mean, you are my go-to person for all things labor market in India, because you're somehow studying it from all different angles — demand side, supply side, field experiments, RCTs, general equilibrium models. Somehow you've managed to cover the gamut.

一、女性劳动力参与率与 Econometrica 论文

Shruti：I want to start with female labor force participation. The headline news is: in India, female labor force participation is both low and declining, and also that there's a fair amount of variation between the states. It's just difficult to get a sense of what the problem is or what the solution is, because there could be so many different factors — demand side factors and supply side factors.

I want to start with one particular paper of yours — your latest in Econometrica, congratulations — with Penny Goldberg, where you build a quantitative general equilibrium model. You look at India's entire labor market: both men and women, whether they choose to work, whether they choose to run firms, whether they are formalizing, or if they're hiring workers, and so on. What you model in particular is gender-specific barriers at each step, and you also treat every state as its own closed economy, which is a lovely way to model this because India has so much regional variation.

The big takeaway from the paper is that women-owned firms end up hiring more women. But before we get to the results, can you walk us through how you actually model something as complicated as the Indian labor market — in particular, female-led firms and female employment — and then what is the exact mechanism through which this multiplier effect is happening?

Gaurav 的回答：为什么要看州级差异

Gaurav：First of all, thank you so much for having me. I've been a great fan of the show and your podcast, and it's so exciting that I'm finally here. So thank you for having me.

To your question — let me preface the thought behind that paper with two things. One thing which I learned very early on is that you can never generalize anything in India, because what works in one part just doesn't work in the other part. So making some general claim about "this is the problem or that is the problem" — in some cases is true, but in many cases is not, because one can always find exceptions. That's coming to your insight about why we look at different states and not just the aggregate.

The aggregate in some sense matters, because of course there's a rich randomized control trial literature trying to look at different barriers to female labor force participation — whether it's work, whether it's the type of work, whether it's where you work, how you get remunerated for it, and so on. The aggregate becomes important from a policy perspective because once you start implementing this at scale, then you have changes in different channels through market responses — women entering the workforce, starting these firms or not starting them if they're facing barriers, and then you might crowd out or crowd in, depending on what the data tells you, either same-gender or male entrepreneurs. Wages, prices — there are lots of other factors that once you start scaling up become important to understand.

Now, the model is obviously a simplification of how this world works, so we don't want to overclaim. But I think it provides interesting insights in terms of understanding this problem.

模型的理论渊源

Shruti：And you do build the model with real world data on the Indian labor market and Indian firms, just to be clear. So it's not an exact one-on-one map of the real world, but it's a pretty close approximation.

Gaurav：Absolutely. It's inspired by this almost — I would say now 25-year-old paper by Hsieh and Klenow (2009 or 2008 paper). It's been almost 15 years, maybe. The idea being: if you observe certain types of distributions in the data, they might be because of two reasons. One is that the fundamentals themselves might be different — women might face different prices or different markets, skill levels might differ. Or it could be these non-economic barriers — culture, norms, other things that are very hard to move from a policy standpoint.

Some of these frameworks I find helpful because they help — to the extent that you believe the framework — very transparently decompose and understand where things are coming from, as opposed to just abstractly thinking "this is how I want to make the world work" and somehow fitting the model. Instead, let the data actually tell you which of these forces are more dominant in what we are seeing in the data.

女性创业者雇佣女性的现象

The thing that also caught our attention — which has been very underemphasized in the literature, and it's not an India-specific story though the paper is about India — is that women-owned firms hire more women. For some reason we didn't find a lot of literature trying to look at that across the spectrum. These are not only small informal firms; these are also large ones — in the formal sector, informal sector. We then use the World Bank data to look across countries, and the pattern is robust across countries, including advanced economies. That we were really struck by.

Now again, you might think: is this — as you said — do women end up hiring other women because of a lack of options? Or is that a preference because of other things that might make the workplace more amenable, whether it's safety, whether it's amenities?

Shruti：And it could also, within entrepreneurship, be the demand versus the supply side, right? Either men have more opportunities so they become more competitive, so the wages are higher, so women are cheaper to hire — that's one possibility. The other is the within-firm transaction cost, which is: men are harder to manage for women entrepreneurs, depending on the social norms. Or men may simply not want to work for a female boss.

So even there, it's nice to study this as the broader general equilibrium pattern, because you can see that the pattern is sticky. Now whether the mechanism is culture, or skills, or wages and competition — that's the question.

模型的局限性与用途

Gaurav：I think that's one of the limitations. I view all of these as tools in a toolbox — some things are great for some things and not for others. One of the things one should be cautious about in these models — at least the ones this paper talks about — is that it's not a policy prescription. It's not going to tell you "should you have policy A versus policy B." I don't think this model or framework is geared towards that.

What it is geared towards is trying to understand how important these things are, as opposed to other things that might crowd in or crowd out participation of women along different dimensions. And it's very rich in terms of a framework — looking at this not only at the state level but also state-sector level. We actually have agriculture, manufacturing, services. We have barriers to entry as entrepreneurs, barriers to formalization of firms. Is it really the fact that you have a lot of informal employment where women work but the real barrier is that they can't formalize their firms and grow their firms? Or is it really, for example, on the demand side — hiring women versus men? We explore a lot of these channels in this paper, which is why I think it's pretty insightful in terms of the patterns.

主要发现：女性雇佣女性的乘数效应

Shruti：What are the broad patterns you can share with us, without discussing every single result — especially when it comes to different states and different kinds of firms?

Gaurav：Two patterns. One is that the "women hiring women" is interesting, particularly from an Indian standpoint. After this paper, I have gotten a lot more interested in looking at labor demand-side policies for female labor force participation as opposed to supply-side policies, because in some sense, norms and culture — as we have seen — are extremely hard to move, and obviously there's little policy can do about it.

Shruti：I'm also not a huge fan of that literature. I mean, there's variation within the literature — we've had some very good people on this podcast talk about it. But the idea that women, especially Indian women in certain states and certain castes, are like this exotic thing, completely bound and trapped by culture and norms — I mean, it's too much of a deviation for me from homo economicus. Everywhere else, markets and prices seem to work. Women are rational too. We just got to figure out what that cost barrier is. So I don't like the supply-side literature sometimes, because I think it makes Indian women a little too exotic in a way that I'm very uncomfortable with.

Gaurav：Totally. And in some sense — of course, much of it is true as well. There's some water to that story, but I think in many ways it's not the entirety of the problem — that "people are just chained to their houses and they can't move." I think it's a combination of the two, but the latter is extremely underemphasized in terms of how the narrative around female labor force participation in India is built, at least to my knowledge.

That's one of the things I think would be nice to emphasize — the labor demand side of things, and the reason female entrepreneurs hire more women. This connects back: in the data, there are very very few female entrepreneurs to begin with. So then the obvious question is: if you have policies that promote female entrepreneurship, apart from just a social equity standpoint, this can actually be efficient for the economy in terms of generating growth and act as a multiplier effect on female labor force participation. By creating one entrepreneur — if that entrepreneur hires five women — then your labor force participation goes up not by one but by six women. There are these labor force participation multipliers, and then that can lead to other things in the economy once you start aggregating things up.

That was one result — very neat and robust across states and across contexts. In fact, the other paper we started working on was for the India Policy Forum, organized every year. They invited us to look at this with more recent data in the Indian context, and again we find very similar things.

创业 vs. 扩张：关键区分

The second thing which was interesting is trying to break — when we think of entrepreneurship, it's important to understand whether this is self-employment, whether it's really owner-operated enterprises, or whether this is really firms in the true entrepreneurial sense.

Well, there's a barrier to just women not working — though there's some recent literature trying to look at this from a measurement standpoint. But even if we were to measure all of these things correctly, it's still too low. Whether it's declining or on the up in the past few years, all of that is a local trend rather than a global optimum.

But what we do is try to look at: there's a clear barrier to labor force participation, but conditional on work, we actually find that women are over-represented in these self-employed owner-operated enterprises relative to men. So it's not the case that entrepreneurship is hard.

Shruti：It's not the case that I just can't start, say, a sewing shop in my house. And that is the classic one — most female entrepreneurs are actually doing sewing work.

Gaurav：Exactly. So there is a barrier of participation, but conditional on participation, it's not really entrepreneurship that is the problem. It is really growing your firms to be larger that seems to be the barrier. Again, these are not policy prescriptions, but it points you towards where we should be thinking from a policy standpoint.

第三个发现：偏好 vs. 约束

The third result, coming back to women hiring more women — I find it fascinating because there are two sides: a preference versus a constraint story. I would love to dig into this more in the future to understand what are these constraints, or are these actually just preferences. There's a homophily literature — men hiring more men, promoting more men. As opposed to constraints: Do men not want women bosses? Do women not want to hire junior men? It can go in many ways.

Shruti：It could be something as simple as: if most of these women entrepreneurs are one or two-person shops in a simple room in the home or joining the home, they may not want a strange man to come to the house. It's just much easier to have a stranger who's a woman come to the house. So the constraints could sometimes be that basic, and we just don't know what they are yet.

Gaurav：Absolutely. This is ripe ground for randomized control trials to figure out at a very micro level some of these barriers — what are the barriers for hiring or growing their firms. That's where the Econometrica paper is situated, and the follow-up IPF paper using more recent data.

二、性别特定的创业障碍

Shruti：One other question on the Econometrica paper — what are the gender-specific barriers to entrepreneurship which are different for men versus women? One, you said, is scale. Women are more likely — India is a country of microenterprises, so that's true across the board, but a microenterprise is under 10 people. I imagine women cluster more around the 0 to 5 or 0 to 4 level. So there's obviously a scale barrier. What are the other kinds? Is it regulatory? Is it the same barriers you have towards workforce participation — you can't leave the house, there isn't good enough public transport, or is it access to credit?

Gaurav：The IPF paper digs into that a little more. We go to another data set called the Global Entrepreneurship Monitor — there they actually ask people questions about aspirations, constraints, how society, media, prestige affect them. The World Bank Enterprise Surveys also — they now have this nice informality module as well. You can look at the owner of the firm, or in many cases whether a majority of the owners in the firm are women or not, and then they have modules on different types of inputs like electricity, water, licensing.

We actually find that many of these come through just accessing services, accessing credit — where women report facing larger barriers. Again, we need to dig into whether these are informational constraints or other constraints — just going to a bureaucratic office and sitting there and getting things done.

That's where there is a nice match to be made between these aggregate patterns and models, with really micro-founded, well-done work — using either RCTs or even descriptive data — to understand what are the functional barriers people face on the ground. It's a combination of many. That's the hesitation in terms of hanging your hat on one — it's going to be a combination of all of these things.

The IPF paper talks about a lot of this. It's not really skills, it's not really confidence, it's not really all of these other things you might be worried about — like are women underconfident? They're not. Are women underskilled? They're not. And of course this could be self-reported, but if anything, self-reported data should bias it even more. So the fact that we don't find this — of course, not causal, but still informative and descriptive — it's access to services, access to credit, access to taxes, dealing with inspectors, labor regulation. There's a lot of that.

贿赂与需求端的隐性障碍

Shruti：The bribe thing is quite interesting. If a traffic cop stops me in Delhi — which is where I'm from — he's more likely to have a conversation with the driver even though I'm the one who's actually going to pay the bribe. They don't want to have this conversation with what they call "ladies log." They will make the demand, but I can't even elbow my way into the conversation.

Gaurav：It's really on both sides. There's a friction. But it could also be — this is where we have so much rich descriptive work on the supply-side constraints but we don't have it on the demand-side constraints.

Shruti：It could be something as simple as: maybe the local bank officer doesn't see the potential in work that is sewing and embroidery. He just doesn't understand the market, and he understands a cycle or a mechanic shop a little bit better. So maybe the constraint might be we need better educated bank officers, or we need more women as loan officers. It could be something that basic, and we just don't have a good sense of it.

各州表现

Shruti：Which are the states that are doing well relative to the ones that are not?

Gaurav：Actually the Northeast is doing excellent in terms of female labor force. The South is doing much better. So it's the usual suspects.

Shruti：And the places that do well on labor force participation also do well on entrepreneurship. And you've just explained to us why — because of the multiplier effect.

Gaurav：100%. And coming back to your early point which I want to double click on — this idea about "men won't talk to you" or "loan officers won't give you loans" — there are randomized control trials that show these biases exist.

Shruti：I feel where the conversation needs to move is not so much towards documenting there is a bias, but what is the source of this bias — which is obviously hard to measure. In a very simple way: is it just taste-based or statistical? If taste-based, certain things we can think about; statistical, certain things we can think about.

与企业合作研究的困难

Gaurav：The problem with working with labor demand — as I have routinely faced — is that just getting firms is hard. No entrepreneur, especially for these big firms, wants to risk. And it's very blatant once you talk to them — they're like "oh, gender is a big issue. If you come out and tell us we're not doing things right, we're going to get into trouble." Really partnering with these firms is extremely hard, especially for RCTs — but I feel even them releasing their own data. Many firms actually have a lot of great data. I've worked with a bunch of job portals — they have rich data on applications, on postings. They just don't want to share it.

Shruti：But that's also because we've pushed this completely on the firms and not enough on the structural broader issues. Because if the answer is public safety, the immediate media and policy lens will be on the firm — "why aren't you providing safe transportation for them?" It's just the way we think about the problem is a little twisted, because we've kind of given up on the state solving a lot of structural barriers.

Gaurav：Exactly. In fact, there are papers that have non-disclosure agreements — they need to not even mention India. So they have things like "a large developing economy," and obviously one knows what you're talking about. That's the extent to which legal teams require you to go to hide identities. And I don't blame them. But that limits our understanding.

That's why I've gotten really excited about the labor demand side of things in the last many years — I think that's the margin we can actually tangibly move, and it will have long-term spillover effects. A great paper was the Goa paper by Rob Jensen back in the day, that shows when call centers opened up, neighboring villages — women started schooling themselves because there were jobs that were accessible, "female-friendly" in these MNCs. Playing around with labor demand, or having policy that is directed towards it, can actually have spillover effects on labor supply. Maybe not in the short run but definitely in the medium run. That does not mean overburdening — there needs to be a needle threaded very carefully when addressing these issues.

三、供给端 vs. 需求端：Andhra Pradesh 契约工的教训

Shruti：The other reason I think labor demand is so critical: we are a little too obsessed with labor supply, not just in the case of women but overall. And this brings me to your paper with Ritum and Vidya. If you obsess so much over labor supply constraints, then you're like "oh, they don't get paid enough, they don't have period leave or maternity leave." Without looking at the labor demand side, you actually implement policy — what you find is that everything becomes upside down.

For those who haven't heard the episode with Ritum, we briefly discussed the paper — a fantastic paper. You look at something so specific — contract workers versus regular workers. Once you start tagging on all these benefits to contract workers, what firms do is not just hire fewer contract workers; they prefer to be informal rather than formal. So actually the supply-side motivated regulation can sometimes be so burdensome that we actually flip it — you tilt every firm and move them back into informality, which is actually worse for both men and women.

Is this one thing I'm learning from your work on why we should pay more attention to labor demand? Are there other things you find like that?

一般均衡分析的价值

Gaurav：Specifically, this paper — apart from the fact that I've written it, so I should like it — this is exactly the test case for why aggregate GE things matter. If you were to purely do a policy evaluation — the policy, just to tell your listeners: Andhra Pradesh back in the day basically said "oh, firms are evading formal, regular workers because once you have regular workers you have to give all these benefits." So how do firms get around this? Hire a bunch of people on contract so they don't have to comply.

Shruti：And this is still all formal employment — this is not informal contract employment, which is a whole other beast.

Gaurav：Absolutely. So Andhra Pradesh one day decides: we're going to ban firms from hiring contract workers — formal sector firms — ban them from hiring contract workers, push them to hire more regular workers. A very well-intentioned policy, because it solves a real problem — workers getting their due benefits within firms.

From a "reduced form" perspective, one would evaluate this and find a lot of success, because that's what we find — formal sector firms do move towards more regular workers and shed their contract workers.

Now, where the aggregation and equilibrium effects come in: once you start building up and saying "let's endogenize a firm's decision to be formal or not," you actually find the margin that the informal sector is just growing. Because obviously no crazy entrepreneur is going to want to formalize and get in the ambit of all these inspectors. What do you do? To some extent, you find the informal sector basically growing.

This marries nicely — here's a well-intentioned policy that wanted to solve a real labor problem, and you just made contract workers more precarious as opposed to less precarious.

技能与培训的困境

Shruti：One thing that comes from that particular paper: it's very sensitive to price and wage. These products are clearly in a highly elastic market. A little bit higher wage is fundamentally difficult for them to pay. So either firms prefer to be informal, or the regulation is so onerous that even in a not-highly-elastic market it's not feasible.

But there's another issue about skill — that firms are not willing to pay a certain price because the skill level is simply not there, and they have to spend a lot of money skilling. Is this a problem across genders? Because there's a lot of work done on female labor force participation and skilling, but to me it seems like men and women in India, when it comes to the labor market, there is both less skill and there is mismatch of skill — complete misallocation in the labor market. What can you tell us about that?

Gaurav：Skilling — there's been some work. Achyuta Adhvaryu, Namrata Kala, Anant Nyshadham have this paper with Good Business Lab that shows firms really underinvest in skilling their own workers, and the returns to skilling are huge. Yet if you go — I've spent a lot of time talking to entrepreneurs across the spectrum — they say "if we skill them, they're going to leave." It's as simple as that. Especially in sectors with a lot of churn, especially in urban areas. People are afraid the returns to skilling are not going to be borne by the firm themselves. And that gets even more precarious once you have contract workers, where you don't have any way of holding workers back for a few months or a considerable amount of time for the firm to actually reap the benefits.

Shruti：Or women, if they go on maternity leave.

技能匹配与保留问题

Gaurav：Coming to the gender aspect: this multiplies in many ways, because there are other constraints that interact with skill acquisition itself, and constraints that impact the way you supply labor.

The basic reason: everybody is appreciative of the fact that more skill matters. We ran a small survey back in the day in Uttar Pradesh. You ask 21-year-olds just entering the labor market — they're coming out of undergraduate colleges, vocational training — they're clearly skilled. Where do you want to find work? They name all these skilled firms. Now flip side, ask these firms what's your biggest problem — the number one thing they'll tell you is skilled workers.

So it's not just a skill acquisition problem — there is a major problem in terms of matching, and more than that, retention. And it's not obvious that lack of retention is a bad thing if people are climbing up the job ladder — but that does not seem to be the case. People who are working delivery kind of jobs are not suddenly quitting to become highly qualified in some other job 6 months down the line. They're doing something else which is parallel in terms of skill requirements and pay.

In some sense, there's also a problem about just documenting panel-level data in India. I haven't seen a good data set with high-frequency collection of data on how people are moving around in jobs for an extended amount of time. People are piecing together, stitching data, making inferences.

Shruti：Because of the level of informality and most of our firms are tiny. It's also the micro-firm nature that is one of the reasons retention is so bad. There isn't that much place to move up. The best people usually want to move up. They don't want to work in a four-person shop or a 10-person shop. If they get skilled, they want to move around. If they get married, they move. The number one reason for migration especially for women is marriage. So there are so many things going on. Micro firms are micro because they don't want to be formal, which means we can't get the data. So we have this problem — your data problem is your regulatory problem is your job problem. It's all intertwined.

Gaurav：But I think you need to start somewhere.

四、职业中断后女性回归劳动力市场 (RCT)

Shruti：One other things you've looked at when it comes to skilling and women — this is like an all-star list of people working on female labor force participation. This is your paper with Ashwini Deshpande, Kanika Mahajan, Nandini, Niharika Singh — and it's forthcoming in the JDE. What I looked at is the design stage, because this is a pre-registered RCT, and you're looking at a small sliver of the labor market — highly educated women in formal employment in IT services. Just a disclaimer: this is not the entire labor market. This is not your general equilibrium paper.

You randomize them into three groups. There's the control group — women coming back from maternity leave 3 years or more, who just get integrated into the workforce. Then two treatment groups — people who get some training and professional support, and people who get professional support plus technical skill training.

I don't know if you have results yet, but I wanted to touch upon this. What are your priors on what you expect to find? If you have any results and are willing to share, that would be great.

研究背景

Gaurav：The reason we got excited about this — in some of my earlier work with vocational trainees (18 to 21-year-olds) entirely in Uttar Pradesh — the number one thing when you ask the girls about jobs, they're clearly extremely excited about going and working. But the number one thing they'll tell us is: "I'm going to get married, and then it's going to be a whole different beast in terms of being able to bargain my way into the workforce later. So maybe I'm going to try this later once I have been married and settled in — then we can think about long-term work strategies."

That got us excited. That was an anecdote. But once you look into the data, actually women who want to come back after a career break — that population is non-trivial in India. It's actually a large population.

That solves many of the constraints of trying to move the needle on 21-year-olds. But what if you're a 25-26 year old? You've been married, you probably have a kid or two, they're starting school soon, and now you're at home with a bunch of free time. That's the set of population we're trying to study.

This is not about informal work at all — largely because of the partner we're working with, who has training programs for highly qualified IT-skilled women. Nevertheless, it solves many of these problems.

两个干预：硬技能与软技能

What are we doing? Basically two things. One is to give them hard skills. One thing you can think about is skill depletion — I'm out of the labor for 5 years, so it's coding, especially now with AI. Second is actually the software side of things — interview skills, CV building, how to answer questions.

Having talked to a few participants, one thing we're finding is that they're searching more intensely. This is still in the field, so we don't have outcomes and employment yet. But they were going to search more efficiently — they know what they want, they know exactly where their skills land, they know exactly what skills they need to work on versus what they can actually remember.

The soft skill is a huge part of this — many of them, going in before the training program, they were like "I haven't been in an interview for many years. What questions will they ask? Who's going to interview me?" Many are concerned that they might have to take a drop-down on their career: "How am I going to go and work with an 18-year-old analyst? I've been a manager in my day, and now I have to go work as an analyst for a few years before I get promoted again."

So my prior is: it's not going to be as slam-dunk of a result as we would hope, but on the margin, trying to understand who this is working for — I think will be the more interesting part.

育儿假 vs. 重返职场支持

Shruti：For me, I love this study for a slightly different reason. India has really good maternity leave — as good as European countries, which seems ridiculous for a country at its GDP per capita, but that aside — the biggest problem for women is not "enough maternity leave" — the biggest barrier might be something like this. So if we do have to focus our energies — whether as a firm giving an incentive or as the government implementing policy — the policy solution may be somewhere else to bring women back into the workforce post-maternity leave. It may not be longer maternity leave. In fact, it may be something completely different and much cheaper.

Gaurav：I agree. There have been papers that have shown that once you think about how firms respond, they reduce hiring of women in these fertility ages. So holistically looking at this is the right answer to figuring out the right way of designing policy support, and I think reintegration is important.

In India, you multiply anything by infinity and it becomes a really large number, just over the scale at which we operate. But the scale also gives us a nice petri dish to observe different kinds of constraints at really minute detail — which I don't think any other country on earth has the luxury of doing.

In this paper, we have women across different cities, not concentrated in one. Across a couple of different occupations. So I'm really excited to see what comes. We are in the endline phase right now — 6 months out after the training program. We're gathering data on employment outcomes. Fingers crossed.

五、结构性转型与全球模式

Shruti：More generally — everything we've been talking about is looking at broad patterns in India, not just one supply-side or demand-side constraint. But the biggest thing about labor force participation, other than the multiplier effect, is what it leads to — which is obviously economic growth.

Women working has been either a symptom, or a consequence, or a cause — it's complicated to disentangle these three — of every single country that has had high growth for lots of years. You have this great broad-based study with Tatjana Kleineberg, looking at female labor force participation from the point of view of structural transformation across a hundred countries.

What is the lesson for us more broadly? India should be studied in its own right, but what can we learn from patterns across the world?

数据与基本模式

Gaurav：Precisely why we started working on this. In this paper, we're looking at a hundred countries over the last five decades — putting together rich data on the type of work you're doing, what occupations you're working in on the job ladder, what sectors, and how does that correlate with economic development.

The first part is documenting patterns. The big pattern: if you go back to Econ 101 development econ, the first pattern you see is that as countries develop, people move out of agriculture into manufacturing and then services. In the last 15 years, we've seen this jump from agriculture to services.

But if you actually look at this from a gender perspective — all of what I just said is a male-dominated story. For women, the actual patterns we find: you get out of agriculture — this is Claudia Goldin's famous U-curve work, so it's nothing new.

职业维度的性别差距

What is exciting and new is once we open up the box of occupations. From an economic development point of view, it's probably helpful to get excess people off the farms and into the firms. But the question is: if all the women are going to become receptionists and all the men are going to become managers, it has very different implications for economic growth than if men and women have equal chances of becoming a manager at a firm.

That's what we dig into in this paper. In low-income countries, there is a gap in the probability that you are a manager versus a worker — but no gender gap in some sense, specifically between manufacturing and services.

Now what happens: as countries develop, the service sector gap basically closes in managerial occupations. Rich countries are able to close this gender gap in managerial occupations. But that's a service sector story.

In manufacturing, the line is basically flat. Whatever you had in low-income countries in terms of male-to-female manager ratios is almost the same as in rich countries. So sector plays a role.

The other interesting thing: if you look at clerical occupations in rich countries, women are three times more likely to be working in these clerical occupations as opposed to men. Whereas in poorer countries, there's a gender gap that favors men in these occupations. With development, how it percolates into gender is extremely uneven.

定量分析结果

Some of this could just be economics — comparative advantage, operating machines versus computers, skill acquisitions. In low-income countries, the first person to get out of school is a woman, because the boy still needs to go to school whereas the girl child can drop out. So this could be skill differences, comparative advantage.

The next part is a quantitative story — similar to the Econometrica paper, we build in this machinery and say: giving it the best frontier models out there right now, can we explain the story completely by just economic gaps? The answer is no.

The quantification is interesting. What we find: gender barriers — these non-economic barriers to either work or earnings — explain about 25 to 30% of the economic growth that we have experienced in these countries over the last 50 years. It's not trivial. 25 to 30% of your growth is explained by the fact that the labor market has become more gender equal. The other 70% is because skill gaps have closed, technology has developed. There's a lot to see about just good old-fashioned development — get people in school, these things work. But there's a non-trivial layer on top which is 25 to 30% that is just about changing some of these underlying constraints women face which are not really economic constraints.

斯堪的纳维亚 vs. 东亚

Shruti：There are two sets of outliers in the global story. In the rich world, the Scandinavian countries. In the developing/middle-income world, the East Asian countries, which have this incredible story where it was partially manufacturing-driven for women. Is there something we can learn from these two clusters?

Gaurav：Now I'm completely going to make claims that are unfounded — Bangladesh and Vietnam being the two posters of really high growth in female labor force participation.

Shruti：Sorry, as a random aside — Bangladesh is the number one reason I hate a lot of the supply-side constraint literature. Anytime someone throws this "norms and women in India are exotic and whatever and cultural" — I'm like "Bangladesh, Bangladesh, Bangladesh."

Gaurav：100%. One of my advisors put it very nicely: if your family is starving, people don't really care whether it's a man or a woman who's working. There is a huge constraint in terms of the jobs.

In fact, Farzana has this amazing paper — they connected a whole bunch of women to job portals. If I remember correctly, women actually don't take up these jobs but their husbands are more likely to get better jobs. So that's telling in terms of how technologies percolate.

Coming back to your question: it's just about good old — the larger scheme seems to be from the government sector again, which is a sector where we have seen a lot of women labor even in India. That's where big firms have entered these sectors and been able to draw women in. So maybe one lesson: if it is manufacturing and you want to view it from a gender equity standpoint, then look at sectors where there is possibility for women to come and contribute effectively.

Scandinavia is a completely different story — probably not the right counterfactual for the Indian perspective. We have these laws — maternity leave in India is amazing on paper, but once you actually look at enforcement, at how firms get around it, these issues become way more binding. So maybe instead of trying to emulate Scandinavia in forming laws, maybe it's time to — as you've argued in many of your pieces — just reduce regulatory burden on many of these things that really allow firms to grow.

复利效应与政治经济学

Shruti：My bias for starting this — even though there are distributional consequences, and yes, this is the kind of awful thing economists say to each other — we say horrible things like "the number of fires in a factory, the optimal number, we'll live with it" — because we understand there's a trade-off between extreme safety regulation and what happens on the ground and whether the firm can absorb the cost. But the reason I have a bias against regulatory barriers, other than that they're stupid and they make people unfree, is: growth compounds. If you can get firms to start growing early, if you can get little green shoots in a particular labor market, that really compounds over 10, 15, 20 years — in a way that if you wait for things to happen and just say "we'll one day reach the level of development that will fit these bad regulations," I don't think you get the same result. We underestimate how much compounding matters in poorer areas.

Gaurav：I completely agree. Just to add — talking to bureaucrats, it's not that people don't know or appreciate this. They know this is the need of the hour. That's where in economics we need more of political economy as mainstream models that can account not only for the efficiency costs. Much of my work will tell you these are the efficiency costs on the economy — you go to a bureaucrat and they're like "yes, we know this. Of course women should be working, of course we should have larger firms."

Shruti：You can tag a number on it and make them realize the severity of the issue.

Gaurav：Where the rubber hits the road: "this is not going to be politically feasible at all."

Shruti：And when we have tried reforms, we haven't tried wholesale reforms. The last time was Rakesh Mohan and group removing license-permit wholesale — you remove the entire command-and-control structure for a wide part of the economy. If you do this piecemeal, you don't know which the binding constraint is. Okay, we can adjust maternity laws a little bit — it still doesn't improve female labor force participation because you don't know if the binding constraint is demand-side or supply-side, or for women of reproductive age, or what. Unless we reform it in a more broad-based manner, I don't think we are going to get the kind of political benefit previous reforms saw. It's also the way we advise our politicians — we make them do tiny narrow things, because we do RCTs on them, and that's just not how the rubber hits the road on the ground.

Gaurav：In fact, the Econometrica paper does this nicely — these frameworks allow you to say: of course we don't observe counterfactuals, but to the extent you believe the estimated model, you can run counterfactuals. If I were to only remove one barrier at a time, would that really generate growth? Basically the paper is very clear: no. The compounding is huge. You really need multiple barriers being alleviated. How much of that policy can push with versus not is a separate conversation. But to the extent one needs to think about these big-bang reforms — in Indian labor force and the labor market — it's a no-brainer. The question is why aren't politicians willing to bet their money on this? Now the current government has put women as a priority agenda, so there is some excitement being generated.

正规化与女性参与率的政策冲突

Shruti：I'm a little alarmed about that — and your research has made me more alarmed. We have two big policy goals. One is formalization of firms. The other is increase in female labor force participation. Your papers show us that sometimes these goals may not be quite compatible — especially the Andhra Pradesh work: when you burden a firm with more goals, more targeted policy objectives, more regulation, they actually flip back into informality. So what alarms me about this dual-goal problem: governments say "we need more formality and that's going to be good for women, so now let's push the female labor force participation agenda to force more formality." Does that make sense?

Gaurav：I think it does. That's where some of these economic frameworks can be helpful — you can exactly model these tensions and at least do a first-order try at understanding how these tensions might interact from a macroeconomic standpoint. I totally agree with you — is formal sector really the goal, especially from a gender perspective? Not really, if flexibility, if informality is what is valued — because that's the society we live in. Obviously everybody understands people are too poor to pay for the goods produced in the formal sector. Some of them can be made available cheaply — data is a good example, clothes are another, where economies of scale might really reduce costs. But to the larger point: absolutely, if you have a ton of laws and come down with a hammer on them and force people to do it, firms are not going to do it. They're going to find ways not to do it. Jugaad in India is great.

Shruti：Jugaad in India is great and bad — because jugaad can only get you up to 10 workers.

Gaurav：Exactly. I meant more like formal sector firms are going to figure out around this.

六、信息摩擦与社交网络：Who Gets the Job

Shruti：Before we get to jugaad and political connections and what firms do in the formal part of the economy, I still want to stick with labor because there's another set of papers of yours — not so much about women and demand/supply or regulatory cholesterol. It is frictions that exist in any job market. We tend to treat the job market as this aggregate thing, but it's actually hugely fractionalized when you start studying the micro data. There is a lot of matching problems and allocation questions — not every software engineer is the same as another. Though that is one particular job where there is a vast amount of similarity, they're still different.

I want to discuss some of these papers — perhaps my most favorite paper of yours. This is titled "Who Gets the Job," with Erin Kelley and Greg Lane, coming out in ReStat shortly.

You're trying to understand information and how social networks are a conduit for information flows — in particular when it comes to job opportunities. You have a field experiment in Bombay University where you look at a particular cohort across different sub-fields and colleges, and you randomly vary whether the job opportunity for that cohort is going to be rival or non-rival. By rival: they have to compete to get that job with the rest of the cohort. Non-rival: if you get the information, you'll get the job. And what happens to information flows within this group?

What you find is not comforting.

实验设计的动机

Gaurav：This came back to my college days — and on the job market as a PhD student — the way people know about jobs, if you look at literally any survey in any developing country, is friends and family. There's a lot of control over who gives their information. Abhijit, Matt Jackson — they have amazing RCTs in the Karnataka area that show gossip matters, nodes matter, and so on. Old work on rumors.

Shruti：Exactly.

Gaurav：And to couple that, there's this entire literature on information flow in agriculture that basically shows: if my neighboring farmer does something with a new technology, I'm more likely to do it. With jobs — with labor market information — the big wedge in this information flow is the fact that information is rival. If I tell you about a great job opportunity and you decide to apply for it, then I'm competing with you for the same job. So that gives me incentives to withhold this information from you.

Shruti：And that has macro effects — this wasn't just a cute experiment. It changes the applicant pool fundamentally at the aggregate level in the labor market.

Gaurav：Absolutely. The reason we landed with college students was twofold. One: where are labor market information frictions probably the highest, where the consequences are going to be quite severe? One pool is college students because they're entering the labor market, it's going to be their first job — we know from a lot of papers that this is an important phase of their careers. B: to be able to work with a group of students where we could observe exactly how information was shared — these are college-going students, in the same classroom, they know each other, networks are very well-defined.

信息的多层次

Shruti：But more broadly, the information — I want to clarify — is not just a job posting. Most people think of information as a job posting or a classified ad or a LinkedIn post, whereas actually the information runs many layers deeper. One: is this within the feasibility set? Is it respectable? Is this the kind of job that's going to be good for me? The third layer: matching — is this actually good for my skills? The fourth: rejection — do I have a shot at it? So there are layers upon layers of information. And I love that you did this in Bombay University because that's exactly the kind of stacked layers of information you can both study and parse out.

Gaurav：Absolutely. This job was not exactly a job from a firm standpoint — we were the firm. The World Bank hired — they needed a bunch of interns, so this was an internship opportunity for these students, which they valued a lot.

The key thing we wanted to vary was to see how much competition was playing a role. Number two: are there forces that can overcome competition? For example: you and I are great friends, so even though we are competing for the same job, the closeness of our friendship might mitigate some competitive concerns.

Shruti：Or you're going to find out eventually anyway if you're such close friends — I might as well tell you before.

Gaurav：Exactly.

Shruti：Sorry for such a cynical view, but reading your paper did not leave me optimistic about the human race.

Gaurav：I'm more optimistic about women — you find that... when we come to the results, we can talk more about the gender angle.

能力与信息网络的相关性

The other wrinkle we wanted to add: if this is going to affect the pool of applicants a firm gets — because the smartest guy in the room never knows about this job — it really depends on the correlation between your ability and ability to gain information. If these are positively correlated — the smarter people are also more connected — then this is not a problem. But if you know a lot of Bollywood and just reality, the nerds are probably not the most connected in their social networks.

Shruti：But there's a second element to it — what you find is something much better: the nerds are deliberately kept out.

Gaurav：Exactly. That was the surprising, and perhaps ex-post unsurprising, thing. What we randomize is basically — after mapping out the social network — every week, who in your class gets information about this internship opportunity. And then we carefully track how that information flows across students within the classroom.

Shruti：That's amazing.

Gaurav：What we find: the nerds don't get to know — or are less likely. The nerds are the higher-ability candidates — not just a pejorative for the studious kids. If someone gets information about a rival job where they have to compete, they are less likely to share it overall. But conditional on sharing, they're more likely to share it with people who are lower on the ability scale than them than those higher. Which basically means the nerds are left out.

Shruti：I was a nerd.

Gaurav：In that sense, I feel there's much to be said. But jokes apart — because we know exactly the social network, we can actually do an analysis at the pair level and look at who on a one-to-one basis gets the information.

非竞争性工作的效果

The surprising thing: making a job non-rival — how do we do this? If I tell Shruti "non-rival" just means if you get this information, you've already got the job.

Shruti：Everyone who has the information has the job — they don't have to compete.

Gaurav：Exactly. That removes your incentive of purely competing for this job. But we do encourage you to still share it, as we do in the rival case. We find this nerd gap disappears completely. So it's nothing to do with networks. It's purely about competition. I know this guy is smart, if I apply and this person applies, he or she's going to get it.

Shruti：Which also brings me back to: if I had to scale up your experiment, demand side really matters. The number of jobs available overall in an economy really, really, really matters.

Gaurav：Absolutely.

性别差异

Shruti：It's the same story over and over again, and you've studied this using different methods, in different sectors. It's an incredible story.

One of the more interesting things you found is this nerd effect. First, men are way more competitive than women. Men share less information. There is a bigger effect when it comes to the nerd effect. Men like to leave men of higher ability out. But these things disappear with women. What's going on?

Gaurav：I don't know. You tell me. You're the woman in our conversation.

Shruti：I have grown up entirely in male networks in economics, so I don't know anymore.

Gaurav：Women share information — we understand this. One thing that might be going on — this may have supply-side factors — if two of my close friends also get the same job, my parents are more likely to allow me to go do it. Or it'll be more fun or we can travel together. You see this in a lot of field experiments. Sharing information and actually applying to the job together, interviewing together, doing the job together is safer, quote unquote, whether in terms of social norms or everything else.

Shruti：Smit Gade has this really nice paper that looks at exactly this issue in terms of traveling together for a job.

Gaurav：Fortunately for us, ours was online, so there was no traveling or interviewing that was the issue. But I agree — men having close male friends is a disaster if you're looking for labor market information because they're competitive.

Shruti：Male friends is a disaster if they're in the same field as yours and competing for the same pool of jobs. That's a well-caveated statement.

Gaurav：But that's exactly right. There's no clear answer. From qualitative conversations, some say "she's a close friend, why would I not tell her" — pure altruism. Others: "there's some reciprocity to it — she has helped me out in the past." Multitude of reasons. Why men don't value it — I have no idea.

Shruti：My hunch is just the Indian job market in terms of really good jobs — but these are internships.

Gaurav：I know, but there is a mindset problem.

Shruti：The mindset comes from what is going on more broadly. We have too few seats — whether at IIT, Bombay University, Infosys hiring, or anywhere else. So everything is a race. You can't blame them in thinking at a very local level that this is a zero-sum game.

Gaurav：Absolutely. And there's more pressure on men.

Shruti：No question.

Gaurav：It's a combination of all these things. But the surprising thing is: when you make jobs non-rival, none of this matters.

Shruti：Right. If there are enough jobs, men would also behave in a sane way.

幽默插曲：女性共著者

Shruti：Is this why all your co-authors are women? Because you've done this study and know exactly what you're doing?

Gaurav：No, it's a happy coincidence.

Shruti：You've worked with a lot of different people from different institutions and countries. Whether working on female labor force participation or not, you have an extraordinary number — above average for sure — of female co-authors. So I'm wondering if this study has —

Gaurav：They want to work with me.

Shruti：No, I'm wondering if the study has something to do with that. You're like "the men are just going to cut me down because of that nerd effect."

Gaurav：True.

Shruti：At least my female co-authors will let me know the opportunity.

Gaurav：I really internalized my own research to a degree that I don't know about it. I'm grateful they want to work with me. Someone else did point to me a few weeks back that "you've got a lot of amazing female co-authors."

Shruti：Did they land on the same reason, or am I —

Gaurav：No, this is the first time I'm hearing about this reason. It's probably not them — it's me who has internalized my own research foundation.

工资翻倍的选择效应

Gaurav：To continue that conversation — the other thing we find fascinating: this is not cute just from a college information standpoint. We actually give them the jobs. You can monitor their entire performance on the job — it really does affect outcomes. The pool shrinks in terms of the quality, the performance of the job.

The last wrinkle: if I'm a firm, what am I going to do to attract talent? I'm going to offer higher wages. So we actually offer double the wages and randomize who gets these.

Shruti：But if you make jobs more attractive, competition goes up.

Gaurav：Exactly.

Shruti：They're even less likely to share.

Gaurav：Exactly. It exacerbates some of these effects. It overcomes information flow constraints — because people are more interested — but exacerbates competitive effects. The traditional way one would say "high quality jobs, offer higher wages, people will come" — yes people will come, but there is selection in terms of who is coming. Nice to study that experimentally.

Shruti：It also matters who your node is within an information network. Your nodes better be really high quality — and more likely women.

Gaurav：Absolutely. From a policy standpoint — for example, online job portals, these new technologies — are they really overcoming some of these information barriers? That's an interesting question to study.

七、就业服务办公室与匹配问题 (Abhijit Banerjee 合作论文)

Shruti：Okay, so I want to stick with the information thing, because this gets me to your next paper — much older paper, with Abhijit Banerjee, also studying labor market frictions. This is very concrete, old-school matching exercise. Here you also have a middleman — you have people looking for a job, firms hiring, and then you have a middleman which is a placement coordinator or hiring manager.

Now there's a question not just of information flow from the appropriate opportunity from the applicant's point of view. It's also for the firm — not just in aggregate terms but for this particular applicant. And now the placement coordinator and what precise information they have about the particular candidate, and if they can actually match them — because matching is really the problem we need to solve, not just hiring random people.

When you ask hiring managers or placement coordinators or HR to figure out preferences of individual candidates, they actually do a terrible job of figuring that out even though that's their primary role. So first: what is the information friction going on? Because on paper, a lot of these jobs — you know a skill from this person in this college is going to be at this level. So this is really about: do they wish to work this job? Do they wish to work these hours? Do they wish to travel? What is it about all this information which is not as explicit as the skill and the degree signal, and how do we overcome it?

偏好的多维性

Gaurav：The placement officers was an interesting exercise, because they play a huge role.

Shruti：I didn't know. I thought they were doing nothing.

Gaurav：One would argue effectively — but to the extent they're incentivized to do a lot. The key was figuring out preferences are multi-dimensional. The thing they get right, unsurprisingly, is that higher-paid jobs are preferred more — right, duh. Where they get it wrong is all the non-monetary dimensions: how much do you prefer characteristic X of a particular job, especially with respect to distance, work hours, how active the job is. Do you really have to go on a delivery scooter halfway across Lucknow, versus a cushy office job where you just type on a computer all day in an air-conditioned office? These amenities — preferences are varied even amongst individuals.

Shruti：And we assume as economists that preferences are given to us. We're not distorting their preferences.

Gaurav：Correct. Students themselves have varied preferences. So what we learned: one part was this information friction, especially on the non-monetary dimension. That begs the obvious question: suppose we know students' preferences — because we measured them carefully — what would happen if you just give preferences to these placement officers? Fortunately, we do find they do pay attention.

Shruti：They won't go looking for the information, but once you give them the information, they act on it.

为什么就业服务办公室不主动收集偏好

Gaurav：They did act on it. People were placed in jobs that — if you take a locus of how far from your most preferred job (multi-dimensional, so we have an index) — they're closer to their preferred index. But they don't actually stick to their jobs. So there were two surprising things.

One: why don't placement officers weight this to begin with? When we talked to placement officers, they accepted the fact that "sure, you might have these preferences, we are never going to be able to find jobs that fit these preferences." The way many placements actually work is bulk placements. There is one employer who wants to hire 40 people, so I don't give two hoots about your preferences.

Shruti：The margins on which you could still make it work is what I got from the paper — a few.

Gaurav：The primary reason placement officers underinvest in this exploration is because in many cases their jobs are just bulk hiring. In Lucknow — this was in UP — Delhi, Kanpur were the main placement areas. They were constrained with the kinds of options they were getting to place their students in, which is why they underinvested.

缺乏保留率的原因

The second part: we actually followed the students over time. Technically, if you were placed in these jobs, you should love it. Very very very few people are actually sticking to these jobs 6 or 9 months later.

Shruti：Which goes back to your earlier point — they don't want to invest in skilling because this churn is real.

Gaurav：Absolutely. And this was after reducing mismatch.

Shruti：You still don't have retention. And the churn comes from mismatch.

Gaurav：Correct. But this was after reducing mismatch. There were two or three reasons that came up.

One: government exam preparation. People told us they were trying for public exams — government jobs.

Shruti：Mangal and all his research — horribly, that distorts the labor market.

Gaurav：Exactly. These were 21-year-olds in UP. In this context, the one thing they wanted to do was appear for government exams — they were not interested in some random delivery job. Which begs the question: why did they want to take the vocational training course to begin with?

性别差异：谁坚持这些工作

Reason number two — this is where gender comes in interestingly — women are actually more likely to stick to these jobs than men. And the reason was very different.

For men, it was the first time they were living out of their household. So the rajabu syndrome — mama-can-handle-anything — was shattered. They would rather come back to their village and just hang out at home than take these employment opportunities in nearby cities.

Shruti：And the cities are cruel, in fairness.

Gaurav：We asked a lot about who they were living with — usually sharing apartments with four or five people. They had to cook their own food. Work hours were grueling. It was very difficult to adjust to this life in a very short time.

Shruti：So the aspiration they have of what kind of job they want, and the kind of job they get in this particular job market — there's a huge gap. So suddenly you feel a little better about applying to the government job lottery.

Gaurav：Exactly. For many men, it was a combination — the job itself wasn't. We asked about the distinction between quality of life versus the work itself. People expected the work to be what it is, reassuringly — they had seen some of this in theory in the vocational training program. Most of the update came from just living in a city and understanding "in a 20,000 rupee job, I'm probably not going to get the quality of life I envision."

Shruti：Which is heartbreaking.

Gaurav：For women on the other hand — we were surprised and cautiously optimistic — it was the first time they were allowed to step out of their household, and they were relishing it.

Shruti：And it probably means they've already overcome the previous barrier — they've figured out their PG situation, or they're living with a family member.

Gaurav：Exactly. Of course, women were more likely to go to Lucknow than Delhi — there were obvious constraints. But to the extent they were able to do it, it was the first time they actually relished their own freedom. In fact, we find women were more likely to send a larger fraction of their salary back home than men. Almost like the price they put on the fact that they could live and work in these cities.

The big drop we still see is just marriage. The minute the family started talking about marriage, they quit their jobs, they were back home.

偏好揭示的可信度

Shruti：One thing I'm now thinking about — when I was reading the paper, I thought it was exactly the way you had set it up: it's the placement officer who doesn't have the information. Now I'm wondering if one big problem is the individual applicants are either not happy to reveal their preference, or they don't even know their preference — because they are not familiar with this kind of job market, especially in a big city given what's happening with structural transformation. How much of that is playing a role? Women are just clearer about what their preferences are — because in some sense their life has been mapped out for them. Families tell them: "you're allowed to study, allowed to work for a few years, then get married by this age, and that's it."

Gaurav：To your first part — how much do we believe these preferences? Within the experiment, we had a sub-experiment where we actually incentivized individuals. The preferences we got were real-world jobs offered to previous cohorts. We presented students with a list of about 8 to 10 jobs and said "go rank them in terms of order of preference." We didn't want to prime them on specific dimensions.

The way we incentivized: "here are 10 jobs offered to previous cohorts. Your preference is going to matter because we're going to ask the placement officer to search in these dimensions depending on what you have." We increased the stakes. We find no difference between incentivized and non-incentivized individuals in terms of the rankings.

Shruti：Do they worry that they won't get the job at all if there is too much of a strong preference?

Gaurav：Potentially, but these were jobs offered to previous cohorts. If everybody just says "job one," then we're all going to compete for job one.

Shruti：This is me speaking as a woman thinking — if we express too much about strong preferences, no one's going to hire us.

Gaurav：Potentially, but this wasn't a preference elicitation where we were going to tell employers. It was: "tell us because we want to match you to jobs you actually want." We find no real difference. It's not that people weren't willing. Talking to these students — they actually want jobs. Coming from a vocational training program, they're excited about experiencing the city and living in these labor markets. So much of it was the update afterwards.

后续研究方向

The two key things Abhijit was excited about were:

  1. Should we have internship programs in the college, where people actually go to these labor markets and firms hire on a temporary basis?
  2. How should the placement process work for these vocational training programs? Retention didn't mean better jobs.

There were some success stories — students who did really well, went into these jobs, loved it, found better opportunities, broke through the Lucknow market. But on average that wasn't the story.

The second part: what should we do about the public sector distorting labor market opportunities? Niharika and Konal are digging into this. Couple this with the social network experiment — if there are few well-sought-after jobs, it really matters who holds that information and how it's conveyed.

求职门户网站的初步实验

Let me add one quick thing — in some follow-up work that is paused right now — I was excited to see whether job portals can break this barrier. We did a small pilot in Jharkhand. What did we try? We showed up, gave them a two-day training on a job portal, helped them create profiles, told them how to filter, what to look for. Then 3 months later we followed up and asked "how did you get a job?"

Placements through online job portals is very very low. They applied to jobs, they searched — but when we asked how they found their job, they said "our placement officer put us there." So networks matter.

Now the reason it's paused: we're trying to unpack what could be driving this. Two channels:

  1. I've increased your outside option as a student. So you're no longer at my mercy as the placement officer. Now I have to work hard to earn my incentive because you can just go find a job.
  2. Purely giving you information doesn't matter — my real monopoly is not on information, it's on the connection to the manager at Domino's who's going to hire you.

I like that story a lot — but seeing what your other research has shown, it's probably the latter.

Gaurav：Exactly. We're trying to dig into that more carefully — whether it's a monopoly on information or connections, as opposed to an outside option going up.

八、3G 手机与结构性转型 (Penny Goldberg 合作)

Shruti：You've done other work on information — literally your paper again with Penny Goldberg, on the digital age and places leapfrogging in terms of technology by getting 2G/3G networks and using these phones to have more information. The information story is not quite as compelling for structural transformation and also matching skills with jobs. So am I reading too much into your paper with Penny on leapfrogging — and how that result is really mixed? You find a few more opportunities through information, but they're not great opportunities and certainly not the kinds you're talking about through a placement officer.

Gaurav：No, absolutely. That's a better summary of the paper than —

Shruti：So why don't you tell me about the paper then?

Gaurav：Sorry, I've read all your work all together much more recently than you have. So this tends to happen.

Shruti：As I've told you before we started this podcast — I think the way you're threading through all of this work, I would have never been able to do that. I'm really grateful you're able to see and connect all of it. You're better at mirroring my own research to me, which I'm now discovering is great for learning a lot of things about the labor market.

You read Marginal Revolution — Tyler and Alex. One of the things I learned from them very early on, maybe 15-20 years ago: don't look at papers but look at literatures. I took this very seriously. I actually like reading papers in clusters — it tells you a lot more about what's going on. What we do as economists is pattern recognition and putting the pieces together. Also, most people are doing partial equilibrium stuff when it comes to these big questions. So it's just easier for me now to read papers as literature. And yours has a very clear through-line to me.

论文内容与发现

Going back to your paper with Penny — this is really relevant for India. You're looking at leapfrogging technology and putting a phone in the hands of people. One: does it matter for structural transformation? What are the differences between men and women?

Gaurav：Does it matter for structural transformation? No, is what we find. But there is a nuance. It matters for jobs.

What is the paper? Putting together data on 3G coverage — smartphones — improvement over a bunch of countries over time. Think about this like: I live in a particular region, and this region now has access to 3G. What do I do with that new technology? The good thing is we have data also on 2G — the not-smartphones.

Shruti：This is not about cell phone versus dumb phones — as someone told me in a talk. So it's not so much about cell phone access as it is about internet on the smartphone.

Gaurav：Right. So it's actually information — and communication. It could be WhatsApp, all these online job platforms. Whereas with the older version of phones, we were just talking to people.

Shruti：Newer, effectively.

Gaurav：Absolutely.

男性与女性的不同路径

What do we find? Basically two things: employment goes up, people are more likely to be employed, more likely to work in wage jobs. Because this is cross-country, we're limited in depth, but the patterns are consistent. And now there's country-specific literature echoing these findings — people are more likely to transition from unpaid employment into paid wage jobs.

Shruti：Just to caveat — unpaid employment is jobs around the house. If you're on a farm, you'd be doing work on the farm which is technically unpaid but is employment.

Gaurav：Absolutely. And that matters for poorer countries and poorer families which are at one end not yet into the structural transformation pipeline — which is why it matters so much.

It matters for women — that's where we find the biggest gender divergence. Why does it not affect structural transformation? Because men are actually moving out of these unpaid household jobs into wage-paid jobs or self-employment. Women, on the other hand — female labor force participation is going up, but they're working on the job ladder that the men have just vacated. They're filling up on farm opportunities. Some do go into wage jobs in the service sector. Everyone is climbing up the job ladder — it's just not gender-neutral in terms of how that progress is made.

On average, everyone's better off. A 10 percentage point increase in 3G coverage raises female labor force participation by about 4.9% — not as much as men, but nothing to sneeze at.

But again, it matters where these women are going. We have follow-up work in Mexico — we've taken one example with great data. One thing I'm fairly sure will survive subsequent analysis: men are moving into better-paying jobs. Because there is entry of women on the extensive margin also into unpaid jobs, average earnings of women are not actually going up. We're trying to unpack those results.

Fascinating in terms of how technology can empower certain things versus the inequalities that persist. With Mexico, we have time use data — people asked "how do you use your smartphones?" We find gender disparity — everybody uses it for entertainment, but information communication channels matter more for women than for men.

需求端约束再度确认

Shruti：This study shows so much that if you don't figure out or crack your labor demand puzzle, relaxing the supply side constraint for women is only going to reduce their wages. This is something I see over and over in what you're doing. If you don't solve labor demand, I'm not saying you're doing women a disservice — I think having a job even if slightly less paid is better than having no job as far as female labor force participation is concerned, especially in the long run for economic growth. But you are going to suppress their wages.

Gaurav：Absolutely. The Econometrica paper makes that point cleanly. If in a counterfactual you only eliminate all labor supply barriers, in the best-case scenario, you go from 24 percentage point female labor force participation all the way up to 70%. But if there are no jobs, because all these demand-side constraints exist —

Shruti：They're going to be treated horribly and paid very little.

工作的心理价值

Gaurav：That's a natural extension. In much of the conversations I've had — people have their own goalpost on what welfare means. There's a really nice paper my co-author Erin Kelley and others have in Bangladesh on the psychological value of work. These are refugees — a different context — but basically showing that just the fact that people have a job really matters to them from a mental perspective.

Shruti：Seeing it in the developed world with all the AI conversation — people are like "we need to work. Just abundance and productivity is not going to hack it."

Gaurav：Absolutely. There's no reason to pick one goalpost over the other, but sticking to one, defining it, and evaluating a policy based on that is much more constructive — because then you can understand the trade-offs.

Coming back to why we need more frameworks and to take them more seriously — usually it's throwing the baby out with the bathwater. People are like "oh, this is a model, why should we care about this? This is not the world." True, but it gives you insights that are very hard to get unless you have really rich long-term data from an RCT perspective.

Shruti：Google Maps is a model, and I learn a lot from it without having to walk every street.

Gaurav：Exactly.

Shruti：So there is something to be said for well-put-together models from actual real empirical work.

结束语

Shruti：This was such a pleasure actually. I feel bad — or maybe good — we've covered only about half your papers. So you have to come back and talk to us about a lot of the political economy work, which I'm even more excited about. This is still George Mason University and we love to talk about rent-seeking and political corruption. So hopefully you will come back.

But this was such a pleasure. Kudos to you for just looking at the labor force participation problem in different countries, different sectors, different income levels, different methods — you're really looking at it from many many different lenses. And I got a lot out of it. Thank you for doing this.

Gaurav：Pleasure has been all mine. Thank you for having me.

观看原视频 →
