## 一、被忽略的"CPI表面数据陷阱"：白线与紫线的暗流交锋
大多数人只看到CPI核心0.2%这个"可接受"的结果，但视频里最刺眼的信号其实藏在那张紫白线图里——**高通胀项目在过去两个月悄悄反弹，低通胀项目却在同步收缩**。这是一个典型的"分布性通胀"信号：均值稳定，但分布在变胖尾。
这里有个跨领域的类比值得警觉——**这跟生态学里的"物种多样性坍缩"高度同构**。当某个生态系统的平均生物量看起来稳定，但优势物种数量在上升、边缘物种在消失时，生态学家会说这个系统正在失去韧性，一次外部冲击就可能引发级联崩溃。通胀数据也一样：当粘性项目（医疗、汽车维修）在集中化上涨，而灵活性项目在被动降温，市场以为的"软着陆"其实是在**用弹性换稳定**。9月降息预期从50%回落到40%，本质上是市场潜意识里嗅到了这种"表面平静，内部僵化"的味道。
## 二、Cerebras叙事里被低估的一个错位：产能才是真正的护城河，而不是芯片
视频里管理层花了大篇幅解释——"台积电给我们锁定了今年和明年的产能"。表面看是供应链新闻，但这条信息的**真正含义比大多数人以为的更颠覆**：
在AI芯片这个赛道

item.title: [All-In Podcast] Rahm Emanuel: Trump's Foreign Policy, China, Europe's Decline, Immigration & DSA vs Democrats
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

三重意外洞察：这不是一次政治访谈，而是一份"大国综合症"诊断书

意外观察一：Rahm 无意中揭示了"超级大国的对称性精神病"

大多数人把中美视为对立的两极，但 Rahm 用一句被埋没的话戳破了这个幻觉——"两个超级大国把世界当作自家国内失灵的倾倒场"。中国倾倒的是经济功能失调（钢铁、汽车、太阳能板的产能过剩），美国倾倒的是政治文化功能失调（选举前 9 天会见 AfD、激化英国种族矛盾、攻击 Maloney）。

这里有个反常识的结论：中美之争的本质不是意识形态对立，而是两个都无法治愈自己内伤的巨人，把痛苦以不同形态外包给世界。这解释了为什么全球中等强国（日本、加拿大、巴西、墨西哥）开始出现相似的"避险语言"——它们不是在选边，而是在同时躲两颗流弹。

意外观察二：教育与国债之间藏着一条"三年级隐形债券"

Freeberg 追问高等教育成本，Rahm 突然把话题拽回三年级识字率。这看似跑题，其实是全场最锋利的一刀——"孩子从大学里辍学，是从三年级开始的"。

跨领域连接来了：如果把美国 40 万亿国债看成一只期权，那么三年级识字率就是这只期权的隐含波动率。50% 的孩子不能在年级水平阅读，意味着未来 20 年美国的 GDP 增长率、税基、创新能力、乃至偿债能力的"标的资产价格"正在被悄悄削减。华尔街定价了通胀预期、定价了 AI 生产力，但没有一个交易员在给三年级识字率定价——而这才是决定 2045 年美国是否能继续借钱的真正基本面。

Rahm 的整套"K-12 到社区学院一体化"方案，本质上是用教育供给侧改革去做"隐形去杠杆"。这比任何减税或加税都更接近财政的长期真相。

意外观察三："普京-习近平-特朗普三角"其实是同一种心理机制

Rahm 用了一个极精准的措辞——"punch down and kiss up"（欺下媚上）。他把它当政治批评说，但其中藏着一个组织行为学的结构性洞察：

特朗普对 Xi 和 Putin 的"追捧"，与他对 Lula、Merz、Maloney、Sheinbaum、Carney 的"打压"，是同一枚硬币。这不是外交策略的正反面，而是同一种不安全感的两种代偿：向上寻求"平等认可"以对抗自卑，向下施加"支配"以获得存在感。

跨领域连接：这与哈佛管理学院多年研究的"中层管理者综合症"结构相同——对老板过度讨好、对下属过度苛刻的经理，其实并非道德缺陷，而是身份焦虑的行为外化。把这个模型套到国家层面，你会得到一个惊人的推论：美国当前的外交政策不是"美国优先"，而是"美国不安"。它的攻击性和它的退缩性，来自同一个心理原点。

而这个结论最反直觉的地方在于——它意味着任何"对抗性"或"绥靖性"的外交回应都不会真正奏效，因为对方处理的不是利益博弈，而是自我叙事。这也是为什么 Rahm 反复强调"经济集团"——他其实是在说：当一个人陷入身份焦虑时，你不能跟他单打独斗，你要用一个稳定的"参考群体"让他重新校准现实。

一个被所有人忽略的隐藏结构：仔细听 Rahm 全程回避的东西——他谈中国、谈欧洲、谈伊朗、谈以色列、谈教育、谈债务，却几乎不谈 AI（只被 Freeberg 逼问了一次，一带而过）。这对一个 2028 潜在候选人来说是致命的盲点，也是全场最耐人寻味的沉默。当一个前政府核心人物在谈"未来 20 年"时把 AI 当背景板而非主角，他其实暴露了民主党建制派的最深层认知延迟——他们还活在"制度可以慢慢修复"的时间尺度里，而 AI 的时间尺度是季度而非十年。这个盲点，可能比 Rahm 讨论的任何议题都更能预测 2028 的走向。

📝 转录文本

开场与介绍

主持人： All right, everybody. We are super pleased to have Rahm Emanuel join us for the all-in interview today. He was the senior adviser of Bill Clinton, last president to preside over zero national debt, and he was Obama's chief of staff, mayor of Shytown, ambassador to my favorite country to visit — Japan — under President Biden.

He hasn't made an official announcement about his presidential run in 2028, nor do I think he's going to make an announcement here, but he's been talking a lot about where the country needs to go in a post-Trump world, specifically in 2028.

Freeberg and I are going to ask Rahm about the most important topics facing America today: the economy, inflation, employment, surging national debt, never-ending wars, the rise of socialism and sadly anti-semitism, immigration (skilled and legal), and how his positions have evolved over four decades of service to America.

Welcome to the All-In Interview. Rahm Emanuel, welcome Rahm.

Rahm: I'm — Yeah.

主持人： Okay, there you go.

Rahm: I didn't know that was the cue. I was like waiting — that felt like an obituary. I was waiting for the rabbi to get up. That introduction is the only one that ever starts with Clinton. Usually they start with my career in Congress, and so I give you a lot of kudos for remembering that I started as senior adviser to President Clinton.

从 Clinton 与 Obama 身上学到什么

主持人： Well, let's start with that. What did you learn under Clinton and Obama? These are — what I would say — the last two sane presidents we seem to have had, who were moderates. In my mind, I'm a moderate, slightly left-leaning, but these seem to have been two great presidential runs that you were involved in. What did you learn from each of those individuals?

Rahm: They have different skill sets. But they had an outlook of the world. They had an outlook of the United States in the world. They had an outlook of a kind of a progressive affirmative view of government.

Most importantly — which I remind everybody — you can't have progressive policies if people think the government can't run and organize a one-car parade. Not possible. They have to have an affirmative view. And the last time you've had a net positive was under Bill Clinton. And actually it wasn't just the balanced budget — it shifts when he signs welfare reform. You can go back and look at the data.

But to their skill set: Bill Clinton was a unique person who, in my view, was able to integrate in three-dimensional chess both policy, politics and press, and understood the presidency in a way that Teddy Roosevelt had redefined it. He was redefining it for the 21st century, and he really meant what he said about being a bridge. Nobody was better — not just at giving a speech, but at taking a policy, being able to communicate, to carry people from where they were to change, and may not make change threatening, and then achieve the objectives you wanted.

That said, President Obama, in my own view, coming at the end — or towards the end — of the Iraq war and the financial meltdown, understood we were at a pivotal, transitional moment for America. Every president gets judged: what's the world you inherited, what is the world you leave behind? Sometimes the harshest critics of both Obama and Clinton come from the left, not the right. And I said, "Is it the peace or the prosperity you don't like most?"

Post-Reagan, Clinton's economy grew the most, jobs grew the most, and income disparity shrunk the most. People were calling it the uni-power — no country, both economically, politically, militarily, had the power the United States had.

The left criticizes Obama for being kind of tepid — but he inherits a country near depression, known as the Great Recession, saves it from that, transitions from losing 800,000 jobs to creating 200,000 jobs, gets America out of two wars, continues the war on terror, and repositions America in the world as a force for good.

There's no to-do kit in the drawer of the resolute desk — but the merging of policy, politics, and communications is what I learned.

美国是否输出了"民主"，还是输出了功能失调？

Freeberg： Did Obama export American democracy as a point of primary policy? And did that lead to this world where there's a pullback, because a lot of what gets exported ends up being one side of the political spectrum, not the other?

Rahm: I made this point recently at the Aspen Security Conference. I'm now writing my next op-ed for the Journal as a curtain-raiser to the summit by Xi and Trump — I'm labeling it "the summit of disruption."

Xi's largest export is not autos or electronics. It's the domestic economic dysfunction of China. They're crushing everybody — other countries' manufacturing base, industrial base, across the world. They have more WTO cases than any other country, and all other cases combined are against China. Chile's steel plant, Indonesia's garment plant, Brazil's four blast furnaces.

We — through Trump — are exporting our domestic political and cultural dysfunction. The two superpowers are holding the world hostage: one through economic dysfunction, one through political-cultural dysfunction. Xi refuses to deal with the real estate bubble popping, a consumer flat on their back, and an industrial base that makes no rational sense. Their auto industry is now exporting more cars, and their profits are down 20%.

Trump — nine days before the German election, meeting with the neo-Nazi party AfD. Race tensions in Great Britain — we seem to want to exacerbate them. We are literally exporting political and cultural dysfunction onto the world.

I happen to think this president stylistically likes to punch down and kiss up to Putin and Xi. But that's a stylistic point. The two superpowers haven't managed their internal problems, and now they're exporting them onto the rest of the world as a dumping ground.

Coming back from Japan, I think that rather than tariffs we should have an economic bloc, so all of us together can withstand China — organize that economic bloc, and then meet China in the marketplace. That's how you win friends and influence enemies.

美国的"文化吸引力"作为国家安全资产

Freeberg： Is that a different view than the Obama-era notion that we should be exporting American culture, American democracy — which then opened the floodgates to exporting our culture wars? Transgender theater in Africa, all that stuff?

Rahm: No, I don't think that's what opened the door. Every country has four tools in their national security toolbox: military power, political persuasion, economic statecraft, and cultural attraction.

American culture large — not just Hollywood — the American brand is a cultural attraction, or was. I actually think this president has hurt the American brand. Our economic statecraft, our market, our technology, our universities and research, our national labs — that is a piece of our economic statecraft, a piece of our national security.

There was a great story the other day by David Graham — only the United States could get Russia and Ukraine around the table. There is no other world power whose political persuasion could do that. It's an asset in our national security toolbox.

The reason I laid out in my speech in Israel the "23-state solution" — China, Russia or Europe cannot do that. Only we can do that.

We have massive political-military power. I happen to think it's not prepared for the future — that's on both parties. We got so enamored with the war on terror we lost sight of the transformation happening on the battlefield. Neither Iran nor Ukraine has a navy, and both control waterways near their fronts. You're not fighting two wars — you're fighting two different types of wars, and we've got to get ready for that.

I don't think Obama representing our cultural attractions around the globe was the problem. America being popular around the globe is a political asset that you then use. Now that America's brand under Trump is in the toilet, that actually hurts America's political power, economic statecraft, and military capabilities.

中国的战略：让世界依赖你，你独立于世界

Freeberg： China's been historically about manufacturing base and energy production capacity — on their way to 8 terawatts of electricity, we're around one. They've got 20 times the manufacturing square footage of the US, much automated. With AI and open-sourcing AI, they're now eliminating our advantage in knowledge, services, and IP. Do we have a response?

Rahm: Xi comes to power and we buy into this "win-win" stuff. It was never win-win. China wants everybody dependent on China, and them independent of you. That is their theory of the case. "Your markets are going to be so big, you can't do anything about it. You're going to be dependent on our markets. We're going to leverage that to destroy, manipulate, and control your sovereignty."

If you give us barley, we'll have five other people give us barley. Look at soybeans — if the US cuts us off, we have Brazil and Argentina. They have duplicity in the system. Maximum latitude for them, minimum for us.

I take a lesson out of COVID. Xi notices that within 12–14 months the United States develops a vaccine with 90%+ efficacy. China takes 18–19 months, efficacy in the 60s. A lot of Chinese leaders quietly took Pfizer/Moderna. They couldn't export their vaccine. Nobody in the Third World wanted it. That was a huge opportunity for America — we squandered it politically, economically, culturally.

Xi then makes a decision: massively invest in life sciences. Within five years, China is at parity pursuit with the United States in life sciences — a place we dominated.

Every Trump budget proposes a 40% cut in NIH. Every budget. Republicans push back and allow 15%. You're not going to cut NIH your way to American leadership. There's a pancreatic drug on the market that came from NIH funding — now looking like it will address three or four other cancers. NIH, National Science Foundation, DARPA, our national labs and national universities are our crown jewel. And what are we doing? We have an administration involved in unilateral disarmament.

Software and manufacturing — we're dominant in software. We shouldn't think it's either/or. We allowed one to atrophy. We allowed a commercialization of our national security. The Business Roundtable, the Chamber of Commerce way over-influenced our national security vis-à-vis China as industry by industry, supply chain by supply chain moved offshore.

What we need to do for the next 20 years: 1. Aggregate allies — Australia, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, EU, friends in Latin America. Don't declare war on Brazil. Isolate the isolator. 2. Use the time of that bloc to organize our research and capacity, and build up what we've allowed to atrophy. 3. Trust American innovation — new technology entrepreneurs, venture capital, DARPA research, and deployment capacity. Give us 5 years — as long as we don't let Raytheon and General Dynamics kill it, and let the Pentagon nurture it.

Right now, the president has isolated America at America's vulnerability.

中东：三大趋势与"23 州方案"

主持人： Where do the Middle East nations fit in? Are they part of the bloc?

Rahm: Three trends going on in the Middle East:

First, the UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait are staying with the United States. Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Jordan on the first list. Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Pakistan, Turkey and Qatar look like they're hedging. They know they're reliant on America but they're not going to be so dependent — because of the lack of leadership in the two wars, Iran and Iraq.

That's one reason I mentioned the India–Middle East–Europe economic corridor — it keeps everybody coming closer to the United States economically and politically on the 23 states.

Second, Iran invested 40 years and $40+ billion in what Israel described as "the octopus" — the proxies. Hamas is degraded to defeat. Hezbollah is cornered. Damascus and Syria has been lost. The Iraqi president seems to be making pretty good headway on dealing with the militias.

You have the Lebanese government working with Israel on cornering Hezbollah. Syria, a non-Assad president, is talking to Israel about a security agreement. That would mean Jordan peace, Egypt peace, Syria security agreement — the three forces of the Six-Day War all came to some resolution with Israel. Massively different strategically.

Syria will be the outlet of a pipeline from Basra to their port for energy around the Strait of Hormuz. These are big opportunities.

Yes — major players in the Gulf would be part of that economic bloc.

台湾：不是 2027 年才要面对的问题

主持人： Let's talk about Taiwan. The Trump administration says China plans on invading in 2027 or 2029. You worked under multiple administrations where strategic ambiguity was the process.

Rahm: Let me say this — we keep the politics ambiguous, but as it relates to using kinetic force to change the status quo, we're not ambiguous. That's a political statement — and "nobody changes the status quo through the use of force." Those are two things. Just to prove somebody knows something about the Taiwan Act as well as policy.

The consequence of the Iran war: China's watching the US bog down in the Strait of Hormuz, resources allocated. Their confrontation with the Philippines has picked up dramatically. Military intimidation of Japan — much more aggressive around the Senkaku Islands. They fired a live missile from a submarine near Australia. Vietnam. The Philippines being the most dramatic in the South China Sea.

China is sending a message to all our allies — Korea, Japan, India, Australia, New Zealand, Singapore, Philippines, Vietnam: your protector is no more.

When the White House becomes a one-ball juggler — this White House is consumed with what's going on and has lost focus on the Indo-Pacific. China has picked up their aggression.

Our long pole in the Indo-Pacific is Japan. They are under economic, political, military pressure. Yes, we've come to the benefit of the yen, but we haven't done anything in and around the Senkaku Islands. We haven't done anything on the economic coercion China's involved in.

So you say 2027 — I'm looking at today and saying you don't get to wait. It's happening now.

The Philippines is not Taiwan. It's a country. It's a treaty ally. It won a 2016 court case. If we don't stand up there — before you get to Taiwan — [we're in trouble].

主持人： So you think we should be projecting force there, putting troops there with our allies?

Rahm: We already have troops there. We already have resources. We need to double them up and give the Philippines confidence, especially given that President Marcos is taking massive risks.

On Taiwan, there are three strategies China could use: 1. Economic quarantine that suffocates Taiwan. 2. Invasion that tries to end this in 96 hours. 3. Take over the three small islands off mainland China's coast associated with Taiwan — a rock, a butterfly, a tree, and a fisherman — and look at the world and say, "You're going to start a war over this?" An incremental strategy.

China has done all three historically with different countries. We have to be prepared for all three.

  • They want 96 hours, not a Ukraine example. We have to say: no, it's going to be 96 days.
  • On quarantine — we need to show through resources (Philippines, Okinawa) that a quarantine can't work — air, naval.
  • On the small islands — we need to project.

There's a security piece and a deterrence piece — and our deterrence piece is very weakened right now.

日本：印太战略的"长杆"

主持人： I want your opinion on Japan remilitarizing and their role, as well as South Korea.

Rahm: Japan is the long pole of America's Indo-Pacific policy. Look at the Quad — India, Australia, Japan, the United States. The trilaterals I worked on: Korea–Japan–US, and US–Japan–Philippines. The one constant is Japan.

Our Okinawa footprint is our largest military footprint in the world in a single country. It's the only place in the world with an aircraft carrier permanently based.

Last five years in a row, number one foreign direct investor in the US: Japan. Last five years in a row, number one foreign direct investor in Japan: the US. Cultural attraction — look at what Japan's done on baseball.

The prime minister had the audacity to say publicly — which we've tried for 30 years to get a Japanese PM to say — that a move on Taiwan would be a national security threat. She says it. China goes crazy because she said publicly what they never wanted announced. Now they're under economic coercion, political coercion, and military intimidation.

I'm happy the administration decided to support the yen — there's a lot of self-interest in that, given our treasuries and dollars and the pressure from our debt. But we have to do more from a military training standpoint. When Russia and China are doing exercises around the Senkaku Islands, we're just not present.

欧洲：不可逆的衰退，还是被误诊？

Freeberg： Before domestic issues — there's an argument that Europe is in a state of irreversible decay. Many point to the AfD in Germany as a response to open-border immigration policy that has drained resources and diluted culture.

Rahm: David, let me say one thing. The German intelligence agency has the AfD under watch. Forget whether I characterize it as neo-Nazi.

Freeberg： Well, US intelligence had Donald Trump under watch too. But I'm not trying to be supportive of the party — I'm trying to indicate there's a reaction to something going on in Europe.

Rahm: There's no doubt on both the cultural side and economic side there's a reaction in Europe, like there is here in the US.

Look at what has happened to incomes. Here in this country, we have a greater share of Americans living paycheck to paycheck — almost two-thirds, 63%. That has changed our politics and our cultural landscape.

Do I think immigration plays a role? 100%, it does play a role. I also think stagnating incomes — when there's greater concentration not just of wealth but where the political system is skewed towards that wealth — all of that gets mixed into the stew. There isn't a separate soup dish for immigration.

Former Italian PM Draghi wrote a good plan for the EU. It is in our interest for strong, robust European economies to be technologically and otherwise contributors to the Western system. In a bloc, you don't want hangers-on — you want people rowing. Europe is important for America's security and economic prosperity.

I do think they have participated in their own suffocation.

Freeberg： This idea that Europe is committing suicide has taken form. Do you disagree?

Rahm: I think Europe has made policy decisions that are not in the best interest of the citizens of Europe.

Freeberg： The policies are arguably leftist policies. The energy policy that gutted Germany's nuclear power and made them dependent on Russian energy was insane. Providing public services and public welfare programs while opening borders to increase population for nonproductive people —

主持人： Wait, Freeberg — for the last 40 years, open borders has been a Republican policy to let as many people in as possible for labor.

Rahm: Is the party affiliation of Angela Merkel a mystery to you, David? You made this broad-brush attack about the left. Angela Merkel came out of the Christian Democrats — the conservatives. It was her decision to cut — wait, no, you're making a point that is historically wrong. I apologize — this will be the last time I'm on your show.

Freeberg： You're welcome to tell me I'm wrong.

Rahm: Put on your seat belt. She's from the CDU. When the Syrian million people come out of Syria, she says "we can handle this" — that's from the Christian Democratic Union, the conservatives, Kohl's party. After the nuclear facility in Japan has its meltdown, she shuts down the nuclear facilities and makes Germany more dependent on Russian energy — and we were the ones that warned against it. So don't tell me this is from the left. You're wrong.

Freeberg： There was a lot of anti-nuclear rhetoric —

Rahm: Who's the chancellor that said shut it down? Merkel. What party is she from? The Christian Democratic Union.

Freeberg： Nowadays I would say far right, but —

Rahm: This is crap.

Now that I've decided to score my Emanuel points on you — on immigration, yes, she opened the borders when there should have been a more thoughtful [policy]. People don't like disorder — not on the border and not on the streets of Minneapolis. Europe responded to disorder, whether in Stockholm or Berlin. Europe is a welcoming continent, but it looked totally out of control, as you saw this weekend vis-à-vis Morocco.

But to say this is leftist is just not accurate. Brussels on the economic front — while trying to regulate — suffocated innovation, entrepreneurship and competitiveness, and they're trying to correct that.

Where I find fault with the Trump administration is we are exacerbating their tensions when they're trying to deal with it. Germany today is losing 5–10,000 manufacturing jobs a month to Chinese pressure. That should be an opportunity for us to come in and say let's work together and confront China — not independently but together. We're not doing that.

Our vice president, nine days before an election, is meeting with the AfD. When there are race problems in Great Britain, we're exacerbating them. When Meloni is dealing with some stuff domestically, we attack her.

主持人： Why does Trump do that? What's the strategy?

Rahm: I've said this before and I'll repeat it: this president punches down and kisses up. He has this fixation about Putin and Xi admiring him as an equal, and they think he's a joke. They think he is not their equal. America is their superior — but he is not their equal.

He then takes a Lula in Brazil, Merz in Germany, Meloni, Carney, or Sheinbaum, and he punches down because he thinks if you're a middle power, "I'm going to show how big and bad I am." He is nothing but a bully, and nobody's buying it anymore. Everybody is looking at the emperor wearing no clothes.

There's no strategy to this. This is all his insecurities. He's just winging it.

移民：Rahm 的"Dignity Act"方案

主持人： Let's do immigration. We had President Trump on this podcast — he promised we'd put a green card on every diploma, then reneged. We're kicking out best-and-brightest we brought here. Almost all our great entrepreneurs are immigrants or sons of immigrants. What's Rahm Emanuel's plan?

Rahm: Bizarrely I'm like the last optimist that you could actually get a deal legislatively. I start with two principles: we're a nation of laws and a nation of immigrants. Whatever we do on legal and illegal has to be true to both.

Nobody likes people breaking the laws and getting a pass — I'm included. I'm the guy for President Clinton who designed Operation Gatekeeper in San Diego, Operation Safeguard in Nogales, Arizona, and the stuff in El Paso. Tough borders, tough enforcement, resources at the workplace.

There's a thing called the Dignity Act — 23 Republicans, 23 Democrats in the House. It's true to being a nation of laws and a nation of immigrants. Is it the bill Jason would write? No. Is it the bill Rahm Emanuel would write? No. Does it achieve the goal? Yes.

Everybody else is hiding, using rhetoric. I endorsed it. If you were doing politics, you'd stay away from this and use just pablum. But we've got to get this problem behind us so we have a future in front of us.

You need leadership out of the White House — not just coming on this show and speaking pablum, and never really following through, like Trump did on Dreamers, like he did on green card on every diploma.

Legal immigration — getting the best and brightest. Going back to China: all these people leading China's life sciences came out of the United States, trained in our life sciences. We kicked them out like fools.

Pass the Dignity Act. Don't mess with it. It's a true compromise. It would stop the civil war.

主持人： What about a point-based system? Japan requires you to speak the language fluently. What are your views on assimilation, language, and point-based systems?

Rahm: Japan isn't a perfect analogy — it's an island, 98% homogeneous, 3.7 million immigrants, and they think they have an immigration problem. Different scale.

The two countries we have a lot to learn from: Canada (point system with a Canadian signature) and Denmark. Because of our dysfunction, Canada is now attracting what used to be talent that would come to America.

Let me give you an example — this is about affordability of higher ed, but relates. I would let universities set a goal — go up to 20% foreign students. Some are at 6%, some more. Divide it between grad and undergrad as you wish. Foreign students pay full boat. It would subsidize our ability to get American students through a three-year BA rather than four — saving mom and dad a year of tuition. Foreign students pay full price, they want the American brand, and since they came here to study, they'd more likely stay and build this country economically.

A lot of immigrants and children of immigrants came because of the university system. That is a political power and capacity the United States has underinvested in.

If you control the border, you send a signal that people who break the law don't get rewarded. I'm angry at my party — not only losing control of the border, but in the 2020 debate, raising your hand and saying "I'm going to give healthcare to people that cross illegally." Forget the immigration policy — the value system. You have American families suffocating under healthcare costs, not everybody universally covered, and you're talking about free healthcare to people who crossed the border illegally. That was foolish by the party.

政府花更多，东西越贵？教育与住房辩论

Freeberg： Over the last 30 years, where the government spends more to make things accessible, costs go up disproportionately. Average inflation has been 2.5%, but housing 5% a year, education 6%+, healthcare 5.5%. All three are areas where the federal government has launched programs to subsidize. In areas where government hasn't — technology, energy, food, consumer services — costs decrease. Is it the role of government to provide these services, or get out of the way?

Rahm: You're wrong. First, the GI Bill was a government initiative — massive increase in housing and home ownership after World War II. Would you have recommended no GI Bill?

Second, you said food costs went down without government — what do you consider the agriculture bill that subsidized big Agra? You say we're not involved in energy — well, we have a tax write-off for drilling.

Freeberg： You could make that case about everything. Our total dollar spend is what I'm talking about.

Rahm: Right now the balance between the private and public sector — when the concentration of both power and wealth gets too much, you [need government intervention]. That was Teddy Roosevelt's redefinition of what government does — to come to the aid of those most vulnerable to concentrations of power.

On housing — that's where government has messed up, but on the local level, not national. In San Francisco, New York — restrictive zoning, building, permitting laws drive up costs.

If I was mayor of Chicago today, I would put all our zoning, building, and permitting laws up against Dallas, Houston, Phoenix. You tell me what we have and why they don't. If you can't justify it, get it the hell out.

The biggest problem in housing is first-time home ownership — a post-2008 problem. The market has gone to the high end and low end; first-time home ownership is stuck. That's a place where both public and private sectors need to address a problem that the private sector alone hasn't fixed in 20 years.

教育：Rahm 的完整方案

Rahm: I spent eight years fixing an education system that was broken. When I was done, Stanford called it the single best of the top 100. We drove graduation rates from 56% to 83%. We drove reading and math scores — at every elementary level, we were six months ahead of our peers.

I'm going to Louisiana at the end of September — the only state whose reading and math scores have gone up to pre-COVID levels — to find out what they're doing.

Elementary level: 1. Created full-day kindergarten and free full-day pre-K. I'm a huge believer in early childhood. 2. Universal accountability — teachers, parents, principals, schools. 3. Reboot teacher education and training — constant, not one-and-done. Redo the entire teacher training program starting at our colleges. 4. Braid resources together so states and cities can meld them — poor students need more resources, but with accountability. 5. Stay at it every day. This is a 20-year project, not a two-year project.

High school — fundamental reform: - We drove 50% of our kids to graduate with college credit on high school day. Goal: 100% through dual credit and dual enrollment with local community colleges. - We're the only school district in America — I'd make it a national requirement: nobody graduates without a letter of acceptance from a college, community college, branch of the armed forces, or vocational school. Every child has a plan. Universal post-high-school education. We accomplished 98% compliance.

Community colleges: - Take $8 billion you're wasting on detention centers at ICE and modernize our community college system — campuses, curriculum, relevancy to industries.

Higher education: 1. 20% foreign students allowed at colleges — they pay full boat. 2. Identify 10% of federal compliance stuff and let colleges keep 100% of those dollars. 3. If a child graduates high school with 20 college credits, three-year BA — Oxford and Cambridge do three-year BAs. 4. If your family income is below $200K — college for free. 5. If income is above $200K — annual tuition doesn't go above inflation.

Get kids minimum four years — ideally three — in universal pre-K. Return to fundamentals. Bring back accountability. Revamp our high school years into college-and-career-driven, not just diploma-driven. And no student is left out.

Freeberg： You haven't addressed that as we pour more into community colleges and federal student loans, administrative staff has bloated from 10% to 60% in 30 years, because the loan program is unrestricted.

Rahm: You haven't addressed the fact that 50% of our kids can't read at grade level. The way you asked that question told me where your priorities are. Kids drop out of college in third grade. That's when they start dropping out. When 50% of your kids aren't reading at grade level, college cost is not your problem. We're going to compete against China with 50% of our kids not reading? That's not how you beat a country three times your size.

Freeberg： I'm not talking about dropping out of college. I'm talking about administrative bloat and how at $30K–$80K a year, higher ed is inaccessible.

Rahm: Two things — you're talking about costs, that is a problem. To me, the problem is we've given up on 50% of our kids. In my view, I have spent more time on education [than most]. I took a system William Bennett called the single worst in America to the single best of the top 100.

Take the high school years — B average, community college is free. 50% (goal: 100%) graduate with college credit. Nobody gets a diploma without telling us what they're doing next.

We're 500,000–600,000 electricians short just for data centers. Broadband: 150,000. You can't build submarines because we don't have pipe fitters and plumbers. You want to be a pipe fitter? Great. Physician? Great. Physical therapist? Great. Have an education system that reflects the economy and skills we need.

债务、增长、税制与最低工资

Freeberg： Zooming out — $7 trillion a year spending, $5 trillion in revenue. $40 trillion in debt. At 5% over 30 years, that's $2 trillion a year in interest. How do we reconcile the fiscal condition?

主持人： And Rahm, this was something Trump promised with Doge and it was all snake oil.

Rahm: I don't accept redistribution and I don't accept corruption. You can't have capitalism or economic freedom with corruption — it's against the rule of law. Redistribution doesn't solve anything as it relates to growth.

Five things essential to grow the economy and incomes so people aren't living paycheck to paycheck: 1. Everything we just talked about on education and training — pre-K to BA. 2. The Dignity Act on immigration. 3. Modernize our energy system — vis-à-vis Texas, best example in the US. 4. A 10% levy on all predictive markets and online sport gaming — has to go to NIH, National Science Foundation, and DARPA. Double our dollars into research. 5. A tax code that does not reward wealth preservation, but wealth creation. This tax code is an abomination as it relates to economic freedom.

Control overall spending for the next 5 years so it can't grow — and start making tough choices within the system. I would not spend $38 billion on detention centers nobody wants. I'd take $8 billion of it and modernize the 1,200 community colleges — the economic backbone of La Crosse, Wisconsin, Spartanburg, South Carolina.

I don't believe in sending ICE agents out with $50,000 bonuses when I'd rather give a bonus to signing up to be a carpenter or electrician. That's more important to America's future than some masked man running around the streets of Minneapolis.

主持人： How do you get Congress along?

Rahm: As the person that coined the term "never allow a good crisis to go to waste" — it's the opportunity to do big things.

The surplus created sloppiness that Bill Clinton left. We tried to fight two wars with two tax cuts. Really stupid. Never been done in American history. We went from a surplus Alan Greenspan described as a danger to America — to running $38 trillion of deficit — because it was reckless.

Now that crisis has come due, and it's going to force some really tough things. We cannot — while AI is hovering, causing further concentration of wealth to a very few — get to fiscal sensibility just talking about cutting. We're going to have to deal with the revenue side as well as the spend side.

We have a tax code that everybody on this show, me included, is rewarded for preserving wealth and passing it on. There was a story in the Wall Street Journal — retreats are being organized to help kids figure out how to handle their inheritance. You have got to be kidding me. And we have a tax code that favors that. You're an idiot if you don't take advantage of preserving your wealth and passing it on.

The step-up basis is a way to avoid all taxes when everybody else is working for a living and can't make monthly bill payments. So it's going to hit everybody, and you're going to make some changes.

主持人： As most capitalists, I wasn't concerned with minimum wage — the free market would work it out. Studies now show 12–20 dollars an hour causes no economic hardship. What's your take on the federal minimum wage?

Rahm: I worked with Bill Clinton when we raised it. When I helped make Nancy Pelosi speaker, that was the last time it was raised — $7.25. As mayor, I raised it. I'd raise it and have it go up each year, as we did in Chicago, coupled with a very generous Earned Income Tax Credit. That's what makes work pay.

If I was waving a magic wand, I'd take the Earned Income Tax Credit, the per-child tax deduction, and do a single family credit — all in one thing.

DSA vs 民主党：我 11 月见

主持人： Let's talk about DSA before we wrap. Last weekend in Chicago, the DSA held their convention.

Rahm: You're not Democrats. You're a separate party. I'll see you in November. You're literally beating Democrats.

I spent my whole life — Bill Clinton replacing George Bush, Barack Obama competing against John McCain, flipping 31 districts from red to blue so Nancy Pelosi would be speaker. I am not into turning a blue district midnight blue. It doesn't do anything for minimum wage. It doesn't do anything for universal pre-K. It doesn't do anything to give 10 million children healthcare who didn't have it. I'm not impressed.

You are a separate party. You're the Democratic Socialists of America. I'll see you in November on the ballot. You had a party convention. You are not a Democrat.

There was a person the other day in Tom Edsall's column — a Justice Democrat, part of the DSA network — who said they're not interested in beating Republicans. I appreciate the honesty. I think Donald Trump is an existential crisis. You think Barack Obama, Nancy Pelosi, or Hakeem Jeffries are an existential crisis? I don't. We have a fundamental strategic difference, a fundamental policy difference, and a fundamental political difference.

Go to your own party. Stay there. I'll see you in November.

收尾

主持人： There you have it, folks. Over-and-out now with Rahm Emanuel. We will have you back in the coming months and years — as this has been amazing — and we got to get you on with Chamath and Sacks next. Thank you so much.

Rahm: Thanks guys.

主持人： All right, besties. I think that was another epic discussion. People love the interviews. I could hear him talk for hours. Absolutely. We crushed your questions in a minute. We are giving people ground-truth data to underwrite your own opinion. What did you guys think? That was fun. That was great.

## 三重意外洞察：这不是一次政治访谈，而是一份"大国综合症"诊断书
### 意外观察一：Rahm 无意中揭示了"超级大国的对称性精神病"
大多数人把中美视为对立的两极，但 Rahm 用一句被埋没的话戳破了这个幻觉——**"两个超级大国把世界当作自家国内失灵的倾倒场"**。中国倾倒的是经济功能失调（钢铁、汽车、太阳能板的产能过剩），美国倾倒的是政治文化功能失调（选举前 9 天会见 AfD、激化英国种族矛盾、攻击 Maloney）。
这里有个反常识的结论：**中美之争的本质不是意识形态对立，而是两个都无法治愈自己内伤的巨人，把痛苦以不同形态外包给世界**。这解释了为什么全球中等强国（日本、加拿大、巴西、墨西哥）开始出现相似的"避险语言"——它们不是在选边，而是在同时躲两颗流弹。
### 意外观察二：教育与国债之间藏着一条"三年级隐形债券"
Freeberg 追问高等教育成本，Rahm 突然把话题拽回三年级识字率。这看似跑题，其实是全场最锋利的一刀——**"孩子从大学里辍学，是从三年级开始的"**。

item.title: [Zhang Xiaojun Podcast] NVIDIA VP Ming-Yu Liu: Cosmos 3, World Models, Kung Fu, What Jensen Taught Me
item.dc:creator: Zhang Xiaojun Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的观察：Ming-Yu Liu 的"低 ego"，其实是 NVIDIA 商业模式的产物，而不是修行的结果

多数人会把他反复强调的"不竞争、不追第一、帮所有人成功"解读为一种个人修养的成熟。但如果你把 NVIDIA 的商业结构叠加上去，会发现一个几乎冷酷的事实：NVIDIA 是全球唯一一家"下游对手越多、自己赚得越多"的 AI 公司。 他所有的世界观——Cosmos 开源、把机器人公司当客户不当对手、不做端到端产品、认为模型能力必然收敛——本质上都不是哲学，而是卖铲人视角下最优的经营策略。所以他能说出"我没有对手"，是因为他站在整个生态最上游的地基上；而一个 Frontier Lab 的研究者，就算再想低 ego，也做不到——他的每一次 benchmark 落后，都是股价、融资和团队士气的直接扣分。

换句话说：低 ego 不是一种性格，而是一种奢侈。它需要你所在位置的博弈结构支持它。

跨领域连接：这场访谈里出现了三个"信息瓶颈"——它们其实是同一件事

一个很少有人指出的模式：Ming-Yu 讲的三件看似无关的事，底层是同一个结构。

  1. CoupledGAN 的核心技巧：把两个 GAN 的生成器 couple 起来，制造"信息瓶颈"，让模型被迫寻找共性——于是学到了"马→斑马"的映射。
  2. Jensen 逼他每天读大量邮件：这也是一个人为的信息瓶颈——只有极高的输入压力，才能训练出"什么重要 / 什么不重要"的判别能力。
  3. LV 减少陈列反而销量上升的故事：22 个模型砍成 1 个 Cosmos 3，也是主动制造瓶颈——去掉冗余，用户和团队反而能做决策。

信息瓶颈是一种通用的"逼出本质"的机械原理。它出现在深度学习的 latent space 里，出现在 CEO 的决策工作流里，出现在奢侈品的橱窗里，也出现在中国武术里——发力时全身劲道必须"过一点"（腰胯的窄通道），才能把地面的力传到拳头。所有真正强大的系统，都在关键位置人为制造一个窄门。 Ming-Yu 20 年的研究和管理生涯，其实是在不同尺度上重复实践同一条物理定律。

一个惊人预测：真正决定物理 AI 是否爆发的，不是模型，而是数据采集设备的人形化程度

访谈里被大多数人忽略的一段是他解释"为什么大家都在做人形机器人"——他给出的第二个理由是：因为人类采集数据用的是手。 这一句话轻描淡写，但如果推到极致会得出一个反直觉结论：

物理 AI 的爆发时间点，本质上不由算法或算力决定，而由"人类采集训练数据的默认工具是双手"这个生物学事实锁定。 因为只要采集端仍然是人（VR、遥操作、egocentric 摄像头），机器人的形态就必须收敛到人形，否则数据不迁移。这意味着：

  • 轮式底盘 + 人形上半身的方案，会在数据端天然吃亏，而不是在成本端。
  • 谁家最先在大规模低成本人形数据采集设备上取得突破，谁就会锁定 Cosmos 那个"ChatGPT 时刻"的时间。
  • 这也解释了为什么 Cosmos 3 突然把 ego-centric 数据作为一等公民——这不是技术选择，这是对整个产业动力学的下注。

跨领域的对照：这跟摄影史上"胶卷决定了取景框的比例，取景框决定了 100 年的电影语言"是同一个逻辑——采集介质的物理约束，会向上游反噬整个产业形态。Ming-Yu 可能自己都还没把这个规律讲透，但他的产品决策已经跟着这条隐线走了。

附带一个不那么显眼但耐人寻味的洞察

他两次提到 Tim Brooks 和 Sora 时的自我反思，用词几乎完全一致："我的决心不够。"——但仔细听下去会发现，他反思的从来不是技术判断错误，而是没有勇气把已经看到的判断做大。这是一种非常罕见的元反思：他知道自己判断对了，但没敢押注。这种"输在勇气而非视野"的失败，比"看错方向"的失败要痛苦一百倍，而这正是他今天推动 Cosmos 时会全部资源砸下去的心理根源——他在为过去的 Sora 补课。

📝 转录文本

NVIDIA VP Ming-Yu Liu：Cosmos 3、世界模型、功夫，以及 Jensen 教我的事

This English translation was generated by AI and is for reference only.

开场：一位"不像研究员"的研究者

Hello, everyone. I'm Xiaojun. Today I'm in Shanghai, and my guest is Ming-Yu Liu, NVIDIA's VP of Research. Our conversation takes place one month after Jensen Huang's recent visit to China.

Ming-Yu has always struck me as someone who dresses very plainly, carrying a somewhat worn crossbody bag, with a very humble demeanor. But people inside NVIDIA told me he doesn't seem like a typical researcher. He's more like an engineering leader. Jensen Huang gave him an evaluation: GSD — getting shit done.

Not long ago, Ming-Yu Liu led his team to release NVIDIA's world model, Cosmos 3. So in this interview, we talked about the Cosmos 3 world model, and also about a researcher's 20-year-long quest. And this researcher's identity is quite special: he works inside NVIDIA, a massive infrastructure-type system, which has changed many of his research approaches. Of course, we also somewhat inevitably talked about some inside stories about NVIDIA and Jensen Huang.

Ming-Yu Liu says that to build models, you have to be low ego. Model competition shouldn't be a Squid Game.

What follows is my interview with Ming-Yu Liu, NVIDIA's VP of Research.

Jensen (Huang) often talks about how he likes this kind of zero-billion-dollar business. It can be unprofitable, but when this business succeeds, it has to be very influential — it has to be enormous.

The prosperity of an economy is measured by how fast money flows from one person's pocket to another's. The prosperity of research should be measured by how fast an idea flows from one person's head to another's.

When we finished Cosmos 1, we asked Jensen whether we should keep going, and Jensen said to me, "You just keep going all the way to Cosmos 97."

Because he's a very disciplined person. Even when something is very important, he'll tell you to pace — pace your steps. He just wants you not to rush. He's good at fighting marathon battles.

Every day he feels the company has only 30 days of cash left, that it will go bankrupt in 30 days.

Now, you happened to have joined NVIDIA exactly 10 years ago. Yes. Have you changed much over these 10 years? How many times has your NVIDIA stock multiplied?

一、来中国、团队与"Cosmos Lab"

Hello, Ming-Yu. Why don't you first say hi to the audience?

Hello, friends online. I'm Ming-Yu Liu.

We just talked about how you've been in the U.S. for 20 years and at NVIDIA for 10 years. Do you still speak Chinese much at the company?

Sometimes I do speak Chinese, but most of the time it's still English, because most of the time many people on the team don't speak Chinese. So communication is mainly in English. But if it's a small group meeting where everyone participating speaks Chinese, then we naturally switch into Chinese mode.

What's your itinerary like on this trip to China? How often do you come to China?

Right now I come to China about two to three times a year, because the main task the company has given me — my personal interest is in Physical AI. Here in China, the development of Physical AI is flourishing. Many companies, many researchers, are making major breakthroughs. We come here to exchange ideas with everyone and to understand how we can help them.

Did you feel anything different this time, compared to before?

This time, what I saw was more and more work on hands — dexterous hands — making breakthroughs in this key technology, and then pursuing the next key capabilities that Physical AI can achieve. Compared to my last visit, I found the pace is very fast — progress is very fast. I learn a lot every time.

This should be your first time doing a Chinese-language podcast. I'd like to help the audience or listeners form an impression. Your current title at NVIDIA is VP of Research. Could you introduce this role, as well as the structure and size of your team?

I'm currently VP of Research, and also VP of the Cosmos Lab. Our team consists of researchers plus engineers. Those reporting directly to me number about eighty to ninety people. In addition, the company has other teams also working on Cosmos — in English it's called a dotted line. Although they don't report to me directly, I'm the overall PIC (person in charge) of the whole mission — the one who calls the shots, the one who decides the direction. So these people also follow my guidance and work together with this team to push the goals forward.

The whole Cosmos effort should have between 200 and 300 people. This is a very significant project within NVIDIA. We invest a lot of resources. We feel this level of staffing is what's needed to produce good results.

二、Deep Imagination 的起点：十年前的一个 Job Talk

I saw that you previously also led a team called the Deep Imagination Research Group. Did Cosmos evolve from it? What's the relationship between them?

Yes. I joined NVIDIA about ten years ago. When I joined NVIDIA, my goal was — back then, in my job talk, when I was pitching myself to NVIDIA, what I talked about in my job talk — that was ten years ago — what I said was: one day, the dominant computation for generating video will be deep learning. It won't be traditional computer graphics.

In that era — computer special effects, movie special effects — using that kind of graphics, using that kind of graphics, the traditional graphic pipeline to generate beautiful graphics — that was the mainstream. I was one of the early people in the field who believed deep learning was the future trend.

I remember back then, with our chief scientist, Bill Dally, in the presentation at that time — my presentation was all about deep learning. Because it's data driven, it can do many things traditional graphics can't. For example, one day I could take a novel as input, put it into this deep learning system, and it would produce a movie. You could do many of the controls that traditional graphics now requires massive manpower to achieve.

Back then, I — the company was very interested in this, and I was honored to join NVIDIA. After joining, I kept working toward this direction. In that period, the dominant model was the generative adversarial network (GAN) — yes, the GAN. I was among the early people in the field working on GAN research.

早期 GAN 工作与 GauGAN

I did several pieces of work I'm very proud of. One of them is — I was the first to propose that you could do this kind of what we call unsupervised unpaired image translation. In AI learning, a lot of the time you rely on supervision. You need corresponding input and output before you can learn this input-output relationship. Unsupervised means you don't have corresponding input-output pairs. You don't know what this person looks like when they smile. You don't know what a horse would look like turned into a zebra. Back then, we were early to use an information bottleneck to be able to do this — what we call unsupervised image-to-image translation.

Back then, when I joined NVIDIA, NVIDIA was not recognized as an AI company. At that time, deep learning wasn't as hot as it is now. NVIDIA had traditionally done computer architecture, designing GPUs. No one was doing research on the application side. I was essentially among the early people to build this direction at NVIDIA.

I did many things. One work was called GauGAN. In Chinese it seems to be translated as "Ma Liang's Magic Brush." It's like a little paint program: you dab a few colors, each color representing a different semantic meaning. After you paint a bit, it can turn into a beautiful landscape painting. That work made me — it helped NVIDIA build an image of being able to not only make great GPUs, but also make great AI models.

Back then, I also had some colleagues working together on StyleGAN research. It was this group of us who made NVIDIA the first — essentially the first to use this kind of generative network for media generation — we brought it to prominence.

从 Deep Imagination 到大模型的觉醒

After doing this for a while, the company felt I was ready, and I could start building my own team. The team I founded back then was called Deep Imagination Research, consistent with the goal from my original job talk.

What year was this?

Between 2019 and 2020. At that time I became a research director. But back then, knowing I was going to build a team, together with a few partners I worked with, we started building this Deep Imagination Research.

Then, after Deep Imagination Research, we kept solving related problems. Step by step, we wanted to go from — toward the goal of putting a novel in and producing a movie. Just moving forward step by step. We made a few interesting demos. One year, Jensen — our CEO — wanted to use a digital human to replace himself to give the keynote. So we helped him make this fake, generated keynote demo. And one after another — that was during the pandemic. During that period, digital humans developed very fast. We also contributed some technology we're very proud of.

Ten years ago, when I gave my job talk, I wanted to work on the problem of turning a novel into a movie. But back then, I felt this problem might take a very long time to solve. I should say, back then I didn't realize we actually already had the conditions. When your compute — when your data is sufficient, you can make such a big breakthrough. But back then, I was busy working on digital humans, busy with all kinds of interesting applications.

Until one day, OpenAI released the DALL·E work — the earliest text-to-image model. Only then did I realize my ambition wasn't big enough. I wasn't brave enough — I didn't have the determination to make this thing happen. In the place with the most compute.

向 Jensen 要 1000 张 A100

Back then, NVIDIA worked like this: if you wanted Jensen to invest compute in you, you had to explain why this matters to the company. I remember when DALL·E came out, I wrote a letter to Jensen, telling him the future is already very clear: it's using deep learning for image generation. Many NVIDIA customers use NVIDIA GPUs with traditional graphics for image generation. We can't fall behind in using deep learning for image generation. We must invest GPUs in our team to help this field grow.

During that period, I also had a lot of collaboration with Getty Images. Because I had been working in this direction, these traditional content companies — they were also very interested in AI, but they were just trying it out; they didn't have enough determination.

After seeing DALL·E, I wrote a letter to Jensen asking for GPUs, and wrote a letter to Getty Images saying we should work together — only then would your future be secured. And then we reached a partnership: they provide the data, we have the compute, and we go build a big model to do text-to-image.

That was the moment I stepped into large models. Back then we started a project called Picasso. Our goal was to build an AI foundry. Some companies have data, but they don't have AI talent; they don't have AI infrastructure. But they have data; they have customers. We would help them build a GenAI model, then give the model back to them, letting them serve their own customers, and both sides profit together. Back then it was with Getty Images, and also with Shutterstock, that we did this.

This was still during the Deep Imagination Research team days. We were doing this work. From here, gradually, my research no longer just produced a model; it no longer just produced a paper. We also produced a product that could help customers succeed. It developed step by step like this.

At the time, I thought I was now determined enough — willing to take on the hardest problems. Because I had already asked Jensen for GPUs.

How many GPUs did you ask for back then?

Back then I asked for 1,000 A100 GPUs.

Right — was 1,000 a lot at the time?

Yes, it was a huge amount. That was still in the Ampere era. 1,000 was already a lot. And to string 1,000 GPUs together and do efficient training was not easy either. That's what we tried back then — whenever we hit bottlenecks, we overcame them one by one.

与 Tim Brooks、Sora 的交集

Because I was among the earliest to work on GenAI in computer vision, I was also honored to work with many outstanding partners. Since I was relatively senior, many promising young people back then, while still students, would come to intern with me, including Yu Jiahui, who's now at Meta, and Tim Brooks, who made Sora. They both interned with me.

I still remember when Tim Brooks first joined my team as an intern, he kept wanting to do video generation — he wanted to do what would become his Sora. But back then we didn't have the technology. We collaborated using GANs. Even then, you could see he was full of determination, full of passion. And of course, he's extremely smart, and incredibly fast with his hands. I learned a lot from working with him. We also wrote a pretty good paper together. After he graduated, I wanted to keep him, but he went to OpenAI. I'm also very happy that he got great development opportunities at OpenAI, and later made the Sora work.

After the Sora work came out, I felt very happy, but I also felt my determination really wasn't enough — still not enough, still not enough. Back then, a few of us working in this field wrote a letter to Jensen together, saying we had to invest more.

三、Cosmos 的诞生

This is how the Cosmos project came about. This group of us scholars — me, and at that time also Sanja Fidler, and Bryan Catanzaro, who leads the NeMo team at our company. Jim Fan was also in that meeting at the time. We discussed together, and we decided to go build a World Model. We felt that for the company — for humanity, this would be an important technology.

Back then Jensen asked me and Sanja Fidler — the two of us — to lead this Cosmos effort together. It wasn't called Cosmos back then. At that time we just knew we wanted to do it. Jensen asked each of us to think about what to call it — what the project should be named. So each of us went back to think about what to call it. I've forgotten how many names were on the table back then, but in the end Jensen said, call it Cosmos. We thought the name Cosmos was very good. So that's how the Cosmos project came to be.

I was still in the Deep Imagination Lab period. In that period, I was originally working on Picasso — AI foundry for this media generation — but at the same time I was also responsible for Cosmos. Later I felt the Cosmos project was more important to the company. And there was no way around it — I was stretched too thin; I couldn't run two major projects at the same time. So I gradually wound down the Picasso project, helped those customers find other tech companies that could keep supporting them, and threw myself fully into Cosmos.

We worked on Cosmos for a while — from 1 to 2 to 3. During this period, more and more customers were using it. You need a certain scale to do the Cosmos project well. You can think of my time in Research as a budding stage. When Cosmos was already relied upon by so many people — whether external customers or internal teams — it reached a stage where it couldn't die; it had to succeed. The resources needed became even more massive.

At the beginning of this year, I left NVIDIA Research. Now I report to our senior VP of software, the most senior leader at our company. Previously you reported to Bill Dally, right? — while leading the Deep Imagination Research team. Now I report to Dwight. He's our company's first software engineer. His story is in Jensen's biography. Right — so now I report to him.

After I left research, we changed the name. I no longer call my team the Deep Imagination Research team. We call ourselves the Cosmos Lab. That's how the whole shift happened.

关于 Sora 的遗憾

I heard Sora didn't come from your team, which was a regret for you, right?

It wasn't exactly regret. I actually felt really happy. That people I once worked with could make such a big contribution — I felt very happy about that. The regrettable part is that every researcher wants to make a contribution. Seeing how big Sora's contribution was, you naturally feel happy. But on the other hand, you also think, where exactly in my decision-making process, in these processes of my judgment, what were the places where I misjudged, which led me to fail, at the right time, to do the right thing? It must be that — I'm someone who really likes self-reflection. I always try to understand how I can make myself better.

Since we're talking about Sora, I'd like to add one more thing. Why do you think OpenAI later basically shut down this product line?

Because Sora is a significant piece of research. And of course it has many applications of its own. OpenAI is a very ambitious company. They have a huge amount of talent. Sam Altman has always been — from his early days at Y Combinator, he was an investor. So of course he wants to have that investor mindset, hoping that within the company there are all kinds of projects, some of which become very successful, a diverse portfolio.

I think over the past year, they came under enormous pressure from Anthropic — huge competitive pressure. They saw Anthropic, with Coding Agents, generating enormous economic returns. Also, when you're chatting with ChatGPT, the number of tokens you generate takes at most a minute to produce. But with a Coding Agent, it can work for 24 hours, 48 hours. The token volume is huge. So they felt this was a very good direction, and focused the company's energy on going in the coding direction.

As The Art of War says, defend everywhere and your strength thins everywhere. Everyone's resources are limited. So they reallocated resources to go toward coding. I don't think they believed that Sora wasn't good work. It's just that, at this point in time, I think the company had more important things that it had to do, so they had to make a difficult decision.

四、NVIDIA 为什么要做研究？

I'm curious — because for frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, doing research is a given, because that is their product. But for a company like NVIDIA — an infrastructure company, or rather a platform company — couldn't you just sell tokens to these frontier labs? Why do your own research too? What does research itself mean to NVIDIA?

Your infrastructure has to be good, and the definition of "good" is that it suits what these application companies need. But if you don't build these applications yourself, you simply can't understand what they need. So you have to walk the paths they might walk, and through that, come to understand. Also, designing chips, designing computer architecture — the cycle is very long. You can't just say, "I'll change it right now." It takes a long period to do this kind of planning. So you have to do research in this area, make these investments, to understand what the potentially important problems to solve are. Only then can I design better chips, better infrastructure, to serve these big AI companies.

I've always felt that in this world, if everyone with ambition and ideals had these tools to do what they want to do, the world would be a better place. On one hand, seeing OpenAI, Anthropic, and several big Chinese companies make breakthroughs, makes me very happy. But our society will keep having a steady stream of ambitious young people, and we hope they'll have their opportunities too. We can build these models, share them with them, and they can build great applications, great extended models, or draw inspiration from them to make even better models of their own.

All these different ideas can be realized. I think when so many diverse ideas have the chance to be realized, and can be presented to users, I think everyone gets more choices, and society progresses better. That's why NVIDIA makes open-source models.

So do your research results create some competition with your customers?

When we do this work — especially when we make these open-source models — we basically put them out for free on the internet, for everyone to use. But actually bringing it to production, truly meeting customer needs — there's still a lot of work to do. Especially in the embodied space, there are many hardware problems, many business problems that must be solved. I think we're giving the community a signal that we will help you.

In this regard, when you see the trend, when you see our commitment — we went from generation 1 to generation 2, to generation 2.5, to generation 3 — going generation by generation like this. You see us, step by step, just trying to make this area better, so that everyone can better anticipate that NVIDIA will keep investing in this and keep improving. Once everyone has this understanding, has this confidence, they can put their resources toward the more critical cutting edges, and make significant contributions.

Because every company — no matter how rich — has limited resources. If you don't find the pain points, find the key points to invest in and make progress, it's hard to stand out. Embodied AI is so hard, with so many problems to solve. I think by making these models and helping share part of the burden, I don't see it as competing. I see it as helping everyone succeed.

为什么选 Embodied World Model 而不是 LLM

Right. Why did you set up a very important project back then, choosing neither the hottest large language models nor models like Sora, but an embodied world model instead?

Large language models — they were already developing extremely well at the time. Also, my background isn't in large language models. I come from computer vision, a CV background. So naturally I stayed around the media space, hanging around image and video. It's probably my past background that led me onto this path. Of course, because of my background, the partners who work with me have similar backgrounds, so we headed in this direction. That's why we didn't go the large language model route. Also, NVIDIA has a very strong large language model team. I didn't feel I had much to contribute there. I think Nemotron is getting better and better. On my side, I mainly want to solve problems better suited to me.

When Sora first came out, it was also a world simulator, but its main applications back then were more like creative applications. Creation is very interesting. Everyone hopes to tell stories in better ways, to present what they imagine — to make it tangible — to help everyone understand the world they see. That's a great application.

But at the time we also saw that Digital AI was developing extremely fast — while many of society's problems need these physical tools — physical tools that can truly change the state of the physical world — to be met. For example, when people get old, they can't drive anymore. And without driving, one's quality of life drops a lot. If there were self-driving cars, elderly people could still have their mobility. Also, many jobs are very labor-intensive and very dangerous. If Physical AI robots could help do these, that could also improve people's lives. And at home there's always a pile of chores — clearing the dishes, tidying up. These aren't necessarily what you most want to do at home. Having a robot help with these things improves people's quality of life.

We saw the contribution world models could make to Physical AI, so back then we moved in this Physical AI direction, rather than the content creation route.

Jensen 对团队的要求

Has Jensen made any demands on this team?

Yes, Jensen's demands on the team are very strict. The bar is high. Of course, the first goal is to help customers. That's not an easy thing, because NVIDIA is a computing company, an AI infrastructure company. What we're best at is the entire compute stack, from the underlying infra to CUDA and all the way up. But we're not a solutions company, like providing a robotics solution or solutions for other applications. But our goal is to help the companies building solutions succeed. Sometimes it feels a bit like scratching an itch through a boot — because you don't really know where the pain points are. When you design a model, when you design a product, if you don't understand your customers, you can't optimize. That's why I often come to China — to understand what problems people are facing and how to help them.

Right, of course that's one of the difficulties, one of Jensen's demands. What we build needs to make impact. Jensen often talks about how he likes zero-billion-dollar businesses — meaning it can be non-profitable, but when this business succeeds, it has to be very influential, something enormous. You can't just be satisfied making $100 million a year. That scale is big for many companies, but for NVIDIA as a company, it's a distraction. You have to solve the most important problems and make the biggest contribution. We believe Physical AI is a big enough problem to make the biggest contribution.

So on this path, you have to be very careful to solve the most important problems, rather than ones that produce short-term results but whose impact isn't that big. That's one of the challenges. Of course, you also have to be the best. That's very hard too.

五、个人成长的三次觉醒

It sounds like over the past 10 years, Ming-Yu has become more and more ambitious at NVIDIA. Next, I'd also like to explore you personally — Ming-Yu Liu the researcher — how you explored your research path step by step.

Before answering your question, let me first finish answering the previous one. I think I've always been very ambitious. Because back then I believed you could generate films directly from novels. It's just that my execution wasn't good enough. My sense of timing wasn't good enough. I didn't really understand — back then I hadn't been in the industry long — I didn't yet understand how to gain support within the company, to get huge resources to pursue a direction. I think through the past 10 years of experience, I've come to better understand how to see clearly, at the right time, how to help the company understand it's an important decision for the company, and how to influence how the company invests. That's the change, I think. Always ambitious, just didn't know how to execute.

从台北到无线通信到 AI

Going back to the beginning, because of my upbringing — I grew up in Taipei, (China). When I was in high school, the hottest technology was wireless communications. Cell phones had just come out back then — still those huge cell phones, it was still the Nokia era. I was very curious about this technology. Also, growing up in Taipei, (China), I always wanted to leave Taipei, (China). So I went to National Chiao Tung University in Taiwan, (China), in Hsinchu, to study wireless communications there.

After studying wireless communications there for a while, I came to understand how it worked. My classmates — those studying together at Chiao Tung University back then, the classmates studying wireless communications — many of them stayed in Taiwan, (China), working, for example, at MediaTek, or some went to TSMC, doing the work that Taiwan, (China) is itself very good at. At that time I started to doubt whether this was the path I wanted to choose. Because growing up, I never actually thought about studying abroad in the US. I never took my English seriously. I thought being good at math and physics was enough.

During that period I began to doubt what path was really right. In my junior year, I got curious and looked at what US graduate schools and PhD programs were working on. I looked at what we had been doing at Chiao Tung University in Taiwan, (China), and then I realized the work was very different. What I was doing then was figuring out how to design a protocol that could make transmission faster. I felt that was an improvement, but not a 0-to-1 change. When I saw what these top universities in the US were doing, I felt that every success there looked like a 0-to-1 change. So at that point I felt I should go out and take a shot.

I remember when I told my parents I was going to study in the US, they were startled, because they'd known me for over twenty years and had never heard me say I wanted to study in the US.

What year of college was this?

My junior year. So they were quite shocked to hear it.

Back then what I wanted to study in the US was quantum communication, because I thought it was magical — using quantum to directly transmit information from A to B. But later, before going to the US, I spent a year at Intel in Taiwan, (China), and met a friend there. We were both interning there. He was working on image recognition there. That was my first exposure to AI, because I'd been studying communications before. And when I saw him doing image recognition, I thought it was magical — he could tell from these pixels what was in there, who it was, what object it was. That's how I first got an impression of AI computer vision.

I got admitted to the University of Maryland in the US, and started my PhD there. The earliest computer vision didn't really work. Most of the research funding came from defense. Maryland is close to Washington, D.C., so back then it gathered some very formidable early pioneers in computer vision AI. After I got to that school, I was originally going to research quantum communication. Later I found they were doing computer vision there, topics very close to what I'd seen during my Intel internship. And I thought, hmm, this looks more interesting. So I sought out my advisor, Rama Chellappa. He was essentially a pioneer in this field, and I started learning AI computer vision from him.

The very first project I worked on was identifying a person from their walking posture in video. Wow, that was a pretty interesting problem back then. That's how I gradually switched tracks into AI. In the earliest days it was image recognition, video recognition. Later during my PhD I also learned how to use things like shape matching, segmentation — these common understanding-direction AI, computer vision research, gradually stepping into AI.

传统 CV 时代 → AlexNet → 生成模型

Back then there was no deep learning. It was the era of traditional computer vision. In traditional computer vision, nothing worked back then. So you had to learn everything. We were doing support vector machines back then. It was a very traditional kind of machine learning approach. Support vector machines are closely tied to optimization. This is something you had to learn, whether continuous or discrete optimization. And I also had to learn some graphical models, energy minimization, and all kinds of 3D calibration, things like that. I learned quite a lot. I'd say my foundation was pretty solid.

But in the year I graduated, ImageNet — AlexNet came out and changed the whole world.

In the later stage of my PhD, I went to a company called Mitsubishi Electric Research Lab. That was a job you took later, right? Yes, it was my first job in the United States. It was in Cambridge, in Massachusetts, right next to MIT. This lab was a very strong research institution in the '90s. Back then it was neck and neck with Microsoft Research. It was a leading research institution in graphics. Many professors at MIT used to be researchers at Mitsubishi Electric Research Lab, including Bill Freeman and Ramesh Raskar. They all worked there. By the time I joined, that era had passed, but many excellent researchers were still there.

After I joined that company — well, several things happened. That was the year AlexNet came out. So the things I had learned started to diverge from where the future world was heading.

Did you feel lost at that moment?

No. I actually — I was very interested in these new technologies. Because in computer vision, since nothing worked, I had already developed this habit of learning everything. Later, when deep learning came out, I found it really interesting. I remember I was in my final year of the PhD program, sort of the senior student in the lab, and I organized the junior students to actively study deep learning — to do research on it. I remember one junior colleague told me that only a few people knew this stuff and there was no point researching it. I ignored him and kept running the seminar.

Later, my first job was at Mitsubishi Electric Research Lab. Research labs usually have a fairly free research culture, so I had a lot of time to learn. So that's where I studied deep learning. Generative models — my advisor Rama Chellappa really believed in generative models. He believed in Bayesian methods, believed you should treat generation as part of understanding. So while I was learning deep learning back then, I was also keeping an eye on the generation side.

Then one year I went to NeurIPS and saw Ian Goodfellow's work on generative adversarial networks. I became very interested in it. After coming back, I started investing heavily in this direction — learning more and more.

It seems you started working on generation quite early.

Yes, I was among the earliest researchers working on generation. Back then, as long as you could generate a 32×32 pixel face that didn't look like a ghost, you felt pretty successful.

So why is generation part of understanding?

Richard Feynman put it this way: "If I cannot create, I cannot understand." It's when you can generate something that you truly, thoroughly understand it. It's a bit like how humans learn. When you can articulate something, it means you've understood it.

Also, in the early days, computer vision had this distinction: discriminative models and generative models. A discriminative model has no generative capability, but it can tell whether this is A or B. A generative model can likewise be used for discrimination, but it also has the ability to reconstruct the signal — it can describe it. When you can describe something clearly, people tend to think you understand it better. So take the earliest AlexNet — it could do ImageNet classification, and we saw it as a discriminative network.

工程师经验的影响

Actually, you spent a year as an engineer early on. Do you think that experience influenced your later research?

Oh, you mean my time as an engineer at Intel? And what do you think is the essential difference between engineering and research? Which suits you better?

That's a good question. The most important part of doing research is asking the right question. When you ask the right question, you've more or less found the right direction. Engineering, then, helps you demonstrate to everyone that yes, this is the right question. You have to actually build the thing. Engineering's ability to implement lets you get things done. And when engineering is done at a large scale, many other things become important too.

In the year before I went to the U.S., engineering's influence on me — probably the biggest influence was becoming aware of this field called AI, computer vision, and in between, I remember hunting down problems for the company inside a huge software stack. That was a very patience-testing process. I think it was all great training.

So AI was something of an accident for you too?

Not really. No — I wasn't the kind of kid who said from childhood, "I want to understand why intelligence can arise." I basically saw this thing step by step, found it fascinating, wanted to understand it, and moved in that direction step by step.

What was it that first struck you? Why did it strike me?

At first? Later on, of course, there could be many reasons. Because I didn't understand it. Didn't understand, yet it was relatively easy to grasp its importance. Some fields of technology — take quantum communication, for example — you have to understand it deeply before you know why it matters. AI is easy to understand: you can recreate intelligence, and some of its behaviors are very much like a human's. That makes you curious. And also, naturally, everyone feels puzzled about their own existence — the whole species — what exactly is a human? How are we different from other living beings? That's a question you naturally ask. I think it's also for this reason that this field draws so many people to devote themselves to it.

研究生涯的三个关键时刻

If you had to pick one moment early on that was crucial to your research career, how would you describe it? Which moment was it?

Too many. Right — so which one mattered most? Or the three most important ones?

第一个时刻：从追求数学之美到贴近问题本质。

I think the first moment is that early on, I loved elegant mathematics, because in the early stages of computer vision, nothing worked. Computer vision used a lot of optimization algorithms. Optimization — it's about finding the optimal solution. For continuous problems, you often run into nonconvex issues — you can't find the optimal solution. For discrete ones, it's these NP-hard problems — you don't have enough compute to find the optimal solution either. But you still develop algorithms to find an answer, though you don't know how far the answer is from the optimum. To make sure your answer isn't too far from the optimum, you need some guarantee. You prove what's called a bound. Maybe the answer you find isn't the optimal one, but it's within, say, 4% of the optimum, or within 20% — better than just any random answer.

To prove this bound, in a lot of early research you start making assumptions. Assumptions make your math cleaner, so you can find an answer, but assumptions also take you further from reality. Back then, early on, I leaned a bit toward pursuing mathematical beauty while neglecting the distance from the real world. After a while, I realized this wasn't the right approach, because AI itself is an applied science — intelligence is meant to be applied. I grew more and more fond of getting close to the essence of a problem, rather than being dazzled by fancy mathematics.

第二个时刻：从"做出来"到"让别人理解"。

Later there was another phase — probably related to my upbringing — I always focused on getting things built, not on making others understand what I'd built. After I started at NVIDIA, I felt my research was pretty good — quite good. Before others had seen this kind of image translation, I had already built it.
