But I didn't really understand how to — I wasn't good at presenting what I'd built in a way ordinary people could understand.

I often say that what I built was 100 points, but my explanation was only 10 points, so others only saw 10 points. Back then I started paying more attention to how to make what I built — how to help others understand its importance, to let them understand the process. I think that's a very important lesson. That was when I was doing GANs in the early days.

第三个时刻：团队协作与 N² 复杂度。

The third one is — I later came to understand, especially once I started working on large models, I began to realize that teamwork is extremely important. Communication between people is actually a high-complexity problem. Say you have — I don't know, call it N squared. Suppose you have N people. Your communication with those other N people is N squared. N squared is a bad complexity in terms of scaling. When you have many people and everyone has to communicate point to point, communication gets hard. Something better would be N — or linear or sublinear.

I began to understand that to make a huge contribution, when everyone needs to work together, you have to explain things extremely clearly so everyone understands, so everyone's goals align. It's not enough that you can build the thing yourself — you also want everyone to understand what is being built, so you can all move in the same direction. This still takes a lot of work — helping everyone understand why this matters. That's something I came to see as very important in my later research — especially research at a large scale. You have to build applications, and you have to sell your work, and you have to collaborate as a team.

GauGAN 与"马良神笔"

Right yes. This is actually your own growth trajectory, isn't it?

Yes, that's right. When I made my first — I had a very popular piece of work back then called GauGAN. Everyone was using it at the time. It's the "magic brush of Ma Liang" I mentioned earlier. Seeing the feedback from users filled me with a sense of accomplishment. And I felt that I could influence not just researchers who read papers, but a much larger group of people. That made me feel my life had more value, and I kept moving in that direction.

Is GauGAN named after Gauguin?

Yes, that's how the name came about. Back then I was working with an intern of mine named Taesung Park. We were researching this direction together, collaborating — also with Jun-Yan Zhu and Ting-Chun Wang. The four of us were working on this problem together. We developed an algorithm back then — we called it SPADE, spatially adaptive normalization. After we built it, I was very happy. I gave a demo inside the company. Jensen saw it and was very excited. He asked me what it was called. I said SPADE, and he didn't like it. The thing is, it's not easy to understand. It's not user language.

Ha — but by then the paper was already written. It had been submitted to CVPR, but hadn't been posted on arXiv yet. When the company saw it, they told me not to post it on arXiv, so that Jensen could, at GTC — that was GTC 2019 — announce it to everyone at his keynote. I was very excited — a great opportunity.

Then they started wondering what to call it. Our company had a marketing genius who thought about what to call it. Back then every algorithm was something-GAN. It was the era of GANs. And that marketing person — his name was Greg Estelle — he proposed calling it GauGAN. Gauguin was French. Once the name was picked, as soon as people heard it, it made sense — a painter, a famous painter. And the application back then was painting, after all. And so it came out.

Originally it was supposed to be at GTC — to be announced at Jensen's keynote. But that year he had too many products to introduce. At the last minute, he — I remember I was still rehearsing with his team on Sunday night, preparing to give a demo on stage. That very evening I got a notice saying there were too many products to cover, and he had decided not to put GauGAN in his keynote. There was still a press release, and we still did demos for media friends, but it wasn't in his keynote. After many media friends saw it, it turned out to be the most talked-about work at GTC. That year was just like that — lots of things like this happened. We made an online app for everyone to try out. From how people used it, we got a lot of great feedback, and we kept moving further toward applications.

GAN 系列工作与"信息瓶颈"

Actually, wasn't GauGAN a step-by-step progression from your earlier research trajectory? It didn't get there on day one. After your PhD, you joined Mitsubishi Electric Research Lab, and computer vision entered the era of GANs. And you did a whole series of work around GANs, including CoGAN, MoCoGAN, and then after joining NVIDIA, things like the GauGAN series of work, right? How did it all evolve?

My very first GAN work was called CoupledGAN. It coupled the generator networks of two GANs together. Coupling them created an information bottleneck. All of deep learning is about learning how to compress information, and a bottleneck gives the network a chance to find the essence. One GAN models one distribution; two GANs model two distributions — one is horses, one is zebras. Once you couple them, there's a constraint, so it looks for commonalities, which lets you do the translation — from horse to zebra. That's the direction it went.

The whole generative network is doing distribution modeling. Distribution modeling means you can sample — produce an image, a mountain, a sea, or a video. But people don't just want to generate — they want to control what they generate. And control requires a signal. There are many kinds of signals.

  • One common signal is using an image as the signal — like, I have a horse here; how do I turn it into a zebra?
  • Another approach is sketch — your own sketch.
  • And another is segmentation — it's like MS Paint: one color means mountain, another color means water.
  • And then there's, say, class labels — this is a mountain, this is a car, this is a motorcycle.
  • The most sophisticated, the closest to natural human language, is text — text-to-image, text-to-video.

That's the most natural form. But the biggest difference between text and something like segmentation is: segmentation is very concrete — it tells you what each pixel is. It aligns everything for you. Text, on the other hand, is quite different. Its structure is very different from image structure, different from video structure. Because the structures are so different, it's harder to learn and requires more data.

So in the course of my work, I understood this problem, and I worked my way up step by step from the easier directions. The easiest were things like segmentation, sketch, or an image. And that's also why I said earlier that DALL·E made me feel my own resolve wasn't strong enough. Because back then I always thought text-to-image was a very hard problem. I felt the field didn't yet have enough data and compute to do it. But actually it did. It was precisely because no one did it that it couldn't be done.

一次预言：语言会最先突破

So you followed the path from image to text, extending bit by bit.

Right. Actually, in the early days, I had a few friends. We attended NeurIPS together every year, and we would discuss. Back then GPT didn't even exist yet. It was all very early days. We were discussing, if AI truly was going to make a real breakthrough, which field would be the first to break through. I told everyone back then that it would be text, language.

What year was this?

It must have been 2016 or 2017.

Even though I didn't work on text myself, I knew that image signals have too much noise. There's a lot of stuff in there. It's relatively far from the essence of knowledge. It's more of an observation of this world. Text is already very pure, closer to symbols. So to produce something like intelligence, language would come first. Although I knew the earliest AI would happen in language, and it really turned out that way, but back then I just liked visual signals more. So I stayed on the side of visual signal generation.

Mm, would you like to talk about those GAN works that came later?

Back then it was image translation. From A — like turning a horse into a zebra, turning a landscape painting into a real landscape. Later we started working on video. We made something called vid2vid back then. It took a car simulator's very simple cartoonish images and turned them into a realistic driving scene. Very close to things like today's World Model.

Right, this was already at NVIDIA. Only CoupledGAN wasn't done at NVIDIA. The rest of the GANs were all done at NVIDIA. Doing this work in those early days — also because of that, with Ian Goodfellow the inventor of GAN, I became good friends. We had lots of discussions. I was also very lucky that at NVIDIA many excellent researchers — Jiahui Yu, Tim Brooks and many others — came to intern with me. I learned from them. We did a whole series of work all revolving around image translation, video translation, moving in that direction.

Scale 与 Muon 的前身

Right, then one year later. During my PhD years what I learned was all traditional computer vision. After I graduated from my PhD the deep learning era arrived. The thinking back then was you shouldn't do handcrafted algorithm design, you shouldn't do handcrafted feature engineering, it should be data driven. I also came to understand back then that a more scalable approach, a simple, scalable approach is more likely to succeed. So I often told myself when you're making choices look for the more scalable ones. Later on, this is what people call the bitter lesson.

I was very happy working on GAN, but I kept thinking whether GAN was really scalable. Because everyone knows GAN is very hard to train. I worried that this thing might not be scalable in the end. That year, when Jiahui Yu came to intern with me, the topic he and I researched was how to scale GAN. It was still very early back then. That's when I saw Jiahui Yu's brilliance. He produced so much. Although we didn't end up writing a paper back then, the amount of experiments we ran was astounding. When I saw his ideas — wow, you can even think about it that way.

For example, back then a GAN has a Generator and a Discriminator. I was fortunate to have a huge number of GPUs back then — a whole cluster to train GAN. And he came up with the idea to put a Discriminator on every GPU but with different weights for each. So it was like many people simultaneously playing against this generative network. In that era being able to implement such a thing was not easy at all.

And then there was another intern back then. His name is Jeremy Bernstein. He's the one who later invented the Muon Optimizer — the Muon Optimizer everyone is using now. He came to intern with me back then. The direction he and I researched was how, at the algorithm level, to use better algorithms to make GAN stable. But in the end, neither of these two directions succeeded. Yet each of them went on to develop extremely impressive, highly accomplished work.

Jeremy started from that time. We wrote a series of papers on how to use the early algorithms behind Muon to stabilize — to make the training more stable. He kept going down that path step by step to develop the Muon algorithm.

从 GAN 到 Diffusion 到 Transformer

It was a very happy period. I learned a lot. Up to a certain year — working really hard. Researching with so many smart people on how to make GAN more scalable. But every result led toward one conclusion: that GAN is not scalable.

I built this team. Back then, people joined because they wanted to work on GAN. That year I told everyone we can't do GAN anymore. We have to move on — this direction is not scalable. Back then we saw diffusion and felt, wow, this method is extremely stable.

That must have been 2017. No, it should be 2021. Around 2021. 2017 was when the Transformer was invented.

Right, the Transformer in 2017. After the Transformer was invented, I have to say I wasn't among the early adopters of the Transformer. Its application back then was still LLM. I had been focusing on GAN all along. Early GANs — the ones that trained well all used Convolution Networks. It was Saining. After he brought in the diffusion transformer, we moved into diffusion and gradually shifted toward the Transformer side.

So from an algorithmic perspective back then we felt GAN was not scalable and I told the team: something that's not scalable won't go far in the end. Go with diffusion. So we started going down the diffusion path and kept going. Right, this was a major transition period. So doing diffusion we started with image then moved to multi-view image. Multi-view image eventually became 3D generation. We did a series of work in this area. The Edify series — the Edify image generator, Edify 3D, Edify video. And all kinds of generation done with diffusion.

关于范式转移与年轻人

Hearing this, two points come to my mind. Throughout your long exploration in CV, the computing paradigm actually changed several times. From traditional methods to GAN and then to diffusion. Each time such a shift happens, what kind of mindset should a researcher have in the midst of it?

I found that things keep getting simpler. You might feel, oh, all my previous work was for nothing. Jensen often says "suffering leads to greatness." Through all these experiences I feel I'm increasingly able to grasp the essence of things. I feel it's a bit like traditional scientific research. You keep working until you truly find the essence. Finding the simplest way to describe how the world works.

I think the current approach is making things simpler and simpler. And on the Cosmos side we also went from several models to the single model we now have in Cosmos 3. It's unified too. Right, we gradually came to understand — OK, so this is the essence of things. Every direction took 5 to 10 years of investment. I think my future decisions are deeply influenced by these past experiences. And I can't say those were wrong either. You can't say it was wrong — the conditions back then, the compute back then, the data back then, doing those things back then was reasonable. What I learned back then is very helpful for my understanding of many things now.

Also, I noticed you've mentioned your interns several times. In an AI lab, do ideas often emerge through interns? Is that a very common thing? How do you view young people?

For example, the prosperity of an economy is determined by how fast money flows from one person's pocket to another's. The prosperity of research should be determined by how fast ideas flow from one person's mind to another's. You hear my idea, you have some thoughts and make it better. I hear your new idea, I think, hey, not bad but this part could be even better. And it keeps flowing, flowing, flowing and the ideas get better and better.

So because I took the industry path rather than becoming a professor at a university — if you only interact within industry all day only with your own colleagues, the diversity of ideas is a bit lower. At NVIDIA, we recruit many interns. We collaborate with these people full of ideas, people from different backgrounds, doing research together, learning from each other. I think this helps me grow and also helps them grow. It's a very important development.

六、加入 NVIDIA：因为想要 GPU

In 2012 you joined Mitsubishi — after your PhD you joined Mitsubishi Research. Right, then in 2016 I joined NVIDIA. How did that later career change happen? How did you join NVIDIA?

Ever since I started doing deep learning I've been a strong believer in compute. Mitsubishi Electric was not a company that valued compute. It valued algorithms. Back then, in order to do research, to do good research, I often asked my manager at the time to buy GPUs. In meetings I'd say we need GPUs to get this done.

At Mitsubishi Electric there was a long-term mentor. His name is Oncel Tuzel. He's also a very well-known researcher. He decided to leave back then and join Apple to work on cars. And I suddenly felt the main reason that kept me at Mitsubishi Electric was gone. I started thinking about whether I should change jobs too.

Changing jobs very naturally meant going to Silicon Valley and talking with the big companies. Back then everyone was looking at Google, Apple, Amazon, Meta — those big companies. Later their recruiter found me. I looked, oh, NVIDIA. Right, I wanted to buy their GPUs all the time. I was so short on GPUs and wanted them so badly. Why wouldn't I join a company that makes GPUs?

So in the end I decided to join NVIDIA. My parents couldn't quite understand it back then. Because NVIDIA was a company they had never heard of. They said, Apple is great, Google is great. Why would you join this NVIDIA?

What I thought back then was that GPU is the most important thing. Especially back then, when I started working on CoupledGAN. It was an unsupervised approach. An unsupervised approach means data is a bit easier to obtain. You don't need labels. I felt the most important things are compute and data. Since my data didn't need labeling, I'd go where the compute is.

One thing is quite interesting. I later found out that my manager at Mitsubishi Electric back then, every time I argued with him about GPUs, as long as I won the argument he'd give me some budget to buy GPUs and at the same time he'd buy NVIDIA stock. He retired later. He didn't tell you at the time, did he? He told me later. He didn't tell you then — otherwise you could have bought some too. Haha yes.

Mm, I saw that during your time at Mitsubishi Electric you already had some collaboration with people at NVIDIA. Right? On some papers.

No, most of those were papers I wrote during that period. Because academic paper review — sometimes you don't get in on the first submission. It might take several submissions before it's accepted. Research done at Mitsubishi might later, after I arrived at NVIDIA get continued improvements on top of it. That's why some papers have authors from both Mitsubishi and NVIDIA. Right, it wasn't that we collaborated back then. Company-to-company collaboration isn't that easy. Oh, I thought there was some prior collaboration which is why you joined NVIDIA. Actually no. It was a normal job-seeking process.

Right, back then I didn't know NVIDIA had a research organization. I thought they mainly sold GPUs. And the colleagues who interviewed me back then — only after talking with them did I learn oh, they're really doing research — only then did I go over. Back then NVIDIA's research organization had no reputation. How many people were there? When I joined, fewer than 100 people. And they weren't purely doing AI research. Most people worked on graphics.

The group that later did StyleGAN wasn't working on GAN back then either. They were working on other things. Something I remember very vividly is that at NVIDIA Research every year there's something called an offsite. They fly NVIDIA Research colleagues from all over the world to California, to a small town south of Silicon Valley called Monterey. There's an area there where we held two or three days of seminars. That's where I first met Tero Karras the inventor of StyleGAN. And also Timo Aila, Samuli Laine — these important GAN researchers. None of them were doing GAN back then. I had already been doing it for a while. When I met them he told me he was going to solve the GAN problem. And I thought you probably don't know how hard it is. I very much hoped they would succeed but I felt they somewhat underestimated its difficulty.

Later they really kept investing in StyleGAN. From 1 to 2 to 3, constantly breaking through. I learned a lot from collaborating with them. They kept doing the unconditional kind, not the controllable kind that I was doing. But their pursuit of detail, their pursuit of results greatly influenced the development of my research.

如何在 NVIDIA 拿到更多 GPU

Mm, joining NVIDIA to do research — did you get as many GPUs as you expected?

Well, nowhere in this world has enough GPUs. Right, you always see where it's not enough. But I was very lucky. I was among the earliest inside NVIDIA to build large models, a researcher using massive numbers of GPUs for generative networks. Because early on I did some highly visible work for the company, many people in the company knew me. Jensen also had quite a lot of trust in me. So I was fortunate to have lots of GPU resources to do this research. But every time I saw others had more GPUs I felt I never had enough.

How do you get more GPUs in a company like NVIDIA? What do you need to learn?

You need to understand what problems the company wants to solve. You need to find a way to explain to the company why what you're doing will have an impact on the company. Every researcher has their own ideas. Everyone wants to solve problems. In a certain sense, researchers are all very high ego. Scholars have always looked down on one another — it's been true since ancient times. Everyone thinks their own idea is better than others'.

But a company's nature is a bit different. A company exists to generate profit for its shareholders. For Jensen, he hopes to take care of family — the whole company, so many people striving together. He built NVIDIA, and he also hopes to help everyone take care of their families. That means the company has to make money.

So one thing I learned is I deeply believe what I do is very important to the world. This thing will bring about change. And that change will help the company. How do I articulate this clearly so that leadership, so that leaders who don't understand AI come to understand that this matters to the company. This was a major change.

三菱电机的往事：Blue Sky Research 的教训

This is the second of the three moments you shared earlier. In which specific project did this shift happen?

The second moment I talked about was how to help other researchers better understand the importance of what you're doing. It's an ongoing process of constant change for me. It's hard for me to say exactly when it happened. But I want to say the Mitsubishi Electric case influenced me greatly.

Because Mitsubishi Electric was very important in the 90s. It was an early place where you could do research without any restrictions. Including many famous people in the field. Like, you know, Bill Freeman was at Mitsubishi Electric Research Labs back then. And Bill Freeman attracted a bunch — Joe Mark, some famous professors all interned there and produced a lot of major research. So back then it could compete with Microsoft Research.

But at a certain point the company's direction changed. They began to question what impact this blue sky research had on the company. It became harder and harder to justify why they should pay these researchers. And then a very famous thing happened. This is something young people today have never experienced. Back then, a whole group of important scholars at Mitsubishi Electric were fired one after another and left the company. Some joined Microsoft. Some joined universities as professors like MIT, Harvard. Some went to Disney. People left one after another. Some of the people who stayed were still doing similar research but it was harder to relate it to the company's direction. For example, Mitsubishi Electric was into cameras. They were very interested in industrial cameras and very interested in robotic arms. So if you did research on those, you could get the company's support and keep going.

By the time I joined, all of that had already ended. But the training I got back then was that blue sky research and the company's interests can also be aligned. And I've often seen, because I've been in the industry for a long time, I've often seen this kind of cycle. Many companies give a lot of freedom at the beginning and lots of interesting ideas come out. But after a while they start tightening up and the people who remain are those whose work aligns with the company's interests. You can see it, whether it's Google or Meta they all go through this process.

I was probably very lucky that early in my career I saw this process happen. So when I was at NVIDIA, I already knew. Back then I always believed — first, I knew that what I was doing — using deep learning to generate images — was definitely positively relevant to the company. And I put even more effort into understanding how to explain to the company's decision-makers why what I was doing mattered.

This is especially important. Maybe when the company is on the rise or in an expansion phase it allows you to do a lot of blue sky exploration. But as soon as it enters a down phase it contracts. It demands that you answer why the thing you're doing matters. What does it have to do with me? Doing deep learning is very expensive. Right, so you have to focus even more on explaining why this is an important investment for the company.

七、Research as Product 与"模型必然收敛"

People will also notice that your research often follows the philosophy of "research as product." Does that have a lot to do with that experience? Did it later influence a lot of what you did at NVIDIA in terms of research and products? For example, your GauGAN, the project you just mentioned, the SPADE algorithm was actually turned into a real-time drawing product. And later you also did video conferencing enhancement — an AI-enhanced product. It seems all of your research gets released as a product.

Yes, I consider myself a lucky person. I'm someone who, as I get older, values efficiency more and more. So I very deliberately turned my research into a product. Well, I can't say GauGAN is a product. There's another thing I learned — an important lesson: AI on its own cannot change everything.

Hmm, what do you mean?

When doing AI everyone is chasing better and better models. But gradually you realize that model performance is slowly converging. Everyone is about the same. Some people will say there's constant progress but what you see is this month Anthropic is better, next month GPT is better, maybe the month after that Gemini catches up. And those strong companies in China — GLM, Kimi, Seed, Alibaba, Hunyuan, DeepSeek, MiniMax. These companies are all constantly making breakthroughs.

So gradually everyone's model capabilities become about the same. When everyone's model capabilities are about the same, you come to understand that relying purely on the model is not enough. I was probably luckier than most. I believed early on that models would converge. I've always emphasized that you can't rely on the model alone. You have to integrate it with the company's other ecosystems.

Look at how well Gemini is doing — it's because Gemini, Google has a whole suite — Google Docs, Search, a whole platform combined together. The more people use your model, the more feedback you get, and the more convenient it is, the easier it is to contribute to the company. When you contribute to the company, the company is willing to invest more in you and you can build even better models. So you can keep pushing the long-term development forward.

So in my early days doing AI I was like other researchers. The way researchers, PhD students graduate is by writing high-quality papers. What counts as a high-quality paper? Usually it means your benchmark results beat others. You need a killer to defeat other people's methods. So scholars tend to look down on each other, always thinking they're better, and keep going that way. So a lot of the time in early research, everyone claims they're better than others.

But later on I gradually came to understand that being better than others is just one way to prove the value of your work. Another way is you can help others and make everyone better. You'll find my thinking now is increasingly about what can I build that helps the whole field improve, rather than chasing being better than others.

Is that a high ego or a low ego?

I don't know if it's high ego or low ego. I've been fortunate to meet many smart people over the past 20 years. I always feel there are so many talented people in this world. Many of my interns are better than me. And I think that's a wonderful thing. I feel that what I can build can serve society, but I don't think I'm necessarily better than everyone else. So I wouldn't say high ego nor low ego. I just feel I'm able to make a contribution.

与 Frontier Labs 的观点分歧

Hmm, you actually just touched on your approach to building models. You believe models will eventually converge and their capabilities may become homogenized. But as I understand it, those frontier labs believe that intelligence hasn't hit its ceiling yet, that intelligence will keep improving at high speed. You don't agree with their view? They're betting on the scaling of intelligence.

On one hand I'm certainly curious. I use these models myself and I do see them constantly improving. But some people always say there will be exponential growth next. If you don't hurry up and invest in this company or join these companies you'll miss out the opportunity. And I think, looking at history, this has never happened in the past. One company holding all the technology with no other company able to catch up — this has never happened in the world. And I don't think AI will be an exception.

Right, I think everyone is smart. Right, people move around. You always work at company A for a while and feel your talent isn't recognized so maybe you jump to company B. And that know-how naturally spreads throughout the field. I just don't think there will be one company that gets massively ahead of all the others. I don't think that's a stable state of society in itself.

Let me extrapolate a bit. If model intelligence reaches a roughly similar level for everyone, what will everyone compete on next?

Integration — integrating with your own ecosystem and with your own products.

That's for big companies. What about startups?

Startups — the advantage of startups is they can take on problems big companies can't. For example, for Nvidia any business smaller than a billion isn't worth pursuing. But some of those things are genuinely worth doing. There's a famous book called Innovator's Dilemma. It's often these small companies heading into areas that weren't favored at first, seeing something that can gradually grow. Many companies rose this way. NVIDIA was like this too. Right, that's how NVIDIA rose.

So I think it's still full of opportunities. Right, I don't think you necessarily have to — if you start a company now and try to do the same thing as OpenAI and Anthropic that's very dangerous. Right, your funding definitely can't match theirs. And you have no customers. How are you going to accumulate? Plus with their massive resources they can make things cheap and it's hard for you to catch up. So you have to solve pain points they can't solve. It's not that they don't want to solve them, it's that they can't. They can't justify why they should solve that problem.

So even if you want to build a large model, in the end you still have to find your own unique niche. Whether it's OpenAI or Anthropic — we can see that Anthropic was considered behind OpenAI early on. Right, but it was the earliest believer in coding. While OpenAI was making diversified investments, not putting all its eggs in one basket, Anthropic made concentrated investments and was the first to build the coding thing. So it saw some opportunities back then and it firmly believed and was determined to make it happen. So I think for entrepreneurs you should have determination to see an opportunity, to see your unique opportunity and use your resources to get things done.

But today, whether in Silicon Valley or China, everyone is homogeneously doing coding, agentic coding. How do you see this phenomenon? Do you think it's right?

Every company doing this has a different purpose behind it. I'm not in their position so I can't speak for them. But from my perspective this is actually a very grueling thing. You mean homogeneous competition? Homogeneous competition is a grueling thing. I think — I think they may be forced into doing this. Because this is itself an important technology. No one wants their core technology to be in someone else's hands. But I don't think this is the entirety of their plan. They must have other plans to create some differentiation. Without differentiation you can't make a distinctive product. In the end you still have to differentiate. I think so.

八、成为 VP：从研究者到管理者

We just went back over a long stretch of your journey. Looking at yourself as a researcher in your first job after arriving in the US — Ming-Yu Liu — and then becoming a tech lead at NVIDIA and now a VP of Research. Do you think the problems you solve in different periods are the same? The scale keeps getting bigger. And this scale doesn't just mean management scale, right?

Not just management scale — whether it's compute or headcount scale. It's also tied to the overall development of AI. AI going from exploration to real-world deployment. That's one change. These different periods each had different experiences.

Sometimes I still miss the old days when nothing worked no matter what you tried, spending all day thinking about what would work. Why? When there are many possibilities, it's actually quite joyful. Multiple choices — having multiple choices gives you a kind of happiness.

Now there are also many choices. I just feel I'm getting closer and closer. I also quite enjoy going back to the very core of things. Now I find it's very much like — the current solutions are all — oh — a heavy sword with no sharp edge; great skill looks effortless. Solidly building the infrastructure step by step and just getting things written.

In this process of execution I also find it a great experience. I've learned a lot from it. How to help the team see the core essence and improve execution. While at the same time, where innovation is possible, enabling the team to make major innovations to keep up with the changes of the era. I think every period has different challenges, and they're all interesting.

Going from a researcher to a VP at NVIDIA — is that common?

I'm probably the first. You're the first. Right, why do you think that is? That's what I want to ask you.

In my first few years at NVIDIA I was promoted one level every year. Jump, jump, jump, jump — all the way to VP. And I think it's because in the early days, when NVIDIA had no AI talent yet, I was there, helping the company raise its profile in the AI community and explain how AI would impact the company. And I personally love landing things in practice. Step by step I earned the company's trust and the company became willing to give me bigger and bigger projects. Like now — think about it — this whole team with so many people using so much compute. Every day it's millions of dollars in compute costs, storage costs. I think over the years the company built a certain trust in me and only then did I get the chance to lead such a big project.

管理者与研究者的张力

Hmm, so aligning with the company is very important, right? The nature of a pure researcher and that of a manager might be somewhat at odds. Right, researchers need to innovate, researchers have high egos, researchers need recognition. And recognition — sometimes the recognition you want is different from what the company wants. So on your path to becoming a manager, was it possible that you had to suppress part of your researcher's nature? Was it like dancing in shackles?

I think I'm still a researcher. I still read papers all the time. And sometimes I do some implementation to understand things. What I worry about most on the road to becoming a manager — the one thing I worry about most is becoming disconnected from the ground level, not understanding where the core of the problem lies. I force myself to review everyone's code, to read papers, to challenge everyone's ideas, to have debates with people, so to speak, to make sure the direction is right. People who work with me all know I'm probably one of the few VPs who still looks at code and still nitpicks the details. I feel if I didn't do this — of course it's not that I want to become someone great at implementation — it's that I feel if I didn't do these things I wouldn't understand where the pain points are. And then I'd be even less able to understand each person's contribution to the project. I just hope to always stay grounded and see everything clearly. That way I can help the team grow and also clearly see who contributed what.

影响最深的三个人

Hmm, if we look at the past 20 years, the 20 years since you came to the US, who are the people that influenced you the most?

The first would be my advisor Rama Chellappa. He brought me into the field of deep learning. He's really brilliant. He's also exceptionally good at communicating. He can fill any occasion with laughter. Even very serious review meetings. He treats everyone with great respect. I learned a lot from him.

And then, during my internship, my first mentor as an intern Oncel Tuzel. He taught me a lot of machine learning hands-on, step by step. He had a huge, huge influence on me.

After joining NVIDIA I mostly learned from peers. Tero Karras the first author of StyleGAN. He influenced me a lot. Right — in what way? He pursues things to the absolute extreme. If you've read his papers you see his experimental analysis, the process of digging out the essence, that persistence. I've collaborated with many different researchers in that period. Many researchers back then were like — one idea, one paper. At the same time they could write 20 papers or 40 papers a year. Tero only wanted to write one paper a year, putting all of his — he works extremely hard too — pouring all his energy into a single idea, digging deeper and deeper to find the essence of the problem and then make a major contribution. That way the pressure is greater. This thing of staying focused I probably learned it from working with people like him. I learned a lot.

Jensen 的影响：First Principles 与 Prioritization

Hmm, and what about Jensen? Did he influence you?

A tremendous influence. He's an extremely hard-working person. When I first joined NVIDIA he would often send me papers to read. Then I'd have to write summaries for him and explain to him what it was about. He's someone who loves learning deeply, always learning, always trying to understand. He didn't know computer graphics back then but he dared to step into making GPUs. He went and learned computer graphics. He didn't know deep learning either but he stepped into AI too and came to understand deep learning. And it's his powerful ability to learn, his powerful curiosity, keeping going forward.

Hmm, if he didn't understand it, why did he dare to invest?

He has his own set of decision-making rules. It's called first principles. He takes the essence of a matter and sorts it out clearly without being disturbed by outside signals. Then he sees very clearly which direction makes the most sense and heads that way. Early on he dared to go all in on deep learning, giving the company a huge lead. Early on he dared to go all in on CUDA, building a great foundation for the company.

Before I got to know Jensen, I feel my decisions tend to be fairly short-term. Watching how he makes these long-term decisions and sticks with them, I think the impact is truly astonishing. There are other amazing things about him. He gets a huge number of messages every day. Emails, you mean? Right, a huge number of emails. But he reads them all very carefully, looking for signals that others can't see and makes major decisions.

He is a very rational person. When you have a lot of things going on, if you can't do prioritization — that is, do the important things — and instead spend your time on unimportant things, you won't get the important things done. So deciding which things are important is a very important thing in itself. That's prioritization. This is how I reason about it myself.

He forces himself to read a huge volume of emails every day, forces himself to decide quickly what is important and what is not. Practicing this every single day, he sees things with great clarity. Okay, once you see clearly what is important and what is not, everything after that is execution. And when many people execute, they mix in their personal feelings — like, this isn't that important but I'm on good terms with that person, should I let him do it? He doesn't do that. His thinking is simply: my job is to take care of the whole company. I just keep making the most important decisions for the company. As long as you stay with the company, I will take care of you.

Right, I learned from him how to do prioritization. And this left a very deep impression on me. I mean, now — back when I was a researcher, handling two or three projects at the same time felt exhausting, switching between two or three topics a day. And now I switch topics almost every half hour. I couldn't have imagined myself doing this before. But being in this state of constant context switching also helps me better understand what really matters.

Right, and that's a very important thing. And there's another thing. If you've studied Computer Science, the most important thing in Computer Science is laziness. Don't compute what you don't need to compute. What can be computed later, compute later. What can be ignored, ignore entirely. You only have so much time in your life. You only have so much energy. If you can figure out what not to compute and just remove it, your life runs much more efficiently. So I think it's still well worth studying Computer Science. Don't stop studying Computer Science just because of AI.

So what has Jensen excluded from his scope of computation?

It's different in every period. Right, it's not fixed forever. Hmm, for example, right now? He has way too many things to deal with. It's hard to say what isn't important right now. What I see and what he sees are on completely different levels. What he sees is — he's essentially a key driver of AI globally. Right, what he sees far exceeds what I've seen. I'm in no position to comment on what he considers unimportant now.

九、功夫、冰浴与生活方式

I heard you practice kung fu, right? Yes. You have a kung fu teacher? I have a kung fu teacher. My martial arts teacher is Xu Ji. He is a very famous martial arts teacher. Yes.

That's quite different from my impression of you. Because every time I see you, you come across as very gentle and humble. But you still do sports that are relatively a bit intense, right? Ice water, martial arts.

十、Cosmos 的愿景：为机器人建造 Matrix

Hmm, let's now focus on Cosmos and world models — which is also your most important topic right now. I saw on your personal homepage that you've been driven by a vision of building a Matrix for robots. Can you elaborate on this vision?

I believe world models can help these embodied intelligences achieve this generalization. I think for any AI problem the problem to solve is generalization. Can you perform really well beyond the training data you've seen? Generalization right? Like in Coding or in Chat, it's all about training a model so it can solve problems it never saw during training, becoming more like a human, right? AI for the physical world is no exception. You have to solve generalization.

And to solve generalization at Cosmos, here's how we want to help. Three points.

  • First, provide better data.
  • Second, provide a better starting point.
  • Third, provide a better environment.

For data, you can generate data. Data is the key to making AI models generalize better. You can imagine, in this world the data you've seen is only so many points. Can you generate some of what you need to see but haven't collected in the real world?

And next — if you can train a good world model, this world model understands how the world works and can predict what will happen in the future. Such a model has a pretty good representation in itself. It can actually provide a physical-world AI — whether it's a policy model or any other model from which you can derive the policy you want. That's a better starting point.

Better data, better starting point. Third — how does a person learn in this physical world? Through experiments — by interacting with the environment. Interacting with the real environment is often expensive. The time you can accumulate experience is limited. That's a limit. If you could use something like The Matrix to generate multiple environments at once, incredibly realistic environments that you can interact with that give you signals, you could learn very, very fast. That's a better environment.

Better data, better starting point, better environment. The most challenging of these is the better environment. I didn't want to write it out at great length on my webpage like an essay. So I put it as something like The Matrix — it's a better way to help everyone understand what we want to do, how we want to help the Physical AI community.

内部立项与 Sora 时刻

How exactly was Cosmos greenlit internally? Was that 2024 or 2025?

2024, I think. We started in 2024. Around March 2024 we decided to do it. That was after Sora. Right, after Sora. It was exactly that point in time. And everyone felt this was full of resolve — we had to do it. I was honored that Jensen trusted me and let me lead this project.

Was it hard to convince him?

On this matter, by then it wasn't hard anymore. Before, it was harder to convince him. After seeing Sora, it wasn't hard. He's a very smart person. One look and he knew what this would mean for the company. Because he's a very disciplined person. Even when something is very important he'll tell you to pace — meaning, don't rush. He's good at fighting marathons. Hmm right. So he's very disciplined, moving toward the goal slowly, step by step.

Why hadn't the timing been right before? Before Sora.

Before Sora — well, first movers have a first mover advantage right? And every company has a different positioning. It depends on what problems you want to solve and how you want to profit. I don't have enough information to judge. But I don't think — look, many companies are doing very well now. The most profitable in video generation right now is probably ByteDance Seedance right? So this trajectory is hard to predict.

By the time Sora came, you felt the timing was right. Did you write him another email?

It was a group of us working on generative models, this group doing media generation, we decided together to write Jensen an email. I guess everyone wrote one. Everyone wrote one? Not one joint letter. We would discuss and then write one together and everyone would add their input. It became a company-wide consensus that we had to build this thing.

Oh, did Jensen reply to that email? Yes — he gathered us together for a meeting. And at that meeting we reached a consensus. Actually, everyone had reached a consensus before the meeting. The meeting just made it more concrete — exactly how to do it, who would be responsible, and so on.

He asked us to come up with a name. At the time I actually already knew he would come up with a better name in the end. Look, we called it Cosmos — it's a universe. Our goal is not to generate content, not to enable content creation — it's to solve problems in the physical world. That's how we gradually moved toward Physical AI. Because Sora is really about serving creators. That's how its early demos framed it.

Why did you choose Physical AI back then? In terms of the market you were targeting.

By then it was gradually becoming clear that Physical AI would be the next revolution. Because it's a rigid demand. Everyone ages. Every place lacks labor. Everyone wants a better quality of life. And on the other hand Nvidia goes after the developer market, helping these developers build better products. We ourselves wouldn't run a social network, nor would we run a creation tool. That's a bit too to C for NVIDIA. So you decided: I want to build a world model and this world model is for Physical AI — to serve the Physical AI community.

十一、世界模型的定义之争

Today, the definition of a world model is still very unclear. Tell us your definition of a world model.

I'm someone who values practicality. Why do people design a model? Because it can be used. There are many uses.

For example, you design a model — design a model to describe this world. Through this model, you can predict what will happen next. So its purpose is prediction. That's one kind of world model, one reason for designing a world model. A use: prediction.

Another is that you want to understand why this thing happened. In a sense all of physics is about building world models to understand how the world works. From Newtonian mechanics all the way to quantum mechanics, it's all about understanding how the world works — also building a model to help us understand how things work. Of course, in deep learning we take this understanding using only some labeled data to teach the model that this thing behaves this way. It's because this thing happened and then with large-scale data generalization, to help when new events happen in the future you interpret the video signals you see to help people understand what happened. For example, in a factory, why did the production line suddenly get stuck here? Maybe some worker earlier forgot to turn something on. This is also one purpose of building a world model — understanding.

Right. And there's another kind of world model whose goal is to reconstruct the 3D world. Reconstructing the 3D world is very useful. You can plan which route your things should take. And you can let people experience it. Even though you're not physically in this real world, you can, in a virtual state, travel around in this world.

So — models for the world. Because your use cases differ, the models take different forms. In the end, we live in the same world. These models, through different observations, describe the same thing. Reconstruction is a very important field. I myself did reconstruction work before. But I no longer do reconstruction now. I now mainly work on understanding the physical world and generation of the physical world — right, things like prediction.

Everyone interprets world models differently. Defining what a World Model is now — a few years ago, the same thing happened when everyone was defining what AGI is. Right. And after all these years, there's still no shared definition. I think defining the World Model will very likely go down the same path. I don't think it's necessarily a very important thing.

Is that because the term is too big? Too general.

Right, it's too general. Once defined, what impact would that have on humanity? Then why is LLM a relatively precise term?

LLM is large language model. The model is very large, and it works on language. Right. So why does everyone have a consensus on this term, a precise definition, while people keep arguing endlessly about world models?

An LLM is an LLM — a large language model. A language model can predict what word comes next. Right? Large means the model is very big. That's very clear. Right? A world model is a tool that helps you model the world. What do you want to use it for? Because the use cases differ, the way you model the world differs. So as long as you have different uses for this model, you get different definitions.

So do you think "world model" can describe Cosmos? Or should another term be used to describe what you're doing?

Yes. At the very beginning, we called Cosmos a world foundation model. Our goal is to build a foundation so that everyone can build the world models that suit their needs. That's why we call ourselves a foundation model, because we hope to be a more fundamental layer that serves everyone. That's how we define it.

Even someone who wants to build a world model can build on top of your foundation model. Yes — you want to provide that base. Right. Because we believe world models will be an important part of Physical AI. But not every company that wants to work on Physical AI has enough resources to build the world model it needs from scratch — yet they need it. So to help them, we built Cosmos, this world foundation model.

与其他 World Model 团队的差异

Since you've also invested in LeCun's AMI Labs and Professor Fei-Fei Li's World Labs, are there differences between the world models you each make?

NVIDIA stands from an enabler's perspective. What we hope is, for any company built on our GPU ecosystem, we hope to help them succeed. We hope everyone can succeed together — win-win. Each company sees things a bit differently and wants to solve different problems. So there are all kinds of them. Fei-Fei's World Labs, Yann LeCun's AMI — they're all different, taking different routes. We help all of them, hope they succeed, and invest in them. We also collaborate with them. If they're interested in our Cosmos stuff, they can use it. Other companies need world models but may not be able to, unlike Fei-Fei or Yann LeCun, who are well funded. They may need help even more. They can leverage our Cosmos. Our goal is to help the whole field succeed.

So do you have competitors? I think NVIDIA's competitors are companies doing the same things as NVIDIA — that is, building this whole AI ecosystem. You said you have no competitors. But some companies also make compute. When I'm working on Cosmos now, I don't think about competitors. What I think about is how to help this ecosystem. Within this ecosystem, those within NVIDIA's ecosystem — using our GPUs, our computing platform, and our software — if they all succeed, then NVIDIA will succeed. Right? Because it gives people not yet in our ecosystem confidence.

I think this is the way to help. I don't really want to compete anymore. I'm past that stage. Like back when, to graduate and get papers published, my algorithm had to be better than others'. Yes. Now my goal is to help this field move forward together.

十二、Cosmos 从 1 到 3：合并成一个模型

From the first to the third generation of Cosmos, it actually went through many changes. In the process from generation one to two, did you accumulate any know-how?

Yes. Well, this was last year's work. Right, the pace is very fast. Back when we started working on Cosmos, I emphasized one point: we must iterate fast. At that time I was deeply influenced by DeepSeek. Because DeepSeek is an astonishing company. It can iterate three times within a year and produce DeepSeek V3. So I kept stressing that our iteration speed must be fast. If iteration is fast, you can keep improving continuously, each generation better than the last.

But the problem we were tackling then was physical world models. At that time, especially in '24, it wasn't very clear. Everyone was still groping around for what kind of world model would help people. As I just said, using a world model is nothing more than how you use it — prediction or understanding — making a video model to help predict the future, or making a reasoning model to explain what happened.

So at the very beginning, we worked with some partners to understand their needs, had some ideas of our own, and built these models. After iterating with these partners, we gradually converged. In the process, we slowly converged. After we did Predict, being able to predict the future, we thought — simulation environments are commonly used, but the video they generate has a certain gap from the real world. Could we use a model to help make it more realistic? So we made Transfer. To explain what happened, we made Reason. At that time there were three.

Later we realized that if I can describe how pixels change, then this pixel change is actually very close to the change in my action. So we made something called Cosmos Policy, a policy model.

Later we gradually realized — as I just said — this is the same world. No matter which angle you look from, you're modeling the same world. Your model is learning an internal representation of the world. That is, this world — in the process of compressing it, what kind of representation you learn. Since it's the same thing, and there's also this thing called foundation model, whose core concept is that it can take in all streams and learn from all kinds of data — a model that learns these patterns. So if you can take the data used to train reasoning, the data used to train predict, the data used to train transfer, the data used to train policy, and combine them all, your model's ceiling is higher. First, you're describing the same world. Second, a foundation model takes in everything, combining things together.

So we gradually moved toward this single model.

22 个模型和 LV 陈列的故事

There's also a practical, execution-level issue in between. I remember when I was building the first version of Cosmos, I did the math myself. Because I hoped the models could really help others — working with these partners, I might need models A, B, C, D, E, F, G. I calculated it myself: back then we might need 22 models.

At that time I had a meeting with Jensen, and I told Jensen that I expected to need 22 models. When Jensen heard that, he thought I was working very hard. And he said, "Very good, work very hard." He said, "But you know what? Louis Vuitton — LV, that store — after it reduced the number of items on display, sales actually went up. You don't want too many things confusing your consumers, so they can't make a decision." That had a big impact on me. I realized that I myself ran into this problem: even I couldn't tell whether to use A or B, let alone other people.

Then there's the execution difficulty. Every time you release a model, it's not like we publish a paper and it's done, then move on to the next paper. We have to help users use it. Whenever a model comes out, we have to maintain it and solve problems. When you have many models, it's really hard. Prepare for everything and your strength is spread thin. It affects your iteration speed.

So when working on version one, during the iteration process, we quickly worked on two. While working on two, we realized no — this wouldn't be sustainable. So we decided to make this only model — the World Model — that is, Cosmos 3. First, they describe the same thing so they can actually be combined. Second, a foundation model absorbs all kinds of data, combined together. It's also much simpler in development. So we went down the path of Cosmos 3.

So 2 to 3 was actually a big change. Yes. The change from 1 to 2 was basically an improvement in data, plus some others — back in 2 we brought policy in. There were some changes. But I think 2 to 3 is a very big gap.

How long did 3 take?

We started on 3 last October, right after releasing 2. It was October when we released 2, right. Actually, we knew even earlier that we had to do 3. But by then we had already started 2.5. We wrapped up 2.5, and only started 3 after wrapping up 2.5. So maybe around September we knew we needed to do 3. Actual execution was probably October, November. It took nearly half a year.

关于"没有大创新"的评价

A Chinese founder working on world models said he spent a week reading the Cosmos 3 paper, reading it every day, and there are lots of details in it. He said their view was that Cosmos 3 doesn't have many big technical innovations, but it has engineering-validated many of the details. Do you think their assessment is fair?

Mixture Transformer was proposed by others before, and Policy Model was also proposed before. We are the first to scale this Mixture Transformer to such a large model, combining audio, video, and action together. Conceptually, these things are just combining things together, but actually making it work is not that easy. Actually pulling it off comes down to these details.

All these large language models use the Transformer architecture. You could say nobody innovated, but it's those details that make some models much better than others. I think after all these years, I value more the effects these things can produce, and I care less and less about whether something is a revolutionary original. To me, it's useful and produces impact. Solving the problems people want solved is the point.

Right. With this paper, we hope to help the entire open-source community build open-source models and help all of Physical AI. The phenomenon we've seen these years is that many Frontier Labs have gone closed-source. Even when they write papers, they won't reveal the key parts. We decided to take a different path. We explain everything we can as clearly as possible. We open-sourced the model, and also the framework for how we train it. We also open-sourced part of the synthetic data. We want to stay transparent and let everyone see how it's done. We also hope others can use our open-source materials to build something similar to Cosmos, if they're interested. Our goal is to enable this entire community.

Right. I'm not worried that others can make an identical thing.

You just mentioned DeepSeek — is your choice to open-source related to it?

Not exactly related. DeepSeek's work has had a profound impact on all of AI — the first company to open-source MoE. And look at its recent models, the care they put in, pushing it to the extreme. These have all profoundly influenced the field. Right, I think this is very important. From the perspective of impact, I think they're connected. We want to make an impact, laying out all these details. NVIDIA has many Physical AI companies built on the NVIDIA ecosystem. We hope to help them succeed. Our goal may be different from DeepSeek's. We hope to help our users succeed. You are inherently this ecosystem. Right, we just hope to help Physical AI arrive in the world sooner.

四种模态与 Action 作为一等公民

Why did you choose this time, first at the input layer, to support inputting language, video, audio, and action at the same time? Was this an important decision?

Yes. I think the world isn't only visual. Right? There's also hearing. I'd also like to add touch, but tactile signals aren't good enough yet. Touch sensors and such are still iterating rapidly. This requires dexterous hands. Right, it needs dexterous hands, it needs data.

I think for large models, there are basically two lines of thinking. One treats language as a first-class citizen, like Coding, like Chat. The other treats visual signals — video — as a first-class citizen, like Seedance, like Veo. We believe the biggest difference between physical world models and digital world models is that physical-world agents take action and change the state of the world. We believe a good physical-world foundation model should also treat action as a first-class citizen. That's why we combined language, video, and action together to build this Cosmos 3.

Right. I remember Yang Zhilin once told me that when they build language models, he treats language as the most important tool for advancing intelligence. They worried a lot that adding vision would affect its intelligence, turning it into a dumb multimodal model. But this year Xie Saining told me he worries about language polluting vision. He thinks language is humanity's scaffolding, not something essential — that's his view. So how do you view these two perspectives of theirs? And when you train all these signals together, does this kind of problem arise? Mutual pollution, that is.

Each of these signals is brought in with its own purpose.

  • Language can bring in human knowledge and also help humans communicate with physical AI.
  • Video provides massive visual information, audio provides massive auditory information, describing how the world works. Using video captures the world's physical workings more precisely. With language, that's actually very hard.
  • Right? But between humans and the model — the model is ultimately built to serve people. If it doesn't understand language, you can't communicate with it. Ultimately the model is meant to help machines take action. So if it doesn't understand action, it can't change the world.

I should put it this way: our purposes are different. My goal is for this to become a good foundation model for physical AI. It needs to understand language, needs to know how things change, and then action, and then use this control to bring them together. My goal is not to pursue AGI. Right, and AGI itself is hard to define. When the AGI you define is purely about understanding the essence of humans, or whatever, doing coding, these visual signals might interfere with you. That's inevitable.

Right? Yes, you could say in the distant ancient past there was no language at all — all of this development of human civilization is generated by observing how the world changes. You could argue that after all, language evolved to suit humans but you don't know whether machines buy into that. Maybe you just, from visual signals, directly learn how the world works and arrive at an intelligence and then develop another civilization. If you look at it from that angle, maybe the language signal is a kind of interference.

I think it depends on what you want. I know very clearly what I want. So I think I need language so that people can communicate with this Physical AI. I need video and audio to describe, from the changes in the physical world, to learn the physical essence. And I need action because in the end I want it to be able to, for Physical AI, to change the world.

模态之间是互补还是干扰？

Right, so all modalities are fused together. Do these modalities mutually benefit each other, or do they constrain each other?

Over the past year, even more than a year, we've been continuously researching the fusion of these modalities. And from various different research efforts we got some clues and combined them in Cosmos 3.

For example, in the Cosmos Policy work, we found that combining video and action helps the action side. When you directly predict action, when we were building the world action model, we found that besides predicting what action to take, you also predict what comes next — the state that results after you take this action, that is, the observation — which helps you train it well. So we know that predicting the video helps the action.

This whole family of world action models — sound can also help video generation. When you know there's a "click" sound, the point of contact — you know the moment of contact is that point. So we know these are mutually complementary.

People who work on video generally know that going from text to video is a process where the amount of information increases, the demand grows larger, which means there are many possibilities. A function with many possibilities is harder to learn. One thing might have 10 possibilities. Then there's no fixed target, so it's hard to learn. So in video or image generation, everyone finds that when your text description is very detailed, it's easier to generate a good video. So you can see that a detailed text description also helps the video.

With Cosmos 3, we wanted to bring together the earlier Cosmos Reason, Cosmos Predict, Cosmos Transfer, Cosmos Policy — all these things together. Combining them has its own benefits — the whole thing gets simplified.

How do these signals get combined so that they complement each other rather than working against each other? This can be achieved through experimental design and by adjusting the proportions of the data. So at the time we firmly believed that these signals all describe the same world and they all contain information about how the world works. There should be a way to combine them so that they help each other. More information helps you understand what the underlying operating principles are. Right, so we had this belief and set out in that direction.

So is there any secret sauce in this, in terms of the mutual benefit?

Actually, there's no secret sauce in building large models. Run rigorous experiments, make hypotheses, run experiments, see the results, accumulate knowledge, then run the next experiment. Just go step by step, do solid work, that's it. There's nothing — I don't think there's any hidden secret. It's just what you pursue: patiently run experiments, validate, and if it checks out, take the next step that way.

为什么是"双塔"设计

Mm. This time you adopted a dual-tower design, one tower processing discrete information and one tower processing continuous information. Why this design?

There are many reasons. In the beginning, Cosmos Reasoning was discrete, starting from a vision language model. Predict, Transfer, Policy were continuous. So we knew discrete works for understanding, and we knew continuous works for generation. Putting them together is a very reasonable choice at this stage.

And another thing, there are many ways to use Cosmos, but the common one is post-training. Maybe you use your video-action pairs to train the generator, or maybe you only want to use the reasoning part and only train it with understanding data from your own domain. When you have two parts that can work together while keeping the gradient influence separated, it makes it easier for customers to use. If we connected everything together, then generation and understanding would be tied together. Now suppose I want to change the generation distribution. In the process, since everything is connected, your data would also change the performance on the understanding side. If you don't have two towers but just one, then since the understanding side will change, and your data has no understanding data in it, the understanding part can easily get lost. That makes it inconvenient for customers to use.

So splitting it into two definitely helps usability. Although it's relatively less elegant, because you still have to decide the architecture in advance. In terms of dependency, ideally the data decides how it's done, rather than you artificially making the distinction. But at this stage, I think this is the more reasonable choice and better suited for practical use.

Speaking of this, people can probably guess that our next goal is to make it simpler. Why two towers? One tower should be enough. But as we move toward the goal of one tower, we have to consider whether users can easily adopt it. Because our goal is to help everyone win, not to produce a model ourselves that can do many things. We believe every robot is different — the number of cameras, the camera positions — and every autonomous vehicle is different too. We feel we need restraint: even if we merge everything to pursue engineering simplicity and perfection, I still have to consider whether users can actually make use of it. That's a problem we must research.

Mm. But relatively speaking, discrete signals are easier to handle; once you fuse in continuous variables, the processing difficulty increases. How do you combine them and scale it up?

Right. There's now a series of works like Transfusion that can handle both discrete and continuous. When doing next token prediction, it's discrete; when doing diffusion, it's continuous. That's within the same tower. During this period there have been many different variants. Everyone is researching this; it's a problem everyone cares about. I think these signals can be represented discretely or continuously. I hope that maybe we can develop an architecture that is all discrete, or all continuous, to make things relatively simpler. But that's an ideal; we're not sure it can succeed. We also need to validate step by step with experiments as we go.

Intuitively, which is easier — discrete or continuous?

Ah, each has its own advantages. Discrete is easier to train. Continuous has its own elegance — that is, when doing Influence, the two have very different shapes. Ultimately, the key point is that customers still have to deploy it. And cost considerations at deployment are very important. So I think in the end it comes down to deployment — what kind of model is best suited for deployment — I think that's what most easily leads to success. So there are many directions, and the discussion should focus there.

一个模型能同时做 Coding 吗？

A researcher asks you: Since you're now training all modalities into one model, then in theory it could also do Coding very well, it could make robots work, and it could generate creator content like what we have today. So is it possible that in a single dimension, say Coding, it could be even stronger than Claude?

I still like what The Art of War says: "He who defends everywhere defends nowhere." If you want to be good at everything, during training you need to be broadly knowledgeable, you have to cover many different categories to raise your level of knowledge. But if you're sure you only need this single application, then are there some adjustments — since you don't care about the other things — is there anything you're willing to give up to do it better? Because if you're not willing to give up anything, you'll have a very hard fight.

I think strategy is often about deciding what you can afford to give up.

Will the two towers improve each other?

We know that — we have an experiment in this paper showing that when you use a reasoner closer to Physical AI, it can help you do better Physical AI generation. We also know that if you can pass the generator's gradient back to the reasoner, in theory it can help your reasoner learn better representations. In this paper, limited by time, we didn't complete all the experiments we wanted to do. There were already many experiments. But this thing — foundation model development itself is very time-consuming. A decision is made two or three months in advance. It's hard to make quick adjustments. We don't see this 3 as the end point. We'll continue with 3.1, 3.2, improving step by step — adding the capabilities we want to build in and the research we want to do that we didn't get a chance to present this time — we'll keep filling those in.

泛化：物理 AI 的核心问题

Mm. Besides possibly being simpler — the two towers might become one — what other changes might people see in future models?

What we care a lot about is how this model can help Physical AI builders. After this model was released, as far as I know, everyone has been discussing it. Some partners, some colleagues have given pretty good feedback. I think generalization is a core problem — a core problem for any AI. And in physical-world AI, I think one kind of generalization we need to achieve is: suppose today I teach a robot that I like my clothes folded this way and placed like this. I show the robot once or twice how I do it — can it then learn it quickly, learn it quickly in real life? If you let the Physical AI read the manual, will it know how to operate the instrument, how to do inspection in a factory? I think these are very important capabilities that Physical AI should be able to achieve. Of course, there are many considerations when deploying these.

What I mean is, in the foundation model part, is there something we can do to help these Physical AI developers? So our improvements will probably all be directed toward improving these generalization capabilities and building these things into the Cosmos model.

For example, what specific optimizations have you made for this? Optimizations like acceleration will definitely happen. Of course we want the model to run faster and faster. Other optimizations are about capability, optimizations for generalization. Right. That might involve changing some architecture, or changing some training objectives, or using some specially curated data for the training. It's not entirely clear; it needs testing. It's an experimental science. Right, it's an experimental science.

I often feel deep learning is a lot like traditional Chinese medicine — it's figured out through trial and error. Through trial and error, right. And in the process of trying, you keep detailed experimental records and from them you understand the underlying principles. I think this is very interesting. I think these two things are very similar. I think running rigorous experiments, controlling variables, and getting some key results is an important step in model iteration.

Some researchers have also suggested that the model's language rendering — could its weighting be increased a bit more? Because they still believe LLMs are the key to improving intelligence. Do you agree?

I think in early image generation research, including Imagen — Google's Imagen — it was already proposed that the stronger your language understanding, when you use a larger T5 model, the stronger your image generation capability. I do believe that. Using a larger semantic representation should help. I agree with that. After all, Physical AI applications are different from what people often talk about — Coding or Chat. So experimental validation is still needed.

What I want to do is understand the real pain points and from those pain points find the right way to strengthen the model's capabilities. There are signals everyone has received that a better model — when you have no resource constraints, of course you'd put it in. But the more challenging thing is when your resources are limited, how do you make the trade-offs?

Mm. So maybe for these scenarios, intelligence may not be the most critical variable. Do you need your robot to solve math olympiad problems? Do you need your robot to solve Coding problems? I think you probably care more about whether it can assemble well what your factory needs to assemble, or handle household chores — do these tasks well. Right. So I think the problem you're solving seems somewhat different from what these large language model companies, these Agent companies, are solving. It's a bit different.

So since it's a different problem, the cost of solving it is ultimately an important — if you want to commercialize, cost is ultimately an important consideration. So under these conditions, will its architecture really be the same as the existing models built for agents? This is a question I've been thinking about. Do you have a preliminary answer now? Any intuition?

Looking across human history, the answer is that it should be different. Right? The tools you make for plowing fields are different from the tools you make for weaving. So they're actually different. In the end, "he who defends everywhere defends nowhere," right? The wisdom of our ancestors still works pretty well.

资源与项目重要性

How many GPUs and resources will you invest in Cosmos going forward?

We've been — the GPU count has been increasing. I'm not sure it's appropriate for me to disclose the number of GPUs. But we're already at the tens-of-thousands level and we hope it can be even more.

Will it be NVIDIA's most important model project?

NVIDIA has several model projects. We mainly divide them into two categories: one is called Agentic AI, that is, doing Coding, Chat — serving customers' needs for agentic, digital-intelligence capabilities. In this category we have the Nemotron model — the Nemotron Ultra their team recently released has achieved pretty good results. On the Physical AI side, the main one is the Cosmos model.

Cosmos is a base model. NVIDIA also cares a lot about autonomous vehicles, cares a lot about robots, and about factories. For us, these are all Physical AI applications. And for autonomous vehicles — it's a specialization built on top of Cosmos, doing the optimizations specifically needed for autonomous vehicles. GR00T does robot-related optimizations on top of Cosmos, and also includes things like whole body control. I see the teams working on autonomous vehicles, internally working on autonomous vehicles, and on robots, as my customers too, and I hope to help them succeed.
