On the Physical AI side, Cosmos is the core, helping these key developers succeed.

So there are mainly two. You ask which is most important — both are very important. Digital AI, how to use agents, how to do Coding is very important. Physical AI is very important too. It's hard to say which is more important. Right. But the fiercest competition right now is in Agentic AI. Physical AI is the next step. How big a market do you think Physical AI will be?

This should be a huge market. Estimating market size is not my expertise, and it's not appropriate for me to speak for the company on how big. But as the population ages, with the demand for autonomy in manufacturing, and all kinds of applications, we believe this will be a huge market.

评估方法与数据

Mm-hmm. Since world models currently lack effective evaluation methods, do you have any good explorations?

World models, large language models — everyone is seeking better evaluation and testing methods. Generally speaking, model evaluation has three steps:

  1. The first is benchmarks — there are some fixed datasets and you test its quality on them.
  2. The second is Arena style — compare A with B and see which is better.
  3. The third is working with experts — with people who really have this pain point, to solve the problem.

I think all three are important. In Physical AI, the third is especially important. Because every Coding Agent is solving Coding problems, digital-use problems, but for Physical AI, each problem to solve is somewhat different. Right, I think we emphasize more working with customers, with partners who are willing to collaborate. Let's also talk about how to evaluate whether a model is truly useful or not. That's not an easy thing to do. It's an important step in guiding model development. I think in the future of development, this step will become more and more important.

Data is also a difficult problem. How did you do it this time?

Data is a difficult problem, and it's especially hard in Physical AI, because in Physical AI, every form factor is different. To collect data, without a physical setup, there's no way to collect that data. And at NVIDIA it's even harder, because we serve all kinds of Physical AI developers. Every robot is different. So what we can do is find the most common ground.

We think there are mainly two types of Physical AI data:

  • One is navigation data, going from A to B.
  • The other is manipulation data — how to use a hand or a tool to manipulate things and complete a given task.

Navigation data is easier to work with. It's just — how a car moves, how a robot moves. These can all be collected. So for robot A and robot B, even if they're different, moving around is just displacement in space, sometimes with some rotation added. So they're relatively similar.

Manipulation is more complex. We've noticed a trend: everyone is increasingly pursuing robot arms that resemble human hands. The argument is that — the human world was built for humans to use, so most tools are designed to be operated by human hands. And AI needs huge amounts of data. The easier your data is to obtain, the faster you can achieve breakthroughs. And most of the data collection is done by people. And people have hands. Okay, so two circumstances — two conditions: hand-based data collection, and the world is largely built for human hands. So that's why you see everyone moving in the direction of human hands.

So with Cosmos 3 this time, we specifically added ego-centric data, which includes how human eyes see things, from a first-person view, and how human hands manipulate objects. Because our goal is not to build a robot ourselves. Our goal is to help everyone build great robots. So we look for the things that are most transferable. I think ego-centric data is very important to everyone.

Given all the current limitations we just talked about, does NVIDIA have any significant advantages?

At NVIDIA, the cost of getting GPU compute is cheaper. After all, we make GPUs. And also, we've been deeply involved in Physical AI for many years. We have the Thor chip, and simulators like Isaac. So I think with all these things combined, we can offer more tools to meet all kinds of needs of Physical AI developers. And one more thing: we genuinely want to help other companies succeed. Because we're very clear about where our own services lie. We don't get caught in constant comparisons. I think customers are often more willing to work with us, because we — we won't go and make exactly the same thing as you and then just — wipe you out. No, that's not our goal.

关于 Cosmos 3 的满意与遗憾

What's the thing you're most satisfied with about this model (Cosmos 3)? And what might you feel a bit regretful about?

What I'm satisfied about is that — I told everyone back then that we could combine all the past models into one and it would be better than all the previous models. And that actually happened. Our current model performs better than each of the standalone models before. Back then many people didn't believe it. I felt very happy about that.

The second thing is — this was the first time we took the whole team, which had been building several models, and merged them to build one model. Getting such a large organization to come together to build this model — I'm personally very proud that this happened smoothly.

What's the regret? I think our model — because of time constraints — well, I think the model could still keep improving, but because of the time limit, we didn't let it fully converge before we had to release it. There are still many things we wanted to fix that we didn't have time to change before. So that's the place where — after all, you always want to pursue a better result, but time is limited. The good thing is we'll keep making 3.1, 3.2, and we'll take the things we didn't do well and put them back in.

Hmm, have you ever thought about what old Huang said — what it would be like to reach generation 97?

When I heard "97 generations" back then, my understanding was — we have the determination to keep building it all the way, to make it great. That's a very big commitment, because building these models is very resource-intensive. He showed his determination to keep going. The confidence I got from it is that — this thing will keep moving forward. World models, in the end, are about — approaching the real world. From — through that model, you can learn the things you want to learn in the real world. So I think we're heading in that direction. Actually, the closest thing to it is — you have the ability to create, at any time, the Matrix from The Matrix. I think that's the ultimate form. I'm not sure whether it needs to go all the way to generation 97. Look, if we do one generation every six months, that's still more than forty years away, right? More than forty years. Right. But I think AI is developing extremely fast now, so maybe it won't take forty-plus years.

十三、数字 AI vs 物理 AI 的架构分化

Your team works both on models for the digital world and on models for Physical AI. What do you think the difference is in training the two types of models? Is the difference big?

The current state is like this: on the Nemotron side, they use something called a hybrid architecture. Some layers are traditional Transformer, but some layers are Mamba-style, close to an RNN architecture. That kind of architecture has its advantages, because RNN computation is — at inference, RNN computation is cheaper than Transformer. An agent has to generate a pile of tokens. Sometimes you need the agent to do things that take a long time, so there's this compute cost requirement.

On the Physical AI side, our architecture no longer follows that route. We still go with the more traditional Transformer, but we move toward Mamba Transformer, adding action into it. So the development of the models on these two sides is — gradually becoming a bit different. But our two teams work very closely together. You can see in the Cosmos 3 paper that many of the authors came from Nemotron. We collaborate with them, drawing on their experience, building some models together.

In the future, could these two models be unified into one larger model?

It's all possible. Our decision-making is very simple: whatever helps the customer the most — that's what we do. Right, we're very low ego.

组织与协作

You also mentioned earlier that Cosmos is a very large team. What do you think is the hard part of driving such a large team to work together? The challenge, I mean. I recall the paper had something like 290-plus authors — under 300 people, right?

Right, this team is very big. The way I see it, it's an organizational design challenge. You want everyone's goals to be aligned, but you also want everyone to be able to make decisions autonomously. When everyone's goals are aligned but nobody can make decisions, progress will be very slow, because only a small number of decision-makers can make decisions. Suppose only I could make the decisions — only I decide how to adjust the data mixture, only I decide how to build the architecture — then our model would not succeed, because my knowledge is limited and my time is limited. What we need is for everyone to be able to make decisions that matter for the organization and the model's development.

And the second thing is, if everyone can make decisions but their goals aren't aligned — I just want to make action great, I don't care at all about how video is doing; I just want to make understanding great, not caring about anything else — then things will diverge. You might end up with different architectures, and it might turn into horse-racing behavior between teams.

I think in running such a big project, the key is to keep everyone's goals aligned while still letting everyone make decisions. In terms of organizational structure, I put a lot of thought into designing how teams operate and collaborate — making information transparent, giving everyone enough information to make the right decisions for the group.

Of course, we also provide room for error, because when someone is afraid of making a wrong decision, they won't make any decision at all. So you have to let them make decisions, while accepting that some decisions will be wrong — but when mistakes happen, you have to correct them quickly. All of this takes some time and some training for the whole team to move in the right direction.

How do you get more than 200 people to all make decisions at the same time? That sounds so hard.

Everyone is clear about — the whole key — what the whole project is ultimately trying to achieve. You have to keep sketching out the future clearly, and tell it to every person. Before the Cosmos 3 paper came out, or before the work was done, I had already talked to the main leaders and the major parts of the team, saying, "The model we build will look like this." Did it turn out exactly like that? Maybe 90% similar, 10% not similar. But when everyone sees the same vision, it's easier to converge. It's like when you're a basketball player — before you take a free throw, you always picture the ball swishing through the net. You set that target first, and then everyone moves toward it. Of course, everyone plays a different role, but when everyone sees the same picture, it's easier for each person in their position to make the right decision for the team.

Mm. What management methods did you design to make information more transparent and collaboration better? What management techniques are there?

Put in more thought. Understand how to say something — so that people get it. Focus on communication.

Do you hold regular meetings, like weekly meetings?

I'm someone who — I care a lot about teamwork and collaboration, so we have a lot of meetings. But not once a week — we probably have ten a week. Per week? Probably more than ten. With everyone, or with how many people? With the main leaders, each — For example, the team doing video — they meet regularly, maybe two or three times a week. The understanding team also meets regularly, two or three times a week. And then for each of the other areas, two or three times as well. So there are quite a lot of meetings. And you can do a lot of communicating in these meetings.

Of course, people often feel meetings are — sometimes very inefficient. One thing I try hard to do is make every meeting more engaging, and let everyone participate. All of this takes some training to get the team to work this way. It's never going to be maximally efficient. You could have nobody hold any meetings and everyone do their own thing — that won't necessarily succeed either. You could also hold meetings nonstop, do nothing, just talk — that won't succeed either. You have to find a balance. At different points in time, there will be different ways to strike that balance. This all depends on the task and the time. There's no fixed formula for which one is guaranteed to work, which one is best.

You see, in Silicon Valley people say OpenAI's culture is bottom-up and Anthropic is top-down. Which one do you belong to?

We're a bit of both. Any single approach taken to the extreme — you know, "long divided must unite, long united must divide" — things always reverse at their extremes. I think you always have to grasp, at that point in time, what the right thing for the team is, rather than blindly following one direction, operating in one fixed mode.

十四、物理 AI 的 ChatGPT 时刻

I understand the moment Cosmos takes off might be positively correlated with Physical AI and robotics taking off. Is that right? Correct? When do you think this market will see a so-called ChatGPT moment?

Everyone is chasing this ChatGPT moment for Physical AI. ChatGPT moment — what is a ChatGPT moment? How is a ChatGPT moment different from a GPT moment? The GPT moment told us that things can scale — that after scaling, model capabilities get stronger. The ChatGPT moment was when everyone could clearly see how such scaling, such a good model, would change people's lives. Everyone realized, here's an intelligent agent you can talk to — like asking a very knowledgeable friend.

So what is the ChatGPT moment for Physical AI? I think it means everyone sees an AI-enabled Physical AI application that makes people clearly see this thing is truly useful. When will this happen? That's very hard to predict. But what I see is the whole field's interest in Physical AI growing, more and more capital flowing in, more and more ambitious people starting companies to solve this problem. Physical AI can leverage the success of digital AI. So I think all the conditions are gradually converging. I hope to see the ChatGPT moment as soon as possible. Maybe this year, maybe next year — I don't know. But I think it's bound to happen.

Do you think humanoid robots will become the mainstream in this space?

I think the advantage of humanoid robots is that they can leverage huge amounts of human data as good material for learning, to improve these results. But humanoid robots themselves — the more human-like they are, with legs and hands, the relatively higher their complexity. A lot of people are building wheeled ones, where only the upper body is human-like, but the lower body is a mobile platform. That kind of platform can also solve many problems. And would you call that a humanoid robot? I'd say yes — the upper half is human-like, right, even if it's not fully humanoid. Among fully humanoid ones, some are closer to human form, and some humanoids are less close to human form.

I think humanoid robots will ultimately be an important key. But exactly how human-like — everyone is still experimenting with that. I think in the very end, fully humanoid may be the best fit for all kinds of manipulation, because the human environment is designed for the fully human form. But in the end, the key still comes down to operating costs — which option delivers the highest economic efficiency. And that's beyond my expertise. I actually don't know. My goal is to help all these different Physical AI builders, so I don't need to make that choice. I just listen to their voices and see what our models can do to help them more.

DeepMind research scientist Jie Tan has a prediction: he thinks 2035 to 2036 might be the tipping point for humanoid robots going mainstream.

Oh, really? I hope it's earlier, but I'm not sure.

Mm. Do you think world models might have a so-called tipping point?

I don't think world models are new. World models have existed for a long time. And I think world models will keep improving in performance. What we've seen with large language models — models getting better and better — right, I think we'll see that with world models too. And this time with Cosmos 3, we've made a rather different kind of world model — this kind of omni-model world model. Right, so I think there are still some changes coming. It will take a bit of time for everyone to absorb and digest it, because after all, this isn't something you can use directly once the model is out. You have to figure out how to deploy it, how to land it in robotics scenarios. I think that takes some time. I think it will keep changing.

如果机器人觉醒了？

Because you said you want to build The Matrix for robots, right? And what The Matrix itself depicts is a world where humans have been reduced to living batteries for machines, living in a virtual world, the Matrix, where an awakened person tries to break free from the fate of this system and end the cycle. So now you're building this Matrix for robots. What if one day the robots awaken and want to break out of this virtual world?

The reason I use The Matrix is to help everyone visualize — that a world model can accelerate learning this fast. Many people worry that when AI becomes too capable, it will take over the world and eliminate us. But I think this society was built by people. These technologies are operated by people behind the scenes. I think as long as everyone shares the consensus, that kind of thing won't happen.

And besides — this gets a bit philosophical. I think pain and suffering is a driver that pushes people to improve — an important key. I'm not so sure whether these silicon-made intelligences experience the same pain and suffering. I have my doubts about that. Of course I know we hope this technology can greatly improve human life and we also need to build the corresponding guardrails to make sure it doesn't disrupt the normal development of the world.

Mm, speaking of world models — other teams working on world models see you as a competitor because everyone thinks you're also building world models. But you keep saying I'm not your competitor. Right? Is there anything you'd like to say to them?

A world model is a tool. Tools are for solving problems. There are many different problems to solve. For the problems you ultimately want to solve, a world model alone isn't enough. It depends on the problem you want to solve. If you say because we want to serve the entire Physical AI system, we build world models for everyone to use. The problem of Physical AI itself is especially hard. There are many other problems to solve. If you can collaborate with us and make use of what we've built, you can go faster and further. Isn't that a great thing?

Right? Everything we do is open source. If you use our work and build a better model than ours, that model is also open source for everyone to use. We're still helping the whole Physical AI system. So you end up better than us and we think that's a good thing too. I think everyone working together to solve hard problems is something well worth doing. When people push against each other, set high bar and keep climbing higher, that's also a very important part of it.

They'll definitely say oh, NVIDIA just wants to sell me GPUs again. Right, but you do need compute. We NVIDIA's ecosystem is right here now. There are so many things you can take advantage of. Why not right? Running any business requires investment. What matters most is how much you earn rather than — take these cloud companies — they bought huge numbers of GPUs but they made even more money. Right?

下一个 CUDA 会是什么？

Do you discuss internally what the next CUDA will be? Could it be Cosmos?

Software in the past was built on logic. CUDA helped convert the logic these applications needed into GPU computation. Future software will be AI-centric. AI is built on top of other AI. So we think the Nemotron and Cosmos we're building could both be the CUDA of the future.

Because outsiders do a lot of post-mortems on CUDA. From your perspective, how do you think CUDA succeeded? What elements did it need to have? For example, which of them does Cosmos have now? And which does it lack? Is it a replicable path?

I'm not sure whether it's replicable. I think when CUDA was first proposed, it was a very forward-looking idea. It was a very risky idea. Back when it was still uncertain whether accelerated computing would be a big thing, our company made that bold investment. All the large models we build benefit from CUDA and can keep moving forward.

I wouldn't equate Cosmos or Nemotron with CUDA because I think the whole landscape has become much more complex now. There are many different — the whole industry is many stacks combined together. I think the combination of them might be the new CUDA rather than saying a single model is a CUDA. You still need to do serving. You still have to build all this infrastructure. Many things have to come together.

Mm, so which elements do you think jointly contributed to CUDA's success?

At the beginning, CUDA was searching for applications. At first it was scientific computing. Then later, after deep learning emerged, CUDA found its most important application and kept going. And CUDA keeps providing all kinds of different applications. I think replicating CUDA is a great idea but I don't think following the original route will take you down the same path. I think the environment is different. Right, I think you need to be adaptive. You have to see clearly what important contributions can be made at which time.

Mm, so you don't go around holding a hammer looking for nails, right? Holding onto "I have to make the next CUDA" just because it was such a successful decision back then — to make today's decisions. Just as Jensen often says, his first principle is based on first principles. He goes with what makes sense and then moves in that direction rather than holding a hammer and looking for nails.

十五、NVIDIA 十年、Jensen、以及"不裁员"

Because you've just hit 10 years at NVIDIA. Yes. Have you changed a lot over these 10 years? How many times has your NVIDIA stock multiplied?

None of this was anticipated. During this period, we witnessed a shift from nobody associating AI with NVIDIA to the whole world associating NVIDIA with AI, to a time when my parents didn't know what NVIDIA was to a time when the whole world knows what NVIDIA is. That's an enormous change.

The journey in between wasn't easy either. If you look at the stock price, the company has had its ups and downs. I remember the year the TPU first came out, the company's stock price dropped by a large chunk. Some colleagues at that time started to think differently about the company's future and left. But later NVIDIA beat the TPU in MLPerf every year, delivering better cost-performance. Eventually we were the only ones left competing. These things are all very hard to predict.

I think these changes are really huge. Over this long period, I've come to better understand what it means to build something slowly. Building slowly means finding a goal you believe in very first-principles and moving forward step by step. You just watch Jensen lead this huge team of the whole company step by step toward today's achievements. I feel honored to be part of it, you know. That's roughly it.

When you joined, you didn't expect any of this. You had other offers back then but didn't take them. Right, it was unpredictable. The reason I joined back then was that I wanted GPUs to support my academic research. It was a very simple reason. In a way, I'm also very first-principles. I thought GPUs are an important tool for doing research. I wanted to go somewhere with lots of GPUs so why not go to the place that makes GPUs.

Who was the other offer from, back then?

I had several offers. One of them was an investment firm. They told me no matter where I went, no matter how much the other side offered me, we'll give you four times that and hoped I would join their company to research using deep learning for investing together. I wasn't really that interested in that. I still wanted to do research so I still chose Nvidia. At the time Nvidia was probably the lesser-known one, right? Yes, that's right.

Jensen 的变化

Do you think Jensen in 2016 and Jensen now have changed much?

His hair has all gone gray. I think the pressure he carries has grown a lot. But he still really cares about employees. He carefully reads the top 5 emails written by company employees to find signals that help the whole company move forward. There have been huge changes. The company's scale has changed enormously. When we joined the company probably had fewer than 20,000 people. Now it's more than double that. Maybe even more. Back then GPUs were still in desktop machines. Now it's all data centers. Right, there was no Physical AI back then. Now Physical AI has become a major focus. Right, the changes are huge.

疫情期的抉择：不裁员，砍差旅

Along the way, have you witnessed any of NVIDIA's pain and suffering?

Jensen often says — he says — of course it's not literally true — he says it every time — that every day he feels the company has only 30 days of cash flow left and will go bankrupt in 30 days. He still says it now. He says it every day. He reminds himself of this at every meeting. Is he scaring the executives? It's about pushing himself to make the most correct decisions for the company.

And then one year during the pandemic the whole economic situation was really bad. At that point many companies started laying people off. I remember at that company-wide meeting we decided what to cut. What we cut was travel. Employees just wouldn't travel anymore. Everything went online. That saved a sum of money. We looked into which tools we could drop. For example, in Silicon Valley many companies use Slack for communication. We considered whether to just drop Slack. After all, we have email. We had two or three cloud services. For example, sometimes we used Microsoft, sometimes we used Google. Could we cancel one of them to save money? You could see the company, in difficult times, making some relatively uncommon decisions.

Some companies cut personnel costs through layoffs but what Nvidia thought about was what unnecessary expenses could be trimmed to take care of employees and get through the hard times together.

Why has Nvidia always insisted on no layoffs? Has it really never laid anyone off?

In all my time at NVIDIA I haven't heard any news of layoffs.

And no bottom-ranked elimination either, right?

We don't have so-called bottom-ranked elimination. We only have performance reviews. Some people leave because they're unhappy with their performance. Some people leave for other reasons. But we don't let you go just because we changed product direction or because your performance was poor during a certain period — we just let you go. We believe trust between people is very important. When an employee identifies with the company and feels secure, they're willing to speak up about things that in a place where people fear being eliminated, they wouldn't dare to say. When there's no such thing as bottom-ranked elimination, people also don't fight so hard to stand out just out of fear of being eliminated. In a place where everyone is fighting to stand out, it's actually harder to foster teamwork.

I think this kind of management approach creates a company culture that's quite different from the culture of companies that do bottom-ranked elimination.

What are its pros and cons?

I think employees dare to speak the truth and are willing to work together. The downside is when a technology gradually matures, these employees need some time to learn new things and transition. Relearning new things takes a bit more time. If you just lay off and hire a new batch of people, you might directly hire people who already know these things. So doing it through transition is a bit slower. But what you gain is the employees' trust and employees who will work together.

Mm, how do you improve organizational efficiency? Is that a problem for you?

As long as everyone is full of passion and feels what they're doing is meaningful, overall efficiency goes up. Everyone has choices. Everyone wants to do things they feel accomplished in. If the company can provide this environment where everyone can shine, then efficiency will improve. Let everyone do what they love most and are best at, while these things are also hugely beneficial to the company. As long as you can achieve that, I think that's a great state to be in.

Mm, it sounds like no layoffs has many benefits. But most companies don't do it this way, right? Why is that? And why did Jensen believe from the very beginning that there should be no layoffs?

I think NVIDIA is a company that wants to be around for the long run. I think it's all these years — Jensen has spent so many years in Silicon Valley and seen so many ups and downs. He must have his reasons for choosing this. I don't think it's a random choice. It's a carefully considered decision about the company culture he wants, the operating model he wants for the company.

So does that mean when new technology arrives, NVIDIA won't be the fastest one? But it relies on laying the groundwork 10 or 5 years ahead so it doesn't demand so much speed of itself?

Nvidia runs a marathon and looks far ahead. Look, CUDA is exactly such a case. It was laid out 10 years in advance. Right, ah, so you need very strong vision. Long-term investment. Right, and you don't do internal horse-racing either, do you? We don't like horse-racing. Because we usually do it this way. You take on this mission and we trust you. But together we set a very high bar for you hoping you'll complete it.

In Jensen's words, it's constantly putting you through pain and suffering — torture you to greatness. Trust in you. Give you trials. Keep tempering you, letting you grow step by step along the way. This is the model we like.

What's the most brutal suffering you've endured at NVIDIA?

Building these large models. These years have all been this hard, pushing forward. The things I just told you about — many of them were learned from mistakes. Many things — at first we didn't realize these were the most important things. To do things well when you get it wrong, how do you slowly improve things. I think this stretch of time — ever since GPT took off, everyone working in AI has felt an inexplicable pressure. During this period with this speed of iteration, everyone has been under tremendous pressure. I think it's all pain and suffering. Especially when you're burning through GPU resources every day, burning through these young people's time, and the results you produce don't reach the outcome you most wanted. I think all of this is an invisible pressure.

生活方式：4-5 点起床

Has your lifestyle changed over these past few years?

Highly efficient. Earlier mornings, later nights. I get up around 4 to 5 a.m.

Oh, that early.

When I get up in the morning — exercise and all that — the time is more continuous. Once I get to the office it's nonstop meetings. I get to the office around 10 — probably around 9 to 10. Because of the whole industry's iteration speed, the pace of life has gotten faster. There's still a lot to learn but there are even more things to handle. So you make yourself more efficient.

Mm, what time do you sleep?

Probably around 10 p.m. Sleep around 10. Around 10 to 11. And up at 4 or 5. Right. It's not fixed every day but that's basically my routine.

NVIDIA 的独特管理

Books about NVIDIA or biographies of Jensen have all talked a lot about his management style. Could you talk about it from a more frontline perspective — some of NVIDIA's distinctive management practices?

We just touched on one: no layoffs. The second is top 5. Employees tell many people the five most important things they're working on. This lets you see all kinds of signals, big and small, across the company. You can see many cases where two teams are doing exactly the same thing and the top five emails naturally reveal it.

Nvidia is a relatively very transparent organization. Apple might be the counterexample. We pursue information transparency. This is also a very different culture. Some of those Jensen biographies are quite dramatic. But a lot of it you can actually feel when you work at NVIDIA. He knows many employees.

We often say mission is the boss, right, so NVIDIA is sometimes like an organism. Without such a rigid framework. When the company wants to move in a certain direction today, teams across different organizations with the relevant skills will automatically align and move in that direction. Like a living organization. Not a fixed framework where if you're in this box, you can't do that thing. It doesn't matter. It doesn't matter where you are in the company. When you're going to move in this direction, if your team can contribute, everyone aligns and it becomes a new direction moving this way.

Cosmos is exactly such a case.

Mm, so many people may not belong to this team but they can all come support the team's work. Right, Mission is the boss rather than your boss being your boss.

These few are the most distinctive features. These are what make the company so alive. Look at the mission is the boss I just mentioned. It's not a rigid framework. It's an organism. And this top five lets tiny signals from every corner of the company spread out. Unwilling — not quick to lay off employees. Emphasizing transformation. Emphasizing torture. Building employees' trust in the company. So they can cooperate with each other. I think these are all very unique things about NVIDIA.

A group of S-tier people working together versus a group of A plus or A-tier people working together — which one do you think is more likely to achieve greater success?

What everyone pursues is 1+1 being greater than 2. Right — whether people can work together in unity to create a greater effect. That's a very important thing. When there are many people, there's a communication cost. The communication cost is negative. You need cooperation between people to produce positive returns while reducing this communication cost. When a group of very smart people work together, of course everyone is smart — they understand things quickly and move fast. But if people can't trust each other it's still hard to achieve 1+1 greater than 2. Everyone is guarding against each other, unwilling to show their best side, or trying to prove "I'm smarter than you." That's not necessarily a good state either.

I actually think it's just like playing a game. You don't want the whole team to be all archers. Maybe some people are in charge of defense, some people are in charge of healing. All these different attributes combined together. I think this kind of diversity is a better state.

十六、低 ego 是修行还是自信？

Hmm, you've said a lot today — you have no competitors, you don't compete with anyone. Everyone is a customer. Everyone is a partner. Is this low-ego state something that happened at NVIDIA? Is it truly low ego, or is it a kind of concealment?

I think it's a kind of confidence. A belief that what we build can help everyone. My goal is to help everyone do well. But I hold myself to very high standards for what I build. I want it to get better. But my goal is not to beat competitors. My goal is to produce great results, to build a better foundation so everyone can move faster.

Did you learn this from Jensen?

Yes, his influence on me runs very deep.

When did you learn this?

If you're a researcher, the way you graduate is by getting your papers accepted at top conferences. Reviewers will question you: is your work state-of-the-art? Being state-of-the-art means you have to beat everyone. So researchers all have this mindset — "My work has to be better than yours." So, following this trajectory, I started out as a highly competitive individual. My work had to be better than yours. That's my demand of myself, and that's fine. You want your work to keep getting better and better.

But after a while you know — you're always state-of-the-art for a while, then the next one comes out. This thing keeps progressing nonstop. And my position today is different too. After becoming a manager I hope to cultivate a new generation of talent to help them grow. And from NVIDIA's position in the ecosystem, I also hope the company gradually feels the benefits. Sometimes when my partners tell me that after using one of our models their efficiency in solving problems improved a lot, I feel very happy. I feel that my effort and the whole team's hard work received some recognition in return. This kind of affirmation is also a wonderful thing. You don't necessarily have to beat others to make a contribution. You don't need to defeat your opponents. I don't like treating them as opponents. I like treating them as partners.

Hmm, look at NVIDIA — including you and including Jensen — he often says "take care of others" whether it's employees or external partners. Is this kind of "take care" genuine? Do you think he really thinks this way?

In NVIDIA's early days we were a design house. We didn't really have any consumer product of our own. We relied on other companies to make the GPU cards for us. We've always had this habit of growing together with the whole ecosystem. Everyone makes money together. It can't be that only we make the money. The ones who help make the graphics cards, the servers — everyone has to be able to keep moving forward together. Because its early graphics cards were used for gaming and we didn't make games. We just kept developing these good libraries to help game companies make games. When we first moved into deep learning there were several frameworks at the time like PyTorch, TensorFlow and also MXNet and those. We supported all of them. Right — later there was the Triton Compiler. We supported Triton. When vLLM came out, we supported vLLM.

Right — I think it's genuine. We genuinely want to help the customers building on our GPU platform succeed even more. The more successful they are, the more customers they can serve. And they'll have abundant opportunities to use our GPUs. It's truly a shared interest — a path to success together. I think that's how it is — he ran the company for so many years to put it in such a good position. Helping others while also profiting yourself. I think that's not easy.

六边形战士

Hmm, you've observed Jensen up close for many years. If you had to describe him in just a few words, how would you describe him?

We call him the "hexagonal warrior". Sometimes in meetings, he can go really deep into registers — registers in computer architecture — extremely fine details. And at the same time he can talk about — even teach everyone how to do marketing. How to do these very high-level things. Handling everything from product pricing to customer relationships. He covers every aspect. He has enormous passion. He gives everything he has to help the company be successful. It's a truly admirable way of operating. He can contribute in every direction and does his best in every direction. He's a truly remarkable person.

Does he encourage you more, or criticize you more?

Generally both. Back when I didn't yet fully understand how he wanted to run the company, there was more criticism. But the criticism always came with encouragement, hoping you could become better. His goal is to torture everybody to greatness. Through this grinding, you come to better understand what it takes to do extraordinary things. This is very energy-consuming. Being willing to spend time torturing others — that's not an easy thing. Torturing others — you yourself carry a heavy burden too. Right? And you only have so much time in your life. You could just not bother and maybe still get what you want. But he's willing to spend time torturing others so everyone keeps improving. That's not an easy thing.

What's a phrase of his that left a deep impression on you?

I remember once we were in a meeting. We were comparing two solutions — two things. I was the one who built one of them and the other was built by someone else. I remember at the time I said "I think the setting they used was an unfair setting so our performance on this front didn't meet our expectations" — falling behind the competing product. And he said to me at that moment, "Are you a quiet baby?" Nothing in this world is fair.

When you write papers, you often say "my setting is different from your setting so you can't compare them directly." But if your goal is to solve a problem, then of course you need the conditions required to solve that problem. If you don't have those conditions, find a way to get them. But that sentence left a very deep impression on me. I became stricter with myself — making excuses is useless. You just have to give everything you have.

And I'd heard this saying before. Some famous books from West Point talk about it too. No excuse — no excuse at all. But when he said it to me, it left an even deeper impression on me because after all, he's a famous figure. I think this sentence had quite a big impact on me. After that, I stopped making excuses.

If, as a researcher, your desire to be number one conflicts with NVIDIA's own business — since NVIDIA doesn't want to become a strong competitor — if a conflict arose, which would you choose?

I think the development of science itself is incremental. It keeps progressing. You can propose an improvement anytime, just taking one more step upward. I think "be the absolute number one" — what does number one even mean? It's hard to define number one. I prefer to look at it this way — train a frontier model. A frontier model, the moment it's built, is number one. That's very fulfilling. But soon after, other models will surpass it.

What I hope for is — you possess the ability to build a number-one model but you do the thing that has the greatest impact on society — the most contributive thing. Right, because you can build a number-one model — or — it could mean letting power become overly concentrated in a few hands, creating some kind of imbalance. I don't think that's necessarily the right thing. Right — I hope to have the number-one capability but to do the thing that contributes the most to this world.

Yes — so what matters most is the contribution at the end. Right? Not the capability itself. Right, right — everyone just passes through this life once. Right? What you leave behind is your impact. So you need to live long. Living longer gives you more chances. I just hope to produce some — to make some contributions to prove I didn't come to this world for nothing. That's how it is.

Hmm, do you have any regrets in your research career? Is there anything you particularly still want to achieve?

I think Physical AI hasn't succeeded yet. The time hasn't come yet to talk about all that. I'm very happy that back then — ten years ago, I was saying deep learning would replace computer graphics and become the most important paradigm for image generation. And that actually happened. I feel pretty happy about it. This thing really happened. I think world models will be an important driving force for the success of Physical AI. That's my next major goal. I hope this can succeed too.

If you compare — you have one best paper award and you think, "I want to win two." Then you find out some people have won a dozen. You can never win them all. Compare paper counts — there are always more papers. Compare citation counts — there are always more citations. Compare money — there's always someone richer. Right? So the point is whether you're proud of your own work. I think a lot of my past work wasn't good enough. But some of my recent work I think is quite good. I accept that. I feel that within the scope of my abilities I've produced work I'm satisfied with. I think that's enough.

So many of the external metrics — they're gradually becoming less important now, right?

Right — when you're young, they all feel so important. Why? "This person has more best papers than me." Right, and more awards than me. Now I feel — gradually I no longer measure myself by those — my focus has gradually shifted to helping others. Maybe what I care about now is whether I've helped enough people.

Hmm, who do you think you've helped this past year?

The users of Physical AI, the users of Cosmos. I think I've quietly helped all of them. And of course my own team. And some people who've had conversations with me along the way. I think, to some degree, I've had an impact on their lives.

十七、中国、大模型格局与未来预测

You also come to China often. How do you view the development of this wave of Chinese models?

Very impressive. Very impressive. Starting from DeepSeek, Qwen, Doubao — let me just name them all — MiniMax, Kimi, MiMo, Hunyuan, Zhipu. They've all done very well.

There's another thing — in the United States, especially at these frontier labs, the current situation is that they rarely take interns anymore. A lot of the know-how, a lot of the research results exist only inside their own labs. What I see in China is these companies all take on a lot of interns, helping to spread this know-how outward. I think for the expansion of humanity's collective knowledge, this diffusion — I think it's a good thing.

Seeing this rapid development I find it very impressive. And at the same time, they pay attention to this diffusion. Everyone is full of passion for AI, willing to give things a try. I think these are all phenomena I've observed.

Xie Saining (co-founder of AMI) told me Silicon Valley has been hypnotized by LLMs. What do you think of that statement?

I don't think it's purely being hypnotized by LLMs. It's undeniable — the leading companies in AI right now, the companies with the leading models, whether it's OpenAI or Anthropic, they all started from large language models. And these models are indeed — I already don't know how I'd get by without a Coding Agent. I really don't know — they're just too convenient. I think they've brought about enormous change. And that's not a bad thing. LLMs have proven enormously useful, helping to improve our lives.

So I think it's very natural that people start thinking "Since this thing is already here, what's the next step?" I think people naturally want to do the next thing. I know some people in the field turn academia into a faith. But I think most people still start from the pursuit of knowledge and truth. Once something has been fully understood, people will find new things to make breakthroughs on. It's hard to imagine a person — someone so smart — spending their whole life only working on LLMs. I think it will just happen naturally. I don't really think there's any "hypnosis." It's just that for those people at this moment in time, working on LLMs might be the right thing to do.

SpaceX went public yesterday. And OpenAI and Anthropic are about to go public too. Will this year's IPOs of these large-model companies have any impact on the industry?

2026 will be a year of huge change. Everyone has seen the news about these IPOs — they'll create a lot of wealthy people. And I know housing prices in San Francisco are soaring. The people who believed in deep learning early, who believed early in this space mission — it's a recognition of their foresight, of their courage, of their determination. A validation. I think it's all very reasonable. These companies have truly made enormous contributions to the world. I think it's fully deserved.

But I don't think technology will stop here. New things will keep happening one after another. The most powerful companies 100 years ago are completely different from the most powerful companies today. Different from 50 years ago. Different from 20 years ago. I think as long as the organizational structure of society remains in a good, healthy state, innovation will keep happening.

模型竞争的终局

What might the endgame of this model race look like? So much has changed in just a few short years. What about looking further ahead?

This might be controversial — I think model capabilities will gradually converge. The model itself won't be the differentiator. You'll have to organize some other things together with it. Leading models have more time to find that differentiation. Strong companies can also strengthen their own — build a strong ecosystem to create some change.

I think it's like when software first came out — very few companies could write software. Now everyone can write software. Every software company has its own way of differentiating. Every software company that survives today has its own differentiation. I see no reason models would be any different. I think it'll be the same. So there's no need to mythologize models or model companies.

I treat it like traditional Chinese medicine. It's a black box. So many people making different attempts and eventually it becomes a body of knowledge. And then many people practice medicine. The key is what you use it for. Right — the key is what you do with it. Some people understand it more deeply. Some people just need a bit more time. This is all just my speculation. I think these things will gradually diffuse.

Now suppose a new company says it wants to train a model — does it still have a good chance of catching up?

It might be two or three years behind the companies ahead of it. Like Kimi or MiMo — these efforts came relatively late. Kimi is okay; MiMo is later. Right, right — there's still a chance. I think there will be a period of time when everyone feels compute is insufficient. But I think compute will gradually ramp up and gradually everyone will find a way to compete. I think there are many people in this world with ambition, determination and the ability to mobilize resources to build a large-model team. And there will be more, right?

I think if large models are an absolute differentiator, then of course there will be more of that. But if it's not an absolute differentiator, then a lot of people will probably find ways that are mutually beneficial. Yes, I think it's a natural state of balance.

How long do you think before on-device models take off?

This is very close to Physical AI. As I just mentioned, I think funding is gradually flowing in, and the technology is iterating fast. I can't say exactly how long it will take, but I hope it takes off quickly.

For this year's and next year's model race, what predictions do you have?

On Physical AI it's hard to say. Creation is still moving fast. I still firmly believe that the capability of World Models is a crucial key to helping these physical-world models strengthen their generalization. How to make it land in practice, what modality to use — these are things everyone is still exploring. ChatGPT moment for Physical AI is coming. That's probably a prediction I can make. As for things like large coding models, I use them myself, but I don't build them myself, so it's hard for me to say. I enjoy using them a lot, but it's hard for me to say what happens next.

中国的机器人公司

You just talked about China's model companies. What about China's robotics companies? You've probably met many of them too. Do you think they're different from the US in any way?

In the US, very few companies build the robot body itself — just Tesla and Figure AI. In China, many companies are building the robot body. Building the body means they can control more things. They can control the model and the software-hardware integration. There's more room to maneuver. I think because of China's strong manufacturing industry, it creates a very advantageous condition that lets these companies do things not easy to do in the US. I think it's all well worth watching — what kind of breakthrough this vertical integration will produce. Yes, I find it quite interesting.

Do you think the US might now be, a little, not valuing hardware enough — that could be wrong?

Hard to say. But if software-hardware integration is a trend in robotics, then having no hardware certainly puts you in a passive position. Right? It's a bit hard to say. There are many things to consider, including the financial model. China clearly has the conditions that let everyone do rapid hardware iteration and software-hardware integration.

The ChatGPT moment in Physical AI — where do you think it might break out?

You see an application where everyone obviously knows it will generate huge economic value. And maybe at that point in time, that application hasn't yet generated economic value. When ChatGPT first came out, it was losing money, right? But everyone saw the trend, and I think that's when it happens. I personally think this kind of thing — where a human simply demonstrates how to do a task, and the robot learns it right there on the spot — I think that's a — If this thing appears, if I see a product like that, I would feel that Physical AI's ChatGPT moment has arrived.

So at its core it's about generalization.

I think it's generalization. It — The core problem of AI is solving generalization.

Mm. When it comes to generalization, what is the single most important problem right now? If you had to name just one?

The problem of generalization — in Physical AI, it's how to learn the required skills from limited signals, and apply them in scenes you've never seen before. This is the main generalization problem to solve in Physical AI: observation to action — the generalization of that pair. You see some — you see this action and observation getting things done. How do you quickly generalize to a new observation with a similar action?

Hey, I'm wondering — if it learns within the Cosmos system, then when it moves into the real world, there's still a sim-to-real gap, right? How do you solve that problem?

That's also a generalization problem. The sim-to-real gap is usually — how we at Cosmos want to help Physical AI builders is through three approaches, as mentioned before: better data, better starting points, and better environments. I think things like better environments haven't happened yet. Everyone hopes to build this matrix, but it hasn't happened yet. There have been breakthroughs here and there, and we've seen some very good work. What's more effective right now is probably better data and better starting points. You take a model that understands the world's physics and use it to predict physics. Understanding physics lets you — well, you can't say it truly understands physics, but it captures the patterns and can predict what will happen in the future. This can perhaps help you generate a better policy, make a better policy. Because its own prior is better suited for generalization, it can perhaps help you build a policy model that generalizes more easily. Right. I think this is what I see as a contribution the Cosmos model could make to Physical AI builders in the near term.

If I interview you again five years from now, what stage do you hope Cosmos will have reached?

Oh, I hope that five years from now, if we have another interview like this, we can clearly state when the ChatGPT moment happened, yes, and where it happened. I hope we can say it clearly and explicitly — down to the year, month, and day. By then there'll be a concrete date. Yes yes hopefully.

In the history of artificial intelligence, how would you like people to remember you?

Let's not talk about me. I'd say talk about Cosmos. I hope Cosmos can be an important driving force helping several important Physical AI builders reach this ChatGPT moment. I think that would make me very happy.

十八、闪电轮：食物、书、忠告

I have a few more rapid-fire questions. Your favorite food, anywhere in the world?

Beef noodle soup.

Your favorite place, anywhere in the world?

Oh, I like the Bay Area. The weather is just so comfortable.

Any music, books, movies, or games you like?

Quite a lot of books. I don't really listen to music. I don't really play games anymore. The last time I played a game was probably over twenty years ago.

Can you share a book that truly changed you or influenced you?

A book Jensen recommended. It's about Positioning. I forget what the title was. A very interesting psychology book. It helps you better understand the essence of a problem. When I was young, I read many different books. Right, I especially loved Jin Yong's novels. That was one part of it.

Did Jin Yong's novels help you later in your research or business management?

Not really. It's more that you get to experience Jin Yong's various fantasies, some beautiful imagery. It certainly pushed me onto the path of learning Chinese martial arts, gaining some training and discipline from Chinese martial arts. I think those were all pretty good experiences.

What advice would you have for young researchers?

Don't be nervous.

Why not be nervous?

I think young researchers nowadays often feel like maybe AI will be over next year, that AI will train itself. Don't be nervous. Have confidence in yourself. Calm down. See clearly where it's worth investing your energy. Don't be swayed by everyone's hype into feeling your path is getting narrower and narrower. Right now is a good time for researchers to enter Physical AI.

A good time — is it a blue ocean?

It's a good time — there are all kinds of opportunities, and many areas — I work on Physical AI, so I know that better — but these advances in AI let us make better materials, better drugs, breakthroughs in biology — I think you can gradually see AI's impact across every industry. I think there are many places worth investing in.

Our studio is called "Language Is the World" Studio. When you first heard that name, what were you thinking?

Using language to describe the interesting things happening in this world.

Do you think the large model race is not Squid Game — or the world model race is not Squid Game? Or is it that for you it's not Squid Game, but for others it might be?

I'm not sure. If everyone is trying to solve exactly the same thing, then it's Squid Game, right? So the model race shouldn't be Squid Game. Right, because there are so many problems in the world to solve, so many things that can provide value, and everyone likes different things. Right, I don't think it should be seen as Squid Game.

Have you ever had a period of particularly high ego?

When I was young. That happens, right? Yes, I always felt my algorithm was the best and the paper I wrote was the most elegant.

You always feel that way.

Algorithms matter, but you need very good data and very good infrastructure so you can iterate on algorithms quickly. Because even if there are two possibilities — one is your algorithm is great from the start, OK, that's great. But even if your algorithm isn't good at first, if you have very good data and very good infrastructure, you can iterate. As long as you iterate with strict discipline, following controlled-experiment principles, your algorithm gets better and better. So I actually think iteration speed is the most important thing. And iteration speed depends on powerful infrastructure to support it. Data is very important, because if a problem can be solved with data, just solve it with data. No need to develop an algorithm, because data is much simpler. Right, so you don't like wasting effort. As long as a problem can be solved with data, go collect data, go create data. And for what truly can't be solved, then use algorithms to solve it.

每家公司都需要自训大模型吗？

Does every company need to train its own large model? You don't think it's necessary, right?

If it's a commodity — do you need to build your own power plant? Does every company need to build its own power plant? OK. It comes down to whether it's economically worthwhile, right? Mm. In the early days, when you were building a car factory, when power plants were scarce, you'd build a power plant, and you could ensure your company ran 24 hours a day. But in this day and age, you probably don't need to, right?

You probably talk to a lot of AI developers, and every one of them feels their AI model is the best.

I don't think this has ever happened in history. I don't think so. Because it's not that easy for people to get along with each other. Look at Dario Amodei and Sam Altman back then — they couldn't get along, right? So he left. And are you sure everyone at Anthropic is exactly the same? I don't think so.

They're all true believers? What if one day you promote A but not B, and B feels — Hmm right? And then might he take a group of people with him to go build something similar? Right, and everyone has data. They have data, and they can buy compute from you. Compute — as long as you have money, you can still buy it, right? So everyone can do it. If you have the determination and the resources, you can do it. It's just that there's no need to.

Is Cosmos a war you can't afford to lose?

If other companies also build open-source models, then it's not. Right. What do we even mean by "war"? It's not like I intend to kill anyone else. I just have to — Oh no — it's that you all have to grow on top of our ecosystem, and NVIDIA keeps growing.

Physical AI is a major market. Right now no household has a robot, but if there were robots, my family might buy two or three. And every robot needs compute. That means the whole world's demand for compute would grow dramatically. If that happens, it's a huge benefit for NVIDIA. Our mindset is not about killing anyone else. Our mindset is: how do we create the market? You know what I mean? CUDA created a market. It created today's AI market. What we think about is how to create the next big market. So you're saying —

Yes. Is it a battlefield you can't afford to lose?

I don't think so either. Not really, because it's something entirely new. I'm not competing with anyone, right? Yeah. It's mutual benefit. Bringing everyone along to build that market together. And then — you make money selling this robot, this thing will need some compute to make money. And of course some companies will develop their own chips, and they'll make money too. Then the whole market rises up from what was originally nothing.

Does Jensen share a similar view?

He says it often, right? He says it often: you have to create markets rather than fight over existing ones. Right. If you read his book, you'll find he says we should do this kind of zero-billion-dollar business. What's a zero-billion-dollar business? It's not a business right now, but once it succeeds, it becomes a billion. Mm. If someone is already doing it now, it's probably not worth doing.

Is this embracing risk, or resisting risk? Is this still a de-risk?

The way we do things is very risky. All of it is — CUDA back then was a very risky thing. It was basically selling at a loss, right? Because we built CUDA in, the price of our entire GPU was higher than others'. For the same FLOPS, we were just more expensive, because we had to support this programmability, right? If you don't do it this way — doing this is very risky, but not doing it is even more risky. Right. If you don't do that thing and someone else does, then for you it becomes very risky. If you don't do it, your stuff gradually becomes a commodity.

Is there anything else you still want to learn from Jensen?

I try hard to learn how he runs other things, and then apply that to running Cosmos.

Why do other companies say the CEO shouldn't be the hardest-working person, but at your company the CEO is the hardest-working person?

Right. Yes. I don't understand that either. Haha. But he — it works. I can not — Right? Nothing in the world is absolute.

What's driving him now?

The drive is to take care of families. Oh. Right. Doing AI itself is a very interesting thing. You — especially from his vantage point, seeing his contributions change the world — I think it's a very fulfilling thing.

Truly worthy of being called the guru.

Haha yes.
