答： 对啊。经常说什么？经常说 造市场，而不是在存量竞争。对，你读他的书就会发现，他讲说我们就是要做这种 Zero billion dollar business。什么叫 Zero billion dollar business？就是现在不是个 business，但以后成功后会变 B 年。如果现在已经有人在做，可能就不值得做。

问： 这是一种拥抱风险，还是一种抵抗风险？还是一个低 risk 吗？

答： This is a low risk. We are very risky in doing things. All of this is a risky thing when CUDA was very risky. It's like a compensation sale. Because we hit CUDA, our entire GPU price is higher than others. The same Flops is higher than others. Because we want to support this programmability, right? You don't do this, you do this thing is very risky. You don't do this thing is more risky. Yes, if you don't do that thing, if others do it, it will be very risky for you.

The world is not absolute.

答： The driving force is "take your families". Doing AI is a very interesting thing. Especially from his perspective, seeing his contribution to change the world, I think it is a very fulfilling thing.

问： You are indeed the leader.

那我个人觉得这种就是简单的人示范一下怎么要的操作，这个机器人就可以就地学会这东西，我觉得这是一个如果这东西出现，我看到这样的一个这样的一个产品，我就觉得说 Yeah, that's a trick for physical AI.

答： 我觉得是泛化。AI 的核心问题就是解泛化的问题。我看过的一个场景里面，这个是 physical AI 里面要解的一个主要的泛化问题：Observation 对 action 这个配合的泛化。你看到 action 跟 observation 是完成事情的怎么样快速泛化到一个新的 observation，那类似的 action。

Sim-to-Real Gap 与 Cosmos 的三大贡献

问： 我在想就是如果他在 Cosmos 这套系统里学习了，然后大家走向现实世界的时候，他还是会有 synth-real gap，对不对？怎么解决这个问题呢？

答： 这也是一个泛化的问题。Synth-real gap，通常是我们 Cosmo 想帮助 physical app builder 是透过三个方式嘛，之前有讲的，就是 better data、better starting point and better environment。

I think better environment hasn't happened yet. Everyone wants to do this. But it hasn't happened yet. There are some breakthroughs. I see some work is very good.

Now the more useful one is better data and better starting point. You take one and understand this. I understand the world more than how to predict the world. I understand physics. I can't really understand physics, but once I get to that mode, I can go to the earth to add and release things. This thing may help you produce better policies. Because its prior is more suitable for emulation, it may help you build a more easy-to-emulate policy model.

答： I hope that if we have an interview five years later, we can talk about it clearly. 切记一瞬间是什么时候发生的？ 对，然后是在哪里发生？我希望这个事情是可以明确的讲出来。纪念七月几日，那时候就有一个具体的时间了。

问： 在人工智能的历史上，你希望别人怎么来记录你？

答： 不要讲我吧，我觉得就是讲 Cosmos 吧。然后希望 Cosmos 可能是一个重要的推手，and help these few important physical app builders to reach this moment of absolute power. I think this is something that I will be very happy about.

快问快答

问： What is your favorite food in the world?

答： 牛肉面（Beef noodles）。

问： What is your favorite place in the world?

答： I like to play games. The weather is so nice.

问： Do you have any favorite music, books, movies, or games?

答： I have a lot of books. I don't listen to music that much. I don't play games that much. I played games for 20 years last time.

问： Can you share a book that really changed you or influenced you?

答： The book that Jensen recommended is about positioning. I forgot the name of the book. It's a very interesting psychological book. 让你更加理解问题的本质是什么。

年轻的时候读了很多不同的书，我特别喜欢金庸小说，那是其中一环。

问： 金庸小说有帮助到你后面的科研或者是写管理吗？

答： I don't have any. I just have the imagination of finance and the beautiful scenery. I have learned the Chinese martial arts path and gained some experience from it. I think it's a good process.

问： What do you suggest to young researchers?

答： Don't be nervous.

问： 为什么不要紧张？

答： 我现在年轻的研究员都往往觉得就是会不会明年这个 AI 就结束了？就 AI 自训练了。不要紧张，对自己有信心。然后冷静下来，看清楚什么地方是值得你投入精力。不要被这些大家的宣传觉得好像自己路越走越窄。

问： 现在研究员进入 physical AI 是一个好时机，是一个狼害吗？

答： 就是一个好时机，就是各种机会，然后还有很多地方。我当然做 physical AI 我比较懂，但这些 AI 的进步，让我们可以做出更好的这些 material，更好的药，这些生物方面的突破，我觉得在各行各业里面都可以渐渐看到这个 AI 的影响，我觉得很多地方都可以去投入。

问： 我们工作室叫「语言即世界」工作室，当你第一次听到这个名字的时候你在想什么？

答： 用语言来描述这世界上发生有趣的事。

问： 你觉得是大模型竞争不是鱿鱼游戏，还是世界模型竞争不是鱿鱼游戏啊？还是说对于你来说不是鱿鱼游戏，对别人可能是吧？

答： 我不清楚，你如果大家想解的东西一模一样，那就是鱿鱼游戏。对吧？所以模型竞争不应该是鱿鱼游戏。对，因为这世界上要被解的问题这么多，然后可以提供价值的东西这么多。也跟喜欢的东西又不太一样。我觉得不应该是看的是猶豫游戏。

关于 High Ego 时期

问： 你有过那种特别 high ego 的时候吗？

答： 年轻的时候。社会的时候。对，就是我总觉得我的算法最好。然后我写的 paper 最漂亮。总是会那么觉得。

算法重要。你需要很好的数据，很好的 infrastructure。那你可以做快速的算法迭代。

Because even if you have two possibilities, one is that you are good at math from the beginning. OK, that's good. But even if you are not good at math from the beginning, you have good data and good infrastructure, you can stack. Then as long as you follow this, it is very strict discipline. Then this kind of control experiment, your math will be better and better.

So I think the speed of stacking is important. The speed of stacking is to rely on strong infrastructure.

Data is very important. If a problem can be solved with data, you can solve it with data. No need to develop a algorithm. Because data is much simpler. So I don't like to waste energy. This problem is as long as the data can be collected, the data will be created. Then the real problem can't be solved with algorithm.

## 一、最出人意料的观察：功夫拳理竟是他管理300人团队的底层操作系统
刘洺堉在访谈里轻描淡写地提到自己练八极拳几十年——师承徐纪，祖师是"神枪李书文"。这看起来是纯粹的个人爱好，但如果你把八极拳的核心心法和他管理 Cosmos 团队的方式并置来看，会发现一件惊人的事：**他管理团队的哲学，就是把武术的"整劲"外化成了组织形态。**
八极拳的核心秘密是：一拳的力量必须从脚起、由腰传、贯于指尖，"发生在一瞬间"却要求全身长路径的高度协调。而他反复强调 Cosmos 团队的两难：**"每个人的目标要一致，但每个人都要能独立决策"**——这正是"整劲"在组织学上的完美对偶。传统管理要么强调 top-down（有整体但每一节僵硬），要么强调 bottom-up（每一节灵活但无整劲）。他找到的解，其实就是拳理里那句"节节贯穿、周身一家"。
更妙的是——他自己说练武是为了"控制自己"，而不是击败别人。这直接对应了他后来对 NVIDIA 竞争哲学的表述："我们不做鱿鱼游戏"。功夫是内向的、非对抗的自我修炼，而他把这种"高手不比武、只求内在完备"的姿态原封不动搬进了顶级 AI 竞赛。

item.title: [Lex Clips] Messi vs Ronaldo: Who is the greatest soccer player of all time? | Khabib Nurmagomedov
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽视的"镜像共生"：伟大是一种相互寄生的现象

大多数人把 Messi vs Ronaldo 讲成"谁更强"的问题，但 Khabib 无意间点出了一个更颠覆的真相：他们不是竞争者，而是彼此的"训练器官"。"Would Messi be Messi without Ronaldo?"——这句问话背后藏着一个进化生物学式的结论：顶级捕食者会因缺乏对手而退化。C 罗和梅西并不是并列的两座山峰，而是一个双星系统——彼此的引力把对方甩离了地表。真正让人意外的是：如果这个假设成立，那么"最伟大的球员"这个概念本身就是伪命题——伟大不是属性，而是关系。

二、Khabib 谈齐达内头槌，其实在谈他自己

整段对话最"莎士比亚"的时刻，不是齐达内的头槌，而是 Lex 追问时 Khabib 的回避："I wouldn't want to judge him."——他说这话的时候，正被 Lex 提醒他自己与 McGregor 的爆发。这是一种共谋式沉默：一个曾经在笼子外扑向对手团队的男人，对世界杯决赛顶爆意大利人的男人不做评判，因为他们说的是同一种语言。可以把它连接到心理学中的"情绪水位模型"（James Gross 的 emotion regulation）——顶级运动员并不是"更能压抑"，而是把 99% 的情绪压进容器里，只允许 1% 在最后 3 秒喷出。这种"迟滞式爆发"是精英竞技的隐藏共性，从 Zidane 到 Khabib 到围棋里的李昌镐迟迟不动的一手，都是同一个心理机制。

三、"魅力（Charisma）"是一种带宽稀缺资源——足球正在耗尽它

Khabib 说不出什么是 charisma，但他列举的名字——Zidane、Beckham、Bartez、Edgar Davids、Oliver Kahn、Roberto Carlos——有一个共同的、几乎没有人指出的特征：他们都有视觉上可被识别的"低分辨率剪影"。Zidane 的秃顶+缓慢+突然加速；Davids 的护目镜+脏辫；Bartez 的光头+狂想；Kahn 的咆哮姿态。跨领域联想：这与卡通角色设计的"剪影测试"（Silhouette Test）是同一条法则——好的角色即使只剩黑色轮廓也能一眼认出。现代足球战术化、数据化之后，球员越来越"高效"却越来越"低剪影"——他们像是被 A/B 测试优化过的产品，失去了轮廓。Charisma 的消失不是球员的失败，而是系统对怪异性的清洗。

四、隐藏彩蛋：Khabib 的"take the ball"哲学，其实是一种反脆弱信条

他反复说"不怕失败的人才能拿球"，甚至举 Ronaldo 罚失点球后再罚一颗的例子。这与 Nassim Taleb 的反脆弱（Antifragility）几乎逐字对应——伟大不是承受风险的能力，而是主动增加风险敞口以换取非线性回报的意愿。反过来说：那些"接球就传出去"的球员，本质上是在做期望值为负的风险规避——他们让整个系统的方差降低了，但也让上限被封死。这解释了一个反常识现象：为什么许多技术顶尖的球员永远进不了名人堂？——因为他们的"技术"是防御性的，而非攻击性的。技术是名词，勇气是动词，只有动词创造历史。

📝 转录文本

An Era That Remade the Game

Lex: I want to ask, because we lived through such a moment in sports history —

Khabib: Mhm.

Lex: — that we might never see anything like it again. I'm talking about this rivalry between Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo. Of course, since you love Real Madrid, you naturally love Cristiano Ronaldo. But what can you say about it? A lot of people call him the absolute best. And for many, Messi is number one. There's also a very good book about their rivalry — I recommend it. It basically tells the story of modern football through their rivalry: Messi versus Ronaldo, one rivalry, almost 20-year era. Two GOATs in an era that remade the world's game. So it's been 20 years — what can you say? Why do you consider Cristiano Ronaldo a great footballer? What do you like about him? Let's start with Ronaldo.

Ronaldo: The Complete Athlete

Khabib: Well, he's a natural-born athlete. God gave him the athleticism, and he managed to maintain it. There are many who have lost it. There are many players who have talent, physical ability, but they are lazy. But he has it all — athleticism, talent, hard work, everything.

And then there's this. He played in Manchester. He moved — he shone in Portugal at Sporting, then moved to Manchester. And it's not easy to make your mark at Manchester. From 2003 to 2008 he became a star there, and what he achieved in 2008 — just look at how many individual trophies he won and how much he won with his team. You can even look it up. Just search what Cristiano Ronaldo achieved in 2008. It's simply unbelievable.

And then he moved from Manchester. He transferred to an even more difficult club — Real Madrid. Nine years at Real Madrid.

Lex: Five years at Manchester United, then nine years at Real Madrid. That's about 15 years. You're under constant pressure at the two biggest clubs in the history of football.

Khabib: And at both clubs —

Lex: At both clubs.

Khabib: — he became the best. That's very difficult. Look here. Three Premier League titles came during his time at Manchester United. Look at 2008 specifically, what he accomplished then. He won the Premier League. He won the UEFA Champions League. Individually he won the Golden Boot, top scorer in the Champions League, the Premier League — every major trophy.

Lex: Right.

Khabib: But the point is that at Manchester he spent 5 years performing at the highest level under enormous pressure. Then he spent 9 years at Real Madrid.

Lex: Yeah.

Khabib: After that, he moved to Juventus, but only for a short time. And this is the part people tend to forget. He spent three seasons at Juventus. And he also won both the Italian championship and the Super Cup there and scored 100 goals. And just the fact that for 20 years — let's say 22 or 23 years — he's been at the highest level. Look at how many goals he scored. And now he's closing in on 1,000. Will Messi ever reach that number? That is the big question. Next season he scores 40 goals in a season and he's less than 40 goals away from the 1,000 goal mark. That's how unique he is in that regard.

Giving Messi His Due

But just because I'm a Real Madrid fan doesn't mean I downplay what Messi has achieved. It's impossible to downplay what Messi's done. You have to give him the credit he deserves. But I wouldn't want to put one of them above the other. If I'm being honest, both of them watching each other, competing with each other — they stay there.

Would Messi be Messi without Ronaldo? Would Ronaldo be Ronaldo without Messi? Those are big questions. I'm convinced they watched each other closely. They always have, and they still do now. For almost 20 years, they've been watching each other, pushing each other, and constantly improving. They were already the best, but that drove them even further. By competing against one another, they pulled so far ahead of the rest — yes, whether you're talking about achievements, trophies, and all that.

And in that sense, their rivalry truly elevated the entire sport. More people started following football because of them watching the games. So I believe both of them deserve tremendous respect.

Lex: Yeah, I'd say I completely agree with you that if Messi hadn't had Ronaldo and Ronaldo hadn't had Messi —

Khabib: Yeah.

Lex: — would they have gone that far?

Khabib: I don't think so.

Lex: That's an open question.

Khabib: I don't think so.

Lex: Yes. But for me, there is nobody like Messi. His pure love for the game, for its own sake.

Khabib: You're a Barça guy?

Lex: Yes.

Khabib: Oh, really?

Lex: Yeah. I can tell from the way you're talking about it — the way you… you got me. Yeah. Yeah.

Khabib: Nothing against it, but — yes, sure. Well, I mean, Iniesta, Xavi, Busquets, Iniesta, Puyol — that was a legendary team.

Lex: Yes.

The Two Greatest Club Teams Ever

Khabib: No, but look, you can compare them like this. Iniesta, Xavi, Busquets, Messi, Ronaldinho, Piqué —

Lex: Ronaldo.

Khabib: Yes, Ronaldinho. He was a bit earlier. That Barcelona team from roughly 2008 to 2012, that 4-year period — only one team in history can compare with them. Real Madrid from 2014 to 2018. They won in 2014, in 2016, 2017, and 2018. The only interruption was Barcelona's team with Neymar.

Lex: With Neymar, yes — with Suárez and Messi. That was 2015.

Khabib: Well, let's leave that aside. But you know — with Modrić, Kroos, Casemiro, Ronaldo, Benzema, Marcelo, Carvajal, Casillas — and this team compared to Víctor Valdés, Piqué, Puyol, Dani Alves, Jordi Alba, Busquets, Xavi, Iniesta, Villa, and Messi. For me those are the two greatest teams. Different generations, different squads. For me, they truly represent true dream teams at football, at club level. That's the comparison.

National Teams: Perfection at the International Level

But if we look at the national team level, you could pick France in 1998.

Lex: Yes, that 1998 France team is very close to a perfect team.

Khabib: And also, 2002 Brazil. In 2002 they were extremely strong.

Lex: Yes. You had Ronaldo, you had Ronaldo, Ronaldo, Ronaldo, Roberto Carlos, Cafu, right? You had Emerson, you had Kléberson, I think, Ronaldinho Jr., Lúcio, Edmilson.

Khabib: And beyond those superstar names, there were also very strong players who kind of stayed in the shadow of those stars. Stayed in their shadow. So Brazil 2002, France 1998, and then later there was Spain — from Euro 2008, the 2010 World Cup, and Euro 2012. At that period, the Spanish national team was close to perfect.

Zidane and the Headbutt

Lex: I wanted to go back to France. You mentioned Zidane. I really, really respect and admire him. There was this moment, psychologically very interesting, almost Shakespearean moment in his career when it ended with — how do you even call it, a headbutt? A headbutt to the chest. What's interesting is — I don't know, looking at your fight with Conor —

Khabib: Mhm.

Lex: — when emotion builds up, for most of it you're focused on the game, but in the end you let that emotion out.

Khabib: Mhm.

Lex: What do you think about that headbutt?

Khabib: I wouldn't want to judge him. Wouldn't want to be some kind of judge of what he did. Well, he did what he did. We don't know what was really going on there. But as a player, of course, he was unique. He won the Euros, the World Cup, reached finals, won the Champions League, the Spanish and the Italian Championships and Cups too. It's just unique.

And the way he played — I just always remembered him for the way sweat was just pouring off him. The way he ran, how he gave everything in every single match. He had incredible stamina, incredible endurance. I think a lot of people listening to this podcast may not have watched Zidane playing live. When I say live, I mean watching him play in real time, right? I personally didn't see his games live. I was younger then, but I did watch many of his matches later on. I remember the goals he scored in World Cup finals in 1998 and 2006, especially the headers, and even that penalty, the Champions League final, European Championships — the way he played, the way he handled the ball, the way the ball was glued to his feet, his movements, and then his charisma. It's rare to find all of that in one player. You don't see that combination often.

What Is Charisma?

There are many very good players, but sometimes they're just not that interesting to watch. You know what I mean? I don't want to give specific examples because someone might take it in the wrong way. So I won't name anyone, but there are players who are phenomenal in terms of their physical attributes — fast, explosive, effective — but they don't have charisma, that energy that makes people want to watch them. And I don't think that's their fault. But with Zidane, everything came together. You always wanted to watch him play.

You always want to watch Ronaldo play. You always want to watch Beckham play. You want to watch Edgar Davids running around the field in those glasses, his hair bouncing behind him, right? You still wanted to watch the way Barthez played in goal — no matter how many bizarre goals he conceded, you still wanted to watch him play. Or Oliver Kahn, the way he stood in goal and directed the whole team, the way he would rush out to the ball, the way strikers were afraid of him. I mean, so many strikers have admitted that they were afraid if they found themselves one-on-one with Oliver Kahn in the penalty area.

You always wanted to watch Roberto Carlos take a free kick or storm down the left flank. You always wanted to see Cafu or Míchel Salgado make an overlapping run. The way Vieira stood there as the defensive midfielder, or somebody like Maldini or like Rio Ferdinand, or somebody like that. You wanted to watch Casillas in goal. So, you know, for me and maybe for our generation, those players had something special.

Lex: Can you try to explain what charisma is? Like you said, there are good players — and then there is a Zidane.

Khabib: It's very difficult to explain. You either have it or you don't.

Lex: Personality, right?

Khabib: Yes. But there are so many different forms of it. Zidane, in a way, almost moved slowly in a way. But he'd carry the ball from midfield into attack incredibly quickly. So it's very hard to put into words. Hard to explain it.

And both Ronaldos had that. I mean, the Brazilian Ronaldo too. The way he played in those World Cups — yes, it was just phenomenal. '98, 2002, even in 2006 when he was already past his peak. He was so fascinating to watch. Seriously, how many people turned on their TVs just to watch Ronaldo? People knew that was it, that in 2010 he wouldn't be playing. And even in 2006, he wasn't really in his prime. But still, so many people turned on the TV just to watch him play.

And Zidane 2006 was really, you know, the peak of that whole generation of legends that had been building since '98, 2000, 2002, and 2004. All the cream of the crop came in. Most of them weren't at their physical peak anymore, but the names were still there. Honestly, I think that for football fans, I'd recommend just looking up the teams and the lineups from the 2006 World Cup. Look at the rosters. Every single team had stars you wanted to watch.

On Taking Initiative — and Risk

Lex: Speaking of teams, what style of football do you like? You prefer short passing, long balls, individual plays — you know, like Maradona carrying the ball, or of course Cristiano Ronaldo taking the ball and scoring himself?

Khabib: Mostly those who take the initiative.

Lex: You like that?

Khabib: Yeah, definitely. I like players who are willing to take the initiative. I was recently talking to Zlatan about this and he said, "It drives me crazy when I have players on my team who, when you pass them the ball, they immediately get rid of it. They don't want to take the initiative. When you have three or more players on the team — if there are three people on the team who are not afraid to make mistakes, that's usually enough. They take the initiative, take control of the game, drive the team forward, make mistakes, but they keep trying. And then there are others who hide." He says they get the ball and immediately pass it to someone else. Just don't give it to me. Not me. Not me. They just want to get rid of the ball.

It's like, you know, it's like something one of Zidane's coaches once said: "If you don't know what to do with the ball, give it to Zidane. He'll figure it out." [laughter]

So, you see, that's the thing. It's a quality. Not every player has it. You're taking the ball, you're taking responsibility, you're taking the initiative. You are not afraid to fail. You're not afraid to make a mistake.

Cristiano had a moment like that. He missed a penalty, and later in the same match he stepped up to take another one. Think about that. You take the first penalty, you miss it, then another penalty comes along and you still step up to take it — because if you miss two penalties in the same game, you're under a lot of pressure, right? But that's the point. You're not afraid to fail. As a leader, you take the initiative and you're willing to take risks.

That's honestly the beauty of it. The beauty of sports in general — the bigger the risk, the bigger the potential for greatness. If there's no risk, then you can't put yourself in the category of athletes people will talk about as some of the best ever, especially when it's a high-level game like the World Cup. And yes — the more risk, the sweeter the victory. There must be risk.

Maradona's Shadow — and Messi Emerging From It

That's why they often speak of Maradona as a great player. There are many great players. He's great — one of them. Yeah. For many reasons. But one reason is that he kind of carried the team on his shoulders. He took the initiative and carried them. That's when he led Napoli. When he led Napoli to the league title — who knew Napoli then? Maradona came from Barcelona to Napoli and made them champions, and the whole stadium was named after him. Many guys played in Napoli, but there was never anyone like Maradona.

And recently, I saw somewhere — or I think someone pointed out — the pressure on the guys who are transferring to Napoli. Whoever you are, you will always be in Maradona's shadow, and you stay in the shadow because fans will never give you the credit you might deserve, because they will always compare you to him. Are you Maradona or not? And if you're not Maradona, you will never get full recognition.

I want to say that one of the things that makes Messi great, I think, is that he really had to live in such a shadow of Maradona, especially with the World Cup.

Lex: Yes.

Khabib: It's not easy. And he came out of it. Hard to emerge from that shadow.

Lex: Yes.

Khabib: And he won the World Cup.

Lex: Yeah.

Khabib: In that sense, you have to give Messi his due. I'm addressing the Real Madrid fans now. [laughter]

Lex: Ours — yours. Both sides. You're explaining it to them.

Khabib: Yeah. Yeah. I got you. Most of them, I think, even if they don't like Barcelona, they still recognize Messi's greatness.

Zlatan: Confidence as an Identity

Lex: I know that you met Zlatan and you talk to him. I think he's one of the most self-confident people in football, in the world in general. What do you think about this confidence? Of course, he's joking around a little bit, but I think he really believes in himself.

Khabib: Well, yeah, he does. He does. I've known Zlatan for years now. We get along well, and I know his kids, and I like his personality. I like his confidence. I mean, he's a unique player. There are not many Zlatans in football. You know, wherever he played, he always scored. He's a goal scorer. He is that kind of center forward and he always carried the team. He was a leader wherever he transferred. It doesn't matter — Milan, Inter, Juventus, when he moved to LA Galaxy or Paris Saint-Germain. He was a leader everywhere he went, with the national team, with his clubs. He was always the guy driving the team forward, taking the initiative. And honestly, he cemented his place as one of the greatest players to ever play the game.

And yeah, maybe he was… [sighs and gasps] when it comes to trophies — not individual achievements, but team honors — Sweden wasn't exactly the greatest team, and some of the clubs he played for didn't always win the biggest trophies. But as an athlete, as an individual, as a person, he is a very strong athlete.

item.description:
## 一、被忽视的"镜像共生"：伟大是一种相互寄生的现象
大多数人把 Messi vs Ronaldo 讲成"谁更强"的问题，但 Khabib 无意间点出了一个更颠覆的真相：**他们不是竞争者，而是彼此的"训练器官"**。"Would Messi be Messi without Ronaldo?"——这句问话背后藏着一个进化生物学式的结论：顶级捕食者会因缺乏对手而退化。C 罗和梅西并不是并列的两座山峰，而是一个**双星系统**——彼此的引力把对方甩离了地表。真正让人意外的是：如果这个假设成立，那么"最伟大的球员"这个概念本身就是伪命题——**伟大不是属性，而是关系**。
## 二、Khabib 谈齐达内头槌，其实在谈他自己
整段对话最"莎士比亚"的时刻，不是齐达内的头槌，而是 Lex 追问时 Khabib 的回避："I wouldn't want to judge him."——他说这话的时候，正被 Lex 提醒他自己与 McGregor 的爆发。这是一种**共谋式沉默**：一个曾经在笼子外扑向对手团队的男人，对世界杯决赛顶爆意大利人的男人不做评判，因为**他们说的是同一种语言

item.title: [a16z] Garry Tan: New Rules for Founders
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、隐藏的"时间旅行者悖论"：Gary 的两次拒绝背后，藏着一个反常识的成功公式

Gary 两次拒绝改变命运的机会——放弃继续做 web 编程转向 Windows Mobile，拒绝 Peter Thiel 亲自开出的 Palantir offer——损失可能高达 20-40 亿美元。但真正让人意外的观察是：这两次错误本质上是同一个错误的重复，而这个错误恰恰是当下 99% 聪明人正在犯的——他们在"看地图"而不是"看地形"。

Gary 说"如果我是时间旅行者，我会给自己发个消息"——但仔细想，他真正需要的不是未来信息，而是信任已经拥有的当下经验。这里有个跨领域连接：这与投资大师 Howard Marks 说的"二阶思维"完全相反。Marks 强调你要比别人多想一层，而 Gary 揭示的是在噪音过多的时代，"零阶思维"——即直接相信一手体验——反而是稀缺资源。华尔街日报、Twitter、投资人的观点都是"地图"；你自己五年的 web 开发经验才是"地形"。这个洞察在 AI 时代放大了 100 倍：模型可以在几秒内合成所有二手观点，唯一无法复制的就是你的第一手体验。

二、"Markdown 文件即员工"——一个被低估的组织学革命

Gary 提出"markdown file is an employee"看似只是工程效率话题，但把它跟他后面讲的日本丰田生产系统放在一起看，就出现了一个惊人的连接：

我们正在经历一场反向的工业革命。第一次工业革命把手工艺人变成流水线工人（去技能化），管理科学把创造者变成层级中的螺丝钉（去主体性）。而 AI 时代做的是相反的事——它把每个个体重新变回"完整的手艺人 + 一整条流水线"。Gary 提到 Brex 的 Pedro 用 agent 监听所有下属会议、直接跨两级做决策——这不是"更好的管理"，这是管理层作为一个物种的历史终结的开始。

跨领域的意外连接：中世纪欧洲的手工业行会消失了 500 年，而 Gary 描述的世界里，"个体大师"这个古老的经济单元正在借助 agent 复活。他说"35-45 岁的创始人 + 400 个自己"能打败任何 Mag7 部门——这不是效率提升，这是把 20 世纪整个"管理者阶级"变成一个可选功能。他称之为"100 年的管理科学是一场干扰"，这句话如果 5 年前说，会被认为是狂妄；今天，它可能是对未来 20 年组织形态最精准的预言。

三、"最不快乐的一天"与"20 年慢"——藏在乐观里的最深悲观

最反直觉的一段：Gary 一边说 AI 会带来"1000 倍更好的产品和服务"，一边又说变革"会比你想的慢 20 年"。这看起来是矛盾，但其实是同一个洞察的两面——人类的"7±2"认知带宽是宇宙常数级别的瓶颈。

这里有个心理学的隐藏连接：George Miller 1956 年那篇著名的《The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two》定义了人类工作记忆上限。Gary 实际上在说：所有现代制度——公司、政府、法律、教育——都是围绕这个数字设计的操作系统。AI 让"三本哈利波特"能塞进你脑袋，意味着整个社会操作系统面临一次内核重写。但内核重写从来不会一夜完成——因为社会的"schema migration"必须让所有活人存活。

真正打破常规的观察是：Gary 把"变化慢"说成"white pill（好消息）"，这与整个 AI 圈的叙事完全相反。所有人都在说"再不行动就晚了"，Gary 却说"你有 20 年"。这背后是一个更深的哲学立场——如果你相信自己是那个 native 于新范式的人，时间就是你的朋友，而不是敌人。就像 2003 年他们是 web native 的一代，如今掌控了世界；今天 18-22 岁的 AI native 一代，将在 2045 年前后接管一切。这个视角把"AI 焦虑"从生存威胁降维成了世代交替——一件人类经历过无数次的自然过程。

最后一个彩蛋：Gary 说"everything awesome in my life is kind of a cult"（我生活中所有酷的事都有点像邪教）。把这句话跟他后面说 Palantir、YC 都始于"违反正统的秘密真理"连起来看，出现了一个让人不安的洞察：创造性和"边缘性"在结构上是同一件事。你不可能既想要突破，又想要主流认同。Homebrew Computer Club "不是能约到姑娘的地方"——但它是 21 世纪的起点。当下你觉得"稍微有点尴尬、有点小众、有点解释不清"的执念，可能就是下一个万亿市场的种子。

📝 转录文本

开场

"We may never achieve a utopia, but it is worthy and worth it to attempt. Everything that's awesome in my life is kind of a cult. We had to go over to the Windows team. They wouldn't reply to our emails. They wouldn't fix our bugs. And we had to go over there with a baseball bat. An org like Microsoft can't." — "Yes." — "But a startup can." — "Yes." — "And every startup must."

—— "Gary, so good to have you, brother. Thank you so much for joining us today." —— "Thanks for having me." —— "Amazing, dude. Well, we're going to cover a bunch of the basics, then we're going to get into the advanced topics to make sure that we uh kind of match the the curiosity, ambition of our audience." —— "That sounds great." —— "Does that work? Awesome."

一、2003 年入行：科技的低谷时刻

—— "Well, dude, maybe talk to me a bit about the beginning of your journey 2003. You know, it feels like what's under discussed is founder psychology and then sort of Silicon Valley culture and how the two are connected. What did it feel like when you first got in the game back in 2003 coming out of Stanford?"

—— "I guess I wanted to work at startups but uh 2003 was funny in that like web 1.0 had just ended, like the you know NASDAQ had just crashed and uh actually there were no jobs that I could even find in the Bay Area other than you know working at GAP IT. And so the two job offers I had were uh Microsoft for Windows Mobile which I was pretty excited about, or Expedia."

—— "Okay."

—— "Yeah. I you know I had student loans and I you know while I wanted to start a company I just you know felt like I needed to get a job. And then actually there were no jobs in the base. It was like kind of hard to believe actually uh that moment was so bleak. And then right before web 2.0…"

—— "It felt like it might have been the end of tech. Huh."

—— "Right. A little bit. Yeah. That's that was the vibe. And then you know at the end of the day like that's the boom that's the bust. Like these things sort of happen over and over again."

—— "So at the time did it feel high status to work in tech or on startups?"

—— "Not at all. I mean you know it's sort of lost to the sands of time but um I was still excited about tech though. Um you know I had done a lot of web programming."

二、第一次错过：追热点而不是追自己知道的事

—— "And then one of my regrets actually was um I was sort of chasing what was hot instead of what was clearly the thing I knew. Mark Zuckerberg was probably doing FaceMash um around then around 2003, and then Facebook didn't even exist yet um and I was getting out of web programming at exactly the wrong time because it felt like that was the smart thing to do."

—— "Yeah, it was smart. And you know I mean this is true now. Um you know in in front of all these people at startup school uh you know I sort of started this 'don't larp' um meme."

—— "I saw that. Uh, but I think like that's that's embedded in this idea that like you should just be earnest."

—— "Yeah. And then you shouldn't follow what the crowd is saying, right? Like at that moment people said the web was dead, but that was sort of the perfect time to work on web and social and things like that. Um, and you know, I didn't do it. I I ran off and said like, 'Oh, well, the next hot thing will be mobile.' So, I wanted to work at Windows Mobile, which was true, but um why I give up like the thing that could have been the next thing?"

认真 ≠ 幼稚，认真 = 勇气

—— "What I love about what you're saying though is often when we hear earnest, we think naive, but actually what it sounds like you're saying is there's like earnestness is a sort of result of maturity and courage. Is that…"

—— "Courage is actually I think the right thing."

—— "Yes."

—— "Like if you know something, it sort of if someone just like comes and contradicts you or even if like a blog post or like someone on Twitter uh contradicts you, you're like, 'Well, I I don't I don't agree with that because I believe my own direct experience.'"

—— "Yes."

—— "I know that I'm not a time traveler because if I was a time traveler, I would have I would have sent a message back to myself and said, 'Just stay on working on web stuff.' Like you literally have um five years of experience on top of everyone else. Like you could do an end run around everyone. Like you could have built like any kind of social software."

—— "Yes."

—— "But instead I was um you know I was 22 so I was like being whipped around by uh whatever I could read in the Wall Street Journal. And you know I the the classic question I'm sure you get that you know all investors get all the time is 'what's hot and what should I work on', right? And that's the wrong question to ask. Like the right question is like what are you interested in? What do you know uniquely?"

—— "And so that's like, you know, one of a great many mistakes I made in my career. I feel like I'm a little bit uh doomed to be the first principal storyteller of uh all the mistakes that I made in my career."

—— "I think that it's it's very inspiring for founders to hear your own journey and your own mistakes and then not feel so bad about the ones that we've all made along the way."

三、当下硅谷：竞争、边缘、部落

—— "Yeah. I mean, maybe talk about the culture of Silicon Valley today. You know, on one hand, maybe it was despondent 20 years ago. It's crazy to think that was just 23 years ago that you're talking about. Um, now you think we would all be incredibly elated. Yet, there's this undercurrent. Maybe it's the larping thing that you mentioned. You know, it's being outside of the light cone, the permanent underclass. Where does that come from? Do you think there's any truth in it? Talk through that."

—— "I mean, I get it. Like, there's just more competition than ever. And then um I think maybe it's just that we're spending too much time in distribution. I think Chris Dixon talks about this all the time where um you know you're in the idea maze but you the cool parts of the idea maze are like the weird fringe parts actually."

—— "It's always like uh what is a toy like? And that's the pattern in Silicon Valley over and over again that bears repeating, right?"

—— "Yes."

—— "Like the idea that you could have a computer on every desk in every home. Yeah. Uh today is like of course like that's what's come to pass. But the people who created that thing they were fringe weirdo punks totally yes they were outsiders. I mean Homebrew Computer Club was not where you were getting laid."

—— "Yeah, that's true. You just were like following this weird obsession that you know actually I want my own computer."

—— "And I think Chris has said this too. I think a good measure of how interesting the thing is is can you find the edge. And for the most interesting things you typically can't. Even if you find the edge of the conversation you can't find the intellectual edge, which I think is a very good sign."

找到你的部落

—— "I mean I had this growing up in the 80s. Maybe you had this too. There was sort of one way to be cool in grade school and probably in high school and maybe when you got to college you kind of found your people. And now I think one of the miracles of being internet native generation is that people find their people much sooner. You find your people on Reddit, you find your people on you know X or Insta or whatever your network is."

—— "Oh yeah. I mean that's the coolest thing today. Like there's probably a subreddit, there's probably um a part of X, like you know some part of teapot that is uh you know this part of Twitter that um is just your set of super weird but like really really into that thing. And you can find your tribe more or less instantly."

四、第二次错过：拒绝 Peter Thiel 的 Palantir Offer

—— "Yeah. Yeah. Can you talk a bit about the culture of Silicon Valley? Felt like 10 years ago it was sort of, you know, it was lower status to work on something like Palantir either because people were nervous about doing things that were too much in the national interest or because it was sort of dismissed as a services business. Now it's clearly one of the most important companies in the world with one of the most compelling CEOs. You were early there. What did it feel like? Why did you do it?"

—— "Yeah, I mean uh I have a worse story than that. I have another mistake story. Okay. Where um uh Joe Lonsdale and Stefan Cohen uh were my fraternity brothers at Stanford Phi."

—— "Okay."

—— "Uh and then I had a job and they were like interns at Peter Thiel's hedge fund."

—— "Okay."

—— "And uh Peter has this thing where you're supposed to like you know when you start a thing you write down on a piece of paper all the smartest people uh who you need to go and hire and like get to join you. And so, uh, they said, 'Oh, both of them were like, oh, let's go get Gary. He's up in Seattle.' Like, they flew me down to have dinner with him."

—— "And he said, you Peter said, 'I'm so sure this is the right thing for you. Like, here's a check for 70 grand.' That was how much I made at Microsoft at the time. Yeah. And I said, 'Thank you very much, Mr. Thiel, but I might get promoted to level 60 this year.'"

—— "Oh, no."

—— "Which I did, but uh I think it's like that was like a $2 billion to $4 billion mistake at this point. No, no."

—— "Um, and I think about it all the time. Like basically I did the same thing again. It was like the same thing that got me to go work on Windows Mobile instead of um just staying on the thing that I knew and loved."

地图 vs 地形：一切美好都始于一种"邪教"

—— "Uh it happened again. I was like, well, I don't know, you know, I was working backwards from the map instead of looking down at the territory and saying like, oh, well, these are the smartest people I know. Like Joe and Stefan were among the smartest people I'd ever met."

—— "Um and you know if not them like who was I gonna you know be a co-founder with, like it just you know the universe was saying like this is the thing you need to do. But all I cared about was what was cool, what was hot, what would a really good investor say."

—— "Um and the thing is like they're like going off of uh a map. Yeah. And like you can see, you can look down, you can look around, you can like have first principles knowledge of what's going on."

—— "Um and you know what they were doing is like they were going to governments and three-letter agencies. Yeah. And it was clear that um the things that really good computer scientists in Palo Alto could do and create."

—— "Yes."

—— "Uh DC did not have access to that. And you know, it's funny how much that thing that they had identified, like Peter and Joe and Stefan and later Alex Karp identified, um that like runs through almost everything that we do um in Silicon Valley."

—— "It's just like uh the future is already here. It's not evenly distributed. Yes. And then that's where like first principles knowledge or like just viewing the world as a scientist is actually very useful."

—— "Yes. Um and what a scientist does is you know sure there's published papers but you go and you examine all the truths. And what you find is that once you go down into the experiment or you go down and talk to the first party people who are experiencing a thing, um then you learn secret knowledge, then you have gnosis."

—— "And so uh you know from Palantir I definitely learned that uh everything that's awesome in my life is kind of a cult. Yeah. That starts with some sort of truth or belief that flies in the face of an orthodoxy which is very punk actually."

—— "Yes. Yes. To dude, that's very Rick Rubin would approve."

五、YC：把外来者变成圈内人

—— "Yeah. Yeah. Well actually what I love about you're saying is that there's a beautiful truth in the fact that you've talked through some of these maybe tragic misses but you know the lessons are courage, the lessons are earnestness right, the lessons are when your instincts are pulling you to work with a set of people."

—— "So, so maybe talk a little bit about, you know, we talk a lot about how Silicon Valley and the magic is it takes outsiders and turns them into insiders. And I feel like YC is the ultimate distillation of that. You know, you go from being two founders perhaps from a foreign country to two people with YC on their LinkedIn and everybody now knows what that means."

—— "Totally."

—— "So, talk about how that happens. Is it a process? Is it a mindset? And how has it changed over the years?"

—— "Um, I mean I have to credit Paul Graham and Jessica Livingston and the original founders including Trevor Blackwell and Robert Morris. I mean uh what Paul and Jessica figured out was that there are lots and lots of really smart people who do not get access um to Silicon Valley."

—— "I mean, I think in the past you had to like go to the right schools, you had to know the right people sort of. And if you didn't, you'd come to Silicon Valley and you try to get invited to the right parties. There's like a social network that you had to crack."

—— "Um, and then, uh, at YC, we have a pejorative for that whole scene, which it's like we call them 'sceners' actually. Okay. Uh, which is I mean, it's sort of a nod to like what you used to have to do. Um, and some people still believe that's like how you do it."

—— "Um, all they did was say, you know what, like here's a here's a website, here's 12 questions. Later, we added like a one minute video. And, uh, people on the other end who are builders are going to try to give you a fair shake."

—— "And so, today we have, uh, you know, 16 equal partners, including myself, and all of us like went through YC and had successful outcomes. And um I think there's something valuable to that that just you know welcome to welcome to Silicon Valley."

—— "We just um celebrated uh 7,000 people coming to San Francisco. The majority of them the very first time they came. It's you know our startup school every single year."

—— "So incredible."

—— "We kind of call it like Birthright but for tech."

—— "It looked like the Roman coliseum dude."

—— "Yeah. It was amazing."

YC 真正给的：一个可以真诚的社群

—— "Yeah. So, you know, I think that that's the coolest thing about Silicon Valley. Like you sort of it sort of doesn't matter where you're from or who you are. It just actually matters what your ideas are and can you execute."

—— "The only other thing that I'd say like why YC people get that a lot of people don't get is um a community of people who you can be super real with. It's like if you go to a TechCrunch event, you look to the left, you look to the right and it's like are you really going to be able to tell them anything real?"

—— "Like you're going to hold your cards pretty close and uh you know you're going to say 'how you doing' and they're going to say 'killing it' and then they're going to ask back and like 'oh I'm also killing it'. I mean honestly founders really need that. Like it's very solitary."

—— "It's um you know on the day that you lose your best customer, on the day that your best engineer quits, like who you going to call? And if you have no one, like I mean the day your co-founder loses hope and you're not allowed to right—that's a tough day you know."

六、Vibe Coding 时代：一个人 = 400 个自己

—— "Talk about the historical upside sort of surprises of like founder types business types and the downside surprises. What have you learned through YC?"

—— "I mean what's we're sort of in the middle of a big transformation now. I think um for the longest time we really really believed that you needed co-founders. And I think that everything else being equal, having co-founders is net really, really good."

—— "Totally."

—— "Um I think some of this is like the beginning of a cult, like you know a cult where there's only one person and that person can't convince anyone else to join them is like you know worse than a cult is just like a crazy person actually."

—— "Right. Right. Right."

—— "Um I think this is like an old Derek Sivers TED talk right where it's like uh yeah one person dancing in a field is a crazy person. Yes. But um you know it's really the second person who like gets up."

—— "That's right."

—— "And joins that person like then you what you find is you know suddenly 10 people are there dancing then it's a party. Yeah. That's literally the TED talk."

—— "Love it."

—— "And um I think there's something to that. But you know I think what's happening right now with vibe coding and agentic coding, um, literally any given person could be 400 of that person like from two years like even like nine months ago. Um, you can be a multiple of yourself."

—— "Amazing."

—— "Yeah. And so…"

—— "Do you think founders are more ambitious than they've ever been?"

—— "They should be. Yes. Um, if anything like that's the number one thing that people should do."

—— "Yes."

—— "Is realize that like don't chase your success or my success. Like that was, you know, when we were coming up like the game done changed, you know, like you actually you can't just do a SaaS thing."

—— "Like you know I was just doing an analysis on like pure SaaS and I was like oh shoot, like you know a pure like per seat SaaS thing like not totally clear it will exist in another five or 10 years. Like it's perfectly fine as a wedge but if you're doing that now in 2026 like you better hope that that's like a leap to some sort of moat around data or network effects or something else, right?"

—— "Um, and that's like, you know, if you if we would time travel to like even two years ago, it's like SaaS was God, you know, like the 10-20x like next 12 months uh revenue multiple was like, you know, iron law."

—— "Yes."

—— "And like it's hard to believe it was like, oh yeah, no, that's not true at all now."

七、代码不再珍贵：GStack、GBrain 与 Agentic Coding

—— "Well, all this, you know, a related thing that I love is that code is no longer precious."

—— "My god."

—— "Like the things that we had to go through to get something shipped. And that's why you had to have this like sense that what you were making was important with a capital I. And that actually flies against the kind of beautiful truth we were just talking about because often earnestness isn't obviously important with a capital I. So you pursue things that seem important when most of the most important things actually start out seeming actually unimportant."

—— "Oh yeah."

—— "I know you've been all over this with GStack and GBrain. And you know when you started out to build those things with the intention to like contribute to the community or just explore your interests."

—— "Oh, I was just messing around. Like you know uh what was it? I think Boris Cherny came on Latent Space podcast right, and I just felt like the urge to you know and a bunch of our mutual friends like all of them uh basically just started coding again. And I was like oh something's happening, I'd better start."

—— "Um and then initially it was just messing around. It's like, oh, I mean, what would it be like to do like make an office hours? Yeah. Um, and then the craziest thing there was like we had just started um like recording all of our office hours actually. And then I could I had like a few months of data and there were like very clear things that um the YC partners used as like rhetorical devices or ways to like draw out like a step function in your ambition."

—— "Um, and then what's funny is I have this markdown file that is basically like the perfect script on how to advise founders to like increase their ambition. And then I actually had to go into Claude and I said 'reduce this by 90%. Reduce the strength and intensity of this prompt by 90%.' And then I open sourced that."

—— "cuz some of it is like you got to come and do YC 100%."

—— "Of course. Of course. Well, we'll take your five. Okay. Thank you."

—— "Yeah. We can't give away the crown jewels like for free."

—— "This just a taste. The first one's free, you know."

只招 Cloud Code Top 10% 用户

—— "Well, dude, Kevin caught this. I think it was a GStack or GBrain. We're deep in the open source. You had said, 'Please apply to YC.'"

—— "Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. But only if you're a top 10% user of Cloud Code."

—— "Incredible."

—— "Like based on whether you're um thinking about users, like thoughtful about your product and your design, like it's not not everyone gets that message actually."

—— "Yes. Yes. Well, dude, I love that you're doing it. And I love that you're doing it so publicly because I think this comes back to the earnestness point which is the whole thing about building intuition at this moment is just using the technology."

—— "Oh yeah."

—— "You know and I think that there's this feeling like oh how can I possibly catch up or there's so much seriousness around it. It's like no just use every model and build completely trivial things for no other reason to have a chassis with which to learn the new technology."

—— "I think the most exciting thing is like you can just have ideas and then in the past it's like oh well I had to be the PM let me write the spec like let me make sure I have you know one or two engineers like oh how are we going to do QA like there's just all this stuff that you used to have to worry about. And then now it's like no slash QA, like it's done. Like you know, yeah we tested it, it's good. Like we have unit tests like 90% test coverage, you know."

—— "Totally. You know, it's like arranging your zen rock garden. It's just fun to do it and the like the output doesn't matter that much, which is why everybody talks about coding agents but very few people are showing their work."

—— "Oh yeah."

It's like, hey, you don't have to have an American vision for how AI impacts your society. If you want the NHS to be incredible, then like you could do that with this technology. So, the kind of the opportunity for ambition to be very localized in our communities, I think, is something really interesting."

—— "Yeah. And so, yeah, act local, like take care of the people right next to you. Like, you know, I I think it's funny. Uh, so many people get very very obsessed with national. I don't even want to look at national generally right now. It's like, you know what? Like, I care about San Francisco. I care about housing. I care about crime. I care about uh, you know, treatment and recovery. And if we do that, like, we can have the society we want to live in."

—— "And then you know if we fix local like state and national will fix itself because like on a five or 10 year basis like the people who win up there like they they will come up through a system that's functional and about saying no to things that don't make sense about saying yes to the things that are awesome for the people."

—— "I love it. All right, Gary. First of many. Thanks, brother."

—— "Thanks, bro. This is great. Cool. Yeah."

观看原视频 →

## 一、隐藏的"时间旅行者悖论"：Gary 的两次拒绝背后，藏着一个反常识的成功公式
Gary 两次拒绝改变命运的机会——放弃继续做 web 编程转向 Windows Mobile，拒绝 Peter Thiel 亲自开出的 Palantir offer——损失可能高达 20-40 亿美元。但真正让人意外的观察是：**这两次错误本质上是同一个错误的重复，而这个错误恰恰是当下 99% 聪明人正在犯的**——他们在"看地图"而不是"看地形"。
Gary 说"如果我是时间旅行者，我会给自己发个消息"——但仔细想，他真正需要的不是未来信息，而是**信任已经拥有的当下经验**。这里有个跨领域连接：这与投资大师 Howard Marks 说的"二阶思维"完全相反。Marks 强调你要比别人多想一层，而 Gary 揭示的是**在噪音过多的时代，"零阶思维"——即直接相信一手体验——反而是稀缺资源**。华尔街日报、Twitter、投资人的观点都是"地图"；你自己五年的 web 开发经验才是"地形"。这个洞察在 AI 时代放大了 100 倍：模型可以在几秒内合成所有二手观点，唯一无法复制的就是你的第

item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib vs Conor McGregor fight: Khabib on why it was the biggest fight of all time
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被忽略的核心：Khabib 不是"心理更强"，而是把自己的自信"托管"到了 Conor 够不到的服务器上

大多数人把这场比赛的心理博弈总结为"Khabib 心态硬，Conor 挑衅无效"。但仔细听 Khabib 的原话——他反复把力量归给两个来源："the almighty gave me this unshakeable confidence" 和"一个父亲的电话胜过窗外一百万人"。

这是一个非常反直觉的结构：Khabib 并没有在心理层面正面迎战 Conor，他做的事情是把"自我价值的认证服务器"迁移到了 Conor 根本无法访问的地方——一个在神学层面，一个在跨洋的达吉斯坦山村。Conor 所有的挑衅、家庭羞辱、宗教触碰，都是在向一个"客户端"发起攻击，但 Khabib 的自我认证根本不在这台机器上。Jose Aldo 之所以被击穿，是因为他的自信来源仍在"世俗竞技系统"内——粉丝、纪录、拳台声誉——这些恰恰是 Conor 最擅长污染的领域。

这不是心理韧性问题，这是架构问题。

二、达吉斯坦式父子距离，其实是一种"高信噪比协议"

Khabib 描述父子关系时说，你不能对自己的孩子做 baby talk，要"像士兵面对将军"。西方现代育儿会立刻把这判定为"情感不足"。但注意他接下来讲的：一个越洋电话、几句简短的建议，就能"charge me up way more than absolutely everything else combined"。

这是通信工程里的一个基本原理：带宽越低、约束越严的信道，单位信号的信息密度就越高。

  • 现代亲子关系是无限带宽（随时发消息、随时拥抱、随时表达情感）——结果是信号被稀释，父母的一句话不再具有决定性。
  • 达吉斯坦父子关系是极窄带宽 + 极强协议约束——恰恰因为父亲不能随便说话，所以他说的每一句都变成了内核指令级别的输入。

这个模式还能在别的地方找到镜像：奢侈品用稀缺制造价值、手写信比短信更重、日式茶道用极端克制反而承载最深情感。限制不是情感的对立面，限制是情感的浓缩机制。Khabib 的心理"钻石"，正是被这种带宽压制"压"出来的。

三、一个跨领域连接：为什么这场比赛能超越体育——它其实是"文明张力"的代理战争

Khabib 提到 Louis vs Schmeling（罗斯福 vs 希特勒）、Ali vs Frazier（越战、种族、宗教）时，说"they simply went beyond sports"。然后他把自己和 Conor 的对决自然地放进了这个序列。

表面上大家会说：因为炒作大、因为人设对立。但更深的结构是：这场比赛在 2018 年正好承载了一组当时全球正在剧烈对撞的文明张力：

Conor Khabib
都市个人主义 山村部族主义
Instagram 表演型自我 传统内敛型自我
后基督教西方（酒、金钱、性） 保守伊斯兰
用挑衅制造真实 用沉默守护真实
品牌化的身份 家族链条中的身份

有意思的是：这些张力不是 UFC 制造的，是 2015–2020 年间整个西方社会自身正在经历的撕裂（后真相、身份政治、传统 vs 全球化）。UFC 只是提供了一个八角笼，让两种世界观进行了一次不需要翻译的物理对决。

出人意料的推论：所以 Khabib 说"下一场同等级别的比赛还会出现"——但它不会因为哪个明星或哪个 promotion 出现，它会在下一次文明张力找到合适的两个人体作为代理时出现。这是历史结构问题，不是 matchmaking 问题。Dana White 找不到，只有时代自己会送出。

四、一个小彩蛋：钻石隐喻的意外精准

父亲用的比喻是"钻石在巨大压力下形成"。这个比喻听起来像是励志鸡汤，但物理上其实惊人地准确——钻石不是被"锻造"出来的，是碳原子在超高压 + 长时间下自动重组晶格结构的结果。它不需要外力雕刻，只需要压力持续存在，且碳自己不逃跑。

Khabib 做的正是这件事：不去反击 Conor 制造的压力，也不逃离它——只是站在那里承受，让压力自己完成结构重组。这可能是全场对话里最深的一句话，藏在一个看似俗套的比喻里。

📝 转录文本

The Biggest Fight in UFC History?

Lex: Your fight with Conor, I think, was the biggest fight in UFC history. That's for sure. Well, actually, in all of sports. Do you think there will ever be another fight of that magnitude in the UFC? Is it even possible?

Khabib: Well, let's look at the history here. I mean, our sport is still very young — say 35 years old, starting from the '90s. Put it this way: take, for example, the sport most similar to MMA, which is, well, let's say boxing. How old is boxing? 150 years? Like, when you think boxing, what pops into your head? Thrilla in Manila?

Lex: Yeah, yeah. Well, I love Mike Tyson a lot, too, so —

Tyson, Ali, and the Missing Rival

Khabib: Well, Tyson had big fights, but Mike Tyson never had that signature rival like Muhammad Ali had in Joe Frazier.

Lex: Mhm.

Khabib: Yeah, he just didn't have one. I mean, who do we have? Evander Holyfield? Look, Holyfield–Tyson is no Muhammad Ali. Take Ali and Frazier — Thrilla in Manila, right? People called it the greatest rivalry. And it still is. In the 20th century, there was nothing that could compare. In the 21st century, the only thing you could compare to it, purely based on the numbers, is Pacquiao and Mayweather. Yes, there was public interest, but there wasn't the energy that there was with Muhammad Ali and Joe Frazier.

Lex: Yeah, if I can just pause for a second, I'll check on Perplexity.

Khabib: Mhm.

Lex: List of biggest boxing fights of all time. It's Ali and Frazier, like you said.

Khabib: Yeah, yeah.

Lex: The first, the third. Well —

Khabib: When he lost. And then the third fight, the Thrilla in Manila.

Lex: And Foreman — I must say, Ali versus Foreman.

Khabib: Well, Foreman — that was the year, I think '74, right?

Lex: The fight was watched by up to a billion people worldwide.

Khabib: Yeah, yeah, yeah. It was one of those things. Politics got mixed into it, too.

Lex: Yeah.

Khabib: It — well, it was actually a very big fight.

Lex: Sugar Ray Leonard, Duran, Sugar Ray Leonard versus Thomas Hearns, Hagler versus Hearns.

Khabib: Well, Hagler — Hagler and Duran in Montreal.

Lex: Yeah.

Khabib: Sugar Ray Leonard and Duran in Montreal — when they fought, when he admitted after the fight that he lost the mental game and broke down before the fight. But then Sugar Ray beat him later.

Lex: Yeah, he came back and won.

Khabib: Yeah.

When a Fight Becomes Politics: Louis vs Schmeling

Khabib: Uh, well, if you look at it, out of everything that stands out, I think you can mention Frazier and Muhammad Ali. And there was also Joe Louis against the German Max Schmeling. Hitler stood behind Schmeling and Roosevelt stood behind Louis. For those who don't know this story — I just watched it recently — it was something incomparable. They were so big. They were two of the most famous athletes of their time. Roosevelt was promoting Joe Louis, you know. At that moment for America, it was something incredible that a white president was promoting a black world champion. And on the other hand, Hitler stood behind Schmeling.

Lex: It was what? 1936, 1938? Did they — they fought twice?

Khabib: Twice.

Lex: Twice.

Khabib: Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah. They fought two times.

Lex: This wasn't just a good boxing match, just a good fight. This was politics. Those were nations.

Khabib: This was politics, this was nations, everything. It all came together.

Lex: And it's the same thing with Ali, too — Muhammad Ali with the Vietnam War, all that stuff.

Khabib: Yes, yes. And his — and even religion is tied into it. Everything here came together.

Lex: They simply went beyond sports.

Khabib vs Conor: Beyond the Sport

Khabib: Yeah. It was the exact same thing when I fought Conor. That fight went beyond our sport. It impacted every sport, because athletes of all kinds of different sports — everyone who loves to compete, it didn't matter if it was football, basketball, soccer, or boxing — everyone was following this. And honestly, will there be a fight like that? Well, it's hard for me to say, but I think it'll happen. It'll happen for sure. There will always be champions, there will always be rivalries — but when it'll happen, that's just a matter of time.

Lex: So it's not entirely about the athletes, it's about everything combined.

Khabib: Yeah, it's everything combined. The way he talked, what he stirred up, the lines he crossed — touching on family, religion — and then somehow on one side you had Conor, this really interesting champion who knew how to hype himself up, and on the other side you had this undefeated somebody from nowhere, from the mountains. You know how it is. It all somehow — all of it — just kind of happened naturally. And it wasn't staged, it was real. We had a real rivalry, unlike the way a lot of people now just hype up interest in a fight — but people feel that energy. It doesn't go anywhere. People can tell what's real and what's fake, and because of that we went beyond our own sport. That's what made this fight so massive.

Emotional Control Under Pressure

Lex: Well, when you look into your heart back then and now, did you have anger? Did you have hatred for him?

Khabib: Back then and even now, I'd still keep a cool head. Nothing has changed. When you let your emotions take over, when they're off the charts, and you completely lose control — that's a very bad place to be. So you'll tire out faster. Uh, you'll fall for any kind of bait, and so on. I just knew that I needed to stay calm, composed, to stick to the plan no matter what happened, and not go beyond my emotional limits. This is a very, very dangerous moment when you give in to your emotions. You have to control them. Every single detail, every little thing has to be perfectly in place. The second you let it all slip, everything becomes a total mess.

So, once the fight was finally done, I just let all my emotions out. I had to step right in and prove it, and punish him, and show them I'm better — that I'm better than him — and put a final end to this whole bitter rivalry. When all of that was over, your emotions came out. That's where my emotions just went over the edge. But until the fight was completely finished — starting from training, you know, at the press conferences, at the weigh-ins, everywhere in front of the media — everywhere I kept myself completely under control, and I was very good at it.

Honestly, looking back, it's been almost 8 years now. Looking back, well, I'm a little surprised. At that point, I was a very emotional guy, too. Over these 8 years, a lot has happened in my life. But I'm surprised that I kept it together. And, well, you know, it wasn't easy for me to keep myself within my limits, to keep myself under control like that.

The Father Across the Ocean

But here, again, I'll come back to what I said — I was very lucky. My father called me. Uh, at that time, I was here 2 months before the fight. His advice helped me out so much, because for me it was not just that it mattered — it was actually the most important thing for me back then, just to know my father's reaction, how he was taking everything that was happening. Because there was just so much media coverage. So I knew my father was watching.

Lex: [snorts]

Khabib: It was important for me to know his take. I'd call and ask, and my father would even tell me things I hadn't even asked him about. He'd bring it up on his own. Because, you know, the way it is with us — between me and my father, in our traditions, in our part of the world, in our family, for generations, in our village — there's just always this distance with your father. Like, when you walk in, there are just so many things you can't let yourself do in front of your father. You have to be sort of like a soldier in front of a general, right? If you can even make that comparison. If a soldier stands at attention like that, then with us it's even stricter.

Like, just to give an example here — for instance, imagine you're a father sitting there, right? And your 2-year-old kid walks up to you and wants to play with you. You can't even do that baby talk thing with your own kid.

Lex: You don't have that kind of friendship.

Khabib: You know, it's a friendship, but it's different, yes. There's a certain distance that you must keep around your father. You always have to be completely buttoned up. Yeah. You have to stand like a soldier in front of your father. You don't let your emotions take over.

At that point, just to know what my father thought — who was all the way across the ocean, who couldn't just fly out and be there to support his son, and just be there by my side — but for me, since he didn't have a visa, I just had to know exactly what he thought. I didn't care what anyone else thought. I didn't care about the opinions of like millions, uh, tens of millions, hundreds of millions watching this fight. I only ever cared about one person and his take — what he thought and what he'd say to me. But I couldn't call him and say, "Father, what do you think about this?" Well, we never had that.

Lex: Well, you had to wait.

Khabib: I would just call and wait to hear what he'd say. And my father, he knew exactly where to draw the line, because he was in the exact same position with his own father — since his own father was still around. And then, he had a son, too, right? And he understood me — how I felt about him, since his relationship with his own father was the same way.

Lex: [sighs]

Diamonds Under Pressure

Khabib: And in that sense, back then, my father really kept me grounded mentally. He even told me — he even told me something once: "Do you know how diamonds are actually made? Under great pressure."

Lex: Mhm.

Khabib: He says, "You're under great pressure and you have a choice. You can break down and give up, or you can get through it all properly, clearly, with dignity. Go in, prepare right, make weight, recover, go in, win, and settle it once and for all." And those exact kinds of moments, they really deeply impacted me.

Lex: So because of those words, you could cut everything off.

Khabib: Yeah.

Lex: Focus.

Khabib: Well, mentally.

Lex: Mentally.

Khabib: Like, if a million people showed up right there and told me — right outside where I was staying, at the hotel, right? — like, if a million people gathered right under my window and said, "Hey, we've got your back." And honestly, just one call from my father — it wouldn't even compare. Because that one call from my father, that one piece of advice, his support, his voice — it charged me up way more than absolutely everything else combined.

Why Conor Couldn't Get In

Lex: But I must say, Jose Aldo, who is one of the greatest fighters of all time, and still Conor was arguably able to psychologically break him. Yeah, but with you, it seems like Conor was not able to mentally affect you. Did he manage to get into your head even a little?

Khabib: No. Not at all. I had a clear understanding that physically and mentally, I was just way stronger than him. I didn't doubt myself for even 1%. Well, people — they can say whatever they want. He's got a massive fan base, too. Maybe they won't agree with that. But the almighty gave me this unshakeable confidence that is just really hard for me to even put into words. Uh, and I just deeply believe that I was better than him, and that I was stronger than him, and that in this matchup, well, I was supposed to win. I just had this rock-solid faith in myself.

The Toughest Fight — Until the Next One

Lex: Up until that moment, is it fair to say that this was your toughest fight?

Khabib: Up until that moment?

Lex: Correct.

Khabib: 100%. Because fighting's all psychology, you know? It's a mental game. Mentally speaking, that was my toughest fight. At that point, yeah. But a tougher fight came later.

Lex: With Gaethje?

Khabib: With Gaethje.

Lex: Hey.

item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib on Joe Rogan podcast | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、藏在"未曾对话"里的悖论

最出人意料的观察是：整段访谈的核心话题——"与 Joe Rogan 的对话"——是一场尚未发生的对话，而这场"关于未发生对话的对话"本身正在用俄语进行。也就是说，Khabib 正在向一个俄语访谈者，用俄语，讨论一个只能用英语进行的对话。语言的边界，正是这段访谈的"隐形第三嘉宾"。 他谈论 Joe Rogan 的方式，几乎就是在描绘一个自己需要跨越的语言/文化对岸——而这种"隔岸相望"的姿态，本身就解释了为什么他把这场对话形容为"不可避免"却又迟迟未发生：有些相遇需要先在语言里发生，才能在物理上发生。

二、"神圣文本流利"与"日常语言失语"——一个被普遍忽视的认知结构

Khabib 说他从小读《古兰经》，熟悉字母、发音、朗读规则，却坦白自己不能用阿拉伯语交谈——这里藏着一个跨领域的深层现象，我姑且称之为"仪式性识字 vs. 生存性识字"的断层。

跨领域连接来了： - 一个古典音乐家可以完美读谱演奏巴赫，却无法即兴演奏爵士； - 一个程序员能读懂整个开源框架的代码，却写不出自己的第一个 idea； - 一个宗教信徒可以背诵经文却无法用同一语言点一杯咖啡。

共同的结构是：输入的完美 ≠ 生成的能力。 我们的大脑在"接收模式"和"创造模式"之间存在一条隐蔽的神经断层。Khabib 无意间揭示了一个 MMA 之外的普世真相：真正的掌握不是能否解读，而是能否即兴。 这也解释了他为什么本能地敬畏 Joe Rogan——因为播客是纯粹的即兴，是"没有剧本的格斗"。

三、"上台前要做功课"——Khabib 用格斗的框架理解播客

注意他描述 Joe Rogan 的用词："mental battle"、"如果准备不足，他会把你活吃了（eat you alive）"。这不是普通的比喻——这是一个终身格斗家不自觉地把播客翻译成了自己母语的认知结构：擂台。

而更深的一层洞见是：Khabib 把 Dana White 排第一（推广者/商业），Joe Rogan 排第二（叙述者/意义构建），这个排序透露了他对"影响力"的隐藏定义——先有系统的搭建者，再有系统的翻译者。这与他自己的父子传承结构惊人一致：父亲搭建了训练体系，Khabib 则是这个体系向世界的"翻译者"。

四、一个大胆预测

Khabib 说学阿拉伯语是"为了理解文化和历史"——但他真正在寻找的，可能不是"更懂伊斯兰"，而是一个能让他在退役后重新定义身份的语言身体。运动员的悲剧在于身体是唯一的表达工具；语言则是身体消退后依然能延展的第二肌肉。他学阿拉伯语的时刻，恰恰是他准备承认"格斗不再是唯一表达"的时刻。这不是学习，这是身份的迁移仪式。

📝 转录文本

关于上 Joe Rogan 播客的可能

You mentioned Joe Rogan. You know, he's a friend of mine. I love listening to his podcast, but I've never actually heard the two of you have a conversation together. Do you think that's something that could happen in the future?

Yes, of course.

I know you have a great deal of respect for him, and he has a great deal of respect for you. I can't wait to hear the two of you talk.

Same here.

对 Joe Rogan 的评价：UFC 不可或缺的第二人

If we're talking about the people most responsible for promoting the UFC, I'd put Dana first. But second place without question goes to Joe Rogan. It's honestly hard to imagine the UFC without him. It'll be hard when he's no longer part of it.

And what he's achieved in his own field, what he's achieved in podcasting, he's the best. And what he's built, the way he commentates, the way he communicates, his knowledge, his charisma, the way he carries a conversation — I think a lot of people could learn from him.

And as for me going on his podcast, I think it's inevitable. God willing, if we're given the time and the health, we'll have a lot to talk about. There are so many different topics we could discuss together. So, a conversation with Joe Rogan would be very interesting. I definitely like to talk to him.

I agree. But it's interesting. Right now, you and I are speaking Russian.

Yes. Language is a tricky thing.

Yeah, exactly. With him, you need to come prepared.

Yes. Because if you show up unprepared, he will just eat you alive. You have to be. It's a mental battle, too.

语言、阿拉伯语与《古兰经》

Yeah. And by the way, you know, you've mentioned a few times that um you'd like to improve your Arabic. Language is such an interesting thing. It opens doors to understanding. It allows you to understand culture and history on a much deeper level.

Absolutely. Without the language, it's very difficult.

I'm starting to study Arabic now, but I've been reading the Quran since I was a child. I know the alphabet very well. The pronunciation rules — I can read it well. But the Quran and Arabic as a spoken language are different. I wouldn't say they are drastically different, but they are different. If you want to speak it conversationally, you need to study grammar and learn it in a different way.

item.description:
## 一、藏在"未曾对话"里的悖论
最出人意料的观察是：整段访谈的核心话题——"与 Joe Rogan 的对话"——是一场**尚未发生的对话**，而这场"关于未发生对话的对话"本身正在用**俄语**进行。也就是说，Khabib 正在向一个俄语访谈者，用俄语，讨论一个只能用英语进行的对话。**语言的边界，正是这段访谈的"隐形第三嘉宾"。** 他谈论 Joe Rogan 的方式，几乎就是在描绘一个自己需要跨越的语言/文化对岸——而这种"隔岸相望"的姿态，本身就解释了为什么他把这场对话形容为"不可避免"却又迟迟未发生：**有些相遇需要先在语言里发生，才能在物理上发生。**
## 二、"神圣文本流利"与"日常语言失语"——一个被普遍忽视的认知结构
Khabib 说他从小读《古兰经》，熟悉字母、发音、朗读规则，却坦白自己不能用阿拉伯语交谈——这里藏着一个跨领域的深层现象，我姑且称之为**"仪式性识字 vs. 生存性识字"的断层**。
跨领域连接来了： - 一个古典音乐家可以完美**读谱**演奏巴赫，却无法**即兴**演奏爵士； - 一个程序员能读懂整个开源框架的代码，却写不出自己的第一个

item.title: [Lex Clips] Khabib on greatness of Islam Makhachev | Khabib Nurmagomedov and Lex Fridman
item.dc:creator: Lex Clips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、真正的"冠军工厂"不是训练体系，而是一条隐形的时间接力棒

大多数人看到 Khabib 谈 Islam，会聚焦于"努力、纪律、牺牲"这些老生常谈的品质。但真正被埋在字里行间的洞见是：达吉斯坦这条冠军链条的核心资产，不是教练、不是体系、甚至不是基因，而是"年龄差"本身。

Khabib 反复强调"我大他 3 岁"——这个数字被提了两次。3 岁，是一个精心校准的生物学间距：足够大，让年长者始终是"前方的墙"；又足够小，让年轻者能真正摸到、追上、吸收。太小则同质竞争、互相消耗；太大则代差过重、无法对练。整个 Nurmagomedov 家族体系其实是一台"错位年龄发生器"——Khabib 追父亲那一辈的老将，Islam 追 Khabib，Umar 和 Usman 追 Islam。

这让我想到一个跨领域的类比：日本传统工艺中的"職人継承"，以及硅谷的 "PayPal Mafia"——真正跨越世代的卓越，从来不是靠一个天才，而是靠一个稳定的"3–5 岁递进梯队"。Khabib 无意间说出的是一条被低估的组织学定律：卓越会沿着年龄梯度往下渗透，但只在特定间距下才会发生。

二、Khabib 对 Islam 的"担忧"里，藏着一个反直觉的真相：轻量级冠军其实是"时间生物"，而不是"技术生物"

结尾那段最容易被忽略——他突然从"Islam 有没有机会成为 GOAT"跳到"轻量级和重量级面对时间的方式完全不同"。这是全场最不加修饰、最锋利的一句判断。

一般人以为技术、经验会随年龄增长而复利；但 Khabib 揭示了一个残酷的悖论：在 155 磅和 170 磅这样的量级里，反应速度是不可替代的底层货币。到了 35 岁，Jon Jones 还能在重量级"用智慧打拳"，因为对手也慢；但在轻量级，对手的神经系统仍然是 26 岁——你老一年，等于对手快一秒。

这跟金融领域的一个概念惊人地相似："久期错配"（duration mismatch）。重量级冠军像是长期国债——利率变化影响小；轻量级冠军像是短期高频交易——毫秒级的反应速度就是他们的全部 alpha。Islam 的 GOAT 之路，不是在跟 Jones 或 GSP 的记录赛跑，而是在跟自己神经系统的衰老赛跑。 Khabib 的"担忧"其实是内行人才懂的时间物理学。

三、"关掉摄像机"是达吉斯坦体系最被误读的密码

Khabib 说"99.9% 的训练没有摄像机"——听起来像是低调、朴素、不爱作秀。但如果你仔细听，他说了一句更奇怪的话："这项运动的准备，发生在这里（指心里）。那个 celebrities matter 的世界，会挡住它。"

这里有一个惊人的心理学观察：摄像机改变的不是别人看你的方式，而是你看自己的方式。 一旦有观众，你会开始为"表演版本的自己"训练，而不是为"真实版本的自己"训练。Khabib 的团队实际上在实施一种"感知隔离训练"（perceptual isolation）——他们刻意剥夺一切社会性反馈，让运动员在没有观众的房间里跟真实的痛苦独处。

跨领域的连接更耐人寻味：这正是禅宗"独坐"、以及顶级古典音乐家"闭门练琴期"的机制。郎朗、霍洛维茨都拒绝在练习时被录像。真正的深度技艺，都需要一个"没有观察者的空间"来生长。达吉斯坦看似是宗教纪律，其实是一套精密的注意力经济学——他们最防范的不是伤病，而是"被观看"这件事对自我认知的污染。

一个隐藏的悖论：Khabib 在一个数亿人观看的播客上，向你解释他为什么不允许别人看他训练。而他之所以能坦然说出这些，恰恰是因为他退役了——他终于可以谈论那个不能被谈论、也不能被看的房间。

📝 转录文本

一、Islam 的起点：同一个街区、同一个师父

Lex： Well, we've talked about different athletes, about Umar, but now let's talk about Islam Makhachev, one of your closest brothers who's at the very top of the world. You've known each other. You've trained together for more than 20 years. In your opinion, what makes him such a special wrestler and fighter? Why has he reached such heights? Why is he a great fighter?

Khabib： Well, let's start with the fact that Islam has been doing this his whole life since childhood. And I've known him since childhood, too. We went to the same school, lived in the same neighborhood, trained at the same gym, and he was my father's student. And it's worth mentioning, he was one of my father's favorite students.

Lex： Yes.

Khabib： One of the best students. My father saw in him this potential for greatness in how hard he trained. That's what I was talking about at the beginning of the podcast. When you go into the dark, uncomfortable room and stay there for a long time, no matter how hard it gets. He knew how to make sacrifices. He was very disciplined. Nobody reaches this level by accident. It's impossible without exceptional natural gifts. And he has them. He's gifted. Allah blessed him with those gifts, and he's deeply devoted to what he does.

二、代际链条：一条从 2003 年延续至今的"接力"

We basically grew up together, right? I'm 3 years older than Islam, and I was always a little bigger, a little older than him. So, when we were amateurs, I competed in slightly heavier weight classes. But we worked together a lot, and Islam benefited tremendously from training with me. We trained together for many years. And he never had to go anywhere to find a sparring partner because he always had one in the gym.

So, I developed by training with the older guys in the gym, the stronger guys, the better guys, when I was young. Then, when they left, I was the one in front. Islam kept growing, growing, growing. Now, I left, Islam is the one in front, and now other guys are developing through him. This is a kind of chain that exists in a gym, in a training system, that produces the best fighters in the world.

And in this chain, Islam was always behind me. If I was behind someone, Islam was behind me. Now, others are following Islam — Usman, Amru, and other guys. You could put them against any of the best fighters in the world right now, and they would perform very well.

So, in this chain we've had since 2003 — and now it's already 2026 — that's 23 years. Islam was the one coming up behind me. And now, there are younger guys coming up behind Islam. And it's no secret that Islam will turn 35 in October. But what makes me happy is that there are younger guys coming up behind him. I left, Islam stepped in. One day, Islam will leave, too, and others will take his place. And this cycle, it never ends. It keeps going, and it keeps pulling the next generation forward.

三、道路越走越窄：为什么只有 Islam 走到了最后

At the beginning, a lot of people are involved. But, as you gradually climb higher, higher, and higher, the road gets narrower, and fewer and fewer people remain. And alongside Islam, a lot of guys were developing while training with me. But Islam made it all the way because of his work ethic, his discipline, and — let's call it — sacrifice.

He gave up a lot to reach this level. This isn't easy. You have to make sacrifices. You have to make sacrifices. You have to give up parties. You have to sacrifice sleep. You have to sacrifice your time. There are so many things you have to give up. You have to dedicate your entire life to this sport, putting aside all the things that can distract you. You train, you sleep, you eat, you wake up, and then you do it all over again. Only then can you reach the level that Islam reached. That's what makes him unique.

四、心理层面的相似与不同

Lex： Were there any small but interesting differences between you and Islam? Psychologically speaking?

Khabib： There are many. Psychologically, he's very solid, too. I've been around him through so many training camps and so many fights. He's built very strong mentally. Of course, we're different in certain things, but in terms of our fighter's attitude toward the work, we have a lot in common. A lot.

Lex： You also train a lot.

Khabib： Yeah, absolutely. A lot.

五、退役六年，依然放不下摔跤

Lex： And I think — he — well, first I have to say, I watched you train yesterday, and it made me really happy to see that you still love this so deeply. You know, it's hard to love something for such a long time. People finish and move on.

Khabib： Yes.

Lex： They retire and move on.

Khabib： But me, it's been 6 years since I retired, and I still haven't let go of wrestling, of competition. I still go to the gym, do cardio, lift, wrestle, grapple. I never let it go. It's still with me. And yesterday I told you that last week I did 200 minutes of live grappling. This week is a little different though because I'm just focused on Umar, traveling, and everything that comes with that. So, this week it's going to be less.

Still, I wrestle. I don't let go. I love it. I love this energy. I love that feeling after wrestling. You wrestle, let's say 40 minutes. Yesterday, I still wanted more. Just now I wrestled with you, with Islam. Maybe 20 minutes, but still it's not enough to get that feeling. That 100% feeling. I need around 40 minutes of wrestling, something like that. I don't think most people listening to us will understand that. But I think some people watching, especially grappling and jiu-jitsu fans, will understand me.

六、关于摄像机：训练之地为什么必须"无人观看"

Lex： Well, to be honest, sometimes there are cameras around you — and for me, at least, that's harder. I like it when there are none.

Khabib： I usually train with no cameras. With you was one of the rare occasions when I come to the gym and you allow —

Lex： When I allow it, yes.

Khabib： Thanks for that.

Lex： Yeah, yeah, yeah. This is very, very rare for me. Even with embedded, with UFC, with everyone who comes, I always say — don't film.

Khabib： Thank you, brother. I don't know why, but cameras get in the way for me. Because this sport, this preparation, it happens here. And that whole world where celebrities matter, it gets in the way.

Lex： Yes, it gets in the way. But 99.9% of our training sessions happen without cameras.

Khabib： Well, thank you, brother.

七、Islam 会成为史上最伟大的 MMA 选手吗？

Lex： Let me ask you this. A lot of people say you're number one, the greatest of all time. Do you think Islam has a chance to become the greatest MMA fighter of all time?

Khabib： Well, I've never said that, and I never set out to become number one or to become the greatest athlete and so on. I never had that. My goal was always to become the best in my sport, to become a world champion, to prove to myself that I could do it.

But it's hard to choose just one person. Even now, look — there's always going to be St-Pierre, there's always going to be Demetrious Johnson, there's always going to be Jon Jones, there's always going to be Fedor. If people want to include me in that conversation, if Islam gets into that conversation, if there's Cain Velasquez, Cormier, and so on, I'd be happy about that, and that's my goal. That someone from our team, from the people closest to me, gets there, too.

If Jon Jones is there, why can't Islam be there? If Demetrious Johnson is there with 11 title defenses, why can't Islam be there? It's a good question. Why not? I'd like him to break all those records, to overtake Jon Jones, Demetrious Johnson, and St-Pierre — no matter how much respect I have for them.

八、时间的物理学：轻量级冠军的隐形敌人

Islam has a chance, but time is starting to run out a little. This worries me because, for example, Jones fought at light heavyweight and now at heavyweight. Time is a little kinder to those divisions. Even at 38, you can still compete at the heavier weights. You don't need the same reaction speed and all that.

But when you compete in lighter weight classes — 155, 170 — age really catches up. I think active fighters, retired fighters, wrestlers, athletes — especially those who competed in these weight classes — will understand what I'm talking about. When you're 35, and when you're 32, and when you're 38, you're a totally different athlete.
