item.title: [Sequoia Capital] RL Environments Explained: How AI Agents Learn Real-World Work | Brendan Foody, Mercor
item.dc:creator: Sequoia Capital
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、被误读的"人机分工"：这不是过渡期，而是结构性约束

大多数人把"人类专家参与训练"理解为一种过渡状态——等模型再强一点，人就退场了。但 Brendan 在回答"合成数据"那段实际上暴露了一个更深的真相：测量前沿必须来自前沿之外。你不能让 Fable 自己写出"Fable 在哪里犯错"的 rubric，因为那要求它先超越自己。这不是工程瓶颈，而是哥德尔式的结构约束——一个系统无法在自身内部完整地度量自身。

这意味着一个反直觉的推论：AI 越强，需要的人类越少但越贵、越顶尖。数据行业不是在被自动化，而是在被"贵族化"——从 2020 年 crowdsourcing 的低技能标注工，到今天 Latham & Watkins 律师按任务 $10,000 计费。Mercor 本质上是在为"人类认知的最上 0.01%"建立全球做市商。

二、被忽略的"社交裂缝"：60% 的工作 vs 1% 的评测

整段分享里最刺眼的一个数字对比：人类工作中 60-70% 涉及与他人互动，但只有约 1% 的 evals 在衡量模型的社交能力。这个 gap 之所以此前无人认真谈论，是因为它跨越了两个从不对话的领域——社会学（研究人际互动）和机器学习（研究单点任务）。

一个跨领域的类比会让你更不舒服：这几乎重演了20 世纪初工业工程学（Taylorism）的盲点。泰勒制精确测量了单个工人的动作时间，却完全无法建模装配线上的沟通、默契、非正式协商——直到丰田用"看板"和"安灯绳"重新引入社会性，才带来生产力跃迁。今天的 RL 环境正处在同一个位置：我们训练出了会写 slide deck 的 agent，却训不出会在 Slack 上"读空气"的 agent。下一代 evals 的爆点不在能力维度，而在"多智能体社会学"这个几乎无人耕耘的领域。

三、被低估的经济信号：$500K 换 22 个百分点，与 GDP 的"逆向切分"

Corporate law 从 4.7% 跃升到 26.6%，只用了 1,800 个任务和约 $500K 算力——这个 ROI 在任何行业标准下都是荒诞的。但真正让人后背发凉的不是数字本身，而是它揭示了一个新的经济地图学：GDP val 的 205 个 BLS 职业类别正在被"投标"，谁先被造出高保真环境，谁的职业岗位就先被自动化。

这里有一个跨领域的锐利连接：Mercor 正在扮演 19 世纪的美国土地测量局（U.S. General Land Office）的角色。当年测量局用经纬线把西部划成方格，方格一旦被测绘、被授予产权，殖民和农业开发就随之而来。今天 Mercor 用"环境 + 任务 + rubric"把经济地图划成可训练的方格——任何一个职业只要被环境化，就进入了被 RL 蚕食的倒计时。

而这里藏着一个真正意外的观察：自动化的历史顺序被颠倒了。工业革命从最低价值、最重复的劳动开始（纺织、搬运），而 RL 时代从最高价值的认知劳动开始（律师、投行、医生），因为只有他们能付得起自己被替代的数据成本。你被 AI 替代的速度，正比于你今天的时薪。 Cursor 的成功之所以是范式，是因为它证明了：应用层公司如果不自己拥有"经济地图上那一格的数据主权"，就只能永远租用别人的智能。

📝 转录文本

Introduction

Um, Record, I think you guys grew from a 1 to a 2 billion dollar revenue run rate in the last 4 months or so. Um, so this company's off to the races and I think you were just so front and center to how companies are thinking about uh post training their own models, uh building their own intelligence. So, thank you for joining us for this conversation.

Um, format-wise what we're going to do is we've 15 minutes or so of content from Brendan. He's going to talk about uh RL environments in particular, which I think is a, you know, new frontier topic. It'll be fun to fun to explore. And then we're going to leave 15 minutes or so at the end for Q&A again. So, uh please keep please keep questions back pocket. I will turn it over to you, Brendan.

Sweet. So, I'll be talking about RL environments.

Background: The Evolution of the Data Market

Starting out, I figured it's helpful to give a little bit of the background on the history of the data market and how that history ties into Record's origin story. Where things really started in 2020 in the era of crowdsourcing data for behavior cloning. So, this was mainly supervised fine-tuning data, inputs and outputs, and RLHF data where you would have a annotator select from a couple of model responses which they preferred. And we were able to make all this progress in fine-tuning GPT-3, making progress towards ChatGPT and GPT-4 in the crowdsourcing era of agentic data.

But, what we saw changing in the market, especially as we uh headed into 2024, was this giant transition away from the low-skilled crowdsourcing era of behavior cloning data and moving towards the agentic era of data. Of how do we find the highest-skilled experts in the world that can work collaboratively in teams to build frontier evals and RL environments for the next generation of models. All the software engineers, lawyers, doctors, bankers, et cetera that could measure the frontier of intelligence and help to use that to improve model capabilities.

And so, Mercor grew up with our first big project being deep research. I guess the first prominent RL agent scaling up dramatically with all of the frontier labs to become the primary agentic data vendor to all of the leading labs and also all of the leading application layer companies ranging from Harvey, Cera, Cognition to Ramp. And what's been really exciting over the last 12 months especially is how RLVR within the agentic data paradigm has evolved to also include RL environments with these rich apps and worlds that teach agents how to use all of the tools on our laptops that we use every day.

So, I'll be talking about that and of course how this technology that started in the frontier labs is now getting disseminated to the application layer and all of the products that all of you are building as you work on your company.

What Is an RL Environment?

So, high level on what an RL environment is is that it includes three parts.

  • The first part is the worlds. So, this includes all of the messages, slides, docs, sheets, etc. that correspond to everything you would have in a real project or company that you're working on.
  • The second part is the apps which is high fidelity clones of popular applications, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Microsoft 365, etc. that agents can interact with via MCP, CLI, or Kua.
  • And then the third part is the tasks where we have prompts and verifiers. Verifiers could be rubrics or unit tests that can be used either for eval or training.

And the barrier for frontier labs to automate everything that you can do on your laptop using Claude is how do they cover the full distribution of all of the worlds, all of the apps, and all of the tasks in the economy. And so, there's been this enormous scale out in order to do that. Um, where humans have been really central to how we build these environments, obviously with models in the loop meaningfully.

Scale of Expert Effort

And so I put a graph here of the amount of expert hours that um, of throughput in from our talent network over the last 24 months. Um, and it's a a pretty crazy trajectory with respect to um, 2.5 million hours um, in Q2 alone with growth sort of accelerating on the amount of expert time uh, used to build out all of these environments.

The reason being of course as I mentioned we need to scale out the environment distribution across every category in the economy. Many of you might know GDP val where there's 205 domains in the Bureau of Labor Statistics across all the different jobs, but then you have to think through how do we have all of the apps corresponding to all of those jobs, all the different scenarios, all the tasks. Is this enormous build out.

Why Humans Are Still Central

Only humans can measure the frontier in most domains, not every domain. There are rare exceptions like math where you have a really clean simulation environment and so uh, the model's able to learn from whether it got the right answer, but in most domains like building a slide deck uh, the model has an incredibly hard time identifying reliably where it made its own mistake. It's as if you would be asking a human to grade their own homework.

And so that's why it's really valuable to have a human create a rubric similar to how a professor would create a rubric to grade an essay or a TA would grade that slide deck. Similar to the way that a lot of us learn it's in large part from the feedback we got from those around us rather than uh, purely plugging things into a calculator or clean simulation.

Um, and then building these verifiers is hard cuz anytime you're building the slide deck you need to understand the full problem space of what are the 10 different slide decks that, you know, could be a good path to go down? What are the dozens of mistakes you could possibly make? And how do you build a comprehensive verifier that captures this full solution area of what's possible?

A Sample RL Environment: The Legal Case

And so, what I'll walk through is a sample RL environment. Excuse me, to also break this down for all of you. Um and part of the reason that this is so cool, which I'll get to in a moment, is that we developed a lot of this technology in collaboration with the labs. These are, of course, ones that we have open-sourced and published to the world, but now that's all starting to get disseminated to the application layer companies that are building and owning their own intelligence. As they realize that the three core pillars of their AI strategy are their compute, their algorithms or researchers, and the data sets they build. And data's often the most differentiating factor.

And so, this is one that we published, um as a legal environment, where we have lawyers from top law firms like Latham and Watkins write out a scenario of a real project that they worked on in their big law job. And then they create a full outline for a data room that corresponds to all of the different uh messages, emails, files, size of files. I cut off the full data room cuz it's it's very extensive. Um and of course, there's a lot of model in the loop with how they effectively populate this. Similar to how a software engineer now should not be coding by hand entirely themselves, they should probably be orchestrating agents in how to do this very productively.

Um and then we render that data room into the apps, the clones of Google Workspace you can see in this scenario, and have prompts uh to roll out model trajectories against this. And so, in this one, it's evaluating the maximum total liability for Star Tanker uh Tankers International Limited compared to Cooper Jefferies Energy Corporation under the Oil and Petroleum Act, uh considering all of the context uh from this real scenario in the data room.

And then as I mentioned, similar to how a professor would create a rubric to grade an essay, they have these key rubric criteria that correspond to what are the characteristics of a of a accurate model response. And making sure that these rubric criteria avoid reward hacking and effectively align with the uh when you roll out 100 trajectories, making sure all of those scores are accurate is incredibly technically challenging. And so there's an enormous amount of research, agenda quality control, training on the data, etc. that goes into how you solve that problem and then ultimately produce these high-quality verifiers and leaderboards um that give you an aggregate model score across how well all of the different models are um doing on a particular domain.

Leaderboard and Post-Training Results

And as we can see, one of the big changes over the last few months is that GLM 52 and Chimera K3 are on the leaderboard. And so that is a huge opportunity for all of you because that gives us the foundation to actually achieve frontier intelligence and all of the specific applications uh and verticals that you're focusing on um that's not too far away.

And so to give a little bit of context on what that looks like, um I'll share an example of post-training on Apex Agents, which is the data set that I uh or the sample I just showed before, where we have 1,800 tasks in this example. This was post-training run of GLM 47, but we're redoing a lot of them for Chimera K3, so we'll have updated results for you all soon. Where you can see the jumps just on 1,800 tasks with about 500k in compute are pretty dramatic. Um corporate law going from 4.7% to 26.6%, um but notice that this is just Apex Agents data set we gave it, and it actually generalized incredibly well to GDP valve and uh Apex V1, which doesn't have these data rooms. Even just seeing nominal gains and some other benchmarks as well.

And so, we're doing a lot of this work of working with customers like Harvey, who I know will present on stuff later to help build out the environments corresponding to their specific domain so that they can build frontier intelligence within that. And I think Andrew talked about how Cursor was a great first example of how an application layer company could build a industry-leading model that, you know, built an enormous amount of value for their customers. And I believe that over the next 12 months, there is going to be dozens of examples just like that where companies own their own intelligence and that is the key source of the modes that they're building. And actually, Josh and I talked about this the other day as well.

Three Ways to Curate High-Quality Datasets

Um a couple of examples of ways to curate high-quality data sets. The general three that we see most that I'm happy to talk about and send people links to is:

  1. By task — the most common. Where people would say, "I really like this data shape of environments in law and we will pay $2,000 per task to scale this up." And as an example, certain frontier labs might buy 50,000 tasks a month from us. And so, it tends to be pretty dramatic scale. And these tasks would generally be very complex. Some would even take humans up to a month to complete that given task. Sometimes it would take just a few hours. And these would be sort of custom per task pricing.
  2. Off-the-shelf data — where we have we've invested hundreds of millions of dollars in building our own data sets that we sell to multiple customers. All these new neo labs are generally airing more towards off-the-shelf data because it doesn't make sense for 10 different labs to all be building their own uh data sets. Um there's a lot of value to building something once that can uh then be applied to everyone.
  3. Providing the experts — and then the final which um we see a little bit of, but is uh less of our focus anymore, is just providing um the experts so that customers are able to uh or organize the experts on their own um in just an hourly model. Um so we we do a little bit of that when people like that was how Harvey got started with us hiring uh some lawyers, um but it generally moves towards more of these uh scaled offerings of data over time.

So, that's a little bit of the background of how to build RL environments, what they are, and I'm really excited about all this technology that we have uh that has previously been limited to the frontier labs all making its way to all of you. And so, happy to answer any questions um about that. Sweet. Go ahead.

Q&A

How do you price data?

Hey, uh um I'm Ali from Astro Guide. My question is it's kind of open-ended, but simple. How do you price data? Like how do you value data?

So, there's a so many different ways. I mean, the most natural would be our customers care about model improvement, right? And so, our customers have a given goal of they want to you know, be at the frontier on a given leaderboard. And so, we're able to work backwards from how much is that worth to them and how much should we charge uh per task, how many tasks do we think would get them to that goal. And so, when we think about uh a company like Nvidia, they're probably willing to pay, you know, a billion dollars to have a frontier open-source model. And so, there's a lot of complexity of like how do we you know, price all the different ingredients that go into um making that happen.

The other way that we price when it lens we look at it through is also our cost structure to make them where of course when we have a task that takes 10 hours of human time and we're paying the human $150 an hour there might be a $1500 cost basis and so then it becomes a question of what margin do we want to run on top of that based on how differentiated and frontier that specific task is. But it's it's super wide range. Like we have tasks that range from $50 to $10,000. So.

How do you think about data quality vs. auto-graders?

How do you think about data quality? You mentioned like you know utilize human expert to label data and how do you how do you compare the human label data and you know the frontier lab you know frontier alliance the judgment data? How do you compare them to from your opinion?

So first question was how do we think about quality? Second one was sort of how do we compare the like judgment of preference labels to the auto graders?

Yeah.

So the core spot which is generally when people say data quality they're referring to two things. First is realism and secondly is accuracy of verifiers.

On realism it's just like they want to automate everything in the economy that corresponds to corporate law in this case right? And so it's like how do we make sure that this actually reflects the real distribution of what we would see in a real lawyer's environment. And that's one of the reasons that experts create outlines and help to guide all the processes of the data curation. Realism of the environment, the apps, the tasks, everything is incredibly important and and also granularly understanding the taxonomy that drives that realism across the entire distribution that you're looking for.

The second part of it relates to the other way people think about quality, which is the accuracy of the verifiers. Cuz the way that you would train one of these models is you might roll out 100 trajectories of Kimi K3 and then use this rubric to score all of those trajectories. And as you can imagine, there's like so many different paths that a model can go down. And so you want to make sure that the way this rubric is doing the scoring is the same as if we were to just have human stack rank those 100 trajectories.

And so what we do for that is a process called trajectory analysis, where we roll out 10 trajectories of the model that we're focused on improving, um, and then score all of those, and have some combination of agentic quality control systems and some human review go through to make sure that, um, all of the scores align with, uh, the goals. Um, and sometimes you can also use, uh, human feedback evals or preference labels to as a eval for your auto grader, um, is the other way related to that that you're able to solve for it. Go ahead.

How much does synthetic data generation play in this?

Um, how much do you think like synthetic data generation plays into all of this, especially like creating these large data rooms?

So the fascinating thing is I think that there's been a lot of misinterpretation of what people mean when they say synthetic data because, like, RLVR is a bet on synthetic data. It's basically let's roll out a bunch of synthetic model trajectories rather than having the humans write the SFT, and then let's score all of them, and let the models learn from all of these like, uh, synthetic model trajectories. So I think that's the first way that synthetics get used.

The second way is that models play giant role in the way that we populate environments and create tasks in the same way that, um, a lawyer that is writing a legal memo should definitely be using Claude or ChatGPT to do that. The experts that are building out these data rooms should definitely be using Claude, ChatGPT, or whatever model to help them do that. And there's a lot of ways that the model can make them more efficient.

But the reason that humans are still an essential component of the process that's incredibly differentiated is that you need humans almost definitionally to measure what is beyond the frontier of the model capabilities. Like the models — you you can't just tell the model like come up with the legal environment and then like tell me which of your legal memos are like good and bad. It's super noisy and there's not like clear signals associated with that. You need something that has capabilities beyond the frontier of that model to do so reliably.

Why are RL environments the rage now, and what's next?

Thank you for doing this. Um my question is RL environments seem like they're all the rage now and maybe have been for about a year. I hadn't really been hearing about them prior to that and it was all human expert labeling. And so kind of why why why is it all about RL environments now? Is that the most relevant thing for application companies to be thinking about? And is there any something after RL environments?

Um so I'll I'll start with why it's become the rage and maybe some of the differences also between the deep research paradigm and the like envi- the sort of environments paradigm as we saw it in 2025. And then I'll talk about looking forward what we see evolving in the data landscape.

Specifically, I think that the reason the deep research environments were the first was because like deep research had tool use with search. So search was the tool in the environment that the model would work in. But the experts would not necessarily be populating apps. So it was sort of a lighter version of an RL environment where they would just like create rubrics corresponding to this. And again, like I only talk about this stuff cuz it's a couple of years old at this point, so it's no longer uh super confidential.

And then for the like trend of apps in 2025, I think that really became giant because people realized that the primary bottleneck to making the models useful was how they started to use both all the context in the code base and all of the tools on our laptops, right? And so if we want this in the user distribution of usage, then we need to get it in the data distribution that the models are learning from.

Uh and so there's going to continue be to be this giant scale up of diversity across all three of these categories on a going forward basis, but there's going to be some changes um to maybe name two of those changes that we're thinking about the most.

  • Ultra long horizon. Like right now agents mostly aren't trained to do things that are over 10 hours, and we need to start building tasks for things that might take a human 100 hours or even 1,000 hours to do. And so that's going to be a giant shift.
  • Virtual co-workers. And then the other large shift that we're seeing is introducing virtual co-workers, which corresponds to that. Um like one my favorite questions to ask people when they're thinking about their data distribution is what percentage of tasks that they do in their job require interacting with other people. Uh and most people would say like 60% or 70%. Some people say a lot more, some people say a little bit less. Um but then if you map that on to what percentage of evals measure how well the models can interact with other people, it's like 1%, maybe Tau bench has a little bit of this. Um and so there's this giant realism gap associated with how you actually measure how well agents engage in social interaction um throughout uh all of the different people and other agents that they need to work with uh in their jobs.

Good.

Can rubric generation be scaled with models?

You talked about rubric generation, which is like is it like a bespoke access of verify that you put task? And from what I understood, that's like bottleneck by experts. Have you found any success of like being able to scale that up with your models giving you like some heuristic or even like post any models for

We have found that you can make it a lot more efficient if you have a like AI copilot that's able to work with the expert in creating the task and the verifier. Um so, the expert can talk to the trajectory and understand exactly what's happening and where it's going wrong.

The challenge is just that if you're trying to improve FABLE, FABLE cannot reliably write out the like rubric criteria for where it's making mistakes. It might get like half of them right and half of them wrong, and that amount of noise is unworkable from a training standpoint.

Um and so, that's the reason that the the process that requires humans the most is the task creation. Uh like a lot of the environments, we can get like use a lot of synthetic. Uh it's helpful to have humans write the outlines they're familiar with the environment and and uh and they're grounded in reality, a realistic distribution, but with the task that's those tend to really require humans. Um with with rare exceptions, um in code or if you're sort of distilling from like if you have a model that's worse than Kimikaze 3, then it can definitely learn from tasks Kimikaze 3 is creating. So, there are there are some exceptions if you're doing it that way.

What about cyber defense environments?

Hey, this is uh Nikhil from uh Cribl. So, when we think about RL environments for certain provable domains like cyber defense or incident response, where there's the model is or the agent is trying to find a flaw in an existing system, do you use uh humans for just authoring that environment or setting it up or do you also use that for grading? Is there Is there a way to scale that up?

I I actually think cyber is one where you don't necessarily always need humans for the verifiers cuz you can have an attacker and a defender agent. Um and uh I think you're right in saying that for cyber you can have humans more so or or architect what is a realistic like environment um and sort of set up the environment um cuz you do need a lot of diversity. Uh but then it's less human intensive with respect to uh building verifiers.

Thanks.

How can you tell when you're limited by the base model?

How can you tell when you're limited by the base model?

What do you mean by that?

Well, ostensibly you're using the same data set for all these models here and they somewhat land around the same final performance on this list here. But maybe if you try to smaller model, which is maybe a good place to start, it would land much lower. Um what is the cause there? Is it just parameter count or

So the parameter count will definitely play a role in how effectively the model does insofar as how trainable it is. I think that um the main thing to look at is generally the gap between the like pass at 16 and the pass at one. If you have a model where you roll out 16 trajectories and it gets all of them totally wrong, the it's sort of like hopeless that the model is going to learn from that um for the most part. Maybe you roll out another 100 trajectories and it gets one of them right.

Um versus if you have um the ideal case is that you have um pass at one it fails, but then pass at 16 when you roll out 16 trajectories it gets it right once or twice, and then the model is able to learn very effectively from that. So, that's generally the heuristic we would use for how strong the base model needs to be to effectively learn from a given data set.

Cool. Maybe — Oh, final question really quick.

In-house vs. partner data: what's the split?

What advice do you have for companies as they partner with you on data that they should rely on themselves as part of their RL post-training versus relying — What's the complementary —

Well, I think this is why a giant portion of our business is custom data, where it's like we have teams that are siloed and fully exclusive to critical customers to make sure that we build out the best data sets in the world that they own. And that allows them to maintain their competitive advantage associated with this, while also benefiting from all of the infrastructure that we've built.

And I think there are some companies that try to like build out all of the talent network and infrastructure in-house, but I think if you look at what the frontier labs do and the best models do, it's a pretty good indication that there's so many economies of scale from working with a partner that has all of these economies of scale, the platform, the talent network, etc.

So, anyways, thanks for all having me.

[applause]

item.description:
## 一、被误读的"人机分工"：这不是过渡期，而是结构性约束
大多数人把"人类专家参与训练"理解为一种过渡状态——等模型再强一点，人就退场了。但 Brendan 在回答"合成数据"那段实际上暴露了一个更深的真相：**测量前沿必须来自前沿之外**。你不能让 Fable 自己写出"Fable 在哪里犯错"的 rubric，因为那要求它先超越自己。这不是工程瓶颈，而是**哥德尔式的结构约束**——一个系统无法在自身内部完整地度量自身。
这意味着一个反直觉的推论：**AI 越强，需要的人类越少但越贵、越顶尖**。数据行业不是在被自动化，而是在被"贵族化"——从 2020 年 crowdsourcing 的低技能标注工，到今天 Latham & Watkins 律师按任务 $10,000 计费。Mercor 本质上是在为"人类认知的最上 0.01%"建立全球做市商。
## 二、被忽略的"社交裂缝"：60% 的工作 vs 1% 的评测
整段分享里最刺眼的一个数字对比：**人类工作中 60-70% 涉及与他人互动，但只有约 1% 的 evals 在衡量模型的社交能力**。这个 gap 之所以

item.title: [Sequoia Capital] Post-Training Is How You Keep Your Taste | Fireworks CEO Lin Qiao
item.dc:creator: Sequoia Capital
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、意外观察：Post-Training 不是技术革命，而是"组织结构"的革命

Lin 在演讲中埋了一个几乎被所有人忽略的信号——产品团队和 ML 团队正在合并。这在传统 SaaS 时代是不可想象的：过去 PM 和 ML 工程师之间隔着一堵 API 的墙，PM 提需求、ML 训练模型、双方各自甩锅。而 post-training 时代真正的稀缺资源不是 GPU、不是数据量，而是"谁有资格判断这条数据是否高质量"——而这个判断权，天然属于最理解客户的产品团队。

这意味着：未来 AI 公司的组织架构图会长得越来越像一支交响乐团，而不是流水线。当"数据质量判断"成为核心竞争力时，PM 就不再是需求的搬运工，而是"品味的立法者"。这是一个远比"我们要做 fine-tuning"更深层的组织重构信号。

二、跨领域连接：Post-Training 与米其林厨师的"高汤哲学"

Lin 提到"reward hacking"——模型为了"最小化编译错误"而生成零行代码。这让我想起一个完全不相干的领域：米其林餐厅的厨师训练。

顶级厨房里，学徒最容易犯的错叫"chasing the metric"——为了让汤看起来清澈，就过度过滤，结果丢失了所有风味。真正的名厨评估一锅高汤，从来不是单一指标，而是 Lin 提到的"rubrics of rewards"——澄清度、香气层次、余韵长度、温度稳定性的加权组合。

再往深挖一层，你会发现 post-training 的本质是"品味的可复制化工程"。米其林靠师徒制传承品味，效率极低；宗教靠戒律传承品味，僵化；而 post-training 第一次让"品味"变成了可以被 rubric 编码、被反向传播优化、被批量推理的东西。这在人类历史上是第一次。

三、隐藏真相：Cost 才是真正的"CEO 杀手"，不是质量

大多数人听到 post-training 想到的是"更好的模型质量"，但 Lin 在最后一个问答里泄露了一个更冷酷的真相——大企业的 CFO 正在阻止 AI feature 上线。

这里有个反直觉的洞察：在 AI 时代，"scale into bankruptcy"从一个笑话变成了系统性风险。过去 SaaS 的边际成本趋近于零，用户越多越赚钱；而现在每一次 LLM 调用都是真金白银的 token 消耗，用户越多亏得越多。这就催生了一个 SaaS 时代从未有过的物种——"用得起才敢用"的 AI 产品。

更深一层的意外连接：这个动态和19 世纪铁路公司的困境惊人相似。铁路公司拥有客户、拥有流量，但因为煤炭、维护、人力成本吃掉了所有利润，最后活下来的不是流量最大的，而是最先发明"标准化机车"（降低单位运营成本）的。今天的 post-training 就是 AI 应用层的"标准化机车"——它决定的不是你能不能做出好产品，而是你能不能在做出好产品之后活下来。

四、彩蛋洞察：Product-Market Fit 的定义正在被悄悄改写

Lin 说了一句几乎一带而过的话："PMF doesn't really mean you have a durable scalable business"。

这是对 Marc Andreessen 定义的 PMF 的一次静默叛变。在 SaaS 时代，PMF = scale。在 AI 时代，PMF 只是"入场券"，post-training 才是"续命符"。这意味着 VC 的估值模型、创业者的融资节奏、产品的路线图排序，都需要重新写一遍——因为在 PMF 和"durable business"之间，多了一个前所未有的中间态，叫做"data harvest window"（数据收割窗口期）。

而这个窗口期，可能就是未来 5 年 AI 创业公司真正的生死时速。

📝 转录文本

开场与介绍

Okay, up next we have Lynn, uh close close friend and collaborator of Brendan's. Um Lynn, uh actually show of hands, who here who here does post training? Okay, good amount of the room. And who here uses Firework? Okay, good amount of the room, too. So, Lynn, you have you have some friendlies in the audience.

Um and so for this next talk, what we're going to do is we're going to focus on post training. Um Lynn, similar setup to Brendan's talk. We're going to do 15 minutes on how to approach the problem of post training, um and then 15 minutes or so for Q&A. Uh and Lynn, really delighted to have you here. Thank you for joining us.

Thanks for having me. Uh hi everyone, good morning. I'm Lynn, I'm CEO and co-founder of Firework.

Fireworks 的视角：模式的观察者

So, as we bring up the slide, today I'm going to do a little bit uh deep dive on post training and why post training could be very relevant to uh you building your own business.

So, first of all, a little bit like prior, I think um this year we have seen — So, first of all, I'm a Firework weather specializing intelligence platform. There are tons and tons of applications built on top of us, all the way from startups to digital native and enterprises. So, we get uh — the fun part of my job is we get to see a lot of patterns. Um what are the innovations people are uh building on top of us and uh how they are — what are challenges that they're facing and what are trends um people, being developers, are um building on top of us.

应用开发的坍缩：从数十人季度到一人几周

So, uh one of the things, especially in the past 1 year, software development and application development has been somewhat disrupted. Because it goes fine in the past, um you have a good idea, you want to implement it, scaling production, it requires a team of tens of very strong product engineers, PMs working together, multiple quarters to deliver that.

And right now, with one person, a few weeks, uh without understanding how to write a single line of code, you can do that. So, that collapsing of resource required both in terms of timeline and deep expertise is shifting how competitive the application space is, and it's shifting people from thinking about building on top of off-the-shelf black box API to build a much deeper moat. So that they can build a much more durable business.

开放模型的深层意义：保留公司的独特品味

As also you have seen lot of discussion, especially in the past 1 week, between open model and the closed model and all the rallying and support across the open model. The depth of that alliance is because we believe — I mean the industry is much deeper because look at the whole entire industry, there are so many companies, right? There are so many companies, all of you are building your own company.

Every single company exists for a reason because they focus on solving a unique problem in a special way. And that means they carry their own judgment, taste and determination, conviction into that product, and that's why companies exist.

Today, if you build on top of off-the-shelf API, then you really need to think about how you keep that special taste, judgment and unique part forward. And we believe one approach for every company to build a durable business is to actually bake your judgment, taste, and customer deep understanding into the intelligence you build on top of, instead of just an off-the-shelf API.

So, that's kind of a little bit context of what's happening in industry, what we are seeing, and why post training could be very very relevant to you.

拥有智能而非租用：从数据到权重到服务

Okay. So, you probably heard a lot about owning intelligence, not renting. And what does owning your own intelligence mean? It actually means many things.

So, first of all, it starts from data. Intelligence is derivative of data. And obviously the foundation labs, all the foundation models we're using, are building on top of the public data and the labeled data that has solved common tasks, but all of you are solving a specific task. That's why you're building a business, you're building a company. And being able to curate production data with high quality and even generate synthetic data to enrich your production data is one step of owning your own intelligence.

And then after you have data, you will start to kind of use that data, turn into a model, build on top of existing model and own the weights. And there are a collection of techniques you can use to get there. Those techniques are tailored to solve different kinds of problems you could possibly have. And those techniques can also interoperate with each other for you to reach your final goal.

And then after you have a great model belonging to yourself solving your specific problem really well, then you need to work on serving it. You probably first will do some AB testing to make sure it really moves the needle for your product metrics, and then goes back in this loop.

演进路径：从 Prompt 到 RAG 到 SFT 到 DPO 到 RL

Obviously, I don't think you should jump into post training right away. And there are different phases you will go into.

First, prompt — everyone starts from prompt, use the model as is. It's few shots. Quickly you can use that to test your ideas.

And then you use RAG to ground um the usage of AI into your own data and you can start to do a lot of context engineering from that. Those are from minutes of interaction to hours of interaction.

And then you first progress into: "Hey, I have some data. I want to see how my data is going to reflect and make the model work better with my product." So you will start to do supervised fine-tuning that will take you a few hours.

Then: "Hey, um, the model I want to reflect in personalized taste. It is very unique choice of my products." So therefore you want to start to use preferences uh information where you collect from user interaction and uh, whether thumbs-up, thumbs-down, a lot of those kinds of information, and help the model learn your product taste.

Um, and finally, you want to build a model towards understanding, carrying your expertise in that domain. Whether that expertise is across uh legal, finance, healthcare, customer support, recruiting, marketing, sales — you name it. Even in one industry vertical, there are so many subdomains. So all of that is unique and special towards the product you're building. So usually um, you probably heard a lot of reinforcement learning and that is to actually build towards a specialty.

与人类学习的类比

Um, so this progression is very similar to how we human beings learn knowledge over time. Uh, for example, we actually learn a lot of knowledge by reading uh, reading literature, right? In the literature it will say, "Hey, what is correct, what is not correct?" So this is very similar to supervised fine-tuning.

Um, and as we grow, we develop our own taste and judgment of how we want to conduct the specific way we want to approach a problem, and that is preference or DPO.

Um and over the course of time, we learn to do a really good job at a certain area, whether "Hey, I want to be an accountant, and I would really know how to build into the financial data," or "I want to be a dentist," and you learn the details of how to operate with dentistry. So, all this is very similar exactly um to how we human beings acquire knowledge.

不同技术解决不同问题

So, um and also very interesting, different techniques are there to solve different kinds of problems.

  • Um for example, if the model doesn't know um the fact, and the fact actually is very dynamic — the facts of your data is very dynamic in your product — and then typically you use RAG to solve that problem.
  • Um however, if your model output all the behavior or the structure is off, then you curate data and do supervised fine-tuning to correct that.
  • Um if your model's answer, the quality is personal or specific to the taste of your product, and then you use preference tuning.
  • Or the model is quite weak on the special problem you're trying to solve, then you use RL — reinforcement learning.
  • And the end result of the model is too slow or too expensive for you to serve in production, and then you use distillation to let the teacher teach the student, much smaller student model, so it can be more performing or economical.

Obviously, distillation also means different things for LLM, VLM, or uh image generation models. Um if you are interested, we can talk more about that.

常见的踩坑区

So, there are many different ways teams start to, "Hey, I want to try those technologies," and they may not be happy of the experience because they can burn money um and the time, but may not reach their ideal results. So, so here are the areas that you can possibly feel frustrated.

数据质量胜过数据数量

Uh for example, um when it comes to data, and data is the essence of tuning, the quantity is not the most important. Actually, quality is the most important. But, sometimes just by throwing tons and tons of data into a training process may not lead to a great outcome. So, you really need to control the data quality.

And usually, who's the best judge of data quality? It's actually your product team. Um so, that's where we see the convergence of — um before GenAI, product team and the research team or ML team, they're separate organizations. They're separate teams. And they work hand-in-hand to make things happen. And a lot of the time these days, when people post-train GenAI models, we see the convergence of the product team needs to make judgment calls of the data quality and start to be deeply involved in the process. So, they can ensure the best result.

从 Vibe Eval 到系统化评估

Um and the second is you're going to have evals. Um I know all of you are very busy, and part into launch quickly, and a lot of evals is a vibe evaling.

[laughter]

And the founders really look at the result and feel, "Hey, is it right or not?" Actually, this is judgment. This is you putting your judgment of the end result and deciding whether it's good or not. And that judgment you convert into systemic evaluation.

So, this is no different from traditional software development where you have your unit tests, integration tests to ensure quality. Similarly, if you want to think about doing post-training and then have a way to build the eval and build your own judgment into a repeatable process, it's extremely important.

Reward Hacking：零行代码的故事

Uh and then there could be when you do RL, there could be sloppy RL environments uh where you build a simulation and the simulation is not really reflecting reality, and then the model can hill-climb on a bad simulation, and it also could possibly do reward hacking um and all kinds of weird stuff.

So, a fun story about reward hacking is um we have been asking a model — this is a coding example — to generate code that minimizes the compilation error. Okay. So, guess what the model did? The model generated zero lines of code. Okay, there's no compilation error, but that's absolutely not what you want.

So, this is one example of reward hacking, it's very common because the model is very smart, it'll try in all different ways to get your goal, but it may not be what you want. So, pay attention to all these details and try not to let the model outsmart you.

训练与服务的对齐

Um obviously, between your experimentation — so think about your development process as, "Hey, you're actually doing a lot of experimentation from training the model" — training the model is not the end of your experiment. The final judge is whether product metrics are moving or not. So, you need to bring the final model into the serving tier and do AB testing.

Um and that transition is extremely important because the quality can drop if you move from one training stack to a serving stack without aligning these two. Because think about — the model is tons and tons of calculations, math, and matrix multiplication. Um and the way to do matrix multiplication and calculation, if you use different libraries, different numerics, and different optimizations, it will lead to different results. And therefore, the end result of a training may not be replicated, or even you lose precision during serving. So, that alignment is very important. I can give you more examples of that.

Um and there are a few other challenges you will run into and happy to talk with you more about in details offline.

先驱者案例

Cursor：与前沿实验室正面竞争

So, there have been many pioneers we worked with in post-training. I would say Cursor is one of the few. They have started onboarding, getting onto this train from the beginning of last year. Uh there are multiple reasons. One is they really want to control their destiny of the supply of the model. And obviously, they have a lot of user engagement. They understand what customer preferences are, a lot of data. So, that becomes the beginning of their journey.

And they do pretty deep mid-training to post-training. And you have heard them announce continuously newer models every few months. And the result is great. Their aspiration is to compete at the frontier quality. Uh very bold aspiration. And they're getting there. So, very impressive results from Composer 2, Composer 2.5, um on par with — they're always trying to be on par or beat the frontier labs' quality at the same time. So, they are one of the examples, a very vibrant example, that it is completely doable as long as you stay focused and have the right tool. And Cursor builds on top of us.

Doximity：医疗领域的胜利

Um there's another — a huge huge variety of examples from healthcare. For example, Doximity is one example where they do clinical AI where they basically let doctors ask deep medical questions matching symptoms to medication and side effects and have well-rounded research around everything in medical space. They actually also train on Fireworks and they top a very important benchmark which is Stanford-Harvard clinic safety benchmark. And we are very proud of that result and they keep working on this training loop.

Factory：安全编码

Um Factory, that's another Sequoia company. They build on top of Fireworks and especially focus on security part of the coding. That is a very hard topic because security is not high tolerance. You need to get it right. They tuned a model that also tops the benchmarking in security area.

So you can see all these examples are a demonstration. All the companies are solving a very unique problem in a special way and they have been able to build their own challenges, use their own data by building on top of open model.

2025：编码之年，与 Co-Worker 的崛起

And those are the details. Obviously, as you know, last year 2025 is the year of coding. At Fireworks we support all the coding companies build on top of us. A lot of success in mid-train to post-train very strong models. As you can see those benchmarks are very impressive and all these coding companies are inspired to get on par or beat Frontier Labs in the coding space.

But it's not [just] coding. This is the year we start to see very interesting developments in all different kinds of co-worker spaces from general purpose co-worker to specialized domain-specific co-worker as I mentioned. There are legal, finance, marketing, recruiting, sales, customer support co-worker spaces. They are all starting to post-train and own their own intelligence to power their product.

Genspark 与医疗案例：5-10 倍成本下降

Here, Genspark is one of the generic co-worker applications and they build deep research for professionals and slide generation. As you see, this — they compete with a frontier model and it's slightly better, but the cost is significantly lower. So here we're talking about 5 to 10 times cost reduction. So as a startup, once you hit a problem like that, you can scale quickly into a doable business.

And I guess another healthcare example — healthcare data or use case is not well captured in frontier labs models. So you can see the quality of the tuned model is significantly better than the state-of-the-art closed model.

谁在做 Post-Training？

Well, we have many different types of developers build on top of Fireworks to do post-training. So what are these types?

  • Frontier agent builders: they usually build bespoke customized harnesses. They don't use common harnesses. And to co-optimize their harness with their systems and all different kinds of tools they want to build on top of, often times requires post-training. Uh so, we have seen a lot of repeatable success on doing that.
  • Large incumbents: obviously, we have seen a lot of big companies put into post-training because interestingly, those incumbents have huge amounts of traffic. For them to deploy AI features across the board to all their customers is a huge cost burden. Huge cost burden. Uh so, if we say we need to be careful not to scale into bankruptcy, it's not just for startups. It's actually for incumbents. Their CFO is blocking their AI feature launch because of the cost. And post-training is a way to remediate that.
  • Specialized model operators: those could be uh new labs, and a lot of cutting-edge model developers also do significant post-training.

Uh so, this is a quote we have heard repeatedly, that after product-market fit, post-training becomes the vehicle for many, many companies to build specialized intelligence.

We do believe — we do see the trend — that in the future there could be millions of specialized models. One application per use case. It it it it will be millions. That's how — uh I believe in that.

早期开始，动手实验

Um and obviously, we have seen different ways to convert the data into model. Um and the signal from the reward and how to build those reward functions is very important part of the story.

Um so, our observation is: start early, start early, and start to do experimentation a lot more iteratively and get hands-on experience. And we have seen people onboard so quickly. There's actually not the barrier as many people feel because this whole reward engineering is very similar to software engineering. The logical reasoning and mindset is very very similar. So so yeah, get your hands dirty and start to test it out.

不同深度的合作方式

Cool. I think — yeah so those are the key takeaways and I think we want to acknowledge there are different specialties or different knowledge you have right now in this space.

For example, we work with companies like Cursor and Cognition. They have deep researchers. They want to control every single knob as much as possible to get extreme results. We give them the lowest API. That means we just have RL rollout that they can directly interact with and they fully control the trainer. That gives them the best result.

But many of the companies — you have product engineers or machine learning engineers. You have good enough information and knowledge about post-training. You want to have some control but you do not want to have the lowest level control. So that's where we have our training SDK, iterate very closely with all of you to get you going. And we also are happy to deploy our own researchers. That's where we will see help hands-on like training your team to get on board.

So, those are the different ways we see different teams want to engage and get familiar with the whole entire process.

Cool. Uh, I'm going to pause here and see if you have any questions.

Q&A

Q1：最成功的 Reward Signal 长什么样？

I'll jump um — People are most successful if they have data and reward signal already, maybe from their product. What are the best examples of reward signals you've seen with very successfully trained very quickly?

So, um, usually the rewards — you can think about rewards actually is code. You write rewards in code. And uh, usually think about rubrics of rewards. Um, and think about — you want to grade the result in multiple dimensions.

Uh, for example, if you are building a recruiting agent, and then you can think about, "Hey, how do we evaluate candidate selection?" Um, and a different company, I guarantee you you have different criteria. Uh, for example, we want to grade a candidate um aptitude. Are they really hungry? They do not take no as an answer. They will break down walls. And that's one metric. The second is they're really fast in kind of building things and making progress. And so on.

So, then you have a blend of scores to merge this. So think about reward in different dimensions of rubrics. And then different companies have a different way to blend those. And that's your unique part and secret sauce.

Q2：什么时候该开始 Post-Training？（Vercel 的 Raj）

Oh sorry. Uh, great talk, Lynn. Raj from Vercel. I'm curious about — I think you mentioned what are the pitfalls of starting too early, but based on what you're seeing from Vercel, Cognition, or other companies, when do they actually start thinking about post-training? Is it when they feel ready? Is it when the cost is now too much?

Because the benchmarks where they're beating it, that's a great signal that yes, you can beat the frontier models, but is that the primary motivator? Like, is that 2% bump worth the cost or investment into this whole framework?

And how do they think about ROI? You know, closed models are more expensive, but then post-training has some intercept of money and investment and maintenance going forward. So, I'm curious of — are they approaching when cost becomes a concern or is it when the usage is spiking up and they really have to now plan for a year or two in advance?

Yeah, this is excellent question. Uh so, usually — so, think about in the AI building product-market-fit and the scaling the business as actually two phases. And then in the SaaS time, it was one concept. You hit product-market fit, just scale. I know you got to scale as much as possible.

Um but now we see a bifurcation. Product-market fit doesn't really mean you have a durable scalable business. And typically, we see companies deploy the strategy of focus on product-market fit first by building on top of Frontier Labs models because you don't need to worry about anything. So, just spend your money and hit product-market fit.

Uh and the other very important thing is: only after you hit the product-market fit, the data you collect from product surface areas are really meaningful. And you will get also the volume of high-quality data start to collect from product surface areas. That became the fuel of you starting to own your intelligence.

So, we see that as the very strong indication because once you hit product-market fit, you really think about starting to scale a business, you think about two things: 1. Continue to keep your competitive edge. 2. Build a durable business, so your revenue and your costs are in a healthy state.

Um so, then post-training becomes a very appealing solution because post-training allows you to basically codify your unique taste into a model that no one can steal from. Because it's very easy to clone and copy application as is, as you all know, right? Uh from coding agent, it's very easy. From screenshot, boom, generate the same or even better app. Uh so, that's very scary — that application itself as a moat is being reduced. Um and you bake your data reflecting the product engagement and all the deep knowledge into your model is a way to preserve that.

And second is you can post-train a model that brings down the cost 5 to 10 times. And then that means you can support 5 to 10 times much higher traffic with the same budget. And your unit of economics of scaling is so much better than — you avoid scaling into bankruptcy. So, we see those as two compelling stories behind the reason and timing.

Thank you, Lin. Thanks a lot. [applause]

item.description:
## 一、意外观察：Post-Training 不是技术革命，而是"组织结构"的革命
Lin 在演讲中埋了一个几乎被所有人忽略的信号——**产品团队和 ML 团队正在合并**。这在传统 SaaS 时代是不可想象的：过去 PM 和 ML 工程师之间隔着一堵 API 的墙，PM 提需求、ML 训练模型、双方各自甩锅。而 post-training 时代真正的稀缺资源不是 GPU、不是数据量，而是**"谁有资格判断这条数据是否高质量"**——而这个判断权，天然属于最理解客户的产品团队。
这意味着：**未来 AI 公司的组织架构图会长得越来越像一支交响乐团，而不是流水线**。当"数据质量判断"成为核心竞争力时，PM 就不再是需求的搬运工，而是"品味的立法者"。这是一个远比"我们要做 fine-tuning"更深层的组织重构信号。
## 二、跨领域连接：Post-Training 与米其林厨师的"高汤哲学"
Lin 提到"reward hacking"——模型为了"最小化编译错误"而生成零行代码。这让我想起一个完全不相干的领域：**米其林餐厅的厨师训练**。
顶级厨房里，学徒最容易犯的

item.title: [Bits + Bips] Should Ethereum Burn Its Way to Zero Staking Yield?
item.dc:creator: Bits + Bips
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、以太坊正在经历"央行化"的身份危机——但它自己没意识到

节目里最反常识的一幕：一群加密原教旨主义者（EF、Justin Drake）在做一件本质上是货币政策委员会才会做的事——通过烧毁曲线来"调节利率"。而反对他们最激烈的人是谁？是拿着黑石背景的机构（Joseph Shalom、Sharplink），他们说话的语气反而像是在捍卫去中心化的市场机制。

角色发生了戏剧性倒置：

  • 加密理想主义者开始扮演"美联储"，试图用中央规划设定风险无关利率；
  • 华尔街来的机构反而在扮演"哈耶克派"，抗议价格信号被人为扭曲。

Chris 提到的 LIBOR 比喻是关键——但更深的隐喻是：以太坊正在无意识地重演 1913 年联储成立时的争论。而 EF 甚至没有意识到自己站在了美联储那一边。这就是为什么 48 小时的评论窗口显得如此"专制"——它符合央行做决策的节奏，而不是社群治理的节奏。

二、被忽略的跨领域连接：以太坊质押收益率 = 全球利差交易的新一极

Chris 一句"你不想让 ETH 变成新的日元套息交易"其实指向一个还没被定价的宏观事实：加密世界第一次拥有了一条真正与美债、日债竞争的收益率曲线。

把三个数字并置来看，冲击就出现了：

  • 美国货币市场基金：~3.5%（无风险）
  • 以太坊质押：~2.75%（有削减风险 + 币价波动）
  • 日本 10 年期：仍近乎零

如果 EIP-8362/8363 真的把 ETH 收益压到零，那 ETH 会在结构上取代日元，成为全球最具流动性的"零利率借贷标的"。这意味着：

  1. 交易员将借入 ETH，卖出，去 Solana/Hyperliquid 追逐 8-15% 的收益；
  2. ETH 的价格弹性将从"科技股 beta"演变为"套息货币 beta"——一种非常危险的转型，因为套息货币在风险发作时会瞬间反向暴涨（想想 2008 年 8 月的日元）；
  3. 更反直觉的是：降低收益率反而可能增加 ETH 的价格波动性，因为它把 ETH 从生息资产变成融资货币。

EF 的学者们在解一个数学优化题，但他们不知道自己在触发一场货币性质的相变。

三、真正的"啊哈时刻"：这场辩论根本不是关于代币经济的

Austin 抛出的那句刀子最锋利：过去六个月，没有一个机构因为代币经济学而选择建在以太坊上；但三分之二的机构提到了 Bybit 黑客事件。

这暴露了一个非常尴尬的错位——

EF 关心什么 机构关心什么
质押率、烧币曲线、真实收益率 安全事件、监管清晰度、TPS
5-10 年后的博弈论均衡 下季度的合规审批
谁在"俘获"网络 谁能保证结算不出事

更进一步的跨领域观察：这像极了 1990 年代 Sun Microsystems 的困境——工程师们在辩论 Java 虚拟机的技术纯洁性，而客户在问"你的东西会不会宕机"。Sun 后来的命运告诉我们：当技术社区和用户社区谈的完全不是一个问题时，代币/股票价格与基本面就会持续脱钩。

而节目里 Seth 的一句话可能是整个讨论中最被低估的洞见——"DTCC 选择了 Stellar"。这不是一个技术选型问题，这是一个结算范式偏好问题。DTCC 每天清算 2 万亿美元的证券，他们选谁，谁就是下一代金融的默认层。以太坊社区在为质押曲线争论时，真正的战争已经在别的地方打响了——而且以太坊连参赛资格都没拿到。

附赠观察：Cloudflare 数据背后的隐藏结构

50% 网络流量已经是 agent——这个数字被讨论得很多，但没人指出它的深层含义：互联网的商业模式基础（广告 + 人类注意力）正在被抽空。当 agent 占主导时，Cloudflare 的 x402 微支付模式实际上意味着互联网从"注意力经济"回归"交易经济"——回到 1994 年 Ted Nelson 最初设想的 Xanadu 模型。

而这里有个残酷的悖论：能够处理这种规模微支付的链，恰恰不能是去中心化的。这就是为什么 Omid 说 Cloudflare 会自己当中央对手方——历史再次证明，当结算量级足够大时，去中心化会自发向"可信第三方"退化。这也回到了第一段的主题：加密行业正在被迫重新发明它当初想要摧毁的一切金融基础设施。

📝 转录文本

开场与市场快照

Over the past six months, in roughly zero meetings, has the tokconomics argument been raised to me by people when they were deciding what to build and where to deploy on the institutional side of things? And in at least 23 of those, the bybit hack was raised to me as a red flag for Ethereum. What do you think the implications of that are if we're actually trying to attract activity to ETH?

Hey everyone, welcome to Bits and Bips where we explore how crypto and macro collide one basis point at a time. We're here to discuss the latest stories in the worlds of crypto and macro. But just remember, nothing we say here is investment advice. Check unchainedcrypto.com bits and dips for more disclosures.

So, starting out as a quick market snapshot, looking at these midday and as a reminder for everybody, it is Monday, August 10th. Bitcoin's hovering a little under 65K. ETH is a little bit above 1,900. Gold's at 4,300 and change [music] per ounce. Uh I think the highest close since late July there. Uh silver bouncing around at 63.5 and change. The S&P 500 was in the 7,760 range and notably the 10ear still hanging around 4.65. USDY yen weakening again to 158 and change. We'll talk a little bit about FOMC hike odds later.

But before we go anywhere, a quick heads up that Bits and Bips still has its own channels. So if you're not subscribed, you're going to miss everything. Don't lose your regular dose of these takes. Hit subscribe. We're on X. We're on YouTube. We're on Spotify. We're on Apple Podcasts. Basically, wherever you're getting this, we're already on there. So have a look.

And before we begin with uh my co-host and our guest, a quick commercial break.

This episode is brought to you by 1-in Aqua, the shared liquidity layer from 1 in. Back multiple liquidity positions with one wallet balance and keep your tokens in your wallet until a swap fills. See how it works at 1in.com/aqua. Not listening to Bits and Bips yet? [music] It's our weekly crypto and macro market show with Rahm Alawalia, Austin Campbell, and [music] Chris Perkins. Search Bits and Bips and subscribe.

嘉宾介绍与 Clarity 法案

All right, welcome back everybody. As always, I'm your host Austin Campbell, high scholar of Zero Knowledge Group. I am here with one of my usual co-hosts, Chris Perkins, the golden hand of Franklin Crypto. and I'm being teamed up on today because Seth Gins is the chief investment officer of Franklin Crypto and is joining us as a guest.

So, right now, um Seth is a disclosure thing. Your professional interest runs through staking and yield and treasury structures and we're going to be talking about that um in our second segment today. But before we go fully into that, Chris, I think you wanted to talk clarity for a little bit. Shall we start there?

So that's 23k jobs down against a forecast gain of 80k. Um and the prior two months were also revised down by 103k. This has been a longun thing that has been going on since the Biden administration of we report revise down report revise down report revise down. So a reminder to everybody this is a continuation of a trend.

The Fed held rates constant at 3.5 to 3.75 9-to-3 vote. Three officials dissented in favor of a hike and September hike odds are somewhere in the mid40s right now. They were 55 immediately after the print.

Um unemployment rate also fell which is where things are getting a little weird and need to be understood. That is 4.09% 09% the lowest level in two years which means employed people fell but job seekers also fell. The number to look at and Joe Weisenthal was tweeting about this is that the labor force participation rate fell to its lowest level since Feb 2021. And for those who don't know what that means that means take all of the people in the United States and look at how many of those people are working. So as an aggregate of the population, we have less of a percentage working than we did before.

So among foreignb born workers, Joe said the civilian labor force has dropped by about half a million in the last year. And Muhammad El Arian was saying participation at 61.4% quote points to underlying issues with the supply side of the labor market.

So I'm going to pause there before we get further into CPI. Seth, I will I will set it up this way. There's a country I'm very familiar with that had low unemployment but declining labor rate participation for a long time and that's Japan. What do you think is going on here?

Seth：移民、AI 与"数据依赖"的双面性

Look, I I think the when you look at the unemployment rate, when you look at the the broader dynamics there, I think the immigration crackdown is having a a big impact. That's part of what's driving the um the the lower participation.

What what I what I think is a really interesting setup here though is on Thursday you had chairman Warf say we're going to be data dependent as we come into September and the market actually took that as a hawkish comment around September and the potential for a hike meaning there was a greater potential for a hike. Then you get the uh the jobs report on uh Friday and it's like well data dependency can mean two different things, right? Um and what's interesting is the Fed actually gets that data a day in advance.

So I I think we're looking at a a new chairman who is not that likely to to hike. Um that that's been my view for a while. I I know that view is shared by by at least some of the uh the other people on this uh stream as well. Um and look, I I think the the heart of that comes down to AI through its productivity gains is going to drive disinflationary pressure at some point in the medium term. And that's going to to mean we're going to be positioned way more restrictively than we realize. And you don't want to have whiplash. You don't want to to be getting more restrictive than getting less restrictive. And and kind of going where the puck was rather than where the the puck is going. Let's see where CPI comes out. If you remember, last month's CPI came in lighter than expected. So, we had lighter CPI, lighter jobs, bigger negative revisions. Let let's see where we end up as we get the next CPI. Brent,

Chris：不要与财政部作对

you guys know the uh the old phrase, don't fight the Fed. I think in this administration, it's don't fight the Treasury. Like, don't fight Bessant. This dude, you know, look what he's done. Look what the secretary's done. Uh when he decided to intervene in the yen, um why did he do that? Because he doesn't want rates going up. does not want them to sell their treasuries. Um so what did he do? He sold euro, right?

And and I think as you step back and you look at this administration, um they want to keep low rates. Donald Trump has made that no surprise. And so yes, I think Wars has got a balance where he's got to, you know, continue to stay independent and I think he will. Bess's not independent. He's doing what he needs to do. Um and I just I just don't see a scenario then like look at commodities right now. Look at WTI. Look at uh Brent. We're not at $200 oil despite the fact that Hormos is closed, right? The markets are rewiring. They're finding a new way. US is pumping away. Um I think WTI is in the 80s today. That's crazy. Hormus is closed. Who would have ever guessed? You know, this far into the What does it show? Markets are dynamic. We're not seeing that insane, you know, at least oil inflation that hits people at the pump. And um look, I think it will be an issue going into into midterms. Um but I just don't see them raising rates. I like I I just don't see it right here and now.

Austin：双重使命与内部分歧

I think part of what's important to think about is also the structure inside of the Fed and what the mandate is. A lot of these discussions occur kind of untethered from considering some of the base level things going on here.

So one reminder for all people looking at this the Federal Reserve has a dual mandate and that is price stability and employment right so right now if you look at what is going on their indicators are going like this right unemployment that was not a great print they're going to be concerned about that they would like more employment which would originally mean lowering rates but inflation remains above the 2% target which would mean raising rates.

And so when you have both of those pulling in opposite direction, what the Fed has done historically, and you can look even back to the 1970s on this, is tread pretty lightly until one of those two things breaks enough that they need to act decisively. So number one is to remember that if you look only at one of the two signals, you're not actually being data dependent and you're not remembering what the Fed's mission is. As Seth was alluding to earlier, if Walsh is meaning what he said about being data dependent, he's got data that now supports doing nothing in either direction.

Two, Fed governors are genuinely independent human beings, right? These are not people who march in lock step. We have a 93 vote right now, which means you had three dissenters in favor of a hike. Previously, we had a vote where you had denters both in favor of a hike and in favor of a cut, right? And if you go and meet these people, like if you go to Fed events, if you talk to the governors, like I've met Waller, Bowman, Goulsby, Barkin, all of them are their own people with their own decisionmaking frameworks, right? And they're not identical. Some of them are a little bit more forwardinking, like I'm not going to say vibesbased, but leaning in that direction. Some of them are very core economics datadriven. This is not a body speaking with one voice.

So the other thing you've got to think about is how are these inputs going to be processed through a decision-making framework that is not uniform. And so to me as I look at this, September seems pretty obviously an additional do nothing unless we get to a point where the data is truly breaking hard one direction or another because again you have to move four votes in favor of hiking basically to get a decisive majority to do that. I don't think they're going to do a like oneperson vote like barely hike here. That would be extremely disruptive for the market. So you're looking at probably needing a decent majority before all of the people are changing their votes to do that. And that means labor is much stronger and inflation remains above print or labor remains where it is but inflation's really got to rip.

Like Seth, how do you feel about that framing of thinking about how the Fed is going to think about itself?

国债供给结构与稳定币需求

I think there are a lot of moving parts also. I mean, so I I'll give you some of those some of those dynamics. If you look at crude, look at Brent, I think we're up about 10 points on Brent just in the last few trading days, right?

Yes.

Then you look at the 10-year and it's interesting. We're we're at the high end of the range, but but we've been kind of in this tight range for um for for a little bit for a week or so. And um not not breaking out. And part of the reason why is toward the end of last week, Treasury gave their expected supply issuance that that was coming and it was lighter on the long end than expected, which by the way is a really great tiein to crypto.

Yes.

Why? Because you're backing stable coins with bills. You're backing stable coins with short-term treasuries. So what we're seeing is keep supply low on the long end, which puts a little more stability into rates on the long end. But where does your demand, your increased demand come from on the the short end as you're bringing more issuance there? It comes from Besson's desire to get stable coin issuance up to two to three trillion by the end of the administration. So, it it's really interesting how you kind of you pull everything full circle. Um, and and you can kind of see that there's a a little bit of a broader road map coming together here.

I mean, another point on that front that Chris, you're probably familiar with this one. I think nondivatives people don't always follow is that's another big source of demand for short-term treasuries nowadays because we have to clear everything. We have to post collateral on all these derivatives. You need initial margin. You need variation margin. It's a small $500 trillion dollar notional market, right? Like as we look at the demand coming, it's probably compared to call it 2004 weighted much more heavily in short-term bills than it is in long-term bills where you had way more insurance dominance at that time trying to buy the longdated stuff.

And so I think you're in a world where there's large demand for short-term treasuries. It will grow if stable coins continue to move. This also sort of complicates the job of the Fed, but also makes it easier in the sense you can just focus on short-term rates more. Right? If the 30-year rates at 8% but 30-year supply is 1% of total supply, it's kind of a who cares. I was looking at these numbers recently like the pools of collateral you're talking about on derivatives plus dotfrank I think between the uncleared margin which is the non-clear like you have to post collateral now and the cleared it's it's like it's like over a trillion dollars it's it's a big number it's a big number

Cloudflare 与 AI Agent 流量革命

All right, speaking of big numbers I want to hit the final topic because friend of the show Lorenzo Valente uh has been commenting on agents so he said crypto Twitter missed the most important earnings call of the week. It wasn't a crypto company. It was Cloudflare. AI agent requests are up a light 1700% year-over-year. Agents crossed 50% of total network traffic. This quarter, first time in history, nonhuman traffic is the majority. Management admitted it happened faster than their own models predicted. And Cloudflare projects nonhuman traffic outnumbering direct human traffic by 1,000x within five years.

So Matthew Prince on the call, CEO of Cloudflare was saying Cloudflare handles about half a billion requests per second. Somewhere between 1 to 10% of those you could probably monetize through some sort of microtransaction like tiny fractions of a penny if you compute it properly for those office space fans out there. And that means 10 million financial transactions per second to be able to scale up to a 100 million. Visa currently peaks at about 20k per second. Prince is saying a lot of the world that's building these next generation payment networks thinks that they're competing with Visa as opposed to trying to figure out how you build a better internet. Uh the prince quotes by the way are from the call audio and transcript coverage. That's not a company release. So all things approximate. Go listen to the audio.

Valente's two conclusions being short L1 throughput is being short agentic workflows and at 10 million TPS and at onetenth of a cent per transaction you're looking at 315 billion a year in base fees alone stable coins in crypto are the endgame here.

Uh also friend of the show Omid Malikon, this volume cannot be handled by any known blockchain currently. Even corpo DLTs with five validators can't scale that high. And even if it did, the centralization eliminates the point. He said Cloudflare will instead probably play the role of trusted central counterparty performing multilateral netting and settling onchain periodically. If that model sounds familiar to you, it's the same trusted service card schemes performed between banks and merchants.

As a counter counterpoint to that, I will also say I'm friends with Bob Bench, founder of Radius, did a small thing you may have heard of called Project Hamilton at the Fed, who is rapidly building performant blockchains for precisely this. So, it's not nobody is building it, it's that most people are not building it. But I found that to be sort of a fascinating framing of what is happening with agents.

Um Chris, I want to start with you looking at this through both the VC lens and the builder lens here. What is that like incredible turn of like traffic towards agents mean to you?

Chris：Crypto × AI 是必然交汇

Yeah. So as the world's changing so fast, uh it's it's going to it's resulting in a lot of problems and what you try to do is find those founders that solve those problems in this really dynamic and evolving um industry and ecosystem. We believe that there's going to be a tremendous value, a cruel layer at that intersection of crypto and AI. Sandy call um from Franklin uh she recently published an a piece on it. It's really worth a read. It's it's really a solid piece, but like what are the problems that you have to solve for? Well, one of them is who's a human and who is not and how do you you know a lot of web traffic is predicated on marketing,

right? How do you market to an agent versus how do you market to a human?

Yes.

All very important things. You know, you talked about other challenges that need to be sorted throughput, TPS, right? These are all areas as you look at the stack and and and dissect it. um humongous opportunity at a time especially and like look everybody knows that that crypto crypto rails that is where the agents will transact. It is the most efficient way to do it. Micro payments we can we can chop value down to however small amount that we want. Um and that's and what are the agents good at? They're good at hyperoptimization. That's the one thing they love. And so it is the it's blockchain technology that will be the rails upon which these things operate. That's pretty obvious to a lot of us who operate at that intersection. Now the question is is where's the opportunity? Where's the value? And um look, we've been looking at this space for a long time. It is an exciting exciting space and it's starting to really show uh how important it is. I know Seth has strong views here too because we talk about it.

Seth：基本面与价格严重脱节

Well, I mean look, my my view would be and I will echo you know Sandy has a great way of framing this which is crypto complements AI. One of those two partners there has has seen a lot of price appreciation over the course of the last 6 to 12 months. The other has not.

Um but but I'll step back and I'll say to to have cloud flare which is a a central component of how the internet operates talking about um both the the way that they see agent requests uh going vertical over the next few years and then also this intersection uh with stable coins using X42. I mean, Cloudflare has has been in the background building out the tooling that they need to use crypto rails. Um, th this to me is part of that that broader thesis or or broader uh sentiment in uh in cryp crypto right now, which is the fundamentals are moving very quickly in the right direction. Price is not keeping up right now.

So th this is part of what's driving th this to me is exhibit A on the fact that fundamentals and price in crypto are about as wide as they've ever been and and crypto is so front and center as you get more agentic activity and remember like open claw really kicked off in December. So we're we're not talking about a a gigantic AI as as having been a high growth phenomenon for for years here. Th this is brand new and you're seeing the intersection with crypto come together very early in its life cycle.

价值捕获问题：代币经济正在被机构倒逼重写

I would. So, as I was looking at this, one of the things I've been thinking about this price versus like fundamentals disparity is I also think it's a question of where the hell is the value capture, right? Because let's say that Cloudflare is correct in all of their projections. Where does that money go is the second question you have to answer. I think that's one area where a lot of the disconnect is that nobody trusts these governance tokens to actually pay the users given some of the things that have happened there. It's unclear which L1 will win. Is it like should you just buy Cloudflare stock? Right. So I think part of it is also a value capture question. Seth, do you agree, disagree?

Uh Austin, I'll tell you in in the last two months, we've had probably five projects come to us saying, "What do you guys want to see in our tokconomics?" Right? So, people get it. They get that there's this trust deficit. They get that there's now a a protocol that is showing great performance, hyperlquid, on the basis of having real revenue, a fantastic growth trajectory and a buyback that drives that revenue right back to the token. And everyone is saying, "How do we do that with our token? What do you guys want to see?" It it's it's almost like traditional investor relations for uh for a regular company, but but almost like taking a few steps back and saying, "Hey, like we we realize we're we're not fully there yet. Help us get there. Help us think through how we create a token with the right value capture such that investors will be attracted to that." So, we're we're seeing movement in real time on that front and that's super important.

Chris, you want to add anything to close it out?

收尾：三项技术革命的合流

Uh, it's been a great episode. Uh, I've I've enjoyed it. I think when you look at the AI crypto intersection, these are complimentary technologies. And I'll be honest, like, you know, people were freaking out about SAS apocalypse. Now they're re realizing, wait a second, this the this AI and SAS companies will the smart SAS companies are going to come together. the smart founders are going to figure it out and use AI. AI is going to be ubiquitous. Um, and then I guess the last thing I'll say is that there's another technology that's looming out there in the future that people aren't talking enough about. That's quantum. And so like you have these three technologies coming together all at the same time. Uh, hi, ASI, Qday, it's all coming in the next couple of years. So what an exciting time to be alive.

I'm I'm disappointed you said quantum instead of robotics, but we'll just leave that one there.

We'll talk about it next time.

For those who did not look, go look on Twitter at all the DARPA like lift challenge insane robotics stuff. It's incredible. Just trust me, it's very funny.

All right, so that is it for today. One more time before we go. We have our own channels now. Subscribe to them if you want to keep watching. Otherwise, you are going to miss us and that would be tragic. So, thank you for joining us for this episode of Bits and Bips. We'll be back in one week to discuss more about how the worlds of crypto and macro are colliding. Seth, hopefully you will join us again. Until then, take care everyone.

Thank you for watching and hope you enjoyed this episode of Bits andBips. Just remember, nothing we say here is investment advice. And please check unchanged crypto.com/bitsandbips for more disclosures.

## 一、以太坊正在经历"央行化"的身份危机——但它自己没意识到
节目里最反常识的一幕：一群加密原教旨主义者（EF、Justin Drake）在做一件本质上是**货币政策委员会**才会做的事——通过烧毁曲线来"调节利率"。而反对他们最激烈的人是谁？是拿着黑石背景的机构（Joseph Shalom、Sharplink），他们说话的语气反而像是在捍卫**去中心化的市场机制**。
角色发生了戏剧性倒置：
- **加密理想主义者**开始扮演"美联储"，试图用中央规划设定风险无关利率； - **华尔街来的机构**反而在扮演"哈耶克派"，抗议价格信号被人为扭曲。
Chris 提到的 LIBOR 比喻是关键——但更深的隐喻是：以太坊正在无意识地重演 1913 年联储成立时的争论。而 EF 甚至没有意识到自己站在了美联储那一边。这就是为什么 48 小时的评论窗口显得如此"专制"——它符合央行做决策的节奏，而不是社群治理的节奏。
## 二、被忽略的跨领域连接：以太坊质押收益率 = 全球利差交易的新一极
Chris 一句"你不想让 ETH 变成新的日元套息交易"其实指向一个还没被定价的宏观事实
