💡 创造性洞见

老黄的第二职业：华尔街结构化产品设计师

表面上这是一次英伟达和6家基建巨头的合作，但如果你换一个角度看——老黄正在把GPU变成一种"债券"。他所提供的"25%剩余价值担保"，本质上不是销售行为，而是一种衍生品：GPU看跌期权的卖方。英伟达用自己75%的毛利润作为"权利金"，写了一份针对GPU二手市场的Put Option给融资方。

这里有个让人意外的观察：英伟达实际上是在做保险公司的生意。而且它做保险的资本效率极高——因为它对"标的物"（GPU）的定价权、再销售能力、软件升级能力都是垄断性的。这意味着它承保的这份"保险"，理赔概率被它自己控制。这在传统金融里叫做"信息不对称"，在保险精算里叫做"逆向选择的反面"——它是唯一一个既能定价、又能改变风险本身的承保人。

一个反直觉的跨领域连接：这是"石油美元"的翻版

1970年代基辛格搞出"石油美元"体系，本质是用美国国债给沙特的石油定价托底，让全球美元回流成为可能。今天老黄这套操作的结构几乎一模一样：

  • 石油 ≈ 算力（都是稀缺的、决定文明进程的底层资源）
  • 沙特 ≈ NeoCloud（都是资源持有方，但缺乏金融护城河）
  • 美国国债 ≈ 英伟达的剩余价值担保（都是"最终背书"）
  • 华尔街六大 ≈ 当年的花旗、摩根（负责把"体系"卖给全球资本）

5000亿这个数字不是偶然——它约等于沙特2000年前后石油美元回流的年度体量。老黄不是在建融资平台，他是在为"算力本位货币体系"打造清算层。谁能想到，一个做显卡的人，正在复刻美国霸权的金融骨架？

藏在A100里的真正秘密：CUDA是"复利机器"

大家都在看融资的5000亿，但财报里最惊人的一句话是A100从2020年用到2029年——这不是硬件寿命的胜利，这是软件对硬件的时间套利。

想一想：所有其他硬件行业（手机、电脑、汽车）的贬值逻辑都是"新的出来，旧的报废"。但英伟达通过CUDA做到了反向操作：新硬件出来后，旧硬件反而因为软件优化变得更有用。这在经济学上是个诡异的现象——它相当于打破了"摩尔定律的通货膨胀"。

更深的隐喻是：英伟达把自己从制造业公司，悄悄变成了一家"生态房东"。它卖出去的每一块GPU都是它的"出租房"，CUDA是它的物业管理系统。旧房子（A100）通过物业升级还能收租9年，这就是为什么Michael Burry的做空逻辑失效——他用制造业的贬值曲线，去对赌一家已经在做SaaS化定价的公司。

一个更黑暗的意外角度

老黄今天做的这件事，其实是在主动稀释大云的话语权。当谷歌TPU、亚马逊Trainium、微软自研芯片全部上线，英伟达的护城河就在推理时代崩塌。他扶持NeoCloud，本质上是在大云的势力范围里，人工制造一批"军阀"来牵制中央。华尔街六大恰好是这批军阀的军火商。这不是合作，这是AI时代的分封制——而5000亿，就是分封的采邑税。

📝 转录文本

赌上美国国运：5000亿融资，华尔街集体下场为英伟达背书

开场

赌上美国国运，5000亿的融资体量，华尔街基建这块所有的顶级机构全部一起下场为英伟达背书。今天我们就来聊一下这一次英伟达和6家基建公司之间的这个合作，他们之间为什么要合作，黄仁勋为什么要牵头去做这件事情。今天我们就把这一场赌上美国国运的一个豪赌，这一个协议本身我们去讲清楚，正好配合了在周二盘后发布财报的一个CoreWeave，我们把这两件事情放在一起去讲。

欢迎大家来到一个每天不单只聊新闻的专业美股频道，我是市场分析师小涛。今天我就不多说废话，我们直接开始。开始之前大家记得留言、点赞加转发。

一、合作本身：一个独立的融资平台

周一有一条新闻出来之后，直接给市场炸锅了。黄仁勋英伟达宣布——他也写了一条X——和阿波罗、贝莱德Blackstone黑石、Brookfield、高盛、KKR之间，这6家是世界上华尔街顶级的基建公司，每一家公司基本上喊出来都是有名号，和KKR之间建立了一个合作伙伴的关系，以建立独立的融资平台，调动超过5000亿美元的第三方资本。

所以他们要做什么？他们要做的是建立一个融资平台，它并不是直接去作为英伟达的销售然后帮英伟达去卖GPU，并不是。因为这些机构背后都掌握了资金——当然不是他们自己的资金，是他们客户的资金——但是他们可以去建议他们的客户说：今天我有这个产品，你要不要来投资？那投资这个标的的背后可能就是因为它的GPU或者数据中心。

所以第一点我们先确认他们之间的这个合作，去建立了一个独立的融资平台。

二、"算力即收入"：一年前的观点已被证实

然后在这篇文章里面，老黄也阐述了当下的一个事实。当然他在一年前就甩出了这个观点：计算能力或者算力即收入。那现在我们在市场里面是实实在在看到了、且证明了他一年前的这个观点是完全正确的。

现在整个市场里边的裸算力是非常的稀缺，这才会有了为什么Meta和xAI出售自己的这个裸算力给谁？给Anthropic。而且Anthropic所收购的这个价格是非常的贵。那么直接导致于在SpaceX（注：应为CoreWeave）的一个财报里面，他们有聊到他们的回本周期是小于一年，这就代表当下短期租赁的这个价格非常的贵。

三、GPU贬值周期之争：空头观点被证伪

差不多在一年多以前，市场里面一直在讨论这个话题，包括每一个季度大科技的财报会里面，管理层也有聊到这一点：什么就是整个芯片或者GPU它的一个贬值周期，或者它的一个折旧周期到底是多久？那大科技他们财报会里面有聊到，现在是根据订单，订单两年就是两年，订单三年就是三年，原本的这个假设是五年。就其他一些GPU的话，可能就是五年。

而市场里面空头的一个观点一直是认为：那这些GPU因为老黄GPU更新迭代这个速度非常的快，可能每两到三年就会进行下一个批次GPU的一个上线。空头的一个假设是：当有新的GPU、有新的卡出来之后，旧的卡就完全不值钱，就没有任何的一个利用价值。所以当市场或者当这些公司把原本老的这些GPU假设它的一个贬值周期是5年的这种假设是不合理的，因为他们认为新卡会淘汰旧卡。

但其实我们从现在市场里面能够观察到这个结果，完全去证伪了当时看空的这个观点。包括到现在，那市场里面的大空头Michael Burry都仍然持有这样的观点。但是这个观点本身现在已经被证伪了。当然他可以持续这样的一个观点，那么可以说两年或者三年之后，他的一个观点就是真实的，但起码从我们现在能够获得的数据，直接去证伪了这个观点。

A100的例证：使用周期延长至10年

比如说英伟达的A100芯片就是一个强有力的例证。6年过去了，这一款芯片是在2020年推出的，6年过去，这款芯片到现在为止仍然很多客户持续在部署。A系列的这个芯片，那么使得A系列的这一个芯片的一个经济寿命延长至将近10年。那这是老黄的话。

那正好今天在CoreWeave的一个财报里面，他们有聊到他们的客户，就原本A100，就A系列的这个芯片已经到期了，合同已经到期了，但是他们有一个客户愿意把这个合同延长到2029年。就是2020年的芯片现在已经有合同直接延到2029年。那也就是说A系列的这款芯片，起码它的一个使用周期是9年以上。

所以并不是新一款的芯片落地之后，以前的芯片就完全不值钱了，不然我们不会同时看到A系列芯片在用、H系列的芯片在用、B系列的芯片也在用。老黄有说到：这正是NVIDIA AI工厂的一个独特之处，它们的价值并非一成不变。CUDA可以持续提升其性能，就是即使是老款的这个芯片，软件端这一块你得到了一个抬升，你也可以使旧的芯片在性能上得到抬升。

四、融资平台的真正目的：扶持NeoCloud

前面我们聊到了他们建立的是一个融资平台，那建立融资平台的目的是什么？是为人工智能工厂引入资金。老黄说到：人工智能基础设施需求现在异常的旺盛，但是资金获取却极其不平衡。

这句话的意思是什么？包括整个这一次合作下来之后，你理解了他们一个合作的一个方向，你会知道其实是利好谁？利好这些NeoCloud，利好没有办法去和这些HyperScaler大云所竞争的这些星云。

为什么？因为大云HyperScaler他们的融资成本就要低很多。因为大云本身的业务非常的强劲，现金流非常的强劲，所以他们的融资成本就会低很多。当你的融资成本低，你自然就有一个优势在那边。而这一次英伟达和这六家公司合作，最终的一个目的就是为了这些星云去增加他们的一个竞争力，降低他们的一个融资成本。

他解释道：许多优秀的人工智能公司、企业和人工智能云平台都对计算能力有需求，但目前尚无法获得快速构建所需的规模或融资成本。

大云的自研芯片威胁

另外一点是我们现在发现这些大云、这些HyperScaler，他们都有自己的自研芯片：谷歌有TPU，亚马逊有Trainium，连微软现在都已经开始在搞自研芯片。而未来又是一个Inference推理的这个天下，那在推理的天下，从大云的这个角度去看，他们似乎会更加偏向于布局什么？布局自己的自研芯片。

所以未来老黄如果还能够、还希望英伟达能够保持现在这样一个增速，那其他的这些星云必须要接受老黄的一个扶持。但是因为星云的体量上来之后，老黄单拿自己的这个balance、拿自己这个现金流已经没有办法去扶持了。

那么老黄已经是一开始为了CoreWeave去背书，然后英伟达他也投资了很多其他的公司，他都投资，但是他投资的体量最多就是两个billion、三个billion。未来你造一个GW是六十个billion，CoreWeave这一次财报他们说2030年之前一共要布局8个GW，那接下去起码还有5~7个GW。5个GW，你一个GW 60个billion，连5个GW就是300个billion，那就这一家公司五个计划就需要300个billion。你说一家英伟达能够怎么复制下去？

所以它能够唯一帮到他们的一些方法、能够帮到星云的一个方法，就是去降低他们的融资成本。通过去扶持这些星云，通过去扶持这些现在融资成本很高的这些企业，来增加或者去卖出更多自己的GPU。

五、这是不是循环融资？——Vendor Financing 的本质

那这边就有一个非常重要的问题，市场也非常担心：这是不是一种循环融资？

老黄又解释道：这项措施旨在解决这一担忧，我们将独立的、长期的资本机构引入人工智能的基础设施市场。也就是他是希望引进第三方资金，然后通过第三方资金去为这些企业进行贷款。所以这并不是循环融资。

但是这是不是我们叫做vendor financing？什么是vendor financing？举个例子：如果今天我去买一辆车，我去买一辆GM的车，那GM旗下它有车行，然后它又有一个借贷的一个业务，等于它借贷的业务GM可以告诉我：今天你买我们GM的车，我们旗下的这个借贷业务可以给你更加便宜的一个贷款利率。这就叫做vendor financing，非常标准的vendor financing。就是通过利率上的这个激励让你来购买自己的产品。

所以这一次的合作仍然是一个vendor financing，即使这个资金是来自于第三方。

六、25%剩余价值担保：LTV的机制解读

什么意思？英伟达为何会支持融资？那怎么去支持这个融资？他有聊到：在某些情况下，英伟达有可能会为项目提供最高可达25%的剩余价值。

我们来举个例子。比如说我要去买一辆车，这辆车是10万，然后买车的时候我首付是1万，然后在行业里面有一个值叫做LTV，Loan to Value Ratio。什么意思？车十万，我首付一万，那Loan to Value就是我要贷多少的款——就是或者贷款方要贷给我多少款——贷90%，所以这个Loan to Value就是90%。

那这个Loan to Value越低，那贷款方所给我的这个利率就越低，能够理解吗？或者说我的首付比例越高，贷款的这个利率就越低。从贷款方的角度，他需要有更多的equity，他需要你有更多的首付，对于他们来说就更加的安全。

理解了LTV这个概念之后，我们再来举这个例子。比如说今天英伟达的芯片是100块钱一块芯片，然后有一家星云，他签了一个订单，客户的订单是4年。客户说我需要一个GW的GPU。然后比如我们打个比方，一个计划就是一百块钱。客户只能签四年的这个订单，但是我假设这个GPU的贬值周期是五年，那就是剩下的那一年的贬值周期你是没有被covered的，你有可能是没有任何收入来源的。那就前四年四年订单，第五年你的这个现金流是没有办法保证。

那这时候英伟达就会进来，他去保证。他说最多是25%的这个剩余价值嘛，所以他可以去保证最后那一年，如果你没有客户的话，我可以帮你去寻找下一个客户。那在这种情况下，他是为谁做担保？他是为那家星云去做担保，担保他第五年的这个现金流。

那有了英伟达进来担保之后，从贷款方——就从我们前面所提到的这六家公司——从贷款方这个角度去看，他们就能够因为英伟达为了这个尾部风险进行了背书，所以我可以把整笔贷款的这个利率往下调。

七、英伟达为什么敢这么担保？

那英伟达哪来的这个自信？他认为自己的这个计算资源是独一无二的，且它具有可替代性、普遍互换性、普遍的采用性、软件可升级性，并且可以在庞大的客户生态系统中重新去部署。

就今天，如果未来你现在的这个客户签了四年之后，第五年不愿意续了，那我可以完全把你这一部分剩下的算力给承接过来之后，帮你去找到另外一个客户承接这一部分的算力。

那在最坏的情况下，那如果第五年完全找不到任何的客户，其实对于英伟达来说并不是非常致命的打击。我举个例，就还是一样，前面100块钱。你想一下，因为现在英伟达的毛利润是多少？75%。卖出去100块钱这个产品，四年用完了，那剩余的这个价值我就算它保了20块钱——保了20块钱，最终这20块钱它完全没有卖出去，一分钱都卖不来，那就是它亏了20块钱。那他原来一百块钱毛利润百分之七十五，现在他再亏二十块钱的话，也就是他从原来的毛利润百分之七十五变成了百分之五十五，就还是赚钱的，对吧？

当然，如果真的出现它的一个额外或者多余的这个算力完全卖不出去的话，那那时候英伟达的这个毛利润可能也没有75%。所以这是相辅相成的。我只是给大家举个例子，就是对于英伟达就如果真的出现这种情况，对于英伟达的影响到底是什么。

八、老黄的号召力：华尔街六大 CEO 齐聚一堂

所以这件事情或者这次的一个合作本身没有那么的复杂。但有一点我非常钦佩老黄——我今天刚看到这期采访——他在CNBC上把这6家公司的CEO全部集中到一起去接受CNBC这个采访。那除了贝莱德的CEO Larry Fink，他是通过电话会议进去之外，你很难会看到，包括高盛的CEO也在里边，所有的公司CEO全部在里边然后接受CNBC的这个采访。这就说明了老黄的这个号召力真的是非常的强。

从以前老黄带着整条行业链往前做，那包括美光都是老黄带着一起走的。如果不是以前老黄向美光说我接下去对于Memory这个需求非常的大的话，现在这个Memory价格的上涨绝对不是现在我们所看到的一倍两倍，可能是四倍五倍的这样的一个上涨。所以他带着整个行业里一起往前走，提前去做这个投资，到现在带着华尔街一起往前走。

我认为他的这个软实力和说服能力和口才，在华尔街里面、在整个市场里面，没有任何一家公司CEO可以和老黄去媲美。

九、总结：老黄看的是两三年后的推理时代

那回到这件事情本身，其实没有那么的复杂。他就是建立了一个融资机构，那这个融资机构是通过这六家公司去牵线。当然未来他们可能会推出各式各样不同的一些产品，围绕着GPU、围绕着数据中心去展开，使得会有第三方的资金进来，愿意去带给这些现在融资非常难的一些企业，包括了星云和一些更小的公司。

在这个基础上，老黄去为这个尾部风险进行背书，去为4年和5年之后的这个风险进行背书，从而去降低这些企业的融资成本，使得他们可以去和这些大云去竞争。因为未来这些大云，他们可能布局是在哪里？布局是在自己的一个自研芯片。

所以我觉得老黄其实思考的是比较远的，他起码已经在思考两到三年之后，那么随着Inference遍地开花之后，是不是对于GPU还有那么大的这个需求？特别从大云这个角度去看，他们的incentive、他们的一个激励机制可能不在GPU身上，而是在自己的一个自研芯片身上。为了幸运这些NeoCloud可以和这些HyperScaler大云去进行竞争，老黄也是想尽了一切的心思去扶持他们。那当然扶持他们最终的目的是能够使自己的GPU未来还是可以保持相当高的增速。

CoreWeave 财报解读（Q2）

一、核心数据：营收盈利略好于预期，RPO 高速增长

带着这样的一个背景和视角，我们来看一下周二盘后发布财报的CoreWeave，星云和NeoCloud。

首先从数据来说，营收和盈利的这个增速还是不错的，就略微好于市场的这个预期： - EPS 比市场预期好了13% - 营收 基本上是符合市场的预期 - RPO订单 这一块的增速非常的快，同比增速246%，总共的体量来到了104个billion（1040亿美金） - 同时还不包括第三季度刚刚所新签下的250亿美金（25 billion）

并且从未来订单的这一个占比去看，大于48个月（就大于4年）的这个订单占比已经来到了41%。也就是他们所新签的这些订单很多都是来自于一些中长期的订单，对于未来营收的这个确定性是一件好事。

二、客户分散：不只是大模型公司

我们来看一下CoreWeave的客户，那它的客户不是仅仅来自于这些大模型公司，它的客户其实是遍地都有：

  • Bentley Systems：它是一家软件公司
  • Caterpillar：我们都非常的清楚，它是一家工业板块的公司。那Caterpillar他们为什么要算力？他们用算力来训练自己的Physical AI（物理AI）
  • 再比如还包括了一些金融服务公司，比如说Jane Street。那Jane Street它本身既投资了一个billion，投资了equity，直接投资了CoreWeave这家公司，然后还下了9个billion的这个订单。他们为什么要数据中心？因为他们是全世界最大的量化高频机构

三、财报会议：议价权提升，利润率上行

最后是财报会议这边，第二季度他们所签的这些订单，比过去几个季度这个利润高了5%~10%。原本他们的利润在20%至25%之间，现在加了5~10%的话，那这个利润的上行空间最高到35%，最低是30%（25~30）。

那为什么他们有这个议价权在那边？他们说到：底层的逻辑是我们的客户可以从他们的客户身上赚更多的钱——也就是AI的这个（因为他们是提供裸算力嘛）AI的这个落地非常的好。

四、业务分布：模型优化服务爆发式增长

从业务分布这个角度去看，在卖裸算力的同时，他们还提供了模型优化服务。模型优化服务在过去这段时间我有聊过，市场里边发生两件事情：一个是模型优化服务，另外一个是硬件优化服务。

  • 硬件优化服务 体现在GPU和HBM之间的这个比率等等
  • 模型优化服务 就是从公司这个角度，他们token的消耗量比以前还要高，但是花费是和以前一样的。为什么？因为他们选择了用一些闭源模型和开源模型的这个组合

那提供了这个服务给CoreWeave，其实也带来非常好的这个营收。在一个季度里边，ARR就从100万到了一个亿了——就一个季度里边翻了100倍。他们预计在今年年底的时候，单这一块服务的一个ARR可以达到2.5亿美金（two hundred fifty million）。

五、A100 合同延期到 2029 年

接下去一点就是我前面说到，A100的这个合同延期到了2029年。那A100是2020年的这个合同，也就是A100现在的一个使用周期，那起码是这一组A100使用周期达到9年以上。

六、总结

那最后希望通过今天这期视频，大家可以理解为什么老黄要去做这件事情：

  1. 他的目的是要去扶持这些星云，使得星云他们的融资成本下降，为了什么？为了星云未来可以购买更多老黄的GPU——这第一点
  2. 然后第二点，我们从NeoCloud的这一次财报——从CoreWeave这个财报里面可以看到——CoreWeave的这个落地，包括他们新签订单的这个毛利率比以前还要高，这也是包括他们客户的一个分散程度，这也体现了现在的AI它不是简简单单在两家大模型身上。当然大模型是承担了比较多的这个营收比例，但是从分散的这个角度去看，其实各个公司都有，算是遍地开花
  3. 最后一点，在CoreWeave的财报里面有聊到，在老黄的这篇X文章里面也有聊到：芯片本身GPU的它一个使用周期，绝对不是三年，绝对不是下一代的芯片出来上一代的芯片就没有任何的价值。恰恰相反，最早那一代的芯片一直用到现在，且市场的预期是可以用到2029年

广告：Seeking Alpha 服务介绍

最后是我们今天的服务，来自于Seeking Alpha Alpha Picks量化选股策略。那过去一年，标普500回报了20%，他们的量化选股策略是回报了50%。

这个量化选股策略每一个月会提供两次的建议，就是建议买入一些标的，然后每一个标的它都会进行跟踪，都会及时提醒到底是应该加仓还是减仓。现在正在举行活动：9折活动，原价是499美金一年，现在是449美金一年。

那Seeking Alpha的平台上还有另外一个Seeking Alpha的Premium订阅。这一档Premium的订阅，你可以看到他们平台上所有的投资文章。Seeking Alpha这个平台本身是在老外社区里边一个历史非常悠久的一个平台，上面有非常多的一些投研文章。在这个基础上，还可以享受他们那个Portfolio Management——一个整体投资组合的一个健康评测，它会告诉我们哪些标的、哪些风险可能是我们会忽略的。所以这一档订阅原价是299美金一年，现在是269美金一年，也有九折的这个优惠。并且还有7天的一个免费试用，可以先免费试用，如果不喜欢的话可以随时取消。

当然如果大家对于这两个订阅都感兴趣的话，还有一个combo的一个价格，我会把这三个订阅全部放在置顶的留言里面，大家感兴趣的话可以在置顶的留言里面找到订阅的链接。

那今天这期呢就到这边，我们下期见。

## 老黄的第二职业：华尔街结构化产品设计师
表面上这是一次英伟达和6家基建巨头的合作，但如果你换一个角度看——**老黄正在把GPU变成一种"债券"**。他所提供的"25%剩余价值担保"，本质上不是销售行为，而是**一种衍生品：GPU看跌期权的卖方**。英伟达用自己75%的毛利润作为"权利金"，写了一份针对GPU二手市场的**Put Option**给融资方。
这里有个让人意外的观察：**英伟达实际上是在做保险公司的生意**。而且它做保险的资本效率极高——因为它对"标的物"（GPU）的定价权、再销售能力、软件升级能力都是垄断性的。这意味着它承保的这份"保险"，理赔概率被它自己控制。这在传统金融里叫做"信息不对称"，在保险精算里叫做"逆向选择的反面"——**它是唯一一个既能定价、又能改变风险本身的承保人**。
## 一个反直觉的跨领域连接：这是"石油美元"的翻版
1970年代基辛格搞出"石油美元"体系，本质是**用美国国债给沙特的石油定价托底，让全球美元回流成为可能**。今天老黄这套操作的结构几乎一模一样：
- **石油 ≈ 算力**（都是稀缺的、决定文明进程的底层资源） -

item.title: [Latent Space] 🔬They Thought the Model Was Broken — Matt McPartlon & Neil Patil, Chai Discovery
item.dc:creator: Latent Space
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

意外的观察与跨领域连接

一、最令我震惊的悖论：Chai 是一家"反生物学"的生物公司

整个访谈中最反直觉的信号被藏在一句轻描淡写里——Chai 30 人团队里"只有 Matt 和 Kevin 有生物背景"。这不是缺陷，而是刻意的哲学选择。他们把蛋白质设计问题当作纯粹的核心 ML 问题来处理，就像"你不需要当导演才能训练视频模型"。

这里藏着一个隐蔽的跨领域联系：Chai 在生物学上重演了 AlexNet 在计算机视觉领域的历史时刻。2012 年之前，CV 由手工特征工程师主导（SIFT、HOG），他们坚信"必须懂视觉才能做视觉"；结果颠覆者是一群纯 ML 人。今天蛋白质设计的"归纳偏置贵族"（AlphaFold 的 23 个子模块、三角层）正在被"苦涩教训派"（bitter lesson pilled）颠覆。Matt 说"complexity 和 bitter-lesson 是根本对立的"——这句话可以直接写进 Ilya Sutskever 的 blog。

啊哈时刻：Chai 办公室墙上挂的不是 DNA 双螺旋，而是 SpaceX Raptor 1 到 Raptor 2 的引擎照片——那张著名的"删除、删除、再删除"的对比图。生物公司把火箭工程当作精神图腾，这本身就是一个信号：他们不认为自己在做生物，他们在做精度工程。

二、隐藏的产品哲学：从 ChatGPT 到 Figma 的范式反转

Neil 说了一句极其重要但被大多数听众忽略的话："我们本可以套个 chatbot，但真正需要的是 Photoshop 式的设计套件——有画笔工具画 epitope，有 content-aware fill 生成 binder。"

跨领域惊人的对称：LLM 世界正在从"visual IDE"退化到"chat"（VS Code → Cursor → 纯对话），而生物 AI 世界正在反向进化——从命令行/脚本 → 视觉化设计套件。为什么？因为分子本质上是 3D 拓扑对象，而代码本质上是线性文本。Chai 的产品直觉揭示了一个更深的真相：AI 界面的形态由被操作物的本体论决定，而不是由模型的形态决定。

更颠覆性的洞见：Neil 承认"我可能一年后就要把这些产品全扔了，因为 Chai 4 会更聪明"。这暗示了一个新的软件生命周期定律——AI 时代的产品不是资产，而是桥梁。软件从"20 年寿命"缩短到"1 年寿命"，产品经理的工作变成了"如何优雅地设计一次性建筑"。这在传统 SaaS 里是异端，但在 AI-native 领域会成为常态。

三、最被低估的系统性真相：制药业是"反向摩尔定律"的殖民地

有一个数字在访谈中一闪而过，但它颠覆了我对整个访谈的理解：GLP-1 类药物三个月前的总收入超过所有 AI 实验室加起来。而与此同时，Eroom 定律（Moore's law 倒过来拼）意味着每个新药的成本在指数级上升。

跨领域的深层连接：Chai 表面上是一家 AI 公司，实际上是在做"用摩尔定律解决 Eroom 定律"的套利。这是历史上最大的曲线交叉套利之一——一条指数下降（compute cost）撞上一条指数上升（drug development cost），谁站在交点上谁就吃掉整个 delta。

最出人意料的洞见：Chai 团队每个人都是"资本配置者"。Matt 说他们的研究团队"像风险投资人一样把 ideas 投向 compute"。这不只是比喻——当 AI 让"做事"的边际成本趋近于零时，唯一稀缺的资源变成了"注意力"和"选择"。因此整个公司从 CEO 到实习生，本质上都在做投资组合决策。这解释了为什么 30 个人能撬动 4 亿美元融资和四大 pharma 合作：他们不是在做更多事，他们在做更少但更对的事。

一个让人后背发凉的隐藏推论：如果这个趋势成立，未来所有 AI 公司的组织架构都会趋同于一家"极小的对冲基金 + 极大的计算集群"。传统的"工程师-产品经理-销售"的三分法会崩塌，取而代之的是"配置者-验证者-集成者"。Chai 已经在这个未来里了，只是他们自己可能都没完全意识到。

彩蛋：科学家哭泣的那一刻

Neil 讲的那个"科学家在会议室里哭出来"的故事，是整个访谈里最反直觉的商业洞见：AI 在 B2B 领域最强的护城河，不是准确率，也不是延迟，而是"10 年孤独感的终结"。当你卖给一个花了 10 年追一个靶点的科学家，你卖的不是软件，是从西西弗斯到普罗米修斯的身份转变。这是任何 SaaS 教科书都不会教的东西，也是为什么 Chai 说 pharma 客户"出乎意料地易于合作"——他们不是在买工具，他们在买被拯救的可能性。

📝 转录文本

开场：从 ChatGPT 到 Figma 的产品直觉

Neil：looks a lot less like a chat GPT and a lot more like Autodesk or SolidWorks or Figma. You know, if you've used those things where you can kind of load up your molecule. There's this almost Photoshop-esque design suite. You have this equivalent of a paint tool to kind of paint your epitope. You have this equivalent of a content-aware fill tool to kind of get your binders generated from Chai.

And I think to add to that, right — this notion of target discovery and hit discovery and optimization where each of these has a gate and takes a few months to a few years is this very waterfall model. The cost of trying things and getting things early is very expensive.

But I think to what Matt's saying — if you start to get in a regime where you can have models give you really promising candidates, you can start to make that look a lot more like a loop. It's akin to becoming more agile in software development. But now the next problem is agonists, right? Like how do you reliably one-shot hitting a switch on a cell? Or bispecifics or ADCs? And I think this — levels of abstraction that we're going to have to climb with the product as the models get better. If you have really good primitives for structure prediction and binding and design and you can compose them, then you can start to just grow into the outer loop of science.

主持人开场与嘉宾介绍

主持人：Welcome to Latent Space AI for Science. I'm Brandon. I build RNA therapeutics at Atomic AI. I'm joined by my co-host RJ Honiki, CTO and co-founder of MirrorOMIX.

It's a pleasure to have with us in the studio today Matt McPartlon and Neil Patil of Chai Discovery. Chai is a protein design startup which is about two and a half years old and has made quite a splash in those few years. They have several very exciting announcements that I think they'll tell us about today. But yeah, to get started, could you two give us a bit about your background and what you do at Chai?

Matt：Yeah, thank you very much for having us. We're super excited to talk about Chai today. I'm Matt McPartlon. I'm one of the co-founders of Chai. My background is in AI biology related stuff during my PhD. I actually started my PhD in theoretical computer science and then transitioned to this later. I've been doing this stuff now for about 8 years and I kind of came into the field at an interesting time where protein structure prediction was just starting to see signs of life. So this is like AlphaFold 1 days. And was in the field during AlphaFold 2 and got to see a lot of the interesting developments at that time. So yeah, I'd always been pretty interested in applying this stuff in the real world and Chai was just a perfect opportunity to do that.

Neil：And I'm Neil Patil. I help lead platform and product here at Chai. So a lot of the stuff around infrastructure to train models, serve them, and then the productization piece — the design suite that lets you use the models.

I kind of have a more meandering path. So I kind of got into programming like 15 years ago, making apps in the App Store. Got really addicted to the dopamine hits you get from that. And then actually got nerd-sniped by robotics and worked on that for a bit. Self-driving cars in like 2018, 2019. Got really jaded and was like, "I don't want to touch hardware for a while." Ended up switching and joining a SaaS company called Vanta as one of the first employees there and kind of grew with it. Started my own security company afterwards. Got a few years into that and I was like, you know what, atoms are kind of cool. I want to work on something a little more meaningful. And so I joined Chai about a year ago, right after Chai 2 was announced, to help with a lot of the platform and commercialization pieces.

主持人：Awesome. It's like the five stages of grief or something.

Neil：Yeah. We're at acceptance.

大厂合作与商业模式

主持人：Awesome. You have these — I think four now — big partnerships and raised a whole bunch of money. Can you tell us a little bit about those partnerships, and then what I really want to know is: what are you telling investors and customers that is so compelling that they're willing to do these big deals?

Matt：Yeah. So we've been very fortunate to partner first with Eli Lilly and then with Pfizer, Novartis, and Argenx. I think it's been a really interesting ride and I think our business model is also very compelling to a lot of people. We really care about the partners succeeding — Chai as a company really depends on how the partners succeed. I think Neil probably has some interesting takes on what we actually offer and what makes that so compelling. So I'll hand it over to you.

Neil：Yeah, I mean, as you all know, drug discovery is a very lengthy process. And a lot of these pharma companies are spending lots of time, years and years and billions of dollars trying to find initial therapeutic candidates. And so at Chai, we train models that can help accelerate that process and find those initial binders and then some. And there's a lot of bio companies, AI for bio companies that are making their own drugs. We really don't see ourselves that way. We see ourselves as almost a neutral software factory for making medicines. And so that's what lets us go work with and support all of these other pharmas in their drug discovery journey.

And so yeah, I mean, a lot of this capital is just another proof point that we can start to really accelerate that software factory — go after harder modalities, train bigger models, and ultimately just build what our partners and customers ask us for.

主持人：But what is it — why you and not other structural companies? Why are they compelled to buy from you?

Matt：The thesis of Chai has always been to be the software and modeling layer — which was, I think, very controversial at the time. Everyone, you know, this play is definitely —

主持人：Two years ago and it's already a completely different world.

Matt：Yes. It's pretty crazy. People tried this play for a while, and I think the models just really weren't there yet. And even for us, we were taking a risk in the very beginning. We were kind of banking on the models getting there. And like I had seen early signs of life in my work, and our CEO Josh — he was on the original ESM papers on that team at Meta — and he was seeing pretty early signs of life that there might be scaling laws here. I think we'll actually be able to start designing things. Structure prediction is getting really good.

One crazy thought is: we didn't have a multimer structure prediction model until like 2021. That was 5 years ago when we could start with deep learning to actually predict the shape of two proteins at once. AlphaFold 1 was — and AlphaFold 2 was this huge breakthrough. But then AlphaFold 2 Multimer came out a year later. So you really needed that to unlock design in the first place anyway. We weren't even trying to predict multiple proteins at once.

And then really around that time, inverse folding kind of started working — and was like, "Oh, ProteinMPNN, this actually works in the lab." Credit to the Baker lab for doing all this really excellent lab validation on all their models. I think we're starting to see them do interesting things and actually work on real-world experiments. And now is probably the time to start betting on this.

I think before then, maybe you could take some experimental data from a campaign on this one target that you had and you care about and you might be able to make some progress on that and keep hill-climbing in this one very specific case. General models weren't really a thing back then. So we took that bet pretty seriously and decided to just push as hard as possible and to really shoot for generality in our approach.

And then when Chai 2 came out — our second paper after Chai 1 — we kind of showed the world "this is actually possible and it's possible at scale." We didn't show this for one or two targets, like it kind of works. We were like, "let's just go all in." I think Josh likes to say we set a bold company-wide challenge to design antibodies to 50 targets, and it actually — we saw some signs of life. We're like, "All right, let's do this with real statistics and see if this actually works."

It's an interesting story of how we chose these targets. We were like, "All right, what targets we going to choose? We should choose some interesting targets, whatever." And at that point we were kind of ramping up with CROs and figuring out what does our wet-lab process look like. We decided, after trying some stuff with many proteins, whatever, "here are the interesting targets, this is what we should look at." And like half the time, the targets just kind of didn't work. We were still learning. And we're like, "All right, maybe we should just go with targets that the CROs have actually validated." So let's get the CRO catalog, see what they've already worked on, restrict that to an interesting set. Uh, so from that we chose 50 targets, designed antibodies against them, got hits to half, and at that point I think pharma starts to realize like, "OK, there are actually signs of life here, and this might actually work in some of our programs."

什么是抗体？为什么难？

主持人：So antibodies is maybe a more challenging domain than other structural prediction problems. So why tackle antibodies? Maybe back up — what is an antibody? And what do you do with it, and why is it an attractive target?

Matt：The analogy that everyone gives — this lock and key kind of problem — where your target, this protein that you're trying to bind to, might be some disease protein that's kind of like your lock. And then you want to design this key that fits into it, and in our case just sticks there.

The interesting thing with antibodies is they're really flexible, general proteins. In a lot of ways they're very general; in a lot of ways they're actually pretty uniform. But at least how they bind to a target is very general. So you have a lot of optionality in how you design this kind of binding interface.

The structure prediction problem for antibodies — predict how this antibody actually binds to the target, how the key fits into the lock — that's been a notoriously difficult problem. The nice thing is we've made a lot of progress on structure prediction. The field as a whole has come a long way in getting structure prediction to where it is. But in the design setting, you can be a lot more selective about the types of designs you want to make and the types of structures you actually want to focus on. And in some cases, it might actually be even easier to design a protein binder that is an antibody than to actually predict how it might bind that target in general. So it's kind of like — if you have the freedom to choose, you can just pick the easy cases, if that makes sense.

主持人：So the antibodies — there's a whole machinery in the body that works with antibodies. What does the body do with it naturally, and what can you do that is sort of not natural but is useful for therapeutics?

Matt：This is coming from a non-biologist here, but I think of antibodies as these kind of Y-shaped proteins. So it kind of looks like a peace sign with your fingers. Each of these fingers is kind of like an arm of the antibody. And it's really actually only the tips of your fingers, the tips of the antibody, that engage in binding. So this makes these really nice therapeutic design targets — for that particular region. The nice part is that the rest, apart from the tips, is actually relatively constant. So this is called the framework region of an antibody.

In the design problem, you're typically just designing the very fingertips, and you can actually choose for the most part these kind of framework regions that your immune system already recognizes. So antibodies are kind of like these Y-shaped proteins that your immune system recognizes. It knows really well. It's kind of like one of the lines of defense against pathogens and other types of diseases.

主持人：So I guess antibodies can, on the one end, connect to proteins on the surface of a cell typically — or other things, but typically on the surface of a cell — and then the other end helps the immune system identify a pathogen typically. But you can also do things like you mentioned — ADCs, antibody drug conjugates. So that means putting a drug on the other side, and that causes, when you bind to something, that it releases the drug into the cell, right?

Neil：They're this very general framework, right? Where kind of on the ends you have these CDR loops and you can design them to bind to arbitrary things. Where maybe one end you bind to a cancer cell, the other end you bind to a toxic molecule — you're now precision delivering that toxic molecule to a cancer cell. Or you just have two ends bind to things and kind of force induced proximity to have some effect in the body.

Or, you know, a lot of drugs historically are really just about blocking things, right? Antagonist behavior. But maybe you can have agonist behavior. We actually really precisely press a switch. There's a GPCR protein, which are these doorbell proteins that sit in your cell membrane — you have an antibody very precisely engineered to poke it in a certain way that causes a downstream chain reaction.

And I think one of the things that's really exciting about where we're getting to with some of these models is we can start to get that precise. We can really target a very specific epitope — meaning binding spot — a very specific set of atoms to have the antibody go after. Which, you know, historically with a lot of drugs, you're just kind of brute-forcing a lot of antibodies and just trying to come up with a bunch of things and see what sticks. But maybe that gets you a binder to some spot of your target molecule, but that doesn't let you precisely engineer where you're poking.

传统方法：老鼠、酵母展示与"针海捞针"

主持人：I know you're not biologists, but do you have any idea about how they used to design these before these models came up? Like what was the grueling process you would do to find — or what still is the state-of-the-art in terms of drugs which have made it to the clinic?

Matt：Josh, our CEO, likes to say that our biggest competitor is the mouse — or nature, in certain ways. So traditionally these types of drug-like molecules were either discovered in these immunization campaigns. So you literally will just infect a mouse with a disease and see what antibodies it makes to try to combat that. Other ways of doing this is super large yeast display, so on.

And so you might start with, "Hey, I really like this framework, and how am I going to figure out the right loops to design to bind this target? I'm just going to try as much as I possibly can and just literally search for a needle in a haystack." And this would be on the order of at least billions of potential molecules that you're screening against this one target. And in that case, you might end up with, you know, one, two, maybe a dozen potential hits to this target. You actually don't know much about those hits. All you know is that they kind of stick to the target. You don't know necessarily where, or if they're even necessarily drug-like.

I think one big separator of Chai — and a thing that definitely our partners like to see — is you can be really intentional with how you want to do this design process. You can say, "I want to bind this target in this particular area." You can even go back and look at the designs after — we validated that our designs. So you can go back and look and say, "Is this antibody engaging the target in the way that I expect? Do I think this will actually have the therapeutic effect that I'm going after?"

选择性与交叉反应性

主持人：One of the cool things about knowing that you have the right binding pose is that you can now also design selectivity into that. Does your platform have some technique for doing selectivity?

Matt：Yeah, there's a nice mix of ideas that went both into the modeling side and especially on the product side for dealing with selectivity and cross-reactivity. So in some cases you want your molecule to bind one target and avoid another one. So you might have healthy variants of protein and disease variant of protein — you want to avoid this disease variant. Or you might have some other similar protein that's not actually harmful in your body that you don't want to just artificially block.

So I think on the modeling side, yeah, we've come up with ways of doing that, but I think it's even more interesting on the product side. So how do you enable customers or partners to go through and actually intentionally design for these things?

Neil：Yeah. And maybe to back up and define cross-reactivity, right — like it turns out when you're developing a drug, you're not necessarily going straight to injecting that into a human. You might want to put it in monkeys first, for example. And the monkey might have a maybe mostly similar but slightly different variant of it. And so your drug not only needs to bind to the human variant, but also the monkey variant.

And so the way we've tried to model the models and the product is to let you account for those very general cases where you say, "Hey, I'm trying to design something that can bind to both of these things so that I can actually go and develop the drug." Let me actually identify maybe the region that's conserved, and then target — conserved means, you know, doesn't change much between the two — and target that exact region.

And then similar with selectivity — maybe you might want to — there's a very similar protein in the human that if you accidentally bind that one, that's very bad, and you only want to bind the target protein. And that's why a lot of drugs fail or are toxic or have really bad side effects. And so it's kind of — you're having this combinatorial problem of "bind only these things and avoid only these" — and I think what's been really exciting with some of the progress recently has been a lot of the improvements we've been able to make on the level of specificity we get with those models.

主持人：So you're not only designing the binder, but you're also making sure that it doesn't bind to another thing. There are other ways that CAR-Ts have tried to tackle this — by having some molecular or signaling pathway that says "I only fire if this one binds and this one doesn't bind." But you're saying you just design an antibody that actually only will bind to the thing that you care about.

Neil：We're getting to the point where in some cases — I mean it's nuanced — but in some cases you can actually try that.

主持人：Okay. That's amazing. So you essentially — call it counter-screen — you have, in part of your platform, you can know reliably counter-screen against a large diverse set of proteins which might be issues for downstream.

Neil：Yeah. I would say the framing is more: you can be very specific about what you care about binding versus what you care about avoiding. But I think, you know, for example, a lot of the money that we're raising now will let us train bigger models that can maybe be even more general and start to account for even more things at the same time.

Chai 模型史：从开源 AlphaFold 3 复刻到 Chai 1

主持人：Maybe we should back up. Let's talk about the history of the Chai series of models.

Matt：We started Chai around two and a half years ago. At first, couple months, we're like, "All right, we're going to work on protein design." And we were working on this. We're making some progress. We're like, "Oh, this is pretty interesting." Like, we had some ideas and models. And then kind of like — that was right when AlphaFold 3 came out. And we'd been talking about like, "Man, we really need an MSA pipeline. We need all this infrastructure."

主持人：MSA is multiple sequence alignment. We've covered this before, but what is an MSA, like in two sentences, and why is it important?

Matt：So if you want to predict the structure of a protein, it might be really useful to see a bunch of very similar protein sequences. And what those protein sequences that are really similar tell you is kind of what positions — which amino acids — end up being conserved across many variants of this protein. And if you see high levels of conservation, or high levels of mutation, correlated mutations, it typically gives you some indication that these amino acids are close in 3D space. So you kind of have this 2D view of a protein which can then be used to help you predict this 3D structure.

主持人：So you're learning from evolution what was conserved, because the things that weren't conserved probably broke the protein and something died or didn't make it.

Matt：Exactly, right. Yeah. It's pretty remarkable that this works, honestly. One of my favorite bio facts here.

So we were kind of thinking like, "Oh man, it'd be nice to have a lot of infra and whatever." So AlphaFold 3 came out, we're like, "Hey, we should open-source this model. We should just bunker down, build all the infra that we need." I think this will pay back in the long term, for sure, of just — as a forcing function to be where we are, and also just to contribute to the community as a whole.

主持人：So it's interesting that you chose — okay, this — we're actually — what we're doing here, we're building a model, but what we're really doing is learning how to build the infrastructure. Is that kind of what you're saying?

Matt：Yeah, that's exactly right. And I had built a lot of similar infrastructure in my PhD, but not at a production level for a company. So at that point I think we were five people. So there were five of us at Chai, and we're like, "All right, this is our forcing function. We have a clear goal to work towards. It's very direct. Let's get this thing going and see how fast we can do it."

主持人：You guys were, at this time, sitting in the OpenAI office. Is that —

Matt：We were sitting in the OpenAI office. Yeah. In the mission.

主持人：Right. So what's the backstory on that? It's really interesting.

Matt：Uh, two of our other co-founders, Josh and Jack, had a relationship with some of the OpenAI people, actually. OpenAI co-led our seed round. So we were kind of thinking like, "All right, should we get an office while we're only five people?" And it turned out that office was mostly vacant. So we got to sit in on the OpenAI offices for a while. Chai 1 built it, open-sourced, learned about infrastructure.

So then after that, we really set the sights down on protein design.

主持人：And worth pointing out, Chai 1 was a structure prediction model, right? So you have the sequence, what is the structure that it folds to. And then that was Chai 2.

Matt：Yeah, Chai 1. Chai 1's finished. One other crazy story there — let's see if we can actually share this — but this is a hilarious one.

So we were like, "Oh man, we really want to be the first to put this out." And we were like, "Okay, we're one week out. The model's almost done training." We're like, "Should we build a web server?" And then we're like, "Oh yeah, maybe not." And then we ended up spinning up this whole web server so people could use it — rather than just download the git repo, it's kind of annoying, especially for biologists. And we actually wanted people to use this. So let's spin up a web server, let's get the technical report out, all this stuff. So we ended up — we were up for like 48 hours straight, just getting the paper over the line, getting all the last things done on the web server. And then Josh was interviewing with Bloomberg TV or something that morning. And we've been up for 48 hours straight. So Josh runs into a room to do this interview on Bloomberg TV. And I think it was like 7:00 in the morning. Everyone's in the office. We didn't want to be seen, whatever. The interviewer is like, "Oh, interesting company. Doesn't look like there are any employees here."

But yeah, it was a really fun time. I think the early startup days were just super fun.

Chai 2：从预测到设计

Matt：So yeah, after that we kind of set our sights on design. And really what we were thinking is — we always had antibodies in mind. We thought of this as the most tractable problem. The nice thing with proteins is you have this beautiful sequence representation. And there's already a lot of research been done in how do you autoregressively generate sequences. This sequence generation problem is well studied.

So we were thinking, "What's a nice area to apply sequence generation to in the bio space?" And it's pretty natural to do linear sequences of amino acids. So we start working on design. A unique thing about Chai is — we're not — like, we're designing antibodies, we're an antibody company — we don't really pigeonhole ourselves into one therapeutic area. So we tried to really tackle this problem very generally. So we were thinking, "Can we design many proteins? Can we design antibodies? Can we scaffold regular complexes?" So really just take a holistic view on how do you design proteins in general.

And that eventually led to the Chai 2 model. So that was our first flagship design model, and that's where the Chai 2 paper and our bold target discovery project came in. So we designed antibodies to 50 targets for that paper. Got binders to about half of them, with I think on average around a 20% hit rate for binding. And then afterwards started working on Chai 3. So that's our latest series of models — but a break there.

结构预测模型的架构解剖

主持人：Before we talk about Chai 3, can you tell us — especially for listeners that may not be familiar with structure prediction models — what does the model look like? How does it work in general?

Matt：Let's take a look at Chai 1. Chai 1 has a tokenizer, a transformer, something that looks like a language model, and then something that kind of looks like an image diffusion model. And they're all just stitched together.

The tokenizer is not your kind of typical words-of-X-style tokenizer. This is like — I have a bunch of atoms in a molecule, and now I want to pull those into what I would call tokens for my LM-looking trunk. And then that conditions this kind of big diffusion model, which will then emit the image, which is some 3D structure.

主持人：So is it atoms or is it amino acids that are the input?

Matt：It's an interesting question as well. So we have all these different input tracks. So one thing about biology is the data is inherently multi-modal in a sense. You have this kind of token sequence representation. Each of these tokens has a set of atoms that kind of dangles off. And then you also have some properties of the different atoms. An atom might have a different charge, it might have a different element type. So periodic table of atoms. And then these kind of all get bunched together into tokens.

Once tokenized, you can kind of process this in very standard ways. But then ultimately you have to get back to these 3D coordinates. So in order to predict the structure — this is just some 3D object — and that object goes through, or to emit that object, you go through what looks like an image diffusion model, where you kind of go back from tokens back to the atom representation.

主持人：I see. So the tokens go in, the transformer establishes the relationship between the different tokens, and then the diffusion model turns that latent representation into a 3D structure.

Matt：That's exactly right.

主持人：Okay, great. So that's Chai 2 — that was Chai 1.

Matt：Chai 1. Chai 1 folds. Yeah. And all this bio stuff sounds kind of scary — atoms, tokens, amino acids. At the end of the day, my background personally is theoretical computer science. That's what I spent all of my earlier years doing, transitioned to this pretty late in my PhD. But I think the background that you need is really similar to the background you need for any other field of machine learning. There are all these domain-specific things that you learn about. But one analogy or anecdote I like to say is: people think you can't work on AI bio unless you're a biologist. But it's kind of like — you can't work on video models unless you're a director or something. There are all these super domain-specific things — like, "Oh yeah, to understand lighting and video, things like that" — but at the end of the day, these are just machine learning problems, and they're all solved the same way.

Chai 2 的架构跃迁与"共设计"问题

主持人：Okay. So then Chai 2 — there's a jump in capability as well as an architectural change, right?

Matt：Yeah. What we've disclosed about Chai 2 is: it is an all-atom diffusion model. So we're trying to predict atoms in 3D space still, but we're doing it in such a way that the model actually has the ability to design atoms, place them, decide which atoms actually are there. So one way to represent an amino acid — like a protein token — is by which atoms are present. So in the Chai 2 case, we were just predicting — all right, show the model, let the model just kind of pick what atoms it wants to keep — and then map that back to what amino acids there are.

主持人：What are you able to do with Chai 2 that you can't do with Chai 1? Is it just better, or are there new capabilities it brings?

Neil：It's design, right? So Chai 1 lets you say, "Hey, I know the sequence of amino acids" — right, that text string — "and I know the structure" —

主持人：That you would get from the genome, or —

Neil：Exactly. Chai 2 says, "Okay, I have a target structure that I want to design a binder to." Chai 2 will then generate candidate molecules, candidate medicines that bind to that target. And so this is kind of a design model, or design family of models. And I think that's where you really cross the threshold of usefulness.

Like Chai 1's very useful because you can at least intuit it and reason about the structure and see what you're looking at. But the ultimate goal here is to design medicines, right? And design new molecules. And I think Chai 2 really crossed the threshold of performance for doing that with antibodies a year ago.

Matt：One analogy here would be — kind of back to the image domain. Chai 1 would be like, "There is a cat in this image. Thanks, Chai 1." And Chai 2 is like — I'll show you a background, maybe I'll prompt you with some image information: "Hey, put a cat in a field." And Chai 2 will actually just give you back an image of a cat in a field. And you're like, "That's a good-looking image" — or it's not. You might have some other model which kind of ranks the image. But fundamentally it's the generative problem.

主持人：Yeah. So taking that analogy a step further, it's maybe more like you show it a background and then it generates "there is a cat," and then it generates an image of the cat at the same time. And it makes sense that there is a cat in this field and also that the cat works in the image. So it is an interesting problem because you have to generate two things at the same time — both the sequence and the structure.

Can you talk a bit about how that works? Like, how do you do that? So you co-design the sequence in a way that the structure also fits and makes sense.

Matt：One way to think about it — kind of like the classic way of doing this. Let's talk about both. In structure prediction: "All right, I know the sequence, and from that I can roughly figure out the 3D shape." And then there's kind of like the inverse folding problem, which is: "Given a 3D shape, give me back a sequence that would fold into this." And now you kind of need to do both things at the same time.

But I think similar principles apply — you can kind of have the model think a little bit about "What should this structure look like?" Then you can have some other part of the model thinking about "Now what sequence would maybe support this?" And then a nice thing with diffusion is you can do this pretty slowly and pretty iteratively. So you can give the model a lot of time to think about "All right, if I change the structure like this, how should the sequence change?" And you can kind of just play this back and forth and back and forth, and eventually it ends up kind of converging on something that's self-consistent.

主持人：It's almost like an EM algorithm.

Matt：Yeah, exactly.

如何验证一个设计？自一致性与"游戏基准"

主持人：So you have this model now, Chai 2, which is able to predict, or to sample, a structure and a sequence which generates that structure. And just because you can generate a structure doesn't necessarily mean it's necessarily accurate enough to do something. So do you have other scaffolding on top of that? Are there additional problems — like are you one-shotting these things, or are you needing to generate thousands of them and then you have a ranking or scoring? Just having a candidate is maybe let's say not enough. So what do you do once you sample a structure?

Matt：Traditionally, what's done — when co-design and protein structure design started to become a thing, we're like kind of at a loss for metrics. Like, how do you know that your protein — you design some sequence and structure — how do I know that this is legit or not? Like, I can tell you it's like anything.

主持人：It's like totally out of domain now, right? By definition.

Matt：Yeah, yeah. And as a human you can look at this thing and be like, "I don't know, it checks out." Like, even biologists are like, "I have no idea if this thing actually folds." Maybe some of it looks right. Even our biologists are surprised, by the way, with some of our designs that do end up working.

What was done at the time is we kind of came up with a bunch of metrics, and AlphaFold really is what enabled this. So you'd take the sequence that you predicted, you'd run that through some totally distinct structure prediction method. So this is completely independent of your model, and you say: if an independent model thinks that this sequence folds to a similar structure, then it has a higher likelihood of being correct than just whatever the prior likelihood would be.

So you can take your sequence now and you can measure: how consistent is this structure prediction method with the structure that you actually predicted for that sequence. You can now compare your design to an independent model structure prediction. And that became a really good way of gaining conviction that your design model was correct.

And people kind of gamed these benchmarks for a while and kept pushing, pushing, pushing. It turns out it's easy to get self-consistency, consistent design of structures, if all of your proteins look identical. There are a lot of problems that this creates, but then people started adding more and more on top of this.

主持人：Yeah, that is an interesting point that some people have acknowledged in the community. So how did you solve that? You can see that if you sort of use your oracle and also your sampler at the same time, you eventually will converge. What do you do to stop that, or to convince yourselves that you're doing something valuable?

Matt：One of the nice things about structure prediction methods is that usually you have some calibration in how confident the model is in its prediction. It turns out these models — they can give you a pretty well-calibrated confidence prediction. So rather than just say "This is what I think the structure looks like," it'll say, "This is what I think the structure looks like, and here are the parts that I'm not really certain about." And you can kind of aggregate this down to a single scalar. And typically what people do is they'll look at "Okay, not only how self-consistent am I — how much does this independent fold model even like the structure that it output?" So that was one way, early on, to just gain confidence.

And then another thing that people often do is they'll look at the diversity of their generations. Because again, you could have a model that's perfectly consistent, gives you great confidence predictions back, might be the same structure every time, same sequence every time. So you also want to see: how diverse are the solutions? How many of these new problems can I solve, in a sense?

湿实验验证与"3 分之一原子"的惊喜

主持人：If I had a whole lot of money to validate, how would you do that? Can I go and do cryo-EM or something like that and try to figure out the structure? Sort of get some ground truth on that.

Matt：It's more that the feedback loop is really slow. So you can validate a few structures like this, but it might take months. And it's just not a very scalable direction. So I think that's a problem for the field as a whole. And I think people are spending a lot of time — even at Chai, I think — thinking about how do we validate these problems at bigger scale. How do we basically increase the throughput of our validation, or increase the cycle time. Because if you're waiting months to figure out "Hey, was my model correct?" — it's just hard to iterate in a research environment that way.

Neil：The good news is that this is getting a lot better. Like, there's a whole network now of wet labs that you can work with that will run these assays, these experiments, and tell you things about "Does your protein that you came up with bind to its target well?" And so, thankfully, we're not at years — we're down to weeks. Which, you know, not as fast as LLM land, where you can just scale up an eval and throw more compute and get results back in hours, but fast enough to where you can start to recursively self-improve.

And we also spend a lot of time figuring out "What are the metrics that we can compute in silico — on the computer — that are predictive perhaps of lab success?" But, you know, to your question about cryo-EM: yeah, I mean, also you kind of have to measure the structure. And as you know, that's so expensive because you have to freeze the protein and shoot these electron beams at it and see how they bounce off.

I remember there's this really funny anecdote — we'll see if I can share it. But the paper in Chai 2 — we actually did that. We took some of the proteins that the model predicted and ran cryo-EM. And we got the results back and we're like, "Wait, the results look wrong." Because we had overlaid the prediction over the electron cloud, the point cloud — we didn't see any difference. And point being: we're getting to the point now where these structure prediction models are within a few angstroms or less of the actual atomic positions that you validate.

主持人：And in this case, it was a 0.33 angstrom error, which is 1/3 the width of an atom.

Neil：And we were like, "This can't even be right. Like, clearly they just sent us back the wrong design."

主持人：They just sent us back our design.

Neil：Yeah, exactly.

主持人：Did you check for data leakage?

Matt：Yeah, in this case there were no — so we actually chose these targets specifically to have no known antibody binder. So if we did get a hit, it was definitely the first antibody hit to this target.

主持人：Yeah. I think that's one of the things I didn't realize about biology — was just how much of it is literally feeling around in the dark. And that's not even a metaphor. You literally can't see how these things look, right? So structure models are so huge, because now you can actually predict within an atom how these things look. And that enables you to then do things like Chai 2 with the design models.

Matt：This, to me, is AI for science — is one of the cornerstone problems, right, is that you don't know — you fundamentally don't even know how to measure your problem in a lot of cases. So it's very difficult to validate.

从 Chai 2 到 Chai 3：赌模型会变好

主持人：Yeah. So you're getting these sub-angstrom predictions with Chai 2. Chai 3 — why Chai 3? What's better?

Matt：Yeah, I think with Chai 3 — so honestly, there was a Chai 2, there's a Chai 2.5, there was a Chai 2.7, there was eventually a Chai 3, and each time we saw better and better performance.

The main thing with Chai 3 is — we look at Chai 2 and we look at the targets it could solve. There was a lot of internal discussion after Chai 2 — like, "Hey, we made successful molecules, binders to half of these 50 targets. What about the other 25? What can we do to make those better?"

And then we were split. We're like, "All right, should we study these targets that we missed and figure out exactly — are there properties of these that we can look at? Or should we just bet on the models — will the models just get there if we put more time into just being bitter-lesson-pilled in that sense and just really bet on the models getting better?"

And we definitely took the latter approach. We bet on the models getting better and we just pushed as hard as we could on that front.

主持人：Scaling up the model, the data, whatever, to just build more accurate models. Is it accuracy? Is that the main thing? Is it binding affinity? What —

Matt：So I think binding affinity is a big one. You can't just bind weakly. In order for this to be a useful tool, especially for our partners, we need to start producing molecules that are at or very close to therapeutic grade — which means they have to bind really tight. They also have to be developable. They have to have all these nice therapeutic properties.

Neil：And developability — we talked about, he mentioned Chai 2.5, which we released a few months after Chai 2. There was a study we did on the developability of the molecule which — you know, for the audience, obviously the molecule has to stick, and stick tightly — but you know, there are these other properties you care about. And to use the non-biological terms: is it safe, is it stable, is it easy to manufacture, does it self-aggregate. And we've been pleasantly surprised at how much we've been able to climb and push the performance in those areas.

主持人：It seems like one of the reasons that you want to do antibodies is because of the developability.

Neil：Yeah, you get a lot for free there with that antibody framework.

主持人：Yeah, it's interesting. I mean, to me, there are many structure prediction models out there. I feel like it's these other ancillary factors actually that are going to probably be the most impactful in the usefulness of a product, let's say.

Matt：Yeah, absolutely. The nice thing about structure prediction is there is a ground truth that you can compare against. For design, you don't really have that. You're like, "Here's some new disease molecule. Give me a binder for that." And if you want to know if this thing really binds, you have to send it off to the lab and wait a while.

For structure prediction, you can be like, "All right, the model hasn't seen this sequence before. It's never seen anything close. Does it actually fold up into the correct shape, and we can just kind of hold that out of the dataset and check?" So I think I've always thought of structure prediction as this really nice speed-run kind of benchmark to validate ideas on.

产品化：从模型跨越到 CAD 套件

主持人：Right. Sorry, I didn't mean to say — I meant, you know, sort of structural models in general. Yeah. So maybe we can talk a little bit more about getting into the product side of things. Thank you for coming.

I actually — like I said, I really think this goes throughout — not only for sort of structural models like this, but also virtual cell and whatever. It's really all the other stuff around the drug development process that is going to have the biggest impact. So can you talk a little bit about that?

Neil：Yeah, I think that's actually a good thing to talk about after Chai 2, because I think Chai 2 is where it started to get really fun from a product perspective. With Chai 2, we crossed the threshold of usefulness. After we released that paper, we had a lot of pharmas and biotechs approach us and say, "Hey, this model might be able to do some stuff for us. Can we use it?" And then we're like, "Oh man, we should build a product. We should build something to let you use that model."

And that's right around when I joined. And there was sort of this mad build-out to both build the product — which we can talk about the shape of — and also go and secure the compute, actually, so we can go and serve those models to our partners.

And I think another third piece there that was really interesting is around security and IP. We want to be a very neutral platform that anyone can design medicines on, but as you guys know, pharma is this notoriously IP-sensitive industry. When I joined, a lot of people told me "This can't be done, like they're not going to put their data in a platform and have all their new medicines be generating out of it." And having a bit of a background in security helped a bit. It was like — no, actually, if you just are really aggressive about how you segment data and set up single tenancy where you're almost deploying a separate version or separate account in the product per customer, you can actually build a platform and then go and ship it to them.

And so through the summer of last year, we started doing that. And we'd been working with, or talking to, Eli Lilly, and they were one of the first partners to really work with us closely on that kind of made — that V1 of that design suite that you can use to engineer some of those molecules on.

And maybe it's worth talking a bit about that design suite. I think — we have these really, really powerful models now that can do all of these crazy things if you condition them in the right way. If you give them the right context about the structure that you're going after, or maybe the constraints around the model, like, "Hey, I want to design an antibody that hits this GPCR protein but doesn't collide with the cell membrane and also targets the specific epitope on that as well."

And we looked at, and we're like, "I guess we could put a chatbot around it — that'd be really easy to talk to." But like, really, you're trying to build something almost very visual. And you can finally build something really visual with some of these structure prediction models.

And so if you look at the Chai product, it looks a lot less like a ChatGPT and a lot more like Autodesk or SolidWorks or Figma — you know, if you've used those things, where you can kind of load up your molecule. There's this almost Photoshop-esque design suite. You have this equivalent of a paint tool to kind of paint your epitope. There's an equivalent of a content-aware fill tool to kind of get your binders generated from Chai. You of course have a lot of the scientific analysis and plotting and whatever to understand the results of the models.

But we've just been surprised at how much complexity is actually just in doing that right, so that you don't shoot yourself in the foot when then you're prompting these models to give you advice.

药化学家、AI 与哭泣的科学家

主持人：So are you sitting with people who are designing these antibodies, and then they're complaining to you or whatever? How do you convince med chemists to use your tools? Because med chemists hate AI tools — notoriously. Like, "I don't want to touch this thing, I don't understand it," and they will not touch things which they do not understand.

Neil：Well, it helps a lot to have the models working really well. So when we had the results of Chai 2 and Chai 2.5, I think that's enough of an activation energy where pharma companies and the scientists within these companies are like, "Oh, let's try it, actually. Can Chai — can you guys just try running the model against a few of these targets and let's look at the results?" And then we do that and the results are good and they're like, "Okay, let me try to get on that product and let me try to use it."

Matt：No, I think pharma is incredibly pragmatic actually. I've been very impressed with everyone that we've worked with so far. They're very — like I was saying — pragmatic about this, and they're willing to be proven wrong. And I actually don't blame them for not trusting the models. Like, I have used these models and, like — rightly so. Like, I am pretty skeptical when I see a new release. I always have been.

So you really just need to show them the proof. And they can give you this target that they are interested in, or maybe it's more of something they've worked on in the past. They probably don't want to share IP right out of the gate, but they can be like, "Hey, I've had trouble with this particular target in the past. Let's see how you guys can do on this." And then once you show them the proof, they almost overwhelmingly are willing to accept that.

Neil：I come from a cybersecurity background, or have worked on security products before, and those were dark, dark years — because you spend a lot of your time actually selling to people who are surprisingly not that technical. You think cybersecurity people are very technical — in many cases they're not. And it is this uphill enterprise slog to this very unsophisticated customer.

I think we've been just pleasantly surprised — I have — by just how much I enjoy working with our partners and our customers. These are scientists who have been spending 5, 10, 20 years of their life working on one target, often in some cases, and they've studied everything about it. They're very sophisticated, they're very smart. Getting to collaborate with them is just a gold mine. And we learn a lot about how to make the product better.

There's this anecdote — a few months ago, we were actually showing some of the results from a target with a pharma partnership, and one of the scientists in the room started tearing up and crying.

主持人：Oh, wow.

Neil：You really hit the head with that one. And she was like — we were like, "What's wrong?" She's like, "No, I've just been — I've literally spent 10 years trying to get an initial binder to this thing, and you guys were able to help me do it."

主持人：Oh, that's —

Neil：And that feels really special.

To answer your question, you know, there's of course the teams of scientists and computational biologists that we're working with within each of our partnerships. There's also the people we have within the building. So one of the things that I really appreciate about Chai is how cross-disciplinary it is. We have people who are maybe engineering experts and less bio experts, like myself. We have great AI scientists, or ML scientists. But we also have a bunch of scientists that we work with and have joined Chai to help us both test the limits of the models — see what is Chai 2 actually capable of, what targets can it do, what can't it — inform some of the research direction there.

Matt：I want to add to that — in the Chai 2 days, we kind of started with a bunch of engineers, and people had AI bio experience. We didn't have a hardcore lab scientist. And one of our first hires on that realm was Nathan Rollins, who — I think he started working in the Baker lab at 14, graduated from Harvard at 18, and got his PhD by 21 or something — in the Marks lab. And he was super skeptical about Chai at first. And then the results start to come in, he's like, "Okay, this is kind of interesting. This could work." And then once the Chai 2 results came back, he was like, "I need to bulletproof this. Like, nobody celebrate yet."

So I think it's been really nice to have that level of rigor, to just have people who have really spent the time in the lab, they've designed proteins themselves. They've literally, in the case of Andy, led several therapeutic programs, brought drugs to the clinic themselves. And we have all these people internally at Chai just using the product and really battle-testing that.

不做自己的管线：如何在没有 in-house 项目的情况下打磨产品

主持人：So if you don't have your own platforms — I mean, so you don't have your own programs, right? You're pure platform, or partnership model. How do you battle-test something if you basically don't have a use case where you have to continuously push it forward? Or if you are just pushing things forward, when you just end up with your own candidates if you're successful, and then what do you do about that?

Neil：I mean, we have benchmarks of our own internal cases. There's a set of targets that have known therapeutics against them. There's a set of targets that we pick to sort of push ourselves. And so we're constantly refining that set and adding to it. And that's what that internal science team that we have helps with — is expanding that and almost running the experiments to try to get initial binders there. We don't care about going and developing those drugs. We just do that in service of validating and making our models better.

And then of course there's a loop with our partners too.

主持人：Would you consider yourself hit discovery, or — I guess using some jargon — hit-to-lead, lead optimization? Like where do you live in this? And hit discovery might be one part of it, which you can do, but the other parts of this are, I think, oftentimes much more bespoke and kind of special. How do you balance that? It seems much more difficult to me to be general than it does to solve general lead optimization than it does to solve like a discovery.

Matt：I think ideally, we really want to be able to — rather than think of this as a bunch of stages. I think part of the reason why we think of it that way is because the initial molecules are usually not good enough to be drugs. And really — we're kind of at the inflection point now. We're really seeing this internally at Chai, where the models are getting pretty close to producing molecules that could eventually — or are very close to — drugs.

So we try not to make too much of a distinction between "Okay, hit discovery, lead optimization, all of the different parts of this kind of pre-clinical pipeline." Our north star is to just really produce drug-like molecules straight out of the models. Of course, this is going to be hard, and there are going to be tons of roadblocks, and you need to be able to actually prompt the model to do this. You need the whole RL stack to learn different properties, things along those lines. But I think it's very achievable.

Neil：And I think to add to that — this notion of target discovery and hit discovery and optimization, where each of these has a gate and takes a few months to a few years, is this very waterfall model. Where the cost of trying things and getting things early is very expensive.

But I think, to what Matt's saying — if you start to get in a regime where you can have models give you really promising candidates, you can start to make that look a lot more like a loop. It's akin to becoming more agile in software development.

Internally, we kind of have two north stars. And at first pass, they almost sound contradictory. But the north star in research is to start to de novo one-shot better and better and better medicinal candidates that are as close to being ready for the next phase as possible.

But within product, we do want to sort of expand into whatever these iterative workflows look like. Where maybe I get a binder, I get some results from the lab, I'm using that to condition my next run of the model.

And I think they sound contradictory, but they're actually not — because I think what's going to happen is the research is going to get better at identifying a de novo candidate for a specific class of drugs. Say like antagonists — blocking things — a little bit easier maybe. Okay, we can get to a state where we can one-shot pretty good drugs there. But now the next problem is agonists — how do you reliably one-shot hitting a switch on a cell? Or bispecifics or ADCs? And I think there's kind of this levels of abstraction that we're going to have to climb with the product as the models get better.

One of the things — I got very existential a few months ago because I was like, "Man, all this stuff we're building in the product to visualize molecules and do this — maybe I'm just going to have to throw it all away when Matt ships Chai 4." But I think that's kind of the reality of building products now. You're actually using them less as an end in and of itself. Maybe you'd have built software that was supposed to last 20 years. Now it's supposed to last maybe one year — but it is the bridge to deliver value and kind of enable the research that then gets you to the next thing.

And so I'd imagine we're probably going to rewrite our product at higher and higher levels of abstraction. Like maybe right now we have something a little bit more akin to Cursor, where you're inspecting the molecule in the same way you're inspecting the code, because you really need to verify the bonds that are forming and the properties of the things that you're getting. But then you get to a point where that stuff is solved enough where now the product is actually just helping you orchestrate these campaigns of hypotheses. Or maybe you have one target and you're orchestrating a bunch of different epitope choices or whatever against that. And then maybe you're going up one level of abstraction where you're now doing a whole campaign against all of the targets within a pathway.

And I think what's really exciting about that is: if you have these really good primitives for structure prediction and binding and design, and you can compose them, then you can start to just grow into the outer loop of science. And then maybe the thing runs itself and you start to really get to some really, really, really cool drugs at the end of it.

Epitope 预测：最难的问题

主持人：I actually want to push on what you just said about epitope prediction. Because I think a lot of people in the field would argue this might be the much harder problem than finding antibodies and binders. Where do you think the state-of-the-art is in general, and also with regards to Chai, in terms of epitope prediction? And is this a problem which has a reasonable solvable time horizon? And also maybe can you define epitope prediction?

Matt：I'll think of this at different levels. So the most basic level is: okay, I have some disease that I want to target, and what proteins are actually responsible there? Like, actually figuring out biologically what's going on — what should I be targeting in the first place with the drug?

I guess once you figure that out, it's kind of like a structural biology problem at that point. You're like, "All right, this set of proteins is responsible, and what's going on there? Well, this is interacting with some other protein that it shouldn't be interacting with." And conventionally, you'd just want to block that interaction, or something within an antibody. But that's kind of where these proteins interact and the type of interactions that you want to disrupt — that's typically the epitope. It's the actual site on the protein that you want to block.

This is a ridiculously hard problem. I'm with you on this. This is the harder problem. Just the amount of context that you need and the global understanding that you need in order to actually figure out what's interacting and how.

主持人：Maybe let's take a few specific cases. Let's think about — what about SARS-CoV-3 comes around, or the new flu or whatever. What would you do there? Is that something that you think you could actually reasonably tackle?

Matt：In that case, you could just run a structure prediction model, maybe, and see where the model thinks this thing will bind. If it's highly confident in that, you might say, "Okay, here is the site that we want to block."

I think in general still very hard. And even structure prediction, it's getting really good, and a lot of people think AlphaFold 2 solves structure prediction. Not really. AlphaFold 2 got — I think the multimer version of this got like 11% of antibody-antigen prediction cases correct. That means 90% of the time it's wrong.

主持人：Yeah. I mean, but AlphaFold 2 solved a certain class of monomeric proteins with MSA. Yeah. And the MSA, I think, might be the key point here. Because MSAs are sort of the magic which makes it all work. It's a template in some sense about what the structure should be. And antibodies, almost evolutionarily, can't have a template, right? Everyone has to have unique antibodies accustomed to the things that they've experienced over the course of their life.

And just to clarify, I had to understand this myself, so maybe I can help the listeners who aren't familiar. An antibody — the whole point of an antibody is it can identify new things that the body hasn't encountered before. So the design of antibodies, as opposed to other types of proteins, is that the system is designed so that you can quickly recombine different components of it in order to match proteins that are from unknown pathogens, more or less. And so this is why it's not conserved in evolution the way that other proteins are.

Matt：Yeah. So back to the epitope prediction problem. I think it's still hard. I think there are a lot of cases that are maybe tractable, but I think in general, if you want to discover this for a new target, still a really difficult problem. Maybe virtual cell would be the closest thing to state-of-the-art there, but that's still a ways out.

从科学到工程：文件格式、简洁性与"苦涩教训派"

主持人：So what is the biggest blocker from going from science to engineering?

Matt：Oh man, there's so many things. That's the thing about biology. I don't even want to talk about this — like, the amount of headaches, like —

主持人：Too late. You already know.

主持人：Opinionated?

Matt：Opinionated. Yes, like, how opinionated should we be in how we do this?
