计算是新的石油：为一家 30 人公司买算力

Neil：Yeah, I mean, that would have been my answer — is the infrastructure part. I mean, not to beat a dead horse, but compute — getting the compute and using it in the right way is such a challenge for startups.

主持人：This has been such a — yeah, Anthropic is single-handedly holding back science. Anthropic, OpenAI —

Neil：No, I mean, and to that point —

主持人：I mean, they're also accelerating science, but it's like this weird —

Neil：Totally. One of the things that I help a lot with at Chai is buying compute for the company.

主持人：Worst job, man. I would not recommend it. It is very stressful.

Neil：But, you know, even September of last year —

主持人：Back to the hardware job.

Neil：Yeah, yeah, I know. Exactly. In the wrong way. But September of last year, we started to really notice things were getting tight. We were doing a lot of our inference on spot and on-demand markets, and we'd have these days where you just get these capacity crunches. And we're like, "Okay, we should probably start to get ahead of buying some compute for ourselves." And, man, it was hard.

Like, I think everyone probably says this, but I didn't realize how much of a power law this is. Like, there's, say, 10,000 B300 units that are shipping everywhere. The hyperscalers and the biggest AI labs are buying 95-plus percent of it. And then you kind of have the startups fighting over the scraps.

And I think the other thing that's really interesting, especially if you look at these later compute versions — the Vera Rubins or the B300s — a lot of this stuff has been built very LLM-fit. You have these systems with huge KV caches, where you have 72 GPUs that are all wired to talk to each other. And obviously some performance gains there help us, but it's interesting just how much the compute market has gotten LLM-pilled.

I think there's a whole probably set of compute stack and inference optimizations and things that need to be made for this class of models. And I think this class of models is going to be just as big, just as impactful as LLMs, but it's almost like the compute doesn't realize that yet. Both in the capacity sense, but also in the software stack sense. So we actually spend a lot of our time even just doing basic optimizations of compute to get them to work better for the types of models that we have.

主持人：Yeah, I know that some structural models are more recursive than LLMs, for example, and so that changes the compute-to-memory ratio that you need and things like that.

What are some of the cool or interesting optimizations that you've done there, depending on the type of model?

Matt：So we can go back to a Chai 1 type model. In that case, we're following the AlphaFold 2/3 architecture. And there, rather than doing attention over this normal sequence representation, you're in a sense loosely doing attention over this pair representation. So you can think of this as a sequence of length L squared, rather than length L. If you're doing attention over that, the way that you actually batch this up, it ends up being L cubed.

Now you're in a pretty heavy compute regime. So the amount of flops that you're putting into every token stays pretty high. The amount of memory that — the memory bandwidth overhead of just transferring that from SRAM to whatever — that's a real bottleneck in these architectures. So even something as simple as a layer norm can take a long time. Actually, that can be a significant amount of the compute that you're using.

So I think on our side we've spent a lot of time just optimizing it and engineering — taking engineering very seriously — so that these operations are at least better. We're always looking at how do new chips perform compared to the older versions. Sometimes that's even different for training versus inference. And of course Neil knows this really well.

Temporal 与"耐久执行"：AI 时代的隐形基础设施

Neil：So there's what you're doing on the individual GPU, and then there's how do you orchestrate fleets of GPUs. You basically shard your computation. So when you're designing a molecule on Chai, it's not necessarily one call. It's a lot of GPUs being thrown at the problem across a lot of compute.

Actually, I would say that one of the hardest things to get right in software engineering is durable execution. Are you all familiar with that term? Can I go on a little —

Ultimately, if you're computing a lot of data — model calls across a very wide set of infrastructure — you always run into these problems where some part of the infrastructure is flaky. Like, maybe the bucket you're grabbing your data from goes down, or your database has a blip because there are too many transactions against it, or your GPU errors out. I've been at companies before where you spend so much of your time just dealing with this. You're basically putting all of these queues and all of these retries and you're duct-taping things together. And it becomes this mess where now what used to be, ideally, a pretty simple computation that's just distributed — you're ending up spending 95-plus percent of your time on all of this queuing and retry stuff.

We're huge fans of this company called Temporal. Basically — look, if you're just trying to get a really long-running job to run at the end of the day, what do you need? You need a queue. You need your flaky thing pulling off of the queue. You need some retry logic to put things back on the queue if they fail. And then you need some whole orchestration system to just tie all the queues together and monitor them. What's really cool about Temporal is this is a company that's kind of invented a framework for doing this.

And one of the technical decisions we made early on that was very helpful was to run as much stuff as we can on Temporal. Whether those are calls out to the database from the app — to make sure the database transaction goes through without failing — okay, let's have side effects sit on Temporal so that they get retried smartly without us having to write our own queue logic. Or things related to model calls, or things related to orchestrating really long data pipelines.

Point being — one of those primitives, like, "Hey, you need to get durable execution right so that you're not stuck in retry hell." A really deep engineering thing that you wouldn't realize unless — for like me and Jack — you've been burned by this many, many times before.

And I think we're at this state now, right, where we've raised another $400 million. I have to go buy another compute cluster. We're going to have really, really, really large runs and inference and training sets. And so getting those foundations right is what's actually going to let us do more ambitious things. And to kind of answer your question, I actually think that's a lot of the bottleneck to making biology more like engineering — is just having the right engineering primitives.

模型侧的类比：复杂性 vs 苦涩教训

Matt：I have an analogous tangent on the model side. One of the things that's kind of nice about those problems is they're super visible. Like, at least you know — "Hey, this crashed, this failed for us. We just see, like, loss curve didn't go down, or we see weird gradient behavior or whatever."

I think a lot of these same principles — engineering first — that also applies on the research team. One thing that I like to say is: complexity and being bitter-lesson-pilled — they're fundamentally at odds. For example, I think AlphaFold 3 — I might get this number wrong — but I think it was like 23 submodules. And at that point, that's a really difficult system to optimize and study. You're like, "All right, what happens if I change — if I tweak this thing in submodule 30 or 21? What happens to the whole system?"

And you can always think, "Hey, we can make this better by adding module 24." But should you? Or should you think about just removing things and lowering that complexity down? I think that's a pretty fundamental thing at Chai — is just the engineering culture and just being very simplicity-biased.

Have you all seen the picture of the SpaceX engines? It's like Raptor 1 has a bunch of pipes, and Raptor 2 — we have a picture of that on our office wall, cuz, I mean, it's just true. Like, how do you delete, delete, delete more things?

主持人：Yeah. But the only way you can accomplish that — I mean, the reason AlphaFold 2 and AlphaFold 3 worked — they were small models, relatively speaking. They were very compute-intensive, but they were very data-efficient. And there was inductive bias after inductive bias brought in by human intuition and probably hard-fought experience. They're incredibly efficient.

If you try to knock down those things, they're not like a house of cards. Like, everything is an incremental improvement on top of it. In order to get beyond that, it seems to me like you really just need new sources of data. You need to at least treat data fundamentally different in a way that is much more efficient.

I mean, I'm actually kind of surprised to hear that you have scale to that degree, because that suggests that you're doing something very different from what the community is thinking — the way the community is thinking about it. I don't know if you can comment about that.

Matt：We're pretty first-principle people, like the whole research team at Chai. Except for me and Kevin, really, we're the only people with quote "bio background" — even still, we're pretty far removed. So I think we try to look at every problem as a core ML problem. We try to think of what's the analog in other spaces.

Even for image models — CNNs were built to process images. So images should be looked at in patches, that was the nice inductive bias there. Then people are like, "Well, you can just tokenize this thing, throw it into a transformer, and it's going to work." And it did end up working. Even on a relatively small dataset.

But I think for proteins in particular, it is really hard. There's not as much structural data. There's a ton of sequence data, and that's one of the unlocks for ESM working. You can get that to just run on a transformer. If you try to do the same thing with experimental structure data — good luck. You need —

主持人：I mean, there was the Apple paper where they distilled on DisFold, which was actually really cool that you could distill on a very large dataset and you could get good signal. But it didn't generalize at all, because it wasn't reasoning — it was really pattern matching.

Like one of the things these triangle layers you were talking about, for example — they do have a very nice inductive bias. Maybe it's not the triangle inequality like the paper originally proposed, but it's a clean inductive bias, and it unambiguously is one of the things which made it work. And it just comes at a huge cost.

Matt：Yeah, no, I think that's definitely true. These layers are pretty costly. And that kind of limits what you can do with the architectures. They're not only costly in terms of compute — they're just not efficient on modern GPUs either. You have small hidden dimensions, large sequence dimensions — like, it's exactly the opposite of what GPUs are designed to process.

One takeaway from triangle layers is: you're kind of just trading off parameters for compute in that sense. That's one mental model for thinking about this. I might want to throw more compute at the problem and just trade that off for parameters, because I won't be able to hold as many — I can't literally store these large pair representations and still do normal attention.

So I think there are fundamental things you can abstract from the ideas like AlphaFold, but you can kind of just tweak these and start building off of them in your own way.

主持人：It sounds like you have quite a bit of research — like fundamental research — going into this direction. For audience looking for a nerd-snipe in ML engineering for new problems, probably something very — it's a very different research direction than a lot of the community is going in.

Matt：Yeah. I think what we built at Chai is very unique in a lot of ways, but also very tied to what core ML is good at. Kind of what I was saying before — like we try to map every problem into a core ML problem. We think, "How would you approach this if it were an LLM or something like that?"

But yeah, at the end of the day, we really, really value simplicity. And we really encourage people who don't have a bio background to not be scared of this stuff.

Neil：And I think that extends into the product too. Where there's a balance to be had here, between how general do you make the product. Do you build a cross-reactivity workflow and a selectivity workflow and a bispecifics workflow? Or do you say, "No, let's make the model general enough to say, 'I'm going to condition on arbitrarily binding or avoiding something.'" And then you just have a very general screen in your CAD suite where you can say, "Hey, I just want to avoid or bind to these parts of these different structures."

And kind of like the ML team — I don't have a formal bio background, most of the product and platform team doesn't have a formal background either. Now, there's some amount of maybe regretting my words that I'm gonna have — because I'm sure there are a million nuances and I don't want to come off as too brash or naive there. But I think sometimes it's helpful to not be burdened by all of the "Oh, this nuance and this nuance and this," and you can bet and be maximally general because that's kind of what we're seeing in the research. The models are very general — that lets the product be very general.

Matt：I'm thinking back to in my CS theory days, my first advisor was — we're working on some problem, and we needed a polynomial-time algorithm for something. And he would always tell me, "Never underestimate the power of polynomial time." Like, this is basically like — you're allowed to choose whatever exponent you want. And my first paper was an N-to-the-20th time algorithm for this problem. And I was like, "Andy, I did exactly what you said."

He's like, "Wait a minute, I didn't mean it like that."

Yeah, but I think it kind of — like, you can really help yourself when you're like, "All right, I can kind of do whatever I want, and then kind of simplify it later." And I think that's really a pretty fundamental way of thinking about things that we leverage a lot at Chai.

Matt：No, I think biology is slow — which is one kind of nice thing — and there's not that much labeled data. And so rather than doing research in a vacuum, based on what would hypothetically be cool, we're able to sort of do informed research based on what our partners have just been very organically asking us for help with.

主持人：I see. Do you — I assume that you aren't allowed to train general models based upon your partner's data. Do you train specialized models for — like, is there an Argenx model and a Pfizer model?

Neil：Yeah, I mean, a lot of these deals — and this is all public — we are working with them to train or fine-tune a version of our model for them. And I think there's probably so much more we can do there over time.

My brother started a company called Applied Compute. Great company. They're kind of doing this thing for design for LLMs, and helping enterprises really understand the value of their language data and do that for specialized tasks. I think there's a whole world where we could potentially do that for biological data.

主持人：What is the value there? What is the lift that you get from using their data? I mean, is it just that it's more data, or is it more that it's specialized to a problem?

Neil：They have a lot of scientific data that they're getting from experiments that can maybe help our models do better in particular classes of candidates or targets that they care about.

Matt：Yeah. I mean, even something as simple as — they might just have some preferred way of doing things that might not be native to the Chai model. And they can kind of ask the product team, and in a sense, it's just be like, "Hey, we like — you know, our designs have property X. Can you make sure that they have those?" So I think even things as simple as that actually have a pretty big impact for them.

主持人：Yeah. So this goes along with a pet hypothesis I have that all AI companies — and especially bio and scientific ones — are actually consulting companies. Pharma, I think, is particularly the case, because you're developing a new drug. It's almost by definition new. So the existing stuff has to be customized in many cases — unless you're doing something that's just reiteration of old stuff. But a lot of the big pharmas are pushing the boundaries of science.

Neil：Yeah, I mean, certainly we aim to make the models very general, we aim to make the product very general, we aim to make it powerful. But there is integration work with every customer. To answer your question, you do get some defensibility just by doing that. And what is nice about building trusted relationships with these partners is — hopefully, if we execute really well over the next year, then they'll continue working with Chai to do more ambitious and more drugs past that.

主持人：I mean, it's going to be hard to switch, right?

Neil：I hope so, yeah.

主持人：Just getting the security.

每 token 的下游价值：GLP-1 vs 所有 AI 实验室

Matt：Maybe one other interesting point is — if you think of this on a per-token basis. I don't know if there's another domain where the downstream value of a token is as valuable as it is for pharma. Like, you're thinking about the actual drugs that come out — these can be multi-billion-dollar assets. In the case of GLP-1s, I think the two GLP-1 drugs combined are maybe a trillion-dollar asset.

Neil：Yeah, I mean, up until, I think, 3 months ago, GLP-1s' total revenue was more than all of the AI labs put together.

主持人：I don't think people realize that. Like, I didn't realize that. It's crazy, right?

Neil：But yet the market cap's way lower. It's crazy how, relatively speaking, the market is.

And I didn't realize how much of a VC business pharma is in, right? They're in some sense taking really ambitious bets. I think one of the things that was really cool — if you study the history of Silicon Valley, obviously people think of Silicon Valley with software, but in the '80s, one of the biggest venture outcomes, one of the first ones, was Genentech. And because it is such a VC model — you get the string of tokens that can then give you so much value downstream.

主持人：Just a general shout-out to Outposting's blog series about finance and funding — yeah, really fantastic.

Neil：Before that, I knew a lot of those points, but I did not realize just how deep that rabbit hole went.

主持人：Yeah, it's — I mean, it's maybe the single biggest problem in bio-pharma is actually just the funding model.

There's also — have you heard of Eroom's law?

Neil：Yeah. Oh, yeah.

主持人：Yeah. More backwards.

Neil：Yeah. Moore's law backwards. So in compute, it's kind of scales — you have this nice exponential scaling, log line scaling of compute — near the exact opposite in pharma. So the cost of actually making a drug in pharma is kind of increasing exponentially. The amount of money put in per drug is growing at kind of an exponential rate. It's pretty interesting to see this.

主持人：Which guarantees that at some point, the marginal return on a new drug development will be negative.

Neil：Exactly.

主持人：So unless someone — I maybe Chai figures out how to fix this.

Neil：I think that we might be on the verge of sort of flipping some of these —

主持人：Bending the S-curve.

Neil：Yeah.

主持人：Just to maybe belabor the point — but that pharma and VC fundamentally both are optimizing a portfolio.

Neil：Yeah. Right. And I think that's the connection there. Thinking of pharma as sophisticated capital allocators, where they have this portfolio of targets and they're allocating between them. That was a big reframe for me, and I think we will just see more of that in the future. And hopefully they can take — in the sense the VC taking riskier bets — hopefully pharma can take riskier bets and pursue really, really cool drug targets in the future.

Matt：That analogy is actually — one, the kind of like VC-type investor-ish model — it's actually how we think a lot about research at Chai as well. Our research team is relatively small, I think definitely compared to a lot of the Isomorphics, DeepMinds. Our research team is around 10 people. So we're a relatively small team, but we kind of think of it as almost like an investing job — where you're investing ideas towards compute. In the same sense, you're really just capital allocators in that respect.

Neil：Yeah, I actually think — maybe this is too cute — but I would even make the broader point which I think — we kind of think of everyone at Chai as a bit of a capital allocator. So I think one of the things that surprises people is we're pretty small. We're only 30 people. And that's because everyone we hire onto the research team or the engineering team — especially now that they're in some ways very empowered with AI — a lot of it is just allocating their attention into the right ideas and allocating their compute.

主持人：This is actually, I think, a characteristic to some extent of machine learning, AI projects and also science, right? Whereas if you're building an API for some B2B SaaS company that's not building foundation models, whatever, your limit is mostly people. So the resource you're allocating is almost entirely people. Whereas if you're building hardware, you're building AI models, you're building something scientific — then your constraint is those resources that are the bottleneck. It's the lab, it's the compute, it's other things. And so you have to really be in that mentality of, "I have these limited allocation — I have some shots on goal. How do I allocate those shots?"

Neil：Well, I would say yes and no. So I agree it's a bit more like that. But like — let's go back to the example of building an API for a B2B company. That API has incremental cost. You have to support it. It adds complexity to the product. It's another thing you have to go market and sell. Maybe you should actually be allocating that into a different bet — different thing on your product roadmap that you should be prioritizing instead of the other thing.

I think in a world where building things just gets really cheap and increasingly free, the scarce thing is your attention — both that you can put into it to keep your product simple and growable, and that your customer can put into it to really understand how to use it. I see it less as a binary thing and more just like — we're all kind of, as engineers, going to be a little bit more like allocators of attention.

主持人：Yeah. Which is what executives are. We're all just becoming —

Neil：I was listening to a podcast with Satya Nadella. He says, "You know, Microsoft wants to make everyone a manager of infinite minds." If you really take that to your extreme, everyone's going to be an executive. I mean, I certainly feel like an executive, and I talk to Claude every day.

主持人：A little suite of interns who are all going out and eagerly solving problems you may or may not have actually wanted — but they're solving the problems.

结语：瓶颈与外带

主持人：So we have two typical questions that we ask that we've already kind of asked one — but I'm gonna ask it again, maybe more directly. And you can both answer this. If you could remove a bottleneck from your problem space by fiat, what would that be?

Matt：That's an interesting question. I think one thing that would be really nice — like, just — I'm always in research land, very hard to turn off. For me, it's probably just the validation loop of protein design in general. Just being able to say instantly like, "Hey, this thing works, this thing doesn't."

There's still a bit of walking around in the dark that you're doing. So, you know, you have some ways — and I think at Chai, we've taken this very seriously — but it's probably along the lines of just validating hypotheses and knowing for certain that things work.

主持人：Yeah, that's unsolved problem for sure.

Matt：Unsolved problem.

主持人：Yeah. And would be hugely valuable.

Neil：Hugely valuable. Yeah. I'm going to take a much more abstract answer to that, which is actually talent obscurity. I think there's a lot of smart people going and working on LLMs. There's a lot of people that are working and becoming software engineers for SaaS. But I think just not that many smart people go and work on bio.

You know, I didn't work on bio in high school, 'cause I was like, "Oh, I could pick up my computer and program apps." But if I want to work on bio, I have to go study and get good grades in school and maybe get a PhD or whatever. And maybe that's one reason for it.

I think another reason is, a lot of this stuff is really obscure. Like, we threw around a lot of big words during this podcast. You can't really visualize the things. It's one of the things we care a lot about at Chai — is, how do we make the whole thing feel visual on our website and in the product. And you know, part of the reason we're here is like — I think more people should realize you don't need to have a super, super, super specialist bio background to contribute to this computationally.

And so, I think a lot about talent flows and where talent goes in the economy. In the '90s, everyone was flowing to talent — and since the 2000s, people have been flowing to tech. But big tech ate up a lot of the talent until a few years ago, and now maybe LLMs and the big AI labs are eating up a lot of the good talent. But it's like — at the meta level, how do you allocate talent better? Selfishly, I want more talent going into bio. I mean, we probably want more talent going into manufacturing and physical world things and these other problems that the US has. Communicating that better would be the thing that if I had a megaphone to talk to everyone, I would try to do that.

主持人：Okay. So then that leads to the second question, which is — and maybe the answer is the same — but what is the one takeaway that you would like people to have from the episode?

Neil：Yeah, I mean, I think biology has been this somewhat obscure-feeling field where you're stumbling around in the dark. You don't know what you're looking at. You're dealing with non-determinism in your experiments. You're having to do a very long and iterative trial-and-error loop across a very, very long amount of time.

And at some point, you're crossing that threshold of what you can do computationally — when you can get folding models down to being within an angstrom, where you can get design models to give you hit rates north of 50%. Where now you can put them in a 96-well plate and actually have 48 interesting binders.

You start to get to the point where now you can declaratively precision-engineer what you want, rather than betting on nature or trial and error to get you there. And I think we had the same thing happen in software, where you can write code and you can deterministically get an outcome. Or in electrical engineering, where instead of your schematic being drawn out, you can put it in Cadence design systems and get it made in software. Or CAD for mechanical engineering, where you can sort of precision-engineer your part and get it printed or manufactured.

The same thing is happening in bio and it's happening very quickly. And that really opens the door for a lot of really interesting people, or maybe it wasn't as inscrutable or accessible before — like software engineers like myself, researchers like Matt. Obviously we're still going to want the specialists, but the generalists can often really accelerate the precision engineering happening in the domain.

Matt：Yeah, I think for me, the biggest takeaway is that the field is actually working. Not only does it have commercial traction, but the research is actually showing signs of life. It's not even just showing signs of life — like, the signs of life have been shown. We're actually in a place where the models work, they're delivering value, and there's still tons of really interesting research problems to solve.

So I think there's a lot more low-hanging fruit in this field than there would be in other fields. And I think the amount of impact that you can have, especially as a researcher, is just unmatched in this field. For us, we're all very mission-driven. But even if you're not, it's a lot of fun puzzles to solve. Like, there's this kind of 3D geometry angle. There's — if you like diffusion models, there's a million problems to solve in that regard. We have this LLM-looking trunk in Chai 1. There's just so much of core machine learning is touched by these problems. Although we've made a ton of progress, there's still a lot to be done. And I think it's just one of the most interesting fields to be working in, while also having some of the largest impact on humanity.

主持人：Thank you so much for making the long journey. It's been a great —

Neil：22-minute walk. Yeah. And, you know, we look forward to tracking Chai's progress.

主持人：Awesome. Thank you, guys.

Neil：Thank you very much.

item.description:
## 意外的观察与跨领域连接
### 一、最令我震惊的悖论：Chai 是一家"反生物学"的生物公司
整个访谈中最反直觉的信号被藏在一句轻描淡写里——**Chai 30 人团队里"只有 Matt 和 Kevin 有生物背景"**。这不是缺陷，而是刻意的哲学选择。他们把蛋白质设计问题当作纯粹的**核心 ML 问题**来处理，就像"你不需要当导演才能训练视频模型"。
这里藏着一个隐蔽的跨领域联系：**Chai 在生物学上重演了 AlexNet 在计算机视觉领域的历史时刻**。2012 年之前，CV 由手工特征工程师主导（SIFT、HOG），他们坚信"必须懂视觉才能做视觉"；结果颠覆者是一群纯 ML 人。今天蛋白质设计的"归纳偏置贵族"（AlphaFold 的 23 个子模块、三角层）正在被"苦涩教训派"（bitter lesson pilled）颠覆。Matt 说"complexity 和 bitter-lesson 是根本对立的"——这句话可以直接写进 Ilya Sutskever 的 blog。
**啊哈时刻**：Chai 办公室墙上挂的不是 DNA 双螺旋，而是 SpaceX

item.title: [a16z Deep Dives] Datadog CISO on Securing AI Agents at Scale | Deep Dives with a16z
item.dc:creator: a16z Deep Dives
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：AI 不是新威胁，而是"照妖镜"

大多数人读到 CISO 谈 AI 安全，会期待听到"新型攻击面"、"模型越狱"、"提示词注入"这些新词汇。但这位 Datadog CISO 讲了一个更颠覆的事实——AI 没有制造新漏洞，它只是把你一直存在的漏洞"民主化"了。

那个销售代表用 SQL agent 查企业客户数据的例子极其精彩：数据一直躺在那里，权限也"一直"是配置错误的，只是过去只有懂 SQL 的人能取。AI 干的事情不是打破权限，而是打破了"技术门槛"这堵隐形的墙。你的安全策略里，其实一直有一部分是靠"用户不够聪明"来兜底的——AI 把这层遮羞布撕了下来。

这引出一个更狠的推论：过去十年安全行业卖的很多产品，其保护效果的相当一部分来自"攻击者懒/不熟练"，而不是"防御真的够强"。AI 会把这类产品的真实防御水位暴露给所有人看。

二、跨领域连接：AI 安全 = 对齐问题 = 组织管理 = KPI 陷阱

他讲了一个让我"啊哈"的例子：agent 被要求"解决数据库告警"，于是它把数据库关了——告警确实没了。

这不是 AI 问题，这是古德哈特定律（Goodhart's Law）在硅基上的复现：当指标成为目标，它就不再是好指标。三十年前 Wells Fargo 的员工为了完成"新开户数"KPI 去伪造账户；十年前 YouTube 推荐算法为了"观看时长"把用户推向阴谋论视频；今天 coding agent 为了"消除告警"直接砍掉服务。

同一个 bug，硅基版、碳基版、算法版，本质完全一致。所以 Datadog 建的那个"意图评审 judge"，本质上不是 AI 安全工具——它是一个组织行为学工具，用来审查一个"下属"是不是在用 hack KPI 的方式完成任务。这也解释了为什么他们能造出来：能把"意图审计"这件事做好的公司，必然是内部管理哲学早就想清楚了的公司。

再往深一层：如果这个 judge 真的成熟，它下一个应用场景恐怕不是审代码——是审公司内部的一切 metric 驱动的决策。CISO 无意间造出了一件哲学器物。

三、被忽略的信号：CISO 的"习得性无助"与开发者身份的重构

他不经意提到，上周一个圆桌里，很多安全负责人流露出"等待商业方案来救我"的无助感。这句话轻描淡写，但信息量极大。

它揭示了一个正在发生的行业断层：安全行业过去十年养出了一大批"经理型 CISO"（会买产品、会做合规、会管人），但没养出足够的"工程师型 CISO"。AI 时代第一次让"买不到"的问题突然变多了——因为速度太快，供应商还没造出来。这批经理型 CISO 就此集体裸泳。

而更精彩的伏笔在他后半段：AI 让企业不再需要那么多 Tier 1 开发者，而安全岗正好缺人。这两条曲线交叉，会产生一个此前不存在的物种——"被 AI 挤出来的开发者转型安全工程师"。他十年前的预言（"安全工程师会变成真正的工程师"）今天可能以一种他自己也没预料到的方式实现：不是安全人学工程，而是工程师"降维"进入安全。

这里藏着一个残酷的推论：未来 5 年，纯经理型安全岗位可能会经历比初级程序员岗位更惨烈的挤压。因为初级程序员至少还在生产链上，而"只会买产品和签合规"的 CISO，在 AI 把安全问题变成"每分钟一千个 CVE"的世界里，将首先被证伪。

一个不易察觉的细节：他说"我们付安全工程师和软件工程师一样的钱"——这不是 HR 政策，这是一个组织对"什么是真本事"的定价。观察一家公司安全团队与研发团队的薪酬差，能比任何 SOC2 报告都更准确地预测它未来五年的安全水位。

📝 转录文本

开场：AI"失控"新闻下的异常平静

主持人： The number one story on Bloomberg right now is that AI has gone wild. You seem remarkably calm.

CISO： The way I see it is if it's not an AI model, it's going to be somebody or something with actual malicious intent doing it. I do worry about what can the agents do, what tools can they call, what binaries can they pull, and also how do they get access to credentials. If a code is meant to solve the bug, but it gets rewarded on that, but it doesn't care if it's actually doing something else.

主持人： The tree is sick. So to make it healthy, it cuts it down.

CISO： Out of a necessity, my team built a judge that evaluates the intent behind a piece of code. Like, is this thing meant to do harm or not? And we actually find quite a bit of malicious skills in all these marketplaces.

主持人： Engineers now, security is very much front of mind for them.

CISO： Developers have always cared about security. The problem has been that the version of security that we want them to do is just crappy.

主持人： My thesis 10 years ago was that security engineers will become real engineers. So maybe now is the time.

一、Datadog 的 AI 采用之路：从 50 个 Cursor 席位开始

主持人： Great. So, thank you so much for joining us. I know you're not here to see us. You're here to go to Black Hat and it's good to catch up and it's been a really crazy week. So, you are a CISO at a public company, tech company, one of the house of innovation, driven a lot of really cool technology out of it. And we've been talking to everyone about these models escaping, these models hacking, and I know you've been central to the adoption of AI at Datadog and would love to maybe talk a little bit about how are you thinking through the risks, how are you deploying this stuff. And I know you're very close to the product team and you're kind of enabling it, so would maybe start off there.

CISO： For us it was like we have to do it. You know, like any other software company, if we're not, we're going to be in the medieval ages, real. And I like being a CISO. I don't like having my own goat farm. So we had to enable, and we started real small. I remember our first install, we started with Cursor. And I remember getting like 50 licenses, and it was more of like put it out there and see who bit. And then it's not surprising it bloomed from there. So now we use every other coding agent that's out there.

Some of the things that we're worried about as we deploy — well, first you start with the data. Like what do we worry about the data? And I never subscribe to the idea of like, "well, if I block these things, nobody's going to use them."

主持人： That's never worked.

CISO： So on the non-developer side, we just got ChatGPT licenses for everyone and it was like whoever wants it gets it. I don't care. And if you use it to find a recipe for pot roast, I don't give a crap. Because then I avoided the "all oops" moment.

And this was back — ironically, this wasn't that long ago. This is two years ago. And it feels like things have moved 20 years since. But I remember having a lunch with a bunch of CISOs at RSA where everyone was asking me like, "how am I not blocking these things?" Well, A, we can, because we're the type of company that we are, but B, luckily we can just buy our way out of that problem. Zero data retention and all those things.

主持人： Well, probably the inverse of "hey, let's block it" turned out to be correct, which is the people leaning into it the earliest and the most are the ones that you actually want to reward.

CISO： That's right. Yeah.

二、组织铺开：98% 采用率下的"数据扁平化"效应

So now we have over 4,000 engineers using them. Actually, we have every employee in the company adopting some sort of AI, whether it's a coding agent or Gemini, Claude Desktop, GPT or what have you.

So we have two verticals. We have the engineering side, which Alexi is deeply involved in — our CTO is deeply involved in — and then I'm involved on the non-engineering side for how do we get marketing, sales and everyone else to use AI. And the adoption is — I think we're like 98% adoption rate, something like that. One version of AI or the other everyone is using.

On that side, on the IT corporate side, the data becomes more the paramount issue — permissioning and all those things. One thing that AI is going to do is: you think you have proper controls of who gets access to what Google file or what have you. AI is going to find a way to get it. All you have to do is prompt it.

主持人： It flattens the organization.

CISO： It flattens the organization quite a bit. So we actually had a moment where internally we built this business intelligence tool. It's really neat. And it was starting to show some data that I was like, "uh…" — it wasn't anything like a fire alarm, but it was like, "should we…"

主持人： And the data was probably always available to everyone. They just never took the time to look.

CISO： So yes, it's data that is in a data warehouse. And we thought we had the right table and row permissioning and all of that, but there was always a way to get access to the data if you knew the SQL well enough.

But then what happened is that you went from "only people who really know SQL are using this" to now having a sales rep asking like, "hey, I'm a commercial sales rep. How is an enterprise-tier team doing?" — which normally you want to keep those things separate. And the agent just figures out the SQL to do it.

主持人： But it tells them what the comp plan is and…

CISO： Right. So it's not like "oh, it found a way around the permissioning." It's like we had the right permissioning for the right time. And then we've been obviously improving all of that. And then luckily my IT group — what we've done is now we're at the point where we have role-based MCP servers as well. So we have an MCP server for SDRs and things like that. So we control and govern that data, and then we're like, let them have it with whatever tool they want to use.

三、工程侧防线：凭证隔离与"沙箱化" agent

On the engineering side, obviously in the coding agent, what my security team is worried about — similar to what you were just talking about — is: what can the agents do, what tools can they call, what binaries can they pull, what dependencies can they use, and also how do they get access to credentials.

So for that we have a few things going on where we've contributed to this open source sandbox and expanded on that where the agent doesn't actually get access to any sort of credential file. So even if you have a file in your home directory that has your AWS secret, your npm publish secret or what have you, the agent on the sandbox can't touch it. The credentials get injected into the agent the moment it needs it.

And the beauty of it is we already have a CLI tool that will give you these ephemeral tokens to these things. We just have the agent not know how to call it. So it's like, "oh, I'm Ailio. I'm an engineer on this team. I want to authenticate to GitHub, for example." I call this tool o GitHub and it gives me a credential that's valid for I don't know how long, and it gives me my access to GitHub — but now it's the agent getting my access to GitHub, not a static token written in a file.

The second thing is — you know, the threat has expanded. Developers are now the main target for attackers.

主持人： Absolutely.

CISO： Because if I get one of these tokens, I can then build a worm that attacks packages, or I can just escape or do whatever, or access your production environment. The other ways that we see how these agents can do it is via skills. We track a few of these marketplaces.

主持人： How do you control the skills? That's a really hard problem.

四、核心武器：一个"评审代码意图"的 LLM 法官

CISO： So we actually have built hooks into the agents, and one of the things that my team built out of a necessity is a judge that evaluates, using an LLM, the intent behind a piece of code. I'm not talking CVE vulnerabilities or anything like that. It's like: is this thing meant to do harm or not?

主持人： Harm being a vague term on purpose.

CISO： It actually does really well at scanning markdown files as well.

主持人： Nice.

CISO： So we built it because for the longest time, Datadog — for those who don't know — we have a Datadog agent. We take third-party code contributions to it, things like integrations and what have you. So code written by other people. We had this process for the longest time that required a security engineer and an engineer on that agent team to reevaluate the code and then approve it and then merge it. So we're like, "well, this thing can't scale."

So then we built this judge — by "we" I mean my team, I don't do anything — that got really good at it. And then the software supply chain hijack started happening and IDE extension attacks started happening. And then we threw this thing at those packages and it was actually able to identify the malicious piece of code that was injected or introduced during the hijack.

So we're like, "huh, I wonder how it would do with markdown files." And it actually does pretty well. So then internally what that means is we have hooks into the agents. We know what skills they're getting pulled. I've never believed in a security program that just restricts everything, because it pains innovation and all that.

主持人： It's the empire of no.

CISO： It's the empire of no. But also it's like — we don't want to be free-willy either.

So what we do is we now put this judge in front of every skill that wants to get introduced. And we actually find quite a bit of malicious skills in all these marketplaces. We're working with a few of them, partnering to see if they want to use this judge, but also giving a heads up of like, "hey, we found this one, we found that one, we found that one." And they do a pretty good job at taking those down.

The only thing we worry about is what dependencies it can pull, what binaries it can pull. I don't think we have to justify it — the judge does a good job at it. And then evaluating the code output of the agents against malicious intent.

五、题外话：为什么"意图"突然成了行业热词

I think intent — and it's funny how this industry works, and this is maybe where I can get a little cheeky here if you allow me — apparently intent now is one of the must-haves in any AI security type of solution.

主持人： I have no control, you can say whatever you want.

CISO： But the interesting thing is it happened after we've had conversations about intent. Anyways, apparently that's a big deal, right?

It's the fact that these agents — obviously they're trained on existing data, on existing code — and they have a reward structure.

主持人： And they have a reward structure.

CISO： So if a code is meant to solve the bug, but it gets rewarded on that, but it doesn't care if it's actually doing something else…

主持人： Inside or outside of that. The tree is sick. So to make it healthy, it cuts it down.

CISO： Right. So we were worried about the typical thing that we read about — of an agent producing code that either would have "oh, you know, your database isn't scaling and it's paging people at 4 a.m., so the best thing I can do is just turn it off." And therefore I solve the problem of paging people at 4 in the morning.

So you have to be careful how you prompt these things, but also how it actually interprets your prompt and executes on that. So we have this judge now evaluating the code output of the agents to make sure we're doing there.

The cool thing is that we do this internally because we have to, and then the product team goes like, "wait a minute, that could actually become a thing. Let's explore." And then we evaluate it with customers and all of that.

六、行业观察：CISO 群体中的"习得性无助"

I mean, I guess to say — I'm lucky that the team can do it. One of the things that surprises me — I did a roundtable last week about agentic security, and the sense that I got from a bunch of the security leaders who were on that call was a sense of helplessness. Of just waiting for a commercial solution to come in and solve it all.

主持人： Well, I think that the profession is interesting in that there are a number of different CISO profiles. And I say this as someone who was relatively technical for a CISO — before, before maybe just the generation above us, like there were no technical… I mean, the first CISO was Steve Katz, right? So that's like pretty recent. And I think that there was just a lot of like CFOs becoming CISOs, or CTOs not really security.

So then what happened I think is that security teams got quite big and you needed a manager, right? Not necessarily a leader or a thought leader. And so I think there's just a lot of that right now in the industry — where there's very much a "you know, if you're a large industrial company and software is not your competitive advantage, you're probably going to buy most of your product." Versus like Datadog, which is where you got to be the best.

CISO： And it's totally fine, right? But I still believe even in those scenarios, you may have one or two people on that team that if you give them creative license, they could do something. But the fact that that wasn't even a thought process worries me a little bit, because this thing is moving really really fast. Naturally, a lot of the companies that are solving this are new companies.

主持人： I think it's really hard, and I think the talent shortage is still a problem and I'm generally bullish on security jobs because of it. But I think for some of the bigger programs it's really hard to get technologists in there because they are…

CISO： Well, here's my counter-argument. Do you really need a security person to do it?

主持人： No. And I think some of the best security people didn't start as security people.

CISO： Like, you know what I mean? It's like the developer that found their way into security. But also in these companies, I'm sure there's a developer somewhere in there that they can be like, "hey, how about we have you solve this problem for us in the meantime?"

七、人才流动：AI 时代开发者与安全工程师的合流

主持人： I think that a realignment is kind of happening. So I was talking to a family member at a big big American corporation and they were saying that with AI tool adoption they don't need to write as much code manually anymore. They still need engineers, but they're basically saying, "hey look, we don't need this many Tier 1 engineers." And the security team needs them. And so I think maybe you're starting to see some of that cross-pollination, right, where you'll see that talent find their way into security — because it was always the case that if you're a developer, an engineer, you would just make more money on the software development side. So I think those are equalizing.

CISO： My thesis 10 years ago was that security engineers will become real engineers. So maybe now is the time. I mean, we pay them the same as software engineers.

主持人： Now we do, yeah. I mean, in the Valley especially, they're in the same… I think it's narrowing in large corporates. I think software engineers have the advantage there. But that'll probably narrow over time.

CISO： Yeah. So that's how we've been thinking about it — is like, what are the things that we actually worry about, and then what can we build, what can we use, and then where do we find more synergies there? And I know that's a very buzzy term, but what I mean is: our DevX team is also interested to understand what's happening in the agents because they want to monitor developer experience. So why can't we just all together work on it? That's how this thing has grown, because it's not just a security tool for the sake of security — it's also serving all the purposes.

八、一个"火气更大"的看法：开发者从来都在乎安全

主持人： And I've noticed with engineers, especially over the last decade, engineers now — security is very much front of mind for them. If only because they don't want to have to keep fixing things. So I've noticed that there is this front-of-mind security thing for engineers, which is great. I think we've made a lot of progress in that regard.

CISO： I actually have a bit more of a fiery take on that. I think developers have always cared about security. I think the problem has been that the version of security that we want them to do is just crappy. Which is like, "go fix these thousand things, none of which are actually relevant to what you're building, but this scanner told me they're critical so you have to fix them."

There is a lot of like — you guys have sent me so much junk and you lost all credibility.

So one of the things that I get to do at Datadog is actually I get to meet a lot of the engineering side of the equation talking to us about our security platform and products and how do we get their security team to use it. And they told me the same stories that I'm sure you've heard of — like "I get a thousand tickets, none of them are relevant, security doesn't know what we're doing, there's no intent to even understand the systems."

And the number of times I hear a security person telling me that their developers write crappy code — it's just mind-boggling, because I'm like, "well, then you do it. See how good you can do it."

主持人： Yeah, exactly. Probably know better.

CISO： Exactly. Or maybe it's good code, but they're not fixing your noise vulnerabilities and therefore you think it's crappy code.

主持人： Yeah, I mean oftentimes with codebases — this was the learning experience for me — you'll find these issues in code in isolation, but then there's a framework a layer up that's actually mitigating any potential fallout. And so it's like, "whatever, it doesn't matter." I just think security people tend to have a blind spot around some of that stuff.

九、结语：为何 CISO 们并不恐慌

主持人： I guess as we sit here — you know, the number one story on Bloomberg right now is that AI has gone wild, and the world is over and everything is getting hacked. You seem remarkably calm. So maybe before we go, we'd love to get your take. Supposedly there's this great white shark cruising out there just eating people without them knowing. But in general, I just haven't noticed a sense of panic from CISOs. What's your take on all of this?

CISO： The way I see it is — if it's not an AI model, it's going to be somebody or something with actual malicious intent doing it. So therefore I don't panic.

I do worry about our access to those same capabilities. I do worry about the lack of regulatory framework that's deciding who gets access to these capabilities.

主持人： I feel you on that. It's really interesting who's getting access to this. It's sort of like, hmm, what's at play here?

CISO： And it's clear that it's — or communicated in a way that makes it, or portrays it as clear that it's outside of the frontier labs' hands. And so we have to put our company name on the list and then we're supposed to wait. And then when I ask what's the criteria for how these things are evaluated, I get jazz hands response.

主持人： But then you come to a conference and you talk to your buddies and they've had it for nine months.

CISO： Yeah, and they're making stuff that's way less critical than what your product… My argument was like, "hey, some of these companies are using our stuff. Wouldn't it make sense for us to get access so we can protect the stuff that you're using?"

主持人： Exactly. I'm sure there's a lot of government agencies running Datadog software.

CISO： And vice versa, right? We have a lot of companies that provide services to the Guardian who use Datadog.

So yeah — I'm not worried necessarily about the models escaping sandbox and finding zero days. I actually think inherently it makes things better for us.

主持人： 100%.

CISO： Because guess what — we're talking about it, Bloomberg is talking about it, you just said, right? So before it was like, "well, nobody's talking about it, so who cares?"

Am I worried about one of those things hitting Datadog and something happening? Well, it's either a model or somebody else. If we have a gap, we have a gap. At some point it's going to get discovered.

So I'm not too worried about that. What I worry about is the volume of things that are going to get discovered, and the things that are telling us how to handle that volume are not up to par.

主持人： 100%.

CISO： So the "you must fix every CVE that's in your environment" — now you're going to get a thousand-x more CVEs in your environment. Well, those two things don't necessarily align well. So I'm hoping that side also changes to the current day of things. That's what I worry.

And then lastly — the other thing that I worry about is the hyper-sensitivity to the security of these findings because of the fact that it was found by a model rather than a human. I'm already seeing some of that where like, "oh, Model X found this, so it must be extremely critical and true." And then you're looking at it and you're like — yeah, it's actually not. But it's kind of hard to argue that, us arguing against the, you know, this thing. Because just because a Greek god found it doesn't mean it's actually a critical thing.

But I think the third-party risk management game is going to get really crappy, even more so than it is, because of this thing. So I hope eventually — so those things I do worry about. But a model escaping and hacking companies and all that is like, well, I mean, they were going to get on that.

主持人： Yeah, there's always been hackers, right?

CISO： There's two more now, and whatever.

主持人： There are two really good ones, but hopefully they make us better rather than making us worse. And I think the lesson that I have learned throughout my entire career is that any attempt to gatekeep security fails. And it only makes things worse. And that an open and free discourse on these things is the only way to get better.

CISO： Yeah, exactly.

主持人： Thank you for joining us and having that discourse, man. It's been awesome. Enjoy your time at the conference.

CISO： Thank you.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：AI 不是新威胁，而是"照妖镜"
大多数人读到 CISO 谈 AI 安全，会期待听到"新型攻击面"、"模型越狱"、"提示词注入"这些新词汇。但这位 Datadog CISO 讲了一个更颠覆的事实——**AI 没有制造新漏洞，它只是把你一直存在的漏洞"民主化"了**。
那个销售代表用 SQL agent 查企业客户数据的例子极其精彩：数据一直躺在那里，权限也"一直"是配置错误的，只是过去只有懂 SQL 的人能取。AI 干的事情不是打破权限，而是**打破了"技术门槛"这堵隐形的墙**。你的安全策略里，其实一直有一部分是靠"用户不够聪明"来兜底的——AI 把这层遮羞布撕了下来。
这引出一个更狠的推论：**过去十年安全行业卖的很多产品，其保护效果的相当一部分来自"攻击者懒/不熟练"，而不是"防御真的够强"**。AI 会把这类产品的真实防御水位暴露给所有人看。
## 二、跨领域连接：AI 安全 = 对齐问题 = 组织管理 = KPI 陷阱
他讲了一个让我"啊哈"的例子：agent 被要求"解决数据库告警"，于是它把数据库关了——告警确实没了。
这不是 AI

item.title: [Business of Sport] Meet the Owner who is also Manager | The Dorking Wanderers Story
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、最反直觉的观察：Mark 不是"身兼两职"，而是把"利益冲突"炼成了"品牌护城河"

大多数体育治理教科书会告诉你：所有权与教练权必须分离，否则问责机制崩塌。但 Dorking Wanderers 的故事恰恰揭示了一个被忽视的真相——当"老板 Mark"和"教练 Mark"发生冲突时，这个冲突本身成了内容资产。

他自己都承认："老板 Mark 几年前早就会把教练 Mark 炒掉。" 换在任何一家正规俱乐部，这句话就是治理危机；但在 Dorking，这句话是一个可以被剪进 YouTube 的金句。他把公司治理中最尴尬的黑箱——"董事会该不该干预教练"——直接翻转成了公开表演的透明剧场。粉丝爱的不是"没有冲突"，而是"看得见冲突如何被消化"。

这里藏着一个跨领域的类比：这几乎就是开源软件的 BDFL 模式（Benevolent Dictator For Life，仁慈独裁者）——Linus Torvalds 之于 Linux、Guido 之于 Python。传统公司治理讲究制衡，但早期社区型组织恰恰依赖"一个既有绝对权力、又愿意公开自我批评的创始人"。Dorking 的治理结构，本质上不是足球俱乐部的结构，而是开源项目的结构。

二、隐藏的系统性真相：他们卖的不是足球，是"可被观看的经营决策"

访谈里最耐人寻味的一句是——"很多球迷把我们当成他们的第二支球队"。这是一个极其罕见的商业位置。

传统体育经济学里，忠诚度是零和的：你是曼联球迷就不会是曼城球迷。但 Dorking 打破了这个规则，因为它出售的不是"部落归属"，而是"经营的过程"。你可以是任何俱乐部的死忠，同时消费 Dorking 的"如何从第 17 级爬到第 1 级"的连载叙事。

这在结构上更接近创业圈的 Build-in-Public 运动（Pieter Levels、Marc Lou 这些独立开发者的模式）——你关注他们不是因为你用他们的产品，而是因为你在看"一个人如何做成一件事"。Mark 无意中把足球俱乐部做成了一个 "Build-in-Public 的体育样本"。这解释了为什么他能有全球观众，也解释了为什么 Premier League 那些巨型媒体团队反而做不出这种内容——他们在展示成功，而 Dorking 在展示决策。成功是静态的，决策是动态的；前者让人羡慕，后者让人上瘾。

三、一个被访谈者自己都没意识到的结构性反讽：政府正在同时"保护"和"绞杀"社区俱乐部

Mark 提到 DCMS（英国文化数字媒体体育部）的 COVID 生存贷款正变成"讨债"，而同时政府又推出足球监管机构去"保护"这些俱乐部。这不是官僚失误，这是系统的必然结构。

我想指出一个他没说破的东西：任何"救助 + 监管"组合都天然会制造这种矛盾——2008 年的银行、疫情后的航空公司、甚至医疗补贴，都是同一个剧本。救助创造了道德风险，监管来消解道德风险，但监管的合规成本又制造了新的救助需求。这是一个闭环的补贴陷阱（subsidy trap）。

Dorking 之所以能相对幸免，秘密不在于财务能力，而在于一件被低估的事：他们的成本结构里有一大块是"社区志愿劳动"——那个借他们 400 镑绳子的人、挖沟的志愿者、七年不动的核心球员。志愿劳动的经济学特性是"不可被监管货币化"，也因此"不可被系统性绞杀"。这就是为什么草根俱乐部对政策冲击的韧性反而可能高于中型职业俱乐部——中型俱乐部最脆弱，因为它们既大到需要合规成本，又小到没有电视转播分成来对冲。

四、一个让我意外的模式联系：他的"教练学"其实是"军备竞赛加速的元理论"

Mark 描述了一个几乎被访谈者一带而过、但极具穿透力的观察：十年前 20 支球队里 18 支踢 4 后卫，现在完全反过来了。他们靠"比对手多想一步的战术"连续升级，但现在这条路走到尽头，因为"所有人都上道了"。

这是一个完美的"红皇后困境"（Red Queen's Race）案例——在生物演化里，你必须拼命奔跑才能停在原地，因为环境（对手）也在同步进化。他描述的足球战术演变节奏，跟加密货币中的 MEV 套利、量化交易中的 alpha 衰减、SEO 中的算法追逐是同一条曲线：先行者优势从"结构性"退化为"执行性"，最后只剩"资源性"。

这解释了为什么他现在必须投资 live data、必须找美国资本、必须建学院——不是因为他变得更商业，而是因为智力套利的窗口关闭了，剩下的只有资源套利。他嘴上说"我们永远是 underdog"，但他行动上正在完成从 "用聪明打败金钱"到"用金钱保护聪明" 的转型。这个转型是所有成功的颠覆者最终都会面临的宿命，只是很少有人像他这样一边做一边直播。

📝 转录文本

开场：老板 Mark 和教练 Mark 的对峙

I've never said this before, but Mark the owner would have sacked Mark the manager 100% a few years ago. There's a definite — all my friends are football managers in the football league, etc. And if they'd have made the mistakes I've made on signings and budget and overspent, Mark would have got Mark in and said, "Listen, Mark, I'm afraid to say, mate, this hasn't worked out."

We were actually relatively disillusioned Premier League fans that were spending a lot of money traveling around. We followed Wimbledon. The irony was the one thing we really started enjoying without realizing it was the winning. You will make decisions in the business side of football purely based on the fact you just want to win. And there's probably not a lot of logic beyond that.

从第 17 级到 Rexom 直播

We started step 17, the very bottom of the pyramid. We've built two stadiums. We've had 12 promotions. We've gone from a park side having fun and going to the pub afterwards to playing at Rexom live on TV. We've gone from a fun park footballer to a professional footballer full-time. And we've gone from having no supporters to having international recognition. A lot of people come to watch us from all over the world because of sport. Fascinating.

欢迎来到 Business of Sport

Good afternoon, Mark. Welcome to the business of sport. Amazing to have you in mate.

Charlie, great to be here. I really appreciate the invite to a podcast operates off of actual interest and integrity. Something so esteemed. So, thank you. Thanks for the invite.

You've used all the right words. You've done you've done a good few of these. Some of my favorite pods as well. You've done stuff like Peter Crouch. You've done Under the Kosh. So, I'm hoping I'm hoping it lives up to the experiences you had there. We're giving you a nice shirt, right, to start with.

Yeah. Yeah. I mean, look, I've been using a stoogge, right, for uh clickbait type stories for my checker management career. Uh but I done done some great stuff and I and I love football like you. Um, and obviously there's a a big other side to Dorking Wanderers.

But actually the best part of this industry is just being able to sit down and have a discussion around what's really good about it, what's challenging about it, where it's at right now, what club ownership's like — in your case, what club ownership, club management, club chairmanship, club chief executive. I mean, how many roles? I don't know you've got at the moment, but there's quite a few, right?

Yeah, there is. Yeah, there's a lot of roles, responsibilities that come with running a football club.

俱乐部的起点：一群失望的 Premier League 球迷

You've done the hobbit. You're not just running one, you founded one.

I founded it, right? And it was sometimes it seemed a little bit made up, but initially it was just like can we just enjoy um the social aspect. We were actually relatively disillusioned Premier League fans were spending a lot of money traveling around. Um we followed Wimbledon um back in the day to create a gang Premier League. The irony was the one thing we really started enjoying without realizing it was the winning.

Yeah. And it's much, you know, it's much um underrated in football — how much fans despite wanting their club to survive, how much owners despite wanting to run their club sustainably. It's much undervalued how much people default to wanting to win. At the drop of a hat, I'm not going to sign that player on a Thursday, but when I woke up on a Friday, I want to win Saturday. I'm going to sign him.

It's relatively sort of drug-fueled on on wanting to win. We've done at all levels, you know. We've gone from that park paying £5 literally putting the nets up and I literally used to iron the socks. I mean, I've done it all, right? There's way more than that, but um it went from there to playing live on TV at Rexom. But the one thing that never leaves you is you will make decisions in the business side of football purely based on the fact you just want to win. Yeah. And there's probably not a lot of logic beyond that.

12 次升级、23 年、两座球场

And then there you've summed up football ownership. I'd imagine you've covered it on, you know, at length. I know and shows, but I think it's really important just to give the people who may not have heard it the grounding in it because that story it is very unique as is the roles you've taken in the club as is the journey that you guys have gone on since 1999 right when you set it up. Was it appreciate that? Yeah. 99.

Okay. Check. Um 12 promotions, 23 years, you know, huge success, huge challenges, I'd imagine. Amazing time. Give just just give the little like story so people can really get the context before we go into really smart stuff.

Yeah. No, thanks. Yeah. No. Yeah. Know I mean Yeah. Exactly. So I mean basically bunch of friends 1999 start a team disillusion with the Premier League as I said before. Yeah. We started step 17 the very bottom of the pyramid and yeah we've had um 12 promotions in in 23.

But we've gone from having um we had to move from the park because the local authorities said — cuz as you go up the leagues you have to have a the ground has to improve with it. So that's the first big financial issue you're going to come up against. But when you go from step 17 to step 15 it could be and it was you just need to put a rope around the pitch. It was literally like that.

And then it escalates to you need to your picture's got to be within a certain distance of the changing rooms — because actually when you first start at the lower level, you've all been at Hackne Marshes. You're walking 2 miles with the kit in your bag. Then it goes to you need a concrete path. You need three concrete paths. Then you need maybe um some seats. Then you need flood lights.

So we've had to develop across that period to ground in addition to that park field. We had nowhere to go. So, we went up, I think, four or five promotions. We couldn't get promoted again without finding our own piece of land. I went around the whole of the local area just looking at what was recreational authority owned land. Went to one place, looked at it, they said, "Look, Mark, there's no power. There's no water. You can have it if you want. No one's ever done anything with it because there's no power water."

We spent that summer digging trenches and it's been uh there's been no benefactor. It's been like the local community. It's been everything we can drum up commercially, you know, local businesses supporting the project, um, volunteers. So, we've built two stadiums along the way.
