And when you get to the EFL, they have a mechanism of four teams up, four down.

So the relegation was um and still is by far the biggest negative in our club. But but it almost showed that the fans uh the ownership group, everybody um yeah, everyone kind of stayed with it.

Do you buy into the very popular now school of thought that you learned more from that failure than you did by continuing on the promotion train?

I think so. Yeah. I mean, we we got found out by slightly too quick um an escalation in promotions. We you know, we were busy building a stadium. I was the you know, involved in that during that year. Um we got found out by getting the player recruitment wrong in terms of age and um you know the sort of a genre person you know um but yeah the learns from it were massive and it's a bit like I in my head and I've never really said this before but in my head like it's a bit like that heavyweight champ. It's a bit like that, you know, they always say, you know, it's almost, you know, bigger accolade to kind of be the sort of like, you know, the two times, you know, three times, whatever. Having them things that knock you down and from our point of view,

I feel like in in my head, we hadn't experienced that and we've now experienced it and it's it's made us stronger.

It light that fire in you even more. Maybe not that you needed it, but —

Yeah, majorly. I mean, I'm, you know, 100%. it it gets me out of bed every day to deliver it is that kind of two times world champ they bounce back and actually then have a shot of the EFL um from ultimate disappointment and that journey because for us because it's all on camera as well and it's quite publicized it's part of that story it's a chapter in that journey

成本、财政与追梦

Yeah I spoken to someone like let's say Spencer again who talked about you talked about the rising cost of going through the leagues but it doesn't necessarily always correlate to increase in revenue. Have you you know which is which is the real challenge I guess. Have you seen that as you've moved around and how much leeway do you give yourself for those promotions where you can go right we can maybe stretch ourselves a little bit further this year knowing that if you then do go back down your cost base may reduce a little bit but the revenue won't change.

Yeah, we've um we I would say we've been relatively optimistic, if I use that as a I'll use optimism as a instead of like um carefree. We followed our nose a lot. We've we listen, we've we've never ever built up massive debt, nothing like that. So, we've never had any kind of like, oh my god, if we get relegated, we can't pay the banks. We can't you know that. So, but um we've always known we can cut our cloth accordingly. We we've always kind of had that delta there to to look at and as protection if you like but we have chased the ace a lot which is what you do in football. We've aim for it.

Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. We lose money. I mean if anyone says they don't then they're they're either bottom of the table or or they're lying. I mean it's just an industry that's a um a money drain.

政府、地方议会与社区俱乐部的困境

I think in non-league football there should be a lot more support from local government um and government. There should be a lot more support. Um because football clubs are heritage um you know when the government says this year well we're going to put national insurance up you know 15.5% lower bracket. Yeah. And all the other trading costs.

Well the irony is right they've recognized the importance of these assets to communities which is why the football regulator has been put in place.

Exactly. Exactly. But there is a you're so right that there such a contradiction in in terms of like the way because these clubs are social hubs um on a huge level whether that's like where the single mom or dad takes her son whether that's where the person without many friends goes to meet people where families meet families they're huge things where people participate as well especially now in nomly football loads of artificial pitches but let me tell you local authorities are charging a bomb uh for people to use them and and government means that if you run a football club, you're going to get charged for that.

And that then goes right down to like we try to run burseries for uh and we run a lot of um football for all schemes in the community where we literally charge no money uh because we know that there are people that want to play football that maybe can't afford it.

So it's it is definitely um um I'm a big in England. This is in fact I'll just sum it up and and anyone watching this with a football club or or in knowledge of a football club will be nodding in Jan this year when we had massive rainfall like you know we had probably 400 kids that didn't even play football because there isn't enough facilities for them in the UK there is very much underfunded by government in terms of facilities unlike most of Europe and in terms of the cost of running a football club.

Um, and that definitely is why it's an expensive game. Back to your original point, do you lose money? Absolutely. Is some of that because we want to win? Yes. Is some of that because it's really expensive to run a football club? Yes.

收入结构与场地经济学

Yeah. Do you make money? How much money based on revenues would you say comes from non-Oing activities? Using the ground, using the club, using the stadium, the license, etc. from stuff as you said outside of it.

Yeah. I think maybe like maybe 35% of our revenue.

So, a third of it. I mean, yeah.

Significant. Yeah. So we get knocked over sideways when the government says actually now this is going to happen or the local council say well we're going to charge you this for the beauty of for the luxury of I mean you go you know if you go and ask you know Berry Council now you know like you know how do you feel now that your football club went out of business and you know you was attracting you know 7,000 people and all the commercial economic benefits of that you know like they then sort of go yeah maybe should have dipped in a bit better.

DCMS 生存贷款：救助如何变成讨债

Quite an interesting one, won't it? If and when, hopefully it won't happen, but if and when a club with a regulator in place hits these challenges, and part of the reason that they've been poorly controlled in their finances is because you've had things like rates go up and you've had actually government schemes come in to screw some of these clubs and their response to the regulator is, well, actually, it's your bosses.

It's brilliant, isn't it? What a — bosses.

Do you know what I I don't mind at all. I mean, I don't mind saying this at all. It's it's not it's not um what's the word? Confidential. They um DCMS provided survival loans funds um and this is a key this just literally proved everything you're saying they previewed uh they called it winter survival funds it kind of postcoid you know coming out of co uh DCMS provided loans um relatively uh low interest to uh football clubs and they are the the pressure they're putting on clubs now I mean listen right we've kept up with our repayments — Every club got them all. That's like a factory setting.

There are clubs now um across the UK that I can tell you now can't afford to pay them back. They're essentially knocking on the door like a debt collector. They're they're they are putting um essentially a charge on their business. So, they're not allowed to borrow money, these clubs, without the DCMS saying, "Well, you can borrow it, but you know, our loan sits ahead of yours."

And there's an absolute kathuffle right now. And these clubs are saying to them, well, what an irony that the money was provided to help community clubs survive at a time where there was no trade, no business. And now you're now making lives more difficult of clubs uh to to get this money back.

And at a time when the government, if you like, has made the cost of running this business ridiculously higher. And football clubs are at the mercy of the economy, right? This is the bit people forget. So, you know, like the the food supplier, you know, their costs have gone up. They're passing it on to the football club, right? Okay. Yeah. The people you employ, you know, their their utility costs have gone up, right? But but in this football club, you got this weird thing where, you know, your supporters through the door are saying, "Well, what are you doing to support the economy?" Because, you know, there's less dispensable income. So, can you put can you you know, can season tickets be less money?

Yeah. I was going to say finish that story, right? And who who ultimately feels the effect of that? Because when you get hit by all of those people, what do you do? You probably put your ticket prices up. And when you put your ticket prices up, hey, we're back round to the old fan. And the old fan's the one that actually is out of pocket.

You've got this kind of B2B and B TOC like mix in a football club that difficult to balance.

收入、损失与可持续性

Yeah, it it's crazy when you when you actually think about it like that. It is crazy. Can you say what what's your what revenues do you do a year?

3 million.

3 million. Okay.

Yeah, about 3 million. And you fund the losses. You, the ownership group, fund the loss.

The ownership group do. Yeah, they're brilliant.

Yeah, the ownership group do. You You obviously you can be successful without making losses, but the reality is anyone who says they are um they would be they'd be probably lying. We we are probably more fortunate than most. Our losses are massively reducing. We're probably getting nearer to the point of sustainability than most, but that's because we've been fortunate to build up with the online, you know, coverage that we've got and commercializing that. So, we're very fortunate, but how some clubs do it, I don't know.

It's not fortunate. That's strategic.

Yeah, I think it's Yeah, it is. It is strategic.

媒体、社媒团队与被低估的机会

I I play a game, right, with football clubs and much higher up than you, but genuinely, I sit here and we'll often have a conversation with someone and they'll say, "Yeah, you know, we've got this media plan. We got a content strategy, blah, blah, blah. We're trying to do it. Okay, cool. How big is your media team? Well, you know, we've got two and a half people. Oh, half a person. Well, yeah, you know, they're kind of crossing over with this. Saying, how many people would you get in your stadium? 25,000 a week. I'm like, you have two and a half people and a content team, a media team, social media team, whatever you want to call it, servicing a fan base that you're getting that into the stadium, let alone everything around it, competing in some of the most competitive sports environments in the year. What the is going on?

I totally agree.

What is going on? But also, you can't that's not like that's just that's not strategic. That's not a content plan. You are not giving yourself a chance to recognize that.

No,

It's not lucky. You're making a choice.

Yeah, we are making a choice. And I mean, we do 10x like you know the likes of Crystal Patterson put it out there, right? Okay. We know our stats. We know we know Premier League stats and we are massive, right?

But if you look at the opportunity to your point that these clubs have got I mean it's uh it's really weird Premier League because um I mean I've known many this is quite strange to get your head around the the managers that run the under 23s in these Premier League clubs they are earning um probably what a London Underground driver earns or less the value they put on this is going come back to your point the value they put on um the bloke that develops all of the young players in the club is is is you the same as a London Underground driver gets in a you know it's it's madness and the the the reserve left back probably gets more than that a week and it goes the same to social media.

I don't think these clubs realize that even though they probably obviously they do yield and make a lot of money through Premier League, the they still got a huge opportunity. And the EFL clubs to similar to the ones you mentioned there, nowhere near it, way off it. They don't even understand really where it where it is and where it's going.

But again, it's the same reasons we've already discussed. You know, if you can then say, well, why is that the case? Go, oh, but you know, and fair enough, it's another line on the sheet, right? It's more expense behind the scenes and that is another revenue well another cost let's say as it's viewed that goes away from how are we going to get promoted from League One to the Championship next season short-term impact the long term of you building up that media team in this day and age will far outweigh financially I think the value of you spending those extra few thousand in in the player but it's very hard for clubs to think outside of it

Yeah it is I think it's common place that they uh they're they're blindsided. Um and it's uh there's so many opportunity video on demand and you know because obviously you've only got to look at what people want to see if they're you know the these kids now 10 12 15 what they want to see is things on demand constantly um and and that is what these clubs aren't very good at doing.

Dorking 的内容策略：Mark 的个性与真实感

Tell us, go on, tell everyone that doesn't know what have you done, how have you approached it, what have you learned, you know, bunch of amateurs, this everything around the media profile that you've built in a club to give you now this exposure, the the opportunity to —

Well, I think we we capitalize on showing people my character and —

What character?

Yeah. The um this is me behaving of any anything.

You say to me before you started, so I'm going to swear — actually you haven't yet, which I'm — I'm so impressed.

Amazed by

I know. But um it's a good opportunity. I appreciate being it's an opportunity to talk about things that you know that I never know people only normally care about when I you know threaten the uh the referee at the end of the York game.

Um I think my character we've got this sort of this natural club trajectory that's um interesting. My character interesting but I said there's a lot of characters in the game. There's loads of people like me.

Um we had a guy turn up rich with a camera said I want to start filming stuff and a lot of it's down to Richard really. It's been a bit of a match made in heaven. sounds a bit crap, but he literally put mics on us and then just said, "Right, do you mind having a mic?" I was like, "I don't really care." Had no idea where it was going to go. He then started showing the content.

Um, and it's kind of like also the timing was important because it was like, you know, YouTube uh starting to evolve, Tik Tok massively starting to evolve, and a lot of short form content that people want to see. And what we've shown people is obviously the real side of a football club, but we're very lucky because a lot of managers can't show the real them because they're worried about getting sacked by either the owner or the fans.

It's your protection.

Mark the owner. Mark the manager. You can go and say that on there. Oh, thanks Mark the owner. That's great.

与裁判的关系与"教练学"

I know. So, we've just been refreshing and uh we we've kind of we've managed to get this kind of mix that I mean we've got a brilliant relationship with referees like even though —

Really?

Yeah. We have like I've now I'm on about my fifth seminar now where I get invited to be speaker with all the referees and such is their respect. They kind of get us. They get that we love football. They get that everything comes from a great place and some of that content they see where I'm trying to get into the fourth official and they but it's true.

They they say it's been it's been eye opening for them. They say well why are you trying to get into the fourth official? And I say well I tell you why. I if you know look at back at the video I didn't try and get into the fourth official until the 15th minute but during the first 15 minutes I noticed he was spending too much time talking to the other manager. So what I want to make sure I do is make sure he's not going to get influence. I'm going to make his job tougher on the day and they go that's a good point. So you think if we probably have a bit more of a you know like uh you know arms length approach it probably avoid — Yeah, absolutely. That's the only reason I do it.

Okay, that's interesting. Mark, why did you tell that ref, you know, why did you tell that ref, you know, why do you shout that ref so bad? So, you know, I'll go, well, because he didn't book me. He didn't book me. So, I'm going to I'm going to I'm going to keep at that ref to influence decisions until the point he deals with me if I because I think he can be influenced. And and and and and this eye opener for for referees. I'm talking top down has been like okay yeah let's really think about it.

So the point is —

And that's content

It's content but like and people love hearing it right and I love talking about it. So the point is the eye opening content um people kind of get its uh it's good for the game. It's um and it's worked out that people value it.

关于真实性与"Welcome to Wrexham"

So, but I hate using the word, but we have to the hardest thing now is the authenticity of that content, right? Because I hear it all the time obviously in what we do doing even this, right? Oh, how great is Welcome to Rexom, you know, we're just going to go and buy an asset or be a part of an asset and we're going to set up a series and we're going to document how we've done it and it's all going to be great. And it's like, well,

yeah, I mean, in theory, there's been a pretty good use point of that. The one challenge is firstly, you're not Ryan Reynolds,

Which for a lot of people is a shame to be. Uh secondly, you have probably completely different points of attraction as an asset or a club or whatever that give you a good reason to do that. So every time people now look at this, yes, there is huge opportunity in content, but you can't just wake up and decide you need to do it. You really have to be clear on what you're trying to achieve from it.

So as you talk around that, whether it's even just as simple as going, we're going to bring my personality out and we're going to show you what it's really like going in from a manager's perspective who's also happens to be an owner to tell the most, you know, incredible story within football. Great. Yeah,

I know what I'm in for.

Yeah, I'm locked in. I'm locked in. If I'm a Premier League club, you talked about doing more than Palace, right? If I'm a Premier League club, what am I actually getting if I'm following a Palace content? Some of the Premier League content stuff when it's been on Amazon all I don't I found the most stale boring often things. The Man City one, no one wants to I didn't want to just tune in and watch them win every week. I didn't I didn't find it interesting really at all. I it it didn't it didn't show me what —

球衣赞助的价值转变

Well I mean if you done a test and said you know you put down all the Premier League teams and said now write down their sponsors on the front of their shirts

Right you you'd be struggling to get past three

Especially now

Right and this is the thing and this is this is this is this is exactly it you know um I I look at

Easy if you're Chelsea

Yeah yeah yeah true but the point is like you know like um growing up you football was in magazines and on TV, right? So, uh sponsors shirt was front and center of all the eyeballs that looked at them. But now, um it's kind of very much that kind of like, you know, stimulative like the billboard thing, you know, once you drive past the billboard twice, you don't recognize it a third time. Fact, right?

And this is um you know, this is where kind of you know, football shirt sponsors now. It's actually lower value, weirdly, than ever before for these people. But if they're in front of like, you know, half a billion people like we were last year, um, online um, and you know, the demographic, it's, you know, it's it's 75 85% male between this age to that age, then I'm preaching to converted here, the worth, the value of that is a is a no market, right?

So do you see compared to other clubs let's say at your level have you seen that revenue needle move in accordance with the success that you've had in those areas you've been able to monetize it

Massively all all people want to do now is get their brand in front of um the right people back in the day I mean you know my background believe it or not is advertising right so there there is a there is a a combination here but back in the day you would say to somebody uh well if you sponsor that football shirt. Loads of people are going to see it. Right. Okay. Can you prove that to me? Well, you know, you like football. Do you ever watch Match of the Day? Yes, I do. Right. Brilliant. There you go. Well, sign up.

Now, you can lally say, "Well, actually, we've got this many million people a week that see our content." Okay. And they're actually between the ages of X and Y, and actually they're from this type of demographic. So, they're interested in that. And they'll go, "Right, well, that's what we sell and that's the people we're trying to target. So here's my money.

So it it's a it's it's a bit like the data on field. It's a science that it's an easy sell. And um yeah, much undervalued. I think you made a great point before about the these people are recruiting for social media managers. They're not even they don't even know what they're recruiting for for starters and it's just so undervalued.

Oh, massive. But a massive opportunity, right? So, as you said, but but if you understand what it is you're doing, you can't you can't just do it and say, "Let's do Welcome to Rex and volume 15 or whatever."

And I see it a lot. I see stuff a lot. I see people saying, "Oh, you know, here's our changing room." And it's like, "Well,

So what?

There's loads of changing rooms."

Yeah. What you doing there?

Who cares?

Yeah.

展望未来：EFL 与两年计划

Um, tell me about — you got the season starting on Saturday, right? Looking forward, you've had all of this story, all the success building up to now. Ambitions, I would imagine, right, let's just head off table, get as high as you can, of course, right? right? You want to do that.

But how do you how do you look at what comes next for the club? How do you look and and keep giving yourself that motivation moving forward? Your role within this whole project, when to bring people in like you have done, when not to. Just interested in in that part of your mind

With a closed shop. I mean, in terms of like um you know, I think owners investment, we're there where we want to be now. I think we've got the people around us to get to the EFL. You have to have a fair wind because this one up — I call it one up because there's playoffs and and you know every year there you know it's it's a coin toss um we've seen uh clubs that have done brilliantly brmley um uh national league league 2 league one stopport national league league 2 league one obviously Rexom anomaly national league championship so we believe with a fair wind we can do um EFL uh we're one of probably 16 17 clubs outside of the football league. Uh maybe more, maybe 20 between the conference and the south and the north that would say this is where we want to be. We're not happy being where we are. We want to get to Wembley. We've got these kind of like school childhood dreams we want to achieve for the club.

Um and I feel like we're not looking any further than that. And I think that's always worked well for us is is having a plan but just not too much because a five-year plan gets changed two years in,

You know. So, is it a two-year plan? You know so —

结束语

Mark, look, it's incredible. I love it. It's such a different story. We, as I said to you at the beginning, you know, you have so many different types of football chats on the show, you never quite know where they're going to go. But genuinely, having the opportunity to look at something properly on performance side, properly tied into executive side and how that works in some miraculous way uh together is is really cool.

But firstly, congratulations on doing everything that you've done today. and fingers crossed you managed to keep achieving everything that that you want to. Um, and most importantly for sharing it because it's great.

Thank you. It's been I appreciate the invite and uh talking about how passionate side of the game.

I love it. You can't beat it, can you?

No, you can't. It's brilliant and we're just uh no matter what when I get back in the car outside, I'll just want to win on Saturday.

Yeah. Well, exactly. I was going to say good luck on the weekend and uh you know, Dag massive game. So, I'm sure I'm sure you'll uh I'm sure you'll do do a great job. I'll look for you on the touch line.

But yes, take care. Thank you.

Thank you, mate. Cheers, Charlie.

item.description:
## 一、最反直觉的观察：Mark 不是"身兼两职"，而是把"利益冲突"炼成了"品牌护城河"
大多数体育治理教科书会告诉你：所有权与教练权必须分离，否则问责机制崩塌。但 Dorking Wanderers 的故事恰恰揭示了一个被忽视的真相——**当"老板 Mark"和"教练 Mark"发生冲突时，这个冲突本身成了内容资产**。
他自己都承认："老板 Mark 几年前早就会把教练 Mark 炒掉。" 换在任何一家正规俱乐部，这句话就是治理危机；但在 Dorking，这句话是一个可以被剪进 YouTube 的金句。**他把公司治理中最尴尬的黑箱——"董事会该不该干预教练"——直接翻转成了公开表演的透明剧场**。粉丝爱的不是"没有冲突"，而是"看得见冲突如何被消化"。
这里藏着一个跨领域的类比：这几乎就是**开源软件的 BDFL 模式（Benevolent Dictator For Life，仁慈独裁者）**——Linus Torvalds 之于 Linux、Guido 之于 Python。传统公司治理讲究制衡，但早期社区型组织恰恰依赖"一个既有绝对权力、又愿意公开自我批评的创始人"。

item.title: [Sequoia Capital] How Harvey Built a Research Lab on a Budget | Gabe Pereyra
item.dc:creator: Sequoia Capital
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

反常识观察：Harvey 其实在玩一场"寄生式创新"的游戏

大多数人以为 Harvey 是"垂直 AI 应用公司"，但仔细拆解 Gabe 的 playbook，你会发现 Harvey 真正的商业模式是把整个前沿生态当作自己的 R&D 部门。他们不试图和 Anthropic、OpenAI 竞争，也不试图取代 Fireworks、Mercor、Snorkel——而是把这些公司当作"外部器官"来使用。这就像珊瑚礁不自己进行光合作用，而是与虫黄藻共生。Harvey 的核心能力，其实不是 AI 研究，而是"生态编排力"——他们同时和多家 Neo Labs（Fireworks、Base 10、N-gram、Trajectory、Applied Compute）合作，本质上是在做多线程赌注对冲，让每一家的研究方向都为 Harvey 的产品打工。这是应用层公司在 AI 时代第一次真正拥有了"帝国式扩张"的可能——你不需要自己养兵，只需要让所有雇佣军都想赢你的战争。

隐藏联系：Julio 的"数据室生成术"其实是逆向工程学的一次范式转移

Gabe 提到他弟弟 Julio 的做法——先设计 rubric（评分标准），再据此反向生成数据——这个动作看似只是解决法律数据私密性的技术 hack，但它实际上暗合了一个跨领域的深层原理：从"数据驱动"到"意图驱动"的范式反转。这个思路和物理学中"费曼路径积分"惊人相似——费曼不问粒子怎么走，而是先定义"所有可能路径"的加权求和；Julio 不问"真实的数据长什么样"，而是先定义"我要检验什么样的能力"，再让数据在这个约束下生成。更进一步，这和好莱坞剧本工业的"高概念反推法"（先想 logline，再倒推情节）本质相同。这意味着：在数据稀缺的领域，未来的护城河不是拥有数据，而是拥有"能定义什么算好数据"的领域专家。 律师的价值从"写文件"变成"设计陷阱"——这是一次职业本体论的迁移，而律师界大多数人还没意识到。

出人意料的战略洞见：Harvey 正在悄悄从"效率工具"转向"组织操作系统"

Gabe 在最后一个问题的回答里，几乎不经意地埋了一个战略炸弹——他说 Copilot、Coda 之类是"个人生产力产品"，而 Harvey 在做的是"组织生产力"。这个跳跃比听起来大得多。个人生产力工具的天花板是"更快的打字机"，而组织生产力工具的天花板是"更聪明的公司架构本身"。 这里存在一个反直觉的连接：Harvey 的终局形态，看起来不像 ChatGPT，更像是麦肯锡 + SAP + Palantir 的合体——它不是替代律师，而是重新组织律所的经济学。当一个律所有 10000 个客户、20 人团队、6 个月项目周期，Harvey 卖的不再是"AI"，而是"新一代事务所的操作系统"。这解释了一个更深层的事：为什么 Harvey 花那么大力气开源基准？ 因为他们要成为标准，而不是产品。开源 Legal Agent Bench 其实是在做"法律 AI 的 ISO 认证"——一旦所有前沿模型都用你的基准发论文，你就悄悄从"参赛者"变成了"裁判员"，甚至变成了"竞技场本身"。这是从产品公司到基础设施公司的隐性升维，而大多数应用层创业者还在纠结"下一个 feature 做什么"。

📝 转录文本

开场介绍

Next up, we are honored to have Gabe with us. Gabe is co-founder and president of Harvey. Um you were a research scientist at DeepMind ages ago, um and then at Meta I think before you showed your college roommates uh what GPT-3 could do. And this duo uh then became Harvey.

Um we're really excited to have you here. I think everybody here in the audience is an application company um thinking about how to start doing their own research, post-training their own models, um and uh create their own labs. And so I think Harvey has really set the example here, and we're really delighted to have you give a talk on how to how you guys built Harvey Labs.

Awesome. [applause]

开篇：一场不公平的游戏

So the alternative title to this talk is building a research lab on a budget. And it's an unfair game competing with the frontier labs if you're an application layer company. There are rich teams, there [snorts] are poor teams, and then there's us in the application layer. The frontier labs have more money, more talent, more compute infrastructure, and data.

So how do you compete? By using the frontier ecosystem.

When we started Harvey 4 years ago, most of these companies either didn't exist or were just getting started. And so we either had to build everything ourselves or in most cases focus on something different. Like building our GTM org and a great product. But today using the frontier ecosystem I think you can compete with the frontier labs and build frontier intelligence.

This talk is going to be our high-level playbook for doing this. And I'm going to talk about how we build benchmarks and training data, how we work with the Neo Labs to do post training and how we serve these models in production.

第一步：先建 Benchmark

To start, you want to build a benchmark. If you don't have a good benchmark, you can't train models, and if you can't train models, you don't need to serve them in production.

So, this year we released three of these data sets that we built:

  • 我们先构建了 Legal Agent Bench——大所律师任务的一个 taxonomy，覆盖多个执业领域，包含起草复杂基金设立文件、判例法研究等复杂任务。
  • 接着构建了一个 contracting data set，让 agent 学会像内部法务部门那样进行谈判。
  • 我最兴奋的是最近发布的大型 diligence data set——可能是目前发布的最大 RL 环境之一，最大的 data room 高达 8000 万 tokens，可以研究超长上下文的复杂任务。

数据集怎么来的：Vibe Coding 式的数据生成

And I think the most interesting thing about these data sets is how we built them. One challenge we always had at Harvey for training models is we can't train on our customers' data. We work with the largest law firms and enterprises, and their legal data is incredibly sensitive. It's privileged, and so you can't put it in generic models. We can't even put it in our models. And so, how do you train models given that?

And the thing that started working really well this year is using domain experts to guide synthetic data generation. And uh Brendan from Reka had a good analogy that the same way that engineers now don't write code, they vibe code and guide these coding models. We're starting to do the same thing.

And so, my younger brother is actually a lawyer at Harvey, and he's gotten very good at using the coding models. He's trained our other lawyers to do that, and they can generate incredibly realistic data sets that we can use for training and also evaluating our product.

And once you've done that, synthetic data isn't good enough, but it's a way to get started. And so, we work with companies like Mercor and Snorkel, who let you scale up this process and build larger sets particularly for training.

让 RL 环境跑得起

Once you've done that, you need to turn these data sets into efficient RL environments. It gets really expensive as these data sets get larger and evaluation gets very expensive. For example, in our diligence data set, we have over 1,000 unit tests that are grading model outputs using LLM as a judge. If you use the largest models and you want to do RL rollouts and things like this, it gets very expensive. And so, there's a lot of work, and here's some we did with LangChain, of making these very efficient.

开源数据集：一个"有争议"的决策

And then the last thing we did that I think was a little controversial at the time, was open-sourcing some of these data sets. And the motivation for this was it's very hard to know your data set is good unless a lot of people train on it.

When I used to do research at Google Brain and DeepMind, the best data sets were open, like ImageNet, CIFAR, MNIST, and everyone used them, and you were able to find all of the issues, and we get a ton of pull requests, we get suggestions. Um and then I think increasingly we're having the labs when they report new models benchmark on our data set.

And then most importantly, we had Elon retweet it.

第二步：Post Training——与 Neo Labs 合作

So, once you've built the benchmark, now you have something to train models against. And the thing that is exciting now is open-source models are getting competitive. In the past, it wasn't worth doing post training because the models were improving so quickly from pre-training that any post training you did quickly got absorbed by the next pre-trained model.

But now with models like Kimmy 3, GLM 5.2, NeMo-Megatron, Inkling, and others, it's possible to take these very strong open-source base models and post train them to levels of frontier intelligence. Maybe not general frontier intelligence, but if you have a specific task like us, they are competitive.

And so, the way we recommend getting started is working with the NeMo labs. They have a bunch of expertise and infrastructure already in place to help you make sure that your training data sets are good. They have recipes. And usually, if you work with them and you're not able to get better results, there's probably something you're doing wrong with your data set, and this is a very good way to bootstrap it.

与多家 Neo Labs 的具体合作

  • Fireworks：训练 GLM 5.1 时用 Fable 或 Opus 4.8 作为 advisor model，得到有趣结果。
  • Base 10：在 KB compaction 上做了有意思的工作。
  • N-gram：企业搜索和事务所知识方面。
  • Trajectory：合作训练 NeMo-Megatron 模型。
  • Applied Compute：在 Vault 产品上做了有意思的工作。

为什么不只选一家？

And I think one question we got is why work with multiple NeMo labs. Why not just pick one? And for us, as we're scaling the research lab, we have more research projects than we have bandwidth to do internally or just with a single Neo lab. And every Neo lab is taking a different bet. They have different ways they think about research. We have different open source models we want to train. And the more we work with, the more we learn.

And it's getting easier than ever to do post training. So one, working with the Neo labs, we're learning a lot in partnership with them. And then we're doing more and more post training ourselves internally with APIs like Tinker and the infrastructure Fireworks and Base 10 have built. It's never been easier to post train these models and then serve them. And there's increasingly more post training talent that we're hiring and is available.

And inspired by Cursor, the goal of these efforts is for us to build our version of Composer one. How do we package all of the work we've done with synthetic data, scaling it with Mercor, the work with the Neo labs, into a model we can serve alongside the closed source models.

第三步：把模型送进生产环境

Now, once you've post trained a model, you need to be able to serve it in production. And this is non-trivial. So I want to start first by talking about our model serving infrastructure because I think sometimes people still think about application layer companies as you're calling a single model endpoint and it's maybe a chat product.

And so a big problem we've solved over the past four years is we operate in 60 countries. We have multiple product surface areas. Customers have different model preferences. And even with the closed just the closed source models, how do you serve these at scale?

And so this matrix gives you a sense of all of the things we need to handle when we're thinking about serving these models at scale. And as a simple example for each of these model families, we need to serve multiple of these models. We need to have fallbacks across providers to hit our SLAs. And now with companies like Fireworks.ai, we can add open-source models into this mix.

上线前的评估流程

In order to think about when you serve models in production and how you modern them modern them in production, you need to have this infrastructure in place thinking of even before you think about post-training.

And so this is how we think about when there's a new model released, whether it's open-source, closed-source, or a model we've post-trained, how we make decisions whether to put it in production. And then once it's in production, how we make decisions whether to keep it in production.

[snorts]

Pre-production 层面：

  • Automated：lab benchmark 快速判断是否为 frontier model、在哪些法律领域强。
  • Human testing：模型之间做 side-by-side 比较。
  • Product-specific：每个产品面都有 critical user journeys 和自动化产品测试——一个模型可能通用能力强但不适合特定产品面。
  • Human product testing。

And then we also have human product testing. And together these signals along with heuristics around cost, latency, region availability is how we decide whether we put a model into production. And I think the important point here is this is the case for post-trained models or non-post-trained models. And so you can reuse this infrastructure and you should have it in place before you think about post-training.

上线后的监控

Once a model's in production, same thing, doesn't matter if the model's post-trained or not. We do AB testing if we're rolling out a large change, we look at engagement to track if this model's performing how we expect. Um and then we look at things like uptime, token efficiency, and then we call it product feedback, I call it angry customer emails.

And so there's There's all of these signals that tell you this is working as expected. And so you need that infrastructure in place before you think about serving models.

简单开源切换（Simple Open-Source Switches）

And then the thing you need to do even still before serving models is what I call the simple open-source switches.

第一步——直接替换： And so the first one is look at all the places you're serving models and find are there places in my product where I can just naively swap open-source models? And so for example, we have parts of our product that generate citations that don't need the largest models and there's opportunities to swap in GLM 5.2 and get cost or performance benefits. And so that's the first thing and doing this builds the muscle of serving open-source models alongside closed-source models.

第二步——模型路由： And then the second which has gotten uh very popular now is model routing. So there could be places where you can't naively swap an open-source model, but what you can do is on certain queries route to open-source models.

And then once you've done this, you have everything in place to start building the post-training flywheel. And once you start serving them in production and collecting feedback, and caveat here, you need to be very careful about what collecting feedback means. In our case, it does not mean training on customer data, but we do get feedback signals from our user testing and other things that can inform how we build future data sets and improve these models.

收尾：Moneyball 时刻

And that is our playbook for building a research lab. We think in the future every AI company—every company is going to need to become an AI company and figure out some version of this playbook. And I think despite that, most people are still betting against this playbook and application layer companies and the frontier ecosystem.

But—

But if we win on our budget with this team we'll change the game.

This is a scene from Moneyball, which hopefully you've seen this movie, where they're talking about we just won 20 games in a row. And Billy Beane says, "It doesn't matter. If we don't win the championship, no one's going to appreciate what we've done here." And the quote is, "But if we win on this budget with this team we'll have changed the game."

And I think now with the frontier ecosystem all of you have the opportunity to do the same.

Go change the game. Thank you.

[applause] Do you want to do Q&A? You okay with that? Yeah, of course. [snorts]

Q&A 环节

Q1：法律专家如何做 "live coding" 生成数据？

Yeah, I'm sorry, who's speaking? Um you talked about the challenges with having uh legal customers with very sensitive data sets and talked a little bit about your brother's lawyer and other in-house experts doing their version of live coding to produce the best work. What does that look Can you give us a little more detail about what that actually looks like?

Yeah, great question. So the biggest challenge with legal work is when you're at a large law firm, the type of work you're doing is, for example, you're representing a company doing an M&A. And you get a data room, which is all the contracts of the company you're trying to acquire, plus there's all these emails and meetings about the negotiation. None of that data is public, and so you don't have this analogy of like open source GitHub repos.

And the biggest challenge you run into when training is you can maybe find some of the final work product publicly, so like a public purchase agreement, but you don't have any of the input data. And historically it was very awkward to get a bunch of lawyers and say, "Hey, make a fake data room." Because these data rooms can be 10,000 contracts. They all need to fit together.

And so what Julio figured out is a very clever way to generate these data sets. And so he started from the rubric, and so he planted all these issues and said, "Here's all the problems in the data room and what I'm going to check for in a scenario, and then use that to generate the data room, so you can plant all of these issues like these contracts don't tie together, this contract's missing, and generate all of the data, and then we'll use Mercor Snorkel to make all the contracts look realistic, but now you have this input data set, and you can have the model generate like a diligence memo, and this way of checking it to say, "Hey, did you catch all of these issues that we know that are in here because we planted them?"

And obviously, depending on the work you're doing, you need to be clever of how you create it, but that to me feels like the really big unlock because now we can start doing this training that before you just you had this chicken-and-egg problem where we'd go to law firms and say, "Hey, we can train you this model on this client data." And they'd be like, "Okay, prove it." And we were like, "Show us the data." And they're like, "No." And so now you can prove it here. And now we have a lot of interest from law firms saying, "Oh, this is really interesting. Can we do it with our data?" Good question. Yeah.

Q2：招聘策略——如何与前沿实验室竞争人才？

Um so, we're also hiring for this. We're also building an implied AI there. Um from a hiring point of view, it's difficult for you to compete with researchers from Anthropic and the labs. Do you try and play that game or do you try and hire domain logic and lawyers and experience? And where has that worked and where has that not worked?

Yeah, I think this was one of the big mistakes I made like when we first started the company because I had worked in these labs and so I knew a lot of the folks and I would say, you know, come work with us and then they were getting these, you know, 100 million plus pay packages and we weren't at the scale where this made sense.

And so I'd say we're now just getting to the company size where I would say we're not competing with kind of the frontier talent, but there is increasingly folks that are doing PhDs, folks that don't want to work at large labs and so I think that is changing.

And then I think the second thing is a lot of why you needed that talent early on was it wasn't just doing the post training, it was you need to build the training infrastructure, the serving infrastructure, and all of those things combined, I think the talent to do that was like very unique. Like my old roommate was one of the folks who like ran post training at OpenAI and he was one of the best researchers I've ever worked with, but now you can use things like Fireworks, uh, tinker-like APIs, and so you don't need to build the training and serving infrastructure, and so I think it opens up the pool of talent and it feels very feasible to get some of this talent now. Yeah.

Q3：Rubric 设计——领域专家如何构建能挑战前沿模型的评分标准？

Uh, yeah, just another question on the benchmark creation. So, when you're like creating these rubrics, you still have to create them in such a way that they're separating them the frontier models and you have to do that with the experts themselves. Like how do you find like navigating that challenge? So, the experts kind of have to create this rubric knowing or like trying to figure out how the models are going to perform on them.

So, the What do you mean separating the—

Uh, I guess so, you have to create the rubrics that can adequately separate separate the front They they have to challenge the the frontier, right?

Yep.

Um, I guess how do you navigate that especially when you're like having these in-house legal experts who might not exactly know how to create that rubric designed for a model.

Yeah, that's a good—So, we think of it more as how do we make them realistic representations of the work our customers are doing? And I think part of why we picked the legal domain is if you just build a realistic client matter that these top firms are working on, like the frontier model still can't do this.

And I think the thing over the past 4 years we've built is So, for example, my brother was one of our first hires. And so, he's been working with the models for 4 years. And so, his intuition of how the models work, how to generate these data sets is incredibly good. And he's trained a bunch of lawyers to do this.

But I would say the focus is still more of how do we build a really realistic data room, and then rubrics for the diligence. And then when we run these models, we find, okay, there's gaps and there's there's room for improvement. But I think depends on the domain.

Uh God.

Q4：端到端管道——哪一层最容易出问题？

Hey, uh Shadeen from Box. Uh sorry, let me do that one and I'll— Great.

I mean, if you think Great talk, by the way. Um Ross from Trolysis. If you think of the uh your you know, the the end-to-end motion is like data generation, the environment piece, then there is the algorithm piece of like what how do we train, etc., the research piece, and then there's the infra piece. If something is not working, like anecdotally, what have you seen? Is it like operationally or dollar-wise or human hours-wise, is it usually in the data layer? Is it in the research layer? Or is it in the infra layer? And how do you go from there?

Who's orchestrating or debugging this whole end-to-end pipeline in some ways?

Yeah, this is This is a great question. I mean, this is a whole 'nother talk. Um I don't think there's a single thing. So, I would say what makes it easier for us is we found product-market fit. We have a product that's being used in production. And we did this largely with the closed-source models to start. And so, that let us build a lot of this kind of confidence in the thing is working end-to-end.

And so, we have a product, people are using it, people have been using it for many years. The models work in this way, we can monitor whether they're working in production. So, that was kind of the point of serving of you need a lot of this in place. And then, we have built the muscle of new models come out, how do we put those into the product, whether they're closed-source or open-source models.

And so, that's you can kind of think about the full cycle. And then, obviously we've done a bunch of work of like Harness engineering and context management and all of these things. And so, now you can think of post-training as one small input into this broader system. And so, we have our team post-train a model, and then you feed it into this broader system of, you know, you treat it just as another new model. And so, then you have all these signals of, you know, what's going wrong.

And so, I would say, but across these steps, there's kind of easy ways to gate it. So, if you start with the benchmarks and you post-train a model and it doesn't work well on those, then it's unlikely to go farther. If it works well on that, and then you put in a product, but someone uses the product and they say things feel weird because, for example, on the benchmarks we've built, there is still things that they definitely don't catch. Like, the best example is you can have a model that does very well on our benchmarks, but they've overfit to some degree, and then you put it in a more generic assistant-like product, and it kind of falls apart for when you go out of distribution. But, yeah, you need to have kind of all of the like stages and gates in place, and then it kind of becomes obvious where things are breaking. But, good question. Yeah.

Q5：开源基准的哲学取舍

Oh, I had a question. Hey, great to meet you. I'm from Rocks. Uh on the on the benchmark side, legal agent, I think you guys had Big Law before, Big Law bench, and then now legal agent of What's your philosophy on open sourcing the benchmark? Because if you open source, of course you're getting traction with other people trying out the benchmark, but the labs can help climb as well. And then if you close source, then there's a question of is this a real benchmark? So how do you how do you how do you how do you what's your philosophy?

I I think that's like a good tension that we think about. I would say even before we open source this benchmark, we already work closely with the labs. And so we share data with them to help them improve their models, which improved our product.

And so I would say the way we think about it is there is a huge advantage in your industry, particularly in legal, in terms of helping our customers understand how good different models are at different things. And so I think when we when I started Harvey I kind of had the intuition of oh, we'll just build the best model and then customers will be happy because it's the best. And it's very clear now that every customer has different preferences, different models are good at different things.

And then I think the second that I didn't anticipate is kind of how big the frontier ecosystem would become. And so now we have so many companies reaching out saying, "Hey, we have this new technique or we did this thing. Can we try it?" And before we just didn't have the bandwidth where we're just like we're working on these other things. But now with this open source data set we could be we can say, "Hey, go try this and if it works, then great. This is something that's interesting to invest in."

Um and then I think the way we think about it strategically is the valuable data for us is going to be helping law firms train their own systems and how they work on private data. And then we want to help everyone improve these systems with synthetic data and kind of some of the data we open source, but obviously a balance for the reasons that you mentioned. Yeah.

Q6：还有哪些开放问题需要帮助？

You mentioned finding a lab. What are the remaining open questions for for that you want help on?

Yeah, that's a great question. Um I would say one big challenge, one of the biggest challenges so we can generate these very realistic synthetic data sets, we can augment them with humans, but the distribution of that data still doesn't match our production distribution. And so I would say these data sets we're generating are somewhat future facing. And so what I mean by that is we can generate a really realistic data room, but right now our our product isn't used purely to do a due diligence. And so if a model does well on that, but then someone uses it to draft an email, maybe it doesn't work as well. And so I think there's still that gap because we can't look at customer data, and so how do you like bridge that gap? So I think that's to me that that's the biggest question on the data set side, and that one that one is challenging.

There is I think there is a bunch of questions around long context, for example, again with the diligence data, like the largest data room is 80 million tokens of context. Like the models don't do a good job of managing this context, and how do you train these models to operate in kind of these very complex environments? So I think that's another one of just there's still a big performance gap.

Um and I would say the third is continual learning—we're making good progress on how do we post train our post train models ourselves, but I think figuring out some form of continual learning is I think the end game here is not for us to build the best legal model. It's for us to help every law firm or enterprise customer customize it to the type of work they're doing. And so just thinking about how do you operationalize that, where you have a large law firm and every time they work on a client matter, their AI system gets better, but you're also protecting the client data. I think that's kind of one huge like both technical, operational, and like AI challenge that that is super interesting. Yeah.

Uh We're done. Or more? I can do more. I can Uh yeah, maybe last one.

Q7：如何与 Copilot、Coda 这类通用产品竞争？

Yeah. So, you know, you talked a lot about like, you know, the the the foundation readiness, right, to compete with Front Row Live, right, including your open source model, including your infrastructure kind of like Ruby. From product perspective, right, Coda as cloud product, they're general product, right? So, from product perspective, how do you guys compete with the, you know, Coda as cloud workflow, methodology, efficiency? How do you think about that?

Yeah. I think the big shift that we're thinking about is like our original product and then things like Coda's Coda Work are very individual-focused products, and so they're about individual productivity. And increasingly, the product we're building is about organizational productivity.

And so, if you think of a large law firm, the problem they're trying to solve is not how do I make my individual lawyers more productive. The problem they're trying to solve is I have 10,000 clients. I'm working on client projects for all of them. I need to make sure that all those client projects go very well, and then I can also do them in a way that's profitable.

And so, a lot of the infrastructure we're building for the law firms is how do you operate that machine? And when you start thinking about an individual client project, most of the challenge is not how do I draft this one section. It's I'm working on this project for 6 months. I have a team of 20, 30 people across the firm. I need to coordinate all of them. I need to make sure that I'm coordinating all the outside parties. And so, a lot of it is starting to look like project management that is orchestrating these humans and these agents.

And that's at the, I would say, at the team level. And then, if you think about it at the organization level, now you have a thousand of these projects, and you need to start thinking about resource allocation, what am I billing, what am I pitching? And then with enterprises, it's even more complicated where kind of a Fortune 500, they're working with a thousand law firms. They have a thousand people internally. What are all the systems to kind of start work is trading that work?

And so I would say the simple answer is just, and this is I think historically what enterprise has has done is how do you just go hyper vertical into your domain in a way that the horizontal products won't. Yeah, good question.

Thank you, Gabe. That was an iconic talk. Thank you for joining us. [applause]
