item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一个反直觉的观察：公共事业板块的"隐藏身份"

小涛推荐 XLU（公共事业）作为防守板块，这看起来是常规操作——但藏着一个巨大的悖论：公共事业本是"寡妇股"、退休金标配的低波动资产，如今却因为 VST、CEG 这类核电/天然气公司被数据中心绑架，摇身一变成了"AI 影子股"。

这意味着一件让人后背发凉的事：你以为自己在买防守，其实你在加杠杆做 AI。当 XLU 的 RSI 跌到 33 的历史性超卖区间，市场正在给你一个错觉——它把"最防守的板块"和"最激进的叙事"打包成同一个 ETF，而多数人不会察觉这层身份互换。这就像 2006 年之前买房地美的债券——它挂着"政府隐性担保"的标签，实际敞口却是次贷。

跨领域连接：英特尔增发与"信号博弈论"

小涛提到一个细节被他自己都感到"意外"——两三周前财报会议上 CFO 只是含糊说"如果业绩好可能 tap the market"，结果两周就闪电增发 150 亿（甚至可能加码到 200 亿）。

这里有一个从扑克博弈论（Signaling Theory）借过来的洞察：管理层的信号密度和时间差，本身就是信息。CFO 越是临时改口，越说明中间发生了不能在公开场合披露的"离散事件"——大概率是一份还未官宣的大订单（可能是政府/主权基金/或某个超大规模客户）。陈立武"没订单不加资本开支"的公开承诺，反过来把这次增发变成了一份自我泄密的通告：他等于告诉市场"订单已经在路上，只是还不能说"。

这和扑克里的"反向诉说"（reverse tell）一模一样——最强的手牌往往通过最反常的时间节奏泄露，而不是通过语言。

让人意外的系统性真相：小涛的"预测框架"其实在自我进化

表面上，这期是常规的市场展望更新。但如果你把他 7 月初的四点展望和这次的修订叠在一起看，会发现一个元层次的模式：他正在从"预测幅度"转向"预测节奏"。

  • 7 月初：预测下半年会有 7-10% 回调（预测幅度）
  • 现在：这波已经走完，剩下 4 个半月还有 5-7% 的回调（预测频率和节奏）

这个转变意味着什么？意味着在 AI 主导的市场里，波动的振幅正在被压缩，但波动的频次在增加——因为流动性、宏观噪音、Kevin Warsh 这类政治变量正在把市场切成更碎的时间段。这和物理学里"高频低振幅"的现象非常像：当系统输入了更多的能量（散户+杠杆+期权+AI 交易），能量不会消失，只会转化为更高频次的抖动。

一个不易察觉的推论：这也解释了为什么"防守板块"（XLU）现在这么值钱——不是因为熊市要来，而是因为碎片化震荡的市场，波动率本身成了最贵的商品。你买 XLU 不是买"跌得少"，你是在做空整个市场的"高频抖动噪音"。

📝 转录文本

开场与议程

各位观众大家好，欢迎来到一个不单只聊新闻、且尽量想做到日更的专业美股频道。我是市场分析师小涛。

今天这期内容首先回顾一下周一资产价格的这个走势，然后其中里边有一个板块，我认为我们是可以关注的，这个板块其实防守属性相对会偏强一些。然后我对于周三的 CPI 数据去做一个展望，包括聊一下周一的和英特尔相关的一条新闻——英特尔进行增发，那对于英特尔来说意味着什么，包括和大家一起去看一下英特尔的一个资产负债表，看一下他们现在的这个杠杆比率。

最后还有另外一点，是我在 7 月初的时候有做过今年下半年的一个指引，我们先快速地回顾一下我当时所做的一些展望，然后展望里边本身有一点我想去做一个更新，主要是针对市场下跌这种情况，好吗？

那我就废话不多说了，直接开始。在开始之前，大家记得留言点赞加转发，让我们一起在留言区里面继续人类大战机器人，哈，开玩笑。

一、周一资产价格回顾

先来看一下资产价格的走势。周一的市场非常的有意思——你很罕见地会看到美元指数上涨，美债收益率上涨，美股几乎是在横盘的，非常小幅度的这个下跌；同时黄金出现上涨。通常来说美元指数上涨，黄金是下跌的，但周一的黄金还是相对比较强一些。再同时，原油又出现了一个上涨。几乎周一所有的资产价格都在上涨，VIX 也出现了 3.8% 的上涨，IGV 也出现了 2.4% 的上涨。

那 IGV 继续保持强势。我们看一下 QTD，就是整个 7 月份到现在为止这个走势——7 月份加 8 月份前几天的这几个交易日： - 标普 500 反弹幅度非常大，3.4% - 纳指相对弱一些，1.5% - 道指 3.2%

那道指和纳指、道指和标普都破了新高了。黄金上涨了 9.5%，原油上涨了 19%。你看，即使在原油上涨的情况下，标普仍然可以出现上涨；黄金仍然可以出现上涨；而且即使是在美债收益率出现上涨的情况下，黄金一样出现上涨。IGV 上涨了 16%，比特币上涨了 9.3%。那记住这些标的的一些涨幅。

二、值得关注的板块：公共事业（XLU）

然后我们回顾一下 7 月初的时候，我做了今年下半年的一个展望。展望里边——我稍后我说，我前面说展望里边有一点我是需要更新的——有一个板块是我想这边聊的。

公共事业在周一出现了 1.1% 的下跌，YTD 到现在为止，公共事业板块只上涨了 1%。 那比公共事业还要差的屈指可数：通讯服务相对差一些，跌了 2.8%，非必需品消费跌了 0.2%，必需品消费也涨了 9.4%。

今天周一晚上我在 a APP 里边做会员直播的时候，有人问我，他说能不能现在去布局一些非、呃、必需品消费啊。你说如果要防守属性的话，公共事业防守属性 OK，那必需品消费也防守，但是你看一下必需品消费，今年到现在为止上涨的幅度其实已经不小了。

为什么关注公共事业？

那我之所以去聊到公共事业：

第一点，公共事业板块，它是防守属性比较强的。那在这一个板块里边，如果指数出现回调的话，它是一个非常好的一个防守属性的一个标的。

另外一点，如果我们去看 XLU 它的一个技术走势的话，我这边是日 K 线，日 K 线截止到周一的收盘，RSI 差不多在 33 左右。那回过头去看过去一年的走势，其实 XLU 从来没有看到过 RSI 是进入超卖的，所以我们可以理解为 33 或者 34 已经在属于一个比较超卖的区间。所以 XLU 现在已经是在一个处于超卖的一个区间。

成分股：VST 的机会

如果我们去看 XLU 里面的一些成分股，NEE、VST、CEG——正巧 VST 和 CEG 这两个标题是我前段时间持有的，然后我把 CEG 卖掉了，换到了 VST。现在 VST 仓位差不多百分之四不到一些。

那 VST 这个仓位，我上周在聊它的一个财报里边我已经详细聊过了，我今天我就不多做展开。那我认为其恰恰好，整个 ETF 的整个板块现在是在一个超卖的区间，然后基本面我又看好，然后技术面个股的技术面现在又是在一个超卖的区间，估值这个角度也合理。

所以现在我认为像 VST 这类的标的，我认为某种程度技术面、估值、基本面出现了一个共振，现在是一个非常好的一个——不说加仓吧，起码是一个非常好建仓的一个区间： - 一来市场如果出现回调，它是一个比较好的一个防守板块，它下跌的幅度也不会非常的大； - 市场如果出现反弹的话，那 XLU 整个这一个板块，我对它的一个期待是它有可能会出现反弹； - 同时 VST 这个标的本身，它又是和数据中心是相关的，那数据中心如果发展得好，对于 VST 来说也是一个利好。

三、下半年展望回顾与更新

好吗，然后回顾一下，在 7 月初的时候做了下半年的这个展望，我主要聊了四点。

第一点：纳指调整幅度更新

那么第一点，我期待是今年下半年会出现纳指 7% 至 10% 的这个调整，是由硬件板块所带领的。那其实截止到现在，我认为这一波调整已经结束了，就起码我们……我认为这波调整在身后，因硬件板块所带领嘛。那只从最高点也回调了应该差不多 10% 吧，但是这个最高点可能是从 6 月份算起。

那有人就问我，那你是不是期待，那么今年接下去的四个半月里边还会有一波 10% 的这个调整？那我的一个回答是：可能没有这、没有那么的期待，或者概率不会那么的高。但是我期待今年下半年可能还会有百分之八九十、百分之九十的可能性，纳指会从最高点回调 5% 至 7%。

某种程度就像我在年终的时候做这个展望是一样的，我说这是一个不是说它一个概率的事，它是一个大概率的事件，就它是正常情况下股市都会发生的一些事情。而且你短期之内如果涨得越高、走得越好，最接下去就越有可能会出现调整。

那所以当时我做出这样的一个展望，我觉得它是市场里、正常市场里面都会发生的情况。上半年 3 月份出现了下跌，然后下半年某一个时间点再出现 7-10 的这个回调，非常的正常。一年里边出现两次 10% 左右的回调经常看到，很少会看到——就当然有小概率的事件，你会看到只有一次的回调，但大概率情况下我们都会看到两次这种调整。股市不可能一年之内持续每个月都出现上涨，不可能的。所以对于剩下的四个多月的时间里面，我认为纳指再出现 5%~7% 的回调是一个大概率的事件。

那这一点是我需要在年终做展望的时候，这一点是需要做更新的。

第二点：仓位平衡与大科技反弹

然后剩下我我基本上没有任何的更新，我还是持有这样的一些观点。我说需要平衡一些仓位，那当时我在 7 月初的时候，我说去配一些医疗板块，去配一些大科技。我说上一年市场就开始担心 AI 这一块的落地，那今年财报已经证明了，但市场仍然去回馈那些收支票的。我说市场当时非常的短视。

嗯，然后这一两周之前，随着呃、微软，然后随着亚马逊的财报出来之后，大科技的反弹就反弹得非常好，微软从最低点反弹 40% 了。当时我也说了，软件板块相当的便宜。

英特尔的话，我说我不减仓，该减仓的时候 5 月 6 月已经减完仓了。减完仓之后呢，对于如果仓位大的人的话，还是应该去做好这个移动指引，那所以 7 月份的回调其实是比较厉害的。

第三点：牛市仍在，宏观噪音持续

第三点，我认为牛市还是在的，主要是以 AI 为主，ROI 那么关注 EPS 这一块的增速，ROI 就是资金回报了的投资回报，现金流为王，软件；然后会有宏观这一块的噪音。

我认为宏观这一块的噪音现在是在正在进行时，ING。从 6 月份当初一次会议之后，表现出了非常鸽派的这个态度。当时很多人和我争，他说你看呀，那天股市是出现反弹的，但接下去你看一下，6 月份美联储会议之后，标普有没有出现回调，纳指有没有出现回调？那这个时间点基本上就是从那次会议之后，那一天上涨之后就开始回调，然后整个 7 月份也回调，纳指的回调幅度会更大一些。

但是 7 月份的那一次美联储会议偏鸽了，就是从 6 月份的鹰派的这个态度然后偏鸽了，往鸽派的这个方向去。所以我们看到股市也出现了反弹，黄金也出现了反弹。啊，所以接下去就市场还会有一个反复，因为确实是在了解凯文·沃什一个过程之中，我自己也在了解他的一个过程之中。

然后宏观这一点、宏观这一块的噪音还有另外一点，就是在上周我和大家分享财政部这块，贝森特和日本财政部那块去救日元这个行为本身，最终的目的是为了去压制美国这边美债这块的一个长端收益率，他不希望看到美国国债的长端收益率继续出现上涨，所以这对于市场来说其实是一个利好。

啊，最后一点，IPO 这一块的一个风险。因为最近这段时间关于这两家大模型公司 IPO 到底什么时候上，今年会不会上，一直在反反复复。对，如果说推到明年的话，那 IPO 的这个风险就降低；那如果还是放在今年的话呢，这个风险还是在今年下半、今……接下去的四个半月里面，我们会看到 IPO 本身对于市场是一个抽水的一个行为。

第四点：AI Agent 落地进展更新

第四点，AI agent 落地比我们想象中的要慢。那这一点其实有些更新了。那么上一周，上周五的时候我说听完了 Cloudflare 的一个财报之后，我看到了 AI Agent 这一块的进展，一个 progress，它是有开始往前进的，就整个过程仍然是在往前进。只是在过去 6 个月里面，我们聊 AI Agent 这个话题聊得会相对会少一些。那但是从一些其他公司财报里面，我们是可以看到 AI Agent 这一块还是在往前进的。

然后我说黄金可以长期布局，比特币也进入一个加仓区间，那对于这两点的话，我仍然保持相同的看法。

四、英特尔增发解读

前面讲到了英特尔，那正好周一的时候有一条英特尔的消息——英特尔接下去将会增发了，增发的这个体量是 150 亿美金。我看到最新的消息，因为需求非常的高，需求好像是 1000 亿美金，然后英特尔好像准备这一次增发的一个体量抬高到 200 亿美金。

那这一个增发的行为本身是自英特尔 1971 年以来首次公开募股。这就说明在过去这段时间英特尔走得有多么的差。

增发背后可能的信号

但不过说实话，因为他们刚发完财报嘛，其实上一次财报会议里边有特地有分析师问了他们的 CFO 这个问题，但是当时他们 CFO 的一个回答里面，他说如果我们公司做的业绩做得非常的好，我们有可能会 tap the market，我们有可能会进行增发，但是没想到在短短的两三周的时间里面就进行增发。这一个决定本身确实是我没有想到，起码在上一次会议里面没有、完全没有透露这个信号，我有点、我我我觉得我有点意外。上次如果透露那个信号的话，也不见得是一件坏事，当时的价格比现在要高，对吧。

当然，这背后另外一个代表什么？另外一个代表有可能，我只是说小概率有可能在过去的一两周之内，接下去英特尔有一个大的一个订单，是在过去的一两周之内所敲定下来。那这个大的订单有可能在接下去通过基本面、通过新闻的这些方式所呈现出来。因为陈立武说过，他说如果说我没有看到确切的订单进来之前，我不会去增加这个资本开支。所以陈立武在资本开支这一块是非常的保守，那现在进行增发，增发就是为了资本开支，为了主主体的这个业务，所以增发本身背后其实代表了有可能基本面这一块仍然是在变得越来越好，甚至有一个非常大的一个利好。

融资方式对资产负债表的影响

在时间线上，通常来说当一家公司选择去融资的时候，其实对于资产负债表是有影响的。那很多时候从公司这个角度，他们有两种融资的方法：一种是举债，一种是直接增发。那举债的话，对于债务会有影响，对于杠杆比例会有影响；而如果增发的话，其实对于杠杆比例是一个利好。

英特尔资产负债表快览

我们来看一些数据。因为资产负债表其实我不大带大家看，我们稍微看一下。这是英特尔的资产负债表：

  • 短期现金：368 亿美金（thirty six, thirty seven billion）
  • PP&E（property, plant and equipment）：112 个 billion——113 个 billion——1130 亿美金

然后这边这个数据挺有意思，就 PP&E，property plant and equipment，这其实就是他们手里的这些半导体的一些仪器，包括 EUV 啊，包括 DUV 这些仪器总共值多少钱。这一个数据就是我用来去衡量英特尔方具（Foundry）这一块的一个业务。

我当时给他 Foundry 这一块的业务的一个估值，就是他现在设备有值多少钱、这些设备就是多少钱、这家公司就 Foundry 这一块的业务就值多少钱。如果你去看台积电的话，台积电也有这个数据，也有 PP&E，台积电的估值是 PP&E 的可能十几倍吧，13 倍、14 倍吧。但是英特尔因为它方具这一块是亏钱的，所以我就当做他方具这一块的业务，最差的情况下，他完全剥离出去，剥离出去的话，他的手里的这些硬件值多少钱，他就卖多少钱。那当然了，你再保守一些的话，在这个硬件的基础上、在手里 EUV、DUV 这些硬件的基础上，你再可以给他打个折扣，打个六折、打个七折，以折扣价卖出去也是可以的。但是无论如何，他方具这一块的业务是值钱的，最低的话怎么也得是 70 至 80 个 billion。那么在 112 个 billion 的这个基础上，给他打一个折扣。

负债端与杠杆比率

然后我们看一下在负债端这一块。负债端的话主要是看 Long term debt，长期这一块的债务总共是 47 个 billion。那看到这边基本上很多时候我们会有一个概念，就是它转短期这一块的现金、手里的现金有 37 个 billion，长端这一块的负债 47 个基点，那就……因为 47 个基点它会有利息这一块的支出，而手里的现金流有 37 个基点，那足以去应付利、利息这一块的支出了。

然后有另外一个可以去衡量公司杠杆的这个比例，我们叫做 debt to equity ratio。举个例子就是你把你所有的债务、短期的债务、长期的债务全部加在一起，然后去除你的资本、除以你的 equity。那英特尔现在这一个刚刚过去的这一个季度是 48%，其实过去几个季度也不是非常的高。

Debt to equity ratio 这一个比率本身： - 如果是在 1 以下的话，杠杆比例属于是偏低的； - 在 1 以上、在 2 以上的话，就属于杠杆比率是偏高的。

就很简单，就我举个例子：比如说如果是 1 的话，就杠杆比、如果是 debt to equity 优秀是 1 的话，什么意思？就是比如说我今天去开一家公司，我自己投了 100 块钱下去，100 块钱本身你觉得你 100 块钱的话，你没有办法把你业务扩张出来，所以你投了 100 块钱下去，建立一家公司，100 块钱可以作为现金流，可以去用来做支付啊等等。然后你再去借了 100 块钱，就是你债务本身是借了 100 块钱，那也就是你的债务除以你的 equity——你自己投进去的 100 块钱就是 equity，就是 1:1 的这个杠杆。如果我花自己投了 100 块钱，去借了 200 块钱，那这个杠杆比例是多少？2:1，就是二倍。

而英特尔现在是多少？英特尔是现在是 48%，算它 50% 吧。那也就是说你每投 100 块钱，他债务借了多少？借了是 50 块钱。所以英特尔的这一个杠杆比例其实是在一个非常健康的位置。

那对于很多企业来说，并不是没有债务就一定是一家好企业，以及很多时候从 corporate finance 这个角度去看，CFO 去承担一部分的债务，从一个效率上来说不见得是一件坏事。

五、周三 CPI 展望

最后我们快速地讲一下周三的 CPI 数据。可能有一部分人有些担心。当然我这边全部是引用彭博 Anna Wang 这个团队他们所给的一些指引。

主要有两组数据我们需要关注的。啊，周三和周四，周三是 CPI，周四是 PPI。

周三 CPI 数据——一组数据关注了核心 CPI： - 市场预期：环比增速 0.2% - 彭博预期：0.1% - 上一个月数据：0%

所以他们的预期是比市场预期要低了 0.1%。

周四 PPI 数据： - 市场预期：0.3% - 彭博预期：0.3%

所以彭博 Anna Wang 这个团队预期 CPI 将会比市场预期要好，然后 PPI 是符合市场的预期。

结语与活动

好吧，那今天这期内容就到这边。然后最后是今天带给大家的活动：福来资付图母母（Futu / Moomoo）—— - 美国市场：这边开户且入金最高可以获得价值 1000 美金英伟达的赠股，闲置资金最高可以获得年化 8.1% 的回报。 - 加拿大市场：这边现在正在举行一个我们这个频道的独家福利，通过开户且入金，最高获得 100 只免费的股票，直接抽免费的股票抽到手软，闲置资金最高年化 6% 的回报，然后前 30 天是 0 佣金交易。

大家如果感兴趣的话，可以在置顶的留言里边找到开户的链接。那今天这期内容到这边，我们下期见。

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 一个反直觉的观察：公共事业板块的"隐藏身份"
小涛推荐 XLU（公共事业）作为防守板块，这看起来是常规操作——但**藏着一个巨大的悖论**：公共事业本是"寡妇股"、退休金标配的低波动资产，如今却因为 VST、CEG 这类核电/天然气公司被数据中心绑架，摇身一变成了"AI 影子股"。
这意味着一件让人后背发凉的事：**你以为自己在买防守，其实你在加杠杆做 AI**。当 XLU 的 RSI 跌到 33 的历史性超卖区间，市场正在给你一个错觉——它把"最防守的板块"和"最激进的叙事"打包成同一个 ETF，而多数人不会察觉这层身份互换。这就像 2006 年之前买房地美的债券——它挂着"政府隐性担保"的标签，实际敞口却是次贷。
## 跨领域连接：英特尔增发与"信号博弈论"
小涛提到一个细节被他自己都感到"意外"——两三周前财报会议上 CFO 只是含糊说"如果业绩好可能 tap the market"，结果两周就闪电增发 150 亿（甚至可能加码到 200 亿）。
这里有一个**从扑克博弈论（Signaling Theory）借过来的洞察**：管理层的信号密度和时间差，本身就是信息

item.title: [a16z] Kavak's Playbook for Rebuilding a Company Around AI
item.dc:creator: a16z
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

从「交易公司」到「关系公司」：一次会计科目的物种变异

大多数人把 Kavak 的转型看成「用 AI 替换人」，但真正发生的是会计范式的更换。旧 Kavak 计算的是"卖了多少辆车、买了多少刹车片"——这是流量指标；新 Kavak 计算的是"1000 万客户的终身价值可激活百分比"——这是存量指标。这与银行从"利差收入"转向"钱包份额（share of wallet）"的进化完全同构。AI 的真正颠覆，不是加速做同样的事，而是让企业第一次有能力承担关系型经济的记账成本——过去只有私人银行家能给顶级客户做的事，现在可以在每一个买二手车的墨西哥打工人身上执行。这是一种"关系经济学的民主化"，而非"劳动力自动化"。

「一客户一 agent」的隐藏拓扑：Kavak 其实在造一个"经济体"，不是一家公司

真正让我意外的是 Ali 说的这句话："过去 4000 年，经济价值由组织而非个人创造，所以要自我改进的应该是组织"。这句话看似平常，其实颠覆了当前整个 RSI（递归自我改进）叙事——硅谷都在赌"更聪明的模型"，Kavak 在赌"更聪明的组织回路"。

跨领域连接来了：这个架构在生物学上是黏菌（slime mold）的拓扑结构——每个 agent 是一个独立细胞核，共享记忆但独立漫游，遇到问题分泌信号（call human API），成功路径被强化。这也解释了为什么他们放弃了「多智能体+图/工作流」——那是神经系统的隐喻（自上而下、结构化），而黏菌式架构是免疫系统的隐喻（分布式、目标驱动、无中枢）。当模型智能超过某个阈值，图结构反而会限制智能表达，就像给爱因斯坦发一张流程图让他做物理。这也是为什么 Opus 4.5 出来后他愿意烧掉两年的架构——不是架构错了，是架构的"智能天花板"低于新模型的"智能地板"。

「Cuernavaca 的 AI 市长」：一次伪装成商业实验的政治哲学实验

Ali 轻描淡写地提到"我们在 Cuernavaca 部署了一个 AI CEO，六周内利润提升 50%"——这条信息如果放在《经济学人》头版，会震动整个管理学界。但更深的含义他没说破：AI CEO 的可行性，实际上在质疑现代科层制存在的合法性根基。

Weber 论证过科层制的必要性来自"人的认知带宽有限"——所以需要分层、需要中层管理者做信息压缩。当一个实体可以同时记住 1000 万客户的每一次互动、每天生成 20 万个专用 agent、且不会疲劳——中层管理者的存在论基础就消失了。Kavak 的"扁平化+资深团队"不是管理时尚，而是科层制的物种退化。

这里有一个几乎没人在讨论的悖论：Ali 说"训练每个人到 Jedi Academy"——但如果 AI CEO 都能跑，为什么还要人类？答案藏在他没明说的一句话里："仍然需要人类的岗位是与物理世界相关的"。具身性（embodiment）成为了新的稀缺资产——不是智力、不是判断、不是策略，而是有一双手能拧螺丝。这是 200 年来第一次，劳动力市场的价值曲线可能会倒转——蓝领的物理直觉将比白领的分析能力更难被替代。Ratatouille 里的 mouse-chef 不是隐喻，是新经济的组织图。

一个反常识的操作原则：踩油门之前先造刹车

Ali 讲了一句令人意外的话："I like to move extremely fast, but in order to move fast, you need to have brakes." 他们在 evals 上花的工程时间、token 和金钱与建 agent 相当。这与整个创投圈"MVP、速度至上"的文化正相反——evals 才是新时代的产品，agent 只是它的副产品。这也是为什么大多数企业 AI 试点失败：他们把 evals 当作"事后测试"，而不是"事前刹车系统"，结果只能龟速前进以避免爆雷。Kavak 的悖论式启示：想让 AI 更快，先造更好的评估器；想让组织更激进，先造更精密的反馈回路。

📝 转录文本

Kavak's Playbook for Rebuilding a Company Around AI

a16z Podcast — 对话 Ali Masa（Kavak AI 负责人）

开场：几个爆炸性数字

"I'm investing more today in tokens than in knowledge workers. We could build superhuman agents. This means that by every dimension that matters, our agents would outperform the best human if we had ever hired."

"The most ambitious companies listening to this will decide to follow suit, which is you decided to build an agent per customer." "Yes. Every day between 100 and 200,000 agents get instantiated specifically for this customer with its own virtual machine."

"There's a lot of people worried about how the organizations of the future are going to look like and the role that humans are going to play. If you haven't faced fear before, if you haven't felt it, then you haven't tried AI."

"We launched a program inside Kavak that's called the Jedi Academy. From the CEO to like AI engineers to mechanics, we train everyone and after 6 weeks, they launch state-of-the-art agents to production."

"What advice do you have to future founders or first-time founders that might be listening? What works right now is..."

一、嘉宾介绍与背景

Welcome back to the ACC podcast. Uh today we have Ali Masa, the head of AI at Kavak. We're going to discuss today the transformation that Ali led within Kavak to turn it into an AI native company. Thank you Ali for being with us today.

Thanks for having me.

Before starting at Kavak, you were running a company called Oppy Analytics.

That's right.

And you were very much into AI before ChatGPT. You want to tell us a little bit about that journey?

Yes, yes, of course. Well, we called it machine learning back then. It was a different family of algorithms and we founded a company with this very like ambitious vision that new machine learning models would be so powerful that they could solve any complex problem. This was pre-transformers, right? This was like 2013. So we started building the company that way and I think we were like 10 years ahead of time. But we built a great company. We served like Fortune 500 companies around like risk algorithms, logistics forecasting, marketing — but really the power of what Transformers and then like the ChatGPT moment, when it arrived, made things very clearly that we could now build a whole new company and way of building companies. And we joined Kavak and Carlos to build that.

二、Kavak 是做什么的？

Amazing. All right. So we're going to spend the bulk of this podcast talking about exactly how you've identified Kavak. But maybe just to start, what does Kavak do and what is your role there?

Kavak started out as a use case as a used car marketplace. So we buy cars, we refurbish them, and then we sell them and finance them. But to do that, we also had to build a fintech and a logistics company and the Carfax and basically all the infrastructure for this to work didn't exist in LatAm. So we had to build everything vertically so we could serve our customers the right way.

三、架构核心：一个客户，一个专属 agent

I'm going to sort of start with the framing of what the architecture looks like. So a consumer comes in and says "I want to sell my car" — like how many agents do they touch? What's the harness look like? Ground us in how you design this.

Right. So we bet the company in transforming to a company run by agents. The questions we ask ourselves is: how would we build Kavak in 2035 with Fable 10 or GPT 10 level intelligence? And actually that company looks very different than what we had built or what we had back then.

So when a customer comes in right now, an agent will get spawned specifically for this customer with its own virtual machine. It'll remember years of interaction of this customer with Kavak — what they visited in the web page, or a call they had two years ago. Remember everything in its memory. Come up with a strategy and set a long-term goal to maximize the lifetime value of this customer and do whatever it takes to make the customer happy and convert them into all our different products across time.

And this is a completely new and groundbreaking architecture at scale. I think because people are still building multi-agent systems with experts, and we realized to bet that long-running agents with hard goals, not just workflows, could maximize our customers' satisfaction and obviously their lifetime value.

四、三个关键决策：不是加 AI，而是重构公司

Awesome. Okay. So we're going to jump to the nuances. But maybe versus many companies that say "hey we want to be agentic" and they try some workflows, you guys took the "just rip" — like we had to make this work. You had to downsize dramatically, it didn't work for a year.

Right.

So do you want to talk through — obviously you had to tune a lot of things to make that work. Like describe the harness at that time and what models you were using and sort of specifically...

Yeah, so there were like three main decisions that we had to make.

决策 1：重新设计整个公司，而不是往旧结构里塞 AI

The first — and this is where I think many companies are stuck right now — is the first instinct is: "okay, let's adopt AI." And you basically leave your structure as it is and just give ChatGPT to your team, and then there are no efficiencies, your customers have the same problems, and nothing happens.

So you need to redesign your whole company around the agents and around the future capabilities. And this means really rebuilding most of your APIs, rebuilding your systems so the agents can use them to perform.

决策 2：打造"超人级 agent"

Then you need to start generating the data and the feedback loops to fine-tune these agents. The only way to really make them work is if you teach them. And how do you teach them? You put them out in the open. You put them in front of customers. You get that data. You get those evals and then you train your agents.

And this is the second bet that we made — that we could build superhuman agents. This means that by every dimension that matters like conversion, lifetime value, customer experience, our agents would outperform the best human we had ever hired. And we put them in front of the hardest problems.

决策 3：从"交易公司"变为"关系公司"

Finally, you start to change how you measure the success of the company. Kavak was a transactional company. We used to measure how many cars we bought, how many cars we sold, how many brake pads we needed to buy.

And we moved to a relational company where now I have 10 million customers in my database and I have agents assigned to most of them with the task of maximizing their lifetime value. Now, we're selling cars and personal loans and very high ticket items. So just activating 1% of this customer base — it's hundreds of millions of dollars if we do it the right way.

So it's a bet that made sense for us because of our industry, because of the ticket, and because at the end of the day, customers need to build trust with a company because they're buying a used car. And the way to build trust is to know them and to plan and nurture a long-term relationship.

五、Evals 才是刹车：为什么评估决定速度

Ali, I just wanted to double click on something. You know, "evals over agent demos."

Yeah.

You probably get pitched a lot of new agents and it's never been easier to build things. But one of the questions is: how do you go about evaluating this? Because not everybody tests them across 90% of the customer interactions to see if they're really working. And I believe about 98% of the interactions are now handled by agents?

Yes. Totally. So to give you a sense of the scale: 96% of all interactions are handled by agents. So no humans there. 95% of all transactions are completely handled by agents. Obviously, you meet a human when you pick up your car — there's someone physically there to give you the keys. But the rest of the experience of the journey is handled by an agent.

Every day between 100 and 200,000 agents get instantiated in a day. They wake up, they work sometimes for three minutes, sometimes for eight hours, sometimes for three days, and they set an alarm clock for their next task and they go back to sleep. So the scale of this is just amazing and it's working.

想开得快，先造刹车

Now, how do you get this to work at scale? And the answer, you mentioned it, is evals. I like to move extremely fast, but in order to move fast, you need to have brakes, right? Imagine a car — you'll hit on the gas just if you have the right brakes. And AI is super powerful. And I've seen many companies get this wrong because they try to go slow because they don't have the right brakes.

So I thought about it the other way around: how fast can we go? Well, it depends on the quality of our evals. So a good rule of thumb here is we spend about the same amount of time, engineer time, tokens, and money on building the evals as on building the agents. And this is how you get better and better and better — not letting evals be an afterthought.

衡量真正的结果，不要虚荣指标

What do we measure first and foremost? Like the results for the business. If my customer is happy, they'll buy a car, they'll get their loan approved, they'll sell a car to us — and that's the first check. Did it convert? And that's where most things break. I see companies measuring number of calls or minutes during the call, or some superficial KPIs that give you some information but that doesn't really work. The important thing is: did this customer convert? Is it bringing value to the customer? And is the customer happy to re-engage with us after a while?

Once you get those evals connected, then it's just optimizing the right agentic architecture and giving the agent skills to scale this and cater to millions of customers.

六、Agent 真的能卖车吗？

Some companies still feel a little bit risk averse about putting agents in front of customers and being able to perform the highest leverage task, which in your case would be selling. Do your agents really sell to customers?

Yes. So we never built customer support or customer service agents. We built sales agents. It's extremely hard to sell a car in Latin America. Imagine someone wanting to buy a car — they can choose amongst 20,000 SKUs. Then they need to pick financing and go through the financing process, insurance and coverage. And then they're probably trading in their car, so we need to quote that car.

So it's a process that if someone does it — or the way Kavak did it back in 2020, 2021 — you need to be extremely good at 15 different things and have 15 different experts in 15 different teams. And usually the person would go and speak with the expert in financing, the expert in car advisory, the expert in buying, the expert in insurance, and they'll build a package and buy a car. That's extremely hard to do.

But the first thing we did was: okay, can we get an agent to be better than the expert in each of these things, and then put it together and have a mega expert that's an expert in insurance, financing, etc.? And that's who we put in front of the customer.

结果：NPS 翻三倍，转化率翻 2.1 倍

The experience for the customer is amazing. We tripled NPS and customer satisfaction score by putting the agent in front of the customer. And at first it converted 50% more than our human team, and now it's converting over 2.1x more.

So it's a completely different concept.

Your agents are better sellers.

Totally better. And you get this right because they're experts and they're infinitely patient and they know all your history and they can plan for the long term and they never get tired. If they make a mistake, they learn it, and the next day not just them, but the other 200,000 agents will have learned from that mistake. So that's the feedback loop that we engaged and that's showing in the growth and results and satisfaction of our customers.

七、金融服务：三分钟批车贷

The world has gotten comfortable with "AI can do customer service." It's still very hard to do well. But there's still a view that customers aren't going to want to buy expensive things from AI — and you are proving them wrong.

The next layer on that is: well, you're not actually going to be able to do regulated financial services end to end with AI. But if you walk through what you're doing, you are underwriting a thin or no file customer, pricing them correctly, doing servicing. So maybe talk through how did you write the evals to get comfortable with that? And versus, I don't know, going to a bank branch or even a fintech — how is that experience?

Yes. So much better.

The first financial product that we launched was a car loan. Usually in Mexico and in some emerging markets, it'll take two months or more to get a car loan approved. We usually approve it in under three minutes. Which is pretty cool because we have all this data around the customer and the car. And if the customer can't pay for the car anymore, they'll just return it to us and we can give them a cheaper car and then they pay a smaller amount each month and they get out of the water — which is amazing about the vertical integration of the business.

But then when we started launching other financial products, we realized that this is a very important decision for the customer. Like they usually take three to four months to make up their mind on buying a car and getting a loan, or getting a personal loan — a large personal loan that we also do. So if you get to know your customer throughout this process and make the process easy for them, then just your conversion and retention metrics start going through the roof.

It's not just the transaction. It's understanding each customer personally and getting them to convert when they're ready with a very deep personalization of the interest rate, the risk, the max amount of the loan — in a way that makes sense for the portfolio as a whole, obviously, but that's optimized to the risk level and probably the other offers that the customer is getting.

八、AI CEO 实验：Cuernavaca 市六周利润 +50%

What is an example of maybe a hard-to-design area for evals, or one where you had to spend extra amount of time — given the fact that there's real money, PII at risk?

Yeah. So when we decided to redesign the company around AI, you ask the question: okay, is AI going to be able to do this job? Like even the CEO job, or jobs where the leadership is? And the answer honestly is probably yes. Like in 2035, with a rate of improvement, it will be able to. So we said, okay, let's try it now. Let's try and build an AI CEO.

So we carved out a city in Mexico — it's Cuernavaca. And we put an agent in one of our harnesses as a CEO and it starts learning and it starts making decisions and evaluating on those decisions. And it's only been running for six weeks now.

The goal of the first month was to double the profits of Cuernavaca. It didn't reach it, but it was 1.5x — like 50% more profits. Just managing the city. Which is crazy, right? It's amazing. And it's the CEO — like, people were like "that was the last job AI was supposed to take." And no it isn't, really.

And how did this happen? It's a very smart person, like Fields medal level smart, going into every single number, every single customer, making the perfect forecast, and going to micromanage every single thing that needs to be executed every day to reach a plan. So it'll literally send messages to all the physical workers in Cuernavaca with their plans for the day and ask them to send voice notes back to know their progress.

Customer satisfaction grew. We got a better inventory. We rotated better. Better financing penetration. Every KPI started to improve. So it's super cool. It's super exciting.

物理世界仍需要人类：Ratatouille 式协作

Now, what are the jobs where we think we're still training and hiring humans? Those are related to the physical world.

When we talk about mechanics, Kavak has around, I think in Mexico, around 800 mechanics. There's lots of dexterity and senses that's super hard to substitute. So there we also build these agents with the exact same harness that's scaling, and the mechanics have the sidekick. It's like the movie Ratatouille — the mouse that's actually a chef collaborating with a human. It's kind of like that. So it's a sidekick. We call it El Mike.

And it tells them how to inspect a car and gives them tips and shows them the way to do it. And the quality of inspections again went through the roof. We're inspecting faster. We're repairing faster. It's cheaper. But most importantly, we're delivering higher quality cars. Warranties came down around 20–26% since we launched, and customer satisfaction again went up.

So it's about this: how would you design your organization from scratch with abundant super intelligence that's cheap? And just go build it.

九、未来组织的形态：Jedi Academy 与扁平化

This is a good segue to a key topic right now in Silicon Valley where there's a lot of people worried about how the organizations of the future are going to look like and the role that humans are going to play. So would love to hear how you guys are thinking about that.

Yes. Totally. So we took that question very seriously three years ago. And the truth is that everyone's job will change. What we were doing a couple of years ago will probably be performed better by an AI agent. So what does this mean? We need to train everyone.

So we launched a program inside Kavak that's called the Jedi Academy where anyone from Kavak — from the CEO to AI engineers to mechanics — going to the academy. It's super hard. I led them myself.

You designed the program.

I designed the program. But constantly — because you need to be upgrading the program because everything's changing so fast. You can't send these people outside to Stanford to learn this because it's new stuff. So we train everyone and after six weeks they launch state-of-the-art AI agents to production. And it's mechanics and finance guys and engineers — like everyone can do it.

And what this generated is — maybe this person won't become an AI engineer (some of them have) — but they know how to collaborate with this new technology.

So the way we looked about it was: guys, there's no way back. This is the way Kavak is going. This is the way the company will look like. These are the changes for the engineering team, the finance team, the product team. This is what's going to change. You have the choice to train and get the skills to perform in this new reality, in this new world. Or maybe leave Kavak if this is not for you, but this is the way we're going.

And it was great. We strengthened the culture. Everyone was super excited. People really know how to build these agentic systems. And then if you look at Kavak now, any process is really a collaboration of agents and humans — and sometimes agents are the bosses of humans, and sometimes humans are designing the agents.

组织结构：极度扁平，团队极度资深

But you do have — or did have — thousands of people. Now agents do most things. So what is the org structure of Kavak? Does the middle management concept even exist anymore? What does your org look like?

Right. So the way it looks like now is: very flat teams, very senior teams, super empowered. If you look at a team, you'll have engineering, AI, operations — like everything. And they're either building the agents, working for the agents, or being in the physical world in front of the customer.

Most of our organization looks like that. So it's really built around the idea of how organizations will look like in the future, and around AI, and really harnessing this new technology.

Obviously, this required lots of retraining because in 2023 or 2022, no one was building agents, no one was helping agents or taking orders from agents. And the way you cater to the physical world or the customers was in a different way than if an agent's telling you what to do or helping you make your job better.

So it's a completely different structure than we had just two years ago.

人类"为 agent 工作"是什么感觉？

Explain — we talked about this before — what "working for the agents" looks like. I think the way you described it was: you have this agentic system, and then sometimes when it fails, it's like "oh that's kicked out to kind of a human queue." But then that's lost.

So we see human-in-the-loops in most of these agentic systems in production right now — large scale agentic systems. Usually if an agent hits a wall or can't perform anymore, it'll send this case or this customer to a tier 2 support and forget about it. That doesn't really work because you don't close the loops. So you don't generate the data to train the agent to do this better.

What works right now is we have an agent that's obsessed with each of the customers — like millions of these. They have access to every single API, every single skill. And we have humans building those skills for them. And then if an agent hits a wall or cancels something, it'll call this API saying "I need help." And on the other side, it's not an agent or software — it's a human helping them out.

But if you map this out in an org chart, it's really human teams that have an agent — I'm getting better results. It's super clear. It makes sense.

十、给其他企业领导者的两点建议

That's actually a perfect segue. I know you get lots of leaders at larger institutions inbounding to you. Maybe this will save you many phone calls. Many leaders of companies intuitively understand this, but it is very hard still to deploy AI through their organization. The models are good enough — it's an org problem, it's a psychology problem. What advice do you have?

建议 1：转型必须自上而下

I think it's two things. The first is: it has to be top down. If you just get adoption, it won't go anywhere because it's hard to generate this taste or strategy for people to bottom-up decide what to build and what not to build, and come up with something that works for the company.

So the transformation has to be top down and leaders need to adopt, and leaders have to have a very clear plan on what to build. I've seen so many companies — it's just like "oh, we're doing a hackathon, people are coming up with use cases, we're sponsoring some of these use cases." That doesn't work.

Be very clear on what the company will look like in three or five years, and then start building that, and be very vertical in guiding your troops towards that. An army doesn't really work if everyone comes up with ideas on the strategy and tactics and goes to the battlefield and does whatever they want. You need a very clear strategy — and that's what we need now. It's a transformation stage.

建议 2：Token 分三个等级，只花有 ROI 的钱

The second one is you need to measure what really matters. And it's evals — but it's also the right evals. So I see a lot of companies spending now huge amounts, and they say "okay, I got adoption, I'm just spending hundreds of millions of dollars in tokens now." What about that? There's quality in the tokens.

So have a framework here that's also useful:

Tier 3 tokens (最有价值): These are the agents where you can get the ROI of each specific token, and I can do that now. That's great news for me because I'm growing and because I know the ROI of each token — because it goes to agents that are performing the job of the organization. These are the best tokens.

Tier 2 tokens: Things that you can measure indirectly. Do I see devs in the codebase? And I can evaluate the value of these tokens at least indirectly, and then push those to production.

Tier 1 tokens (最没底): Where most companies are — people are just using Claude Code or ChatGPT or Cursor or whatever. What happens with those? I have no idea.

So it's not just about adoption. It's really about having a very clear vision and then measuring that each token you spend is bringing you those benefits. And just iterate, iterate, iterate from there.

十一、Per-Customer Agent 架构的进化：为什么要推翻重来

I want to — we touched on this a little bit, but I think it's worth a dive — maybe the most ambitious companies listening to this will decide to follow suit, which is you decided to build an agent per customer versus per task. And then discovered along the way that each one of those agents needs its own micro virtual machine. So maybe walk us through those decisions and that architecture.

Yes. And I think we're seeing these results now, but it was a really risky bet. Because people usually go from workflows — like if I could advise everyone: don't build agentic workflows — to graphs or functions or objectives. And we built that, that these are multi-agent systems that can perform a whole function for complex goals like the ones I told, that to sell a car you need to do financing, purchasing, recommendations, etc.

And we had thousands, like tens of thousands of these agents working at scale running the business back in December.

Opus 4.5 后的推翻：智能升级让旧架构变成枷锁

But then Opus 4.5 came out and I realized this isn't the right paradigm anymore. The intelligence now doesn't need the graph and the multi-agent lattice and harness because it will constrain this level of intelligence.

So we decided to destroy everything we had been building for two years — that was working, that brought us to profitability, that brought us amazing growth — and start over with a harness that we thought would be robust and scalable and leverage recursive self-improvement or new, more intelligent models coming out every month.

So the way this looks like: it's a virtual machine with an agent with access to memory and evals and the CLI, where they can access every tool and every API in my company, and the long-term goal. And I instantiate hundreds of thousands of these each day with long-term goals like maximizing the lifetime value.

The self-improving organization.

自我改进的应该是组织，不是模型

Exactly. The self-improving organization. And I think people are super obsessed with RSI now and this will improve the models. But if you look at it this way: economic value in humanity for the past 4,000 years has been delivered by organizations, not by individuals.

So what you want to self-improve and to engage in that loop is the organization that can deliver more economic value. That's the loop that I think companies will start to focus on. Because if you get that loop working, and it's an organization that is really self-improving and harnessing the newer models and the better intelligence that we're getting every couple of days now — then you hit the exponential not just in intelligence, but in the value that you can generate as a company.

So that's really exciting. That's what we're working on.

十二、创造性毁灭：为什么初创公司会赢

You mentioned that because of all the challenges on adopting AI, you saw the biggest opportunity on net new companies being formed working on this new way and then disrupting markets. You want to talk a little bit about that?

Yes. There's this concept in economics about creative destruction from Joseph Schumpeter. What it says is that the way innovation hits the economy isn't by companies adopting the new technology, but by companies remaining the way they were, and incumbents with the new technology destroying the old companies.

So this destroys value in the short term in the economy, but in the long term it's better for everyone because these new, more efficient, more effective companies will provide better products and services for the economy as a whole. And this has happened in the past like industrial revolutions.

This is a great opportunity for entrepreneurs and people today because it's hard to adopt AI deeply. It's really hard for a CEO today, especially of a large or public company, to go and say "hey, I'm betting everything on AI. The company has to look this way. I'll destroy and rebuild everything I've been building for the past 40 years to become an AI native company." How many CEOs will do that in a company at scale?

So while they adopt, new companies can be formed that are built around the strengths of AI and take over and bring new products and services to the masses.

电力革命的历史类比：福特工厂本可以早 40 年出现

This has happened before. This happened with electricity. This is a story I always tell my team. The technologies for Ford's production line were developed in 1879 and 1881. Edison started commercializing electricity in New York and then London, and he invented a dynamo that was extremely efficient. So you could have built Ford's factory 40 years before Ford. The technology was there, everything was there.

But the way people adopted electricity and Ford's dynamo was: "okay, I'm going to leave my factory like four floors, shafts and belts, and just change my coal engine for an electric engine." And this will bring you benefits, yes, but like 6% efficiency.

What needed to be done was to destroy that factory, build it in a flat surface — not in the center of New York, but in Connecticut or New Jersey — and redesign your whole factory around small dynamos and electricity. And then you get the 3x improvement in productivity that powered the US during the 20th century.

And the same happened again with the computer. And the same is happening again today. People want to adopt it, but they're not willing to redesign the whole company and they just adopt it superficially. And in the end, that'll give you a 6% or a 10% improvement — not a 10x improvement.

It's like the innovator's dilemma at an industrial scale.

I think you've just made an amazing case for any future founders out there — that it's time to build.

It's time to build.

十三、给创业者的最后寄语

Maybe a great place to end is: you've built and scaled your own company, you've now turned Kavak fully agentic. What advice do you have to future founders or first-time founders that might be listening?

So, this is the most exciting time in human history. I believe that we're living in the most exciting time in human history and it's the most exciting time to be a founder — because it's the first time that anyone has access to the most powerful tools and intelligence in the world, for almost free or for $20 a month.

So literally, the democratization of the tools for people to build has never been this way in human history. And there's so many problems to be solved and a new reality to be built around this new paradigm.

So just go for it — but go for it deep. Like, imagine what the future around AI will look like.

It's just — it's not even an exponential. Just just map a trend that's linear. If AI keeps getting better at a linear scale — just build for that, and you'll come up with wonderful ideas that will bring a lot of value to the world.

Amazing. Ali, thank you for joining us.

Thanks for having me.

观看原视频 →
item.description:
## 从「交易公司」到「关系公司」：一次会计科目的物种变异
大多数人把 Kavak 的转型看成「用 AI 替换人」，但真正发生的是**会计范式的更换**。旧 Kavak 计算的是"卖了多少辆车、买了多少刹车片"——这是流量指标；新 Kavak 计算的是"1000 万客户的终身价值可激活百分比"——这是存量指标。这与银行从"利差收入"转向"钱包份额（share of wallet）"的进化完全同构。**AI 的真正颠覆，不是加速做同样的事，而是让企业第一次有能力承担关系型经济的记账成本**——过去只有私人银行家能给顶级客户做的事，现在可以在每一个买二手车的墨西哥打工人身上执行。这是一种"关系经济学的民主化"，而非"劳动力自动化"。
## 「一客户一 agent」的隐藏拓扑：Kavak 其实在造一个"经济体"，不是一家公司
真正让我意外的是 Ali 说的这句话："过去 4000 年，经济价值由**组织**而非个人创造，所以要自我改进的应该是组织"。这句话看似平常，其实颠覆了当前整个 RSI（递归自我改进）叙事——硅谷都在赌"更聪明的模型"，Kavak 在赌"更聪明的组织回路"。

item.title: [Business of Sport] “Infantino is a Symptom of the Problem”: What Really Needs to Change at FIFA
item.dc:creator: Business of Sport
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、真正的"病灶"不是英凡蒂诺，而是"一国一票"的数学结构

大多数评论把矛头对准英凡蒂诺个人的贪婪与傲慢，但节目里最锋利的一句话是："Infantino不是问题本身，他是问题的症状。" 真正的病根在于FIFA的投票算术——211个成员国里，大约90个是非洲和加勒比小型足协，凑够110票就能当选主席。于是任何一位主席，只要想连任，都会被这个数学结构"锁死"在同一条路径上：用小额转移支付（每年5–6百万美元）批发换取选票。这也解释了为什么从阿维兰热到布拉特再到英凡蒂诺，三代主席在完全不同的时代、不同的性格、不同的出身背景下，却都不约而同走向了近乎相同的丑闻剧本——这不是人的败坏，而是制度的引力场。

二、一个跨领域的意外类比：FIFA其实是"资源诅咒"的翻版

这里有个让人意外的连接——FIFA当下的困境，与政治经济学里的"资源诅咒"（Resource Curse）几乎同构。石油国家因为坐拥现金流，统治者不需要向本国纳税人负责，只需要用石油美元维稳精英即可；而FIFA主席因为坐拥世界杯这口"油井"，也不需要向真正贡献收入的欧洲和南美负责，只需用分成"维稳"最贫穷的成员国即可。贡献收入的一方没有话语权，掌握话语权的一方不贡献收入——这套结构在委内瑞拉、在尼日利亚、在很多石油国家反复上演，而FIFA只是把石油换成了转播权。

更耐人寻味的是，这种"倒挂"制度的破裂方式也高度一致：并非来自内部改革，而是来自被剥夺方的"退出威胁"（exit threat）。UEFA这次做的事，在博弈论上其实等价于1992年英超脱离英足联下级联盟的那次分裂——都是"出钱最多的一方"第一次真正拿起"我不玩了"这张牌。

三、被忽略的观察：英凡蒂诺其实是被"提前逼宫"救了

主流叙事是：英凡蒂诺因为提前推出20%世界杯私有化方案而"暴露自己、加速倒台"。但如果反向阅读节目里的时间线，会得到一个更反直觉的结论——如果这套方案没被Ziggler提前泄露、而是在2027年3月他连任成功之后才推出，那么UEFA大概率只会"骂几句然后忍下来"，因为届时他还有四年任期护体，各方会算计"忍他到2031年就好"。真正毁掉他的不是方案本身，而是方案在他"续命之前"就曝光了——他被迫在没有连任背书的裸奔状态下，直面欧洲的核按钮。

这里藏着一个更普适的洞见：权力最脆弱的时刻，往往不是它最弱的时候，而是它自以为最强、还没来得及"锁定"的时候。英凡蒂诺栽在了自己对连任的过度自信上——他先把"必然连任"当成资产提前变现，结果反而把"连任"本身变成了负债。这是典型的"路径依赖式傲慢"：当一个人在体系里赢得太久，他会开始把"体系规则"和"自己的意志"混为一谈，直到体系用它最古老的语言提醒他——你只是一个赛事组织者。

四、给读者的一个反常识收尾

节目结尾那句"如果换成Montigliani当主席，civil servants还是会告诉他：想连任十年，就得继续讨好非洲和加勒比"——这句话本身就是对"换人式改革"最锋利的判词。在一个结构错误的系统里，换一个更好的人，只会让这个系统运行得更"高效地错"。 这也是为什么Charlie最后说"nothing really changes unless the voting system changes"——足球世界这一轮最需要的，不是道德觉醒，而是一次冷酷的、结构性的、带有胁迫色彩的权重重置。

📝 转录文本

开场：一周之内的剧变

Let's talk FIFA. A lot's happened, Charlie.

I mean, I will pat on the back maybe where credit is due. We recorded last week, I think on the Wednesday, a lot happened after the Wednesday before we released on Friday. The main thing being the UEFA stance, which basically led to the UEFA nations saying that they will not participate in FIFA tournaments.

Now, the reason I say credit where it's due is because actually it didn't date the show — considering we'd already suggested that that would be the main way to deal with the situation. And if that did indeed happen, then the plan in essence would be dead in the water, because without the European countries all the value of this scheme kind of fell out at the bottom of it.

So that having happened, and then obviously the very quick withdrawal of the scheme on I think Friday night when Infantino finally realized that this was probably over, um, has kind of brought an end to those four — sorry — days. But of course with this, and I think this is where we're particularly interested to speak as well as what happened, the huge conversation now is what goes on moving forward.

计划已死，那英凡蒂诺本人呢？

Yeah. So the question you're asking is: has this been terminal not just for Infantino's plan to sell off 20% of the World Cup, but is it also terminal for Infantino himself and his presidency?

It kind of looks both, doesn't it?

Well, the plan for sure. The plan, Infantino, as you say, has already accepted is dead in the water. And I will say that, you know, we did predict that. We predicted that UEFA would kill it, torpedo it, and they did.

He was virtually untouchable, right? He was virtually untouchable. I was going to put this out there. He came out of that World Cup. We had all of the stuff that went on with Balagan and Trump, and you had all of this conversation about 64 teams, and some people going, "How can we do that? That's crazy."

But do you know what? We still looked at the voting systems and where the money was going to be going. And we said, "Look, the reality is, unfortunately, until he decides — well, until he sees out his final term in presidency, i.e. 2031 — it's highly unlikely he's going to remove himself. Then he has played an absolute blinder, as the only person that could cause himself any issues, he has done exactly that."

And it is a classic case of even with seemingly unending power and influence, he has found his Achilles heel, and the hubris of the whole situation will be his downfall. And to be honest now, you know, fingers crossed, now is the time where you really need those organizations that we've talked about potentially having power — i.e. the FA, but really it was UEFA as a block — standing up and actually, for the first time, as you said in your memo this week on Substack, for the first time standing up and actually acting with the power that they have to show, in your words, whether the emperor really has any clothes.

And it looks like to me this whole situation has shown now — with UEFA pulling the lever that they did — that the real power in football is not a glorified tournament organizer, really, if I can say it, in FIFA. But it is the people that have the block of countries that they need to participate in these tournaments to make them valuable.

英凡蒂诺不是病，是症状

Yeah, exactly, Charlie. Really the issue now is not so much about, you know, Infantino. We can come to Infantino and the specifics of that. The issue really is more to do with the status of FIFA within the power blocks within the game.

Because don't forget that Infantino — I know it's hard for people to think this way given what a total clown he's made of himself in recent weeks, months — Infantino is not himself the problem. He's a symptom of the problem. Let's not forget Infantino was the secretary general of UEFA, right? Infantino doesn't come from the African, um, you know, conference. He doesn't come from the Oceania conference. He's a UEFA guy, right?

So effectively, you have to ask yourself the question: why does Infantino, and indeed previous presidents of FIFA, end up doing things which either are on the margin sort of corrupt or, as I put in my memo, sort of blackguard? Right? That's one bit of it.

But the other bit of it is becoming very beholden to, in particular, the African nations on the one hand and the Caribbean nations on the other hand, which are the poorest federations in the world in terms of their own revenues. Right?

"一国一票"背后的数学现实

And this is where I get into, you know, roots of problems versus symptoms of problems. Because effectively, to become president of FIFA and then particularly to stay as president of FIFA, what you become aware of quite quickly is that under one member, one vote — where there are 211 member nations, of whom about 90 are either African or Caribbean nations, i.e. federations with very little money — in your aim to get 110-odd votes, you can wrap up pretty much all the support you need simply from the African and Caribbean nations.

And this is something which Blatter did before, and Havelange did before that, etc.

And the reason why that is so corrosive is because those federations, which are constantly struggling for money, they don't have money themselves. So we're talking about federations that have annual revenues of $5 million, $6 million bucks a year, compared to our football association with revenues of £600 million pounds. Right?

So for these small federations, handouts of $5 or $6 million a year are transformational for them. It changes everything. Now, of course, one would love to think that all of that extra $6 million went into football development and lovely schemes overseen by Arsène Wenger, and some of it does. Let's not imagine for a moment that part of this isn't used to prop up those federations, prop up the people who run those federations — who, don't forget, are significant people within their own country's, you know, political ecosystem.

And you know, it's the difference between the president of one of those federations being able to pay himself a $100,000 bucks a year and $200,000 or $300,000 bucks a year. It's the difference between them being able to travel first class to various locations around the world and having to travel in the back of the plane. It's the difference between them being able to look after people within their own football ecosystems with handouts here and there to keep everybody else in line.

买票的最便宜方式

You know that. So Infantino, Blatter, Havelange have been confronted with a mathematical reality, which is that the cheapest and easiest way of keeping your 120-odd votes that you need is by giving enough money on an individual basis to the poorer federations, right, to keep them happy with you, because they're not going to debate you long and hard about the big stuff you're doing.

So when you come up with some scheme to, you know, have hydration breaks or hold the World Cup every two years or whatever it might be, the head of the federation of a small African country is not going to take to the New York Times and give an interview about how this fundamentally undermines the future governance of world football. He just says, "Give me my $5 million bucks and you can do what the hell you want." Right?

That's the underlying reality of how FIFA works.

So whereas he could come to the English FA — I mean, you know, supine and hopeless though it is — and say to them, "Oh, by the way, you know, I'm going to do something here which means I'm going to be able to give you an extra $5 million bucks." And the FA would be like, "Well, that's sort of rounding error for us. Um, Johnny, it doesn't make any difference to us. Like, that doesn't mean that in a year's time we're just going to say yes, yes, yes when you want to go and hold a World Cup every two years and that type of stuff. We'll take the money, sure, but then we reserve the right to debate with you going down the track whether the stuff you think is reasonable and fair."

换个人不解决问题：以Montigliani为例

So effectively, you know, as I said, we in Infantino — we'll get on to a moment whether Infantino himself does survive this. But my point is this: let's just say for a moment that Infantino goes, but he's replaced by Victor Montigliani from Concacaf, right? Let's just say.

So Montigliani comes in, perfectly good guy. I know people who work with him. I know people who know him, etc. You know, he himself has got basically a good reputation, as Infantino did before he became FIFA president. Infantino did not have any stink surrounding him when he was the secretary general of UEFA.

But let's just say that Montigliani is then in power within FIFA, right? And he then wants to get two terms. Doesn't want to be a one-term president. He wants to have his full 10 years. Okay, the civil servants within FIFA tell him, "Well, look, the only way you can do that under one member, one vote is by keeping the African and Caribbean nations happy. Once you start annoying those guys, then you're always going to have problems with the Germans. You're always going to have problems with the Brazilians. You're always going to have problems with the Russians. Just keep the Africans and Caribbeans happy."

And that then drives the relentless short-term desire to increase revenues, because that's how you keep those guys happy. And that's why they come up with all these madcap schemes to try to increase revenue rather than thinking about the medium to long term of the sport.

分水岭时刻：治理必须重写

So, you know, I'll ask you in a moment your view about whether he does or doesn't survive this. But at the same time, the point of my memo was to say that this watershed moment has to be the moment for a fundamental change in FIFA's governance.

And what that really means, right? It doesn't mean some report that takes 6 months. It simply means UEFA saying, "Right, from now on, basically, we are going to run this and you are a competition organizer." As you said, you are a competition organizer for the world, and we're fully on board with there being really good equal distribution of money that comes out of the stuff you do — no problem with that.

But let's be clear: that money that you're distributing is our money. That's our member nations' money. That's our fans' money. And those players are players that are employed by our clubs. So never think for a moment, whoever you are, that you are going to be able to do this from now on by just getting together the support of the African and Caribbean nations. From now on, basically, you need to answer to us. Right?

加权投票：英超的历史类比

Okay, so can I ask you — a weighted system like that would make sense. Like, if they do implement that, what's the danger? Like, what's the cost of doing that? What will people fear? Why would people push back on it and say, "Actually, no, you couldn't do that"?

If you look back to why the Premier League was actually formed, and you read the memoirs of various English football industry people from around that time. What had happened during the late 1980s, mid to late 1980s, where English football also had one club, one vote — so Man United had one vote and Walsall had one vote — is on a continual basis, when the big clubs, who had senior managing directors, more senior people involved, when they would say, "Well, one way in which we think football in this country can progress is this, this, and this," then there would be a block of the lower division clubs who go, "No, I don't fancy it. Don't fancy it. So, um, you know, let's just carry on as we are. Or actually, if you want us to vote for you on that one, you're going to need to give us more money or help us in some other way."

To the point where eventually the big clubs said, "Look, sorry, this isn't working. It's our money. It's our fans mostly. And therefore, we — I'm sad to say — but we're going to need to break away, to be able to do the things that we think need to be done to progress the whole game. And you guys now are going to have to look after yourself."

Now, I don't think it'll be quite as simple as that with FIFA, and I don't think it should be quite as simple as that with FIFA, but I do think that a weighting is required.

加权方案的具体设想

Now, in the memo I suggested, I think something along the lines of you'd have a top council where you had, let's say, four members from UEFA, you had two members from Conmebol — which is a Latin American block — and then you had one member each for the Asian Football Federation, the African Football Federation, Concacaf, Oceania. Right?

So that UEFA couldn't just simply get its way all the time. It would have to persuade somebody else to get on board with them. And it would recognize that the other big power block in world football is Conmebol, which is Argentina, Brazil, and Co., and would give them slightly more weight.

At the moment, Conmebol is even worse treated than UEFA, which is they've only got 11 votes because they've only got 11 countries, because they're all quite big countries in Latin America. So even though they are providing a lot of the revenue and a lot of the fans, they've only got 11 votes. UEFA have got about 50 votes. And then Africa have got about 50 votes, and Concacaf have got about 50 votes.

So effectively, UEFA and Conmebol together are 60-odd votes, 65 votes, whereas the African Federation and Concacaf, who in terms of global revenues are minimal, right, are 100 plus votes.

So this just needs to be — not even looked at — this just needs to be changed by force. Um, and I hope that Čeferin, who is a pretty tough operator, as I noted in last week's show, presses home his advantage now and says to the European member nations, "If you want to stop this happening again, don't imagine that Infantino going is going to be the thing that makes the big difference. We need to change the governance."

Well, it feels — it's that watershed moment, isn't it?

It is. At least it should be. At least it needs to be.

英凡蒂诺会走还是会留？

So let me come on to the question, Charlie, which I'll put over to you. Okay, having said that whether Infantino stays or goes is not quite as significant as some people might think — do you think he does stay or go?

I find it very hard to see how he stays and FIFA retains any sort of credibility.

Look, one thing it certainly does, Charlie, I think, is it means that he will not go into the next election uncontested. So there's going to be an election for the FIFA presidency in 2027 in Rabat, in I think March of next year.

March. Yeah.

Now, previously all the conversation was: no one's going to stand against him. It would mean he does another four years and he goes to 2031, and at 2031 he could no longer take up another term of presidency — which interestingly was where this whole scheme was coming in, because it was assumed he would then go and run the FIFA Enterprise scheme, uh, as, you know, I guess a private entity, um, alongside FIFA, and obviously take a very nice salary in the process.

So he had this very nice plan laid out, I think, in front of him that, as I said at the beginning, was kind of virtually impossible to see how you could change that. This whole situation now, if you're really looking at it — and I noted, Charlie, the some of the commentary that came out internally from FIFA when something like this happens, right — you've got people that are very quick to move away from it and they don't want the association.

And he was very much put forward by some of the top people in FIFA — this was his idea. If you listen to comments on Friday, you know, he actually used these — these are the words, you know, in our quotes — he used the words that they, the staff, had been "deceived", and he said it was "the project of one person". Now, that's your COO of FIFA. You had Arsène Wenger — we were recording on Wednesday — come out last night, all this morning, um, saying that he didn't know about it and was very surprised about the situation.

So you're looking at some very top people in FIFA who are now standing back and disassociating themselves with Infantino and his presidency and this decision. How you maintain the authority that's required to run FIFA and the global game into another cycle is — it's virtually untenable.

罢免主席的三条路径

The interesting question, Charlie, I think is: does he get removed now, or does he go into that election and see whether he gets removed?

Now I just wanted to just touch on this again, because we mentioned it on a previous show, but, you know, I think it's really important to people to understand what has to happen for a FIFA president to be removed or to not be in position. There's three things.

Firstly, he can resign. I mean, still even now, I just can't see that happening.

Um, secondly, the member associations that represent 20% of the membership — which is 43 out of 211 countries — they can formally request what they call an extraordinary FIFA Congress. So if they call that, it basically then goes to a vote, and it will be a vote on whether he does stay or go.

The third way is obviously to lose in an election.

So if you're now looking at this, previously, Charlie, I think we said it's highly unlikely that even number two would happen, because while countries may disagree with his presidency, I don't think they're going to call a special meeting to do it. It does look increasingly like that could happen, particularly with UEFA saying, "You either resign or we will just activate all of our members, i.e. 55. We will call that meeting and we will vote against you."

So taking all those things into account, trying to take all the emotion out of it, I just don't see how anyone in that position who has gone through what he has gone through in a week stays in position and keeps the power that he wields.

Yeah.

I don't know what you think.

傲慢的时间线错误

It was an act of astonishing hubris to start bringing this plan forward before he'd been re-elected. Cuz let's play it a bit differently.

Let's imagine that actually we hadn't heard anything from now until the FIFA elections in March 2027, and that with him having been re-elected — which he would have been. Don't forget, even our own football association in England was formally backing him for it, despite not —

like you would know that now, obviously.

You certainly would not know. There's a very, very funny picture, isn't there, Charlie, um, which I bet she wishes she could take back, of Debbie Hewitt holding the England shirt with her. I mean, you know — anyway, that's a story for another day.

But it was an act of astonishing hubris to start doing this so soon after the World Cup, when there was still a bit of a stench in the air about a few of the things that happened in the World Cup, but also with his re-election still not guaranteed. It was almost as if he banked his re-election up front, right? "I'm definitely going to get re-elected. So on the basis I'm definitely going to get re-elected, I might as well crack on with my massive money-making scheme." Right? Why?

民族国家式的自我幻想 & 泄露的时间点

Two things on that. Two things on that, right?

Firstly, I think you're right, but it plays into what we've discussed again before, which is him genuinely seeing himself in a completely inflated manner as almost the head of a nation state — the power that he wields being equal to those top political leaders.

And look, we joke about — and people have joked about — the relationship with Trump and how close they are. But, you know, you can absolutely see spending the amount of time around him and having him in your ear talking about how powerful you are, saying, "I'm going to put you up for the secretary general of the United Nations" or whatever hogwash that, you know, that this whole stuff was — that, you know, this Gianni brain inside is just getting more and more influenced and convinced of the power that he really wields, versus, as we've just shown, you know, the real power that actually exists within football and who controls it.

The second part, though, I do think, which is important, is: they didn't want this to come out now, right? They didn't want this to come out now.

So this wasn't a FIFA-planned press conference to announce a brand new scheme. This was really from the Times of Martin Ziegler, who everyone — and, you know, quite rightly — has been praising for a lot of very good journalistic work to get this out in the open, has obviously got hold of. And how that's happened and the people privy to this information — you know, someone's leaked it, considering top members of FIFA are even claiming to have had no knowledge of it.

But really, they were caught off guard. They had to react to this. It was going to come out. And, as you said, if he had been able to run this through to next March or so, then it could have been in a far more concerning situation.

Um, but would it really — does it change anything? Because I still think that whether it's now or whatever, the reaction would have been the same. UEFA would have reacted the same. UEFA pull out — and as we've said, UEFA pull out, the whole value of this thing falls out the bottom. There is no $15 to $20 billion valuation on a World Cup commercial enterprise if you don't have the key countries participating in those tournaments. So that if you're looking where the real power is, that's where it is.

时间点为何加速了他的政治死亡

I totally agree with that. My point was simply: if he'd managed to get himself re-elected and was then in for the next four or five years in any case, and this had come out, um, first of all, he would have had a bit more time to buy off some of the support that he needed to buy off to get the thing across the line. He would have known that UEFA were going to be against it, whatever. I mean, that was always going to be clear.

But the problem was he hadn't ticked all the boxes even in terms of his own payroll vote in Africa and Concacaf. So, um, my point was, even if it then got knocked back after his re-election, he probably wouldn't have lost his job as a result of it. They probably would have gone, "Do you know what? You know, he's only here for an extra four years. Just let him hobble on for a bit, and we'll keep him on a bit of a shorter lead" or something like that.

What's added real spice and urgency into this, as you noted, is that there is an election in March, and therefore there is a clean way of getting rid of him by putting up a candidate against him, or more than one candidate against him.

各联合会的态度扫描

Now I think if you look at the federations and their current body language, UEFA are clearly not just against the plan but against Infantino, and very explicitly so — like, this calls into question the whole leadership of FIFA. It's very clear. It's very, very clear that UEFA wants him out.

Concacaf have come out against him. Um, and again, Concacaf is a coming together of the small Caribbean nations and then the larger Concacaf nations of Canada, America, Mexico, um, and some of the other Central American countries that have reasonable football heritages.

Now the head of Concacaf, Victor Montigliani, is a Canadian, and he was already aspiring to replace Infantino. Okay. So that has been in the undergrowth for some time as a likely successor. So from Montigliani's point of view, this is great timing. This is fantastic timing — which is, rather than having to wait an extra four years to challenge Infantino, which is, well, not to challenge — for the FIFA presidency when Infantino leaves — he can now become a sort of, you know, neutral peaceful power broker, you know, sort of, you know, "compromise" guy who comes through the middle. You know: "Me, Victor, everyone knows me, I'm a good guy, I've never, you know, ruffled any feathers, I've always done a sort of, you know, a reasonable job of keeping Concacaf together."

So he is leading Concacaf to come against Infantino's position, and that's problematic for Infantino because a lot of the Concacaf nations are, constitute his power base — the Caribbean nations.

Yeah.

It's pretty clear that the African Federation is going to continue to support Infantino. Right. So conspicuous by its absence has been any clear declaration from the African nations, um, or from CAF itself, against this whole thing.

And then you've got Asia, which looks like it's split. There are some Asian nations who have come out against this. There are some who seem to be either keeping quiet or even somewhat supporting Infantino in general.

And then you have Oceania — people don't — that's not very clear. New Zealand have been very much against it, as you'd expect. Probably Australia will be as well. But the smaller Oceania countries, we don't know. And since they constitute a majority in that confederation, we don't know how they're going to go — but again, they're only 11, they're only 10 or 11 votes as well.

And Conmebol, Latin America, have been, um, fence-sitting, I would say.

So at the moment, you have UEFA and Concacaf that constitute about 100 votes between them — 105, 110 votes — who appear to be coming out against Infantino's presidency. But again, probably in Concacaf's case, not en masse — I imagine there will still be nations within that who don't necessarily back Montigliani in that. And then you've got the other federations who are either fence-sitting or who are still in support of Infantino.

结语：换头没用，除非改结构

So going back to your point, which I think was a point well made earlier — which is, I don't see Infantino resigning here — I think he'll still back himself to try to pick off enough of the individual nations in the meantime to be able to hang on in power. Um, because if he's got all the African nations, he's only 50 away then, isn't he, from having enough to hang on in there.

So anyway, look — watch this space over the next weeks and months. Gradually the politics bit will become apparent.

But in a way, that horse-trading that I've just mentioned — what's this federation saying, what's that federation thinking, all this stuff — in a way, that's all the problem, right? Which is: actually it doesn't matter, because all that really matters is what UEFA think, really. Right?

And — but also, just to leave it on this point — your point really: you can, we can talk about this for days, get blown in the face, nothing really changes unless the voting system, the structural elements of FIFA change. So, you know, it's interesting to look at Infantino, it's interesting to assess the power dynamics, but really, as you said, you're just replacing — it's a different head, right?

And ultimately, as you said, when Infantino came in, Sepp Blatter was the greatest enemy of football. And now he's the spokesperson for integrity and righteous behavior. If you've been following his Twitter feeds — uh, sorry, X feeds — it's been brilliant.

You know, I think you sit this one out, Sepp, I reckon. [laughter]

item.description:
## 一、真正的"病灶"不是英凡蒂诺，而是"一国一票"的数学结构
大多数评论把矛头对准英凡蒂诺个人的贪婪与傲慢，但节目里最锋利的一句话是：**"Infantino不是问题本身，他是问题的症状。"** 真正的病根在于FIFA的投票算术——211个成员国里，大约90个是非洲和加勒比小型足协，凑够110票就能当选主席。于是任何一位主席，只要想连任，都会被这个数学结构"锁死"在同一条路径上：**用小额转移支付（每年5–6百万美元）批发换取选票**。这也解释了为什么从阿维兰热到布拉特再到英凡蒂诺，三代主席在完全不同的时代、不同的性格、不同的出身背景下，却都不约而同走向了近乎相同的丑闻剧本——**这不是人的败坏，而是制度的引力场**。
## 二、一个跨领域的意外类比：FIFA其实是"资源诅咒"的翻版
这里有个让人意外的连接——FIFA当下的困境，与政治经济学里的"资源诅咒"（Resource Curse）几乎同构。石油国家因为坐拥现金流，统治者不需要向本国纳税人负责，只需要用石油美元维稳精英即可；而FIFA主席因为坐拥世界杯这口"油井"，也不需要向真正贡献收入的欧洲和南美负责，只需用分成"维

item.title: [All-In Podcast] Google’s AI Brain Drain, SpaceX's Huge Quarter, Airtable’s 90% Collapse, US Data Fuels China AI
item.dc:creator: All-In Podcast
item.content:encoded:
💡 创造性洞见

一、"人才外流"其实是资本配置的物理定律

Google 失去 Jeff Dean 和 Demis 的降级，表面看是硅谷版的"帝国黄昏"，但真正的驱动力是一个被忽略的会计事实：加速折旧的 Capex 抵税，让基础设施投资的税后回报率碾压了模型研发。当 26% 的企业税率允许你把每一美元资本支出当年全部计入费用，数据中心就变成"高 alpha、低 beta"，而前沿模型是"高 alpha、高 beta"。

这里有个反直觉的洞察：科学家的出走不是 Google 的失败，而是 Google 财务模型的成功。当董事会把钱都投向 GPU 出租业务（因为 ROIC 更可预测），研究员自然会离开去做他们真正想做的事——用 VC 的钱冒险。Google 在无意中把自己变成了"AI 界的中石油"：它不生产最好的智能，但拥有最好的管道。而 Jeff Dean 去创业，本质上是用 LP 的风险预算替代了 Google 股东的风险预算——同一个人做同一件事，只是风险载体换了。

二、SpaceX 的隐藏套利：把火箭工程学套用到数据中心

大家都在算 Elon 每瓦 30-50 美元的算力现货价，但没人注意到一个跨领域的诡异连接：SpaceX 之所以能比 Microsoft、Google 更快地立起 gigawatt 级数据中心，是因为造数据中心比造火箭简单太多。Elon 在电话会上那句"data centers is not rocket science"不是玩笑，是一个残酷的产业事实——硬件制造的"垂直整合肌肉记忆"是无法用软件公司的资本堆出来的。

更让人意外的是 Starlink 与 Starship 的耦合关系：V3 卫星单次发射的带宽是 V2 的 20 倍以上。这意味着 Starship 每成功一次，Starlink 的边际带宽成本就断崖式下降一次。这不是线性改进，而是一个"发射即降价"的通缩螺旋——传统电信运营商 AT&T、Verizon 面对的不是一个新对手，而是一个每次爆炸测试都在变得更强的对手。Huenet、Viaat 的股价已经告诉你结局。

三、Airtable 的死亡与 Vibe Coding 的诞生：SAS 的"熵增诅咒"

Airtable 以 12 亿美元卖身（峰值 117 亿），大部分人解读为 SAS 泡沫破裂。但真正的洞察藏在 Sachs 那句被忽略的话里："only 30% of Airtable's sales team was making quota"。这个数字暴露了 SAS 行业的一个结构性诅咒——当 PLG（产品驱动增长）撞上 VC 期待的曲棍球杆增长时，创始人被迫嫁接一个自己不擅长的 sales-led motion，最终把公司拖入"既非高增长也非高利润"的死亡地带。

跨领域的连接来了：Airtable 的困境和 Google 的 Demis 出走本质是同一件事——当组织的能力曲线与资本方的期待曲线错配时，管理层要么被迫做违反自己 DNA 的事（Airtable 加销售），要么让核心人才出走去做他们本来擅长的事（Demis 去创业）。资本的错配比技术的错配更致命。

而最出乎意料的洞察是关于 AI 与遗留代码的关系：Sachs 指出 AI 让"维护模式"变得极其容易，因为不再需要 institutional memory。这颠覆了软件行业 40 年的一个铁律——过去，代码库的历史知识是一种"人质"，让公司无法轻易裁员。现在，AI 可以瞬间"考古"出任何代码库的意图。这意味着 Bending Spoons 这类"SAS 殡葬公司"将成为未来五年最赚钱的商业模式之一：它们买下的不是产品，是"被 AI 解放出来的现金流"。Airtable 只是第一个，不是最后一个。
